paragraphs:
I have always considered that one of the most thrilling and dramatic
of the many adventures I have shared with Poirot was that of our
investigation into the strange series of deaths which followed upon
the discovery and opening of the Tomb of King Men-her-Ra.

Hard upon the discovery of the Tomb of Tut-ankh-Amen by Lord
Carnarvon, Sir John Willard and Mr. Bleibner of New York, pursuing
their excavations not far from Cairo, in the vicinity of the
Pyramids of Gizeh, came unexpectedly on a series of funeral
chambers. The greatest interest was aroused by their discovery.
The Tomb appeared to be that of King Men-her-Ra, one of those
shadowy kings of the Eighth Dynasty, when the Old Kingdom was
falling to decay. Little was known about this period, and the
discoveries were fully reported in the newspapers.

An event soon occurred which took a profound hold on the public
mind. Sir John Willard died quite suddenly of heart failure.

The more sensational newspapers immediately took the opportunity
of reviving all the old superstitious stories connected with the
ill luck of certain Egyptian treasures. The unlucky Mummy at the
British Museum, that hoary old chestnut, was dragged out with fresh
zest, was quietly denied by the Museum, but nevertheless enjoyed
all its usual vogue.

A fortnight later Mr. Bleibner died of acute blood poisoning, and
a few days afterwards a nephew of his shot himself in New York.
The “Curse of Men-her-Ra” was the talk of the day, and the magic
power of dead and gone Egypt was exalted to a fetish point.

It was then that Poirot received a brief note from Lady Willard,
widow of the dead archaeologist, asking him to go and see her at
her house in Kensington Square. I accompanied him.

Lady Willard was a tall, thin woman, dressed in deep mourning. Her
haggard face bore eloquent testimony to her recent grief.

“It is kind of you to have come so promptly, Monsieur Poirot.”

“I am at your service, Lady Willard. You wished to consult me?”

“You are, I am aware, a detective, but it is not only as a detective
that I wish to consult you. You are a man of original views, I
know, you have imagination, experience of the world, tell me,
Monsieur Poirot, what are your views on the supernatural?”

Poirot hesitated for a moment before he replied. He seemed to be
considering. Finally he said:

“Let us not misunderstand each other, Lady Willard. It is not a
general question that you are asking me there. It has a personal
application, has it not? You are referring obliquely to the death
of your late husband?”

“That is so,” she admitted.

“You want me to investigate the circumstances of his death?”

“I want you to ascertain for me exactly how much is newspaper
chatter, and how much may be said to be founded on fact? Three
deaths, Monsieur Poirot—each one explicable taken by itself, but
taken together surely an almost unbelievable coincidence, and all
within a month of the opening of the tomb! It may be mere
superstition, it may be some potent curse from the past that
operates in ways undreamed of by modern science. The fact
remains—three deaths! And I am afraid, Monsieur Poirot, horribly
afraid. It may not yet be the end.”

“For whom do you fear?”

“For my son. When the news of my husband’s death came I was ill.
My son, who has just come down from Oxford, went out there. He
brought the—the body home, but now he has gone out again, in spite
of my prayers and entreaties. He is so fascinated by the work that
he intends to take his father’s place and carry on the system of
excavations. You may think me a foolish, credulous woman, but,
Monsieur Poirot, I am afraid. Supposing that the spirit of the dead
King is not yet appeased? Perhaps to you I seem to be talking
nonsense——”

“No, indeed, Lady Willard,” said Poirot quickly. “I, too, believe
in the force of superstition, one of the greatest forces the world
has ever known.”

I looked at him in surprise. I should never have credited Poirot
with being superstitious. But the little man was obviously in
earnest.

“What you really demand is that I shall protect your son? I will
do my utmost to keep him from harm.”

“Yes, in the ordinary way, but against an occult influence?”

“In volumes of the Middle Ages, Lady Willard, you will find many
ways of counteracting black magic. Perhaps they knew more than we
moderns with all our boasted science. Now let us come to facts,
that I may have guidance. Your husband had always been a devoted
Egyptologist, hadn’t he?”

“Yes, from his youth upwards. He was one of the greatest living
authorities upon the subject.”

“But Mr. Bleibner, I understand, was more or less of an amateur?”

“Oh, quite. He was a very wealthy man who dabbled freely in any
subject that happened to take his fancy. My husband managed to
interest him in Egyptology, and it was his money that was so useful
in financing the expedition.”

“And the nephew? What do you know of his tastes? Was he with the
party at all?”

“I do not think so. In fact I never knew of his existence till I
read of his death in the paper, I do not think he and Mr. Bleibner
can have been at all intimate. He never spoke of having any
relations.”

“Who are the other members of the party?”

“Well, there is Dr. Tosswill, a minor official connected with the
British Museum; Mr. Schneider of the Metropolitan Museum in New
York; a young American secretary; Dr. Ames, who accompanies the
expedition in his professional capacity; and Hassan, my husband’s
devoted native servant.”

“Do you remember the name of the American secretary?”

“Harper, I think, but I cannot be sure. He had not been with Mr.
Bleibner very long, I know. He was a very pleasant young fellow.”

“Thank you, Lady Willard.”

“If there is anything else——?”

“For the moment, nothing. Leave it now in my hands, and be assured
that I will do all that is humanly possible to protect your son.”

They were not exactly reassuring words, and I observed Lady Willard
wince as he uttered them. Yet, at the same time, the fact that he
had not pooh-poohed her fears seemed in itself to be a relief to
her.

For my part I had never before suspected that Poirot had so deep
a vein of superstition in his nature. I tackled him on the subject
as we went homewards. His manner was grave and earnest.

“But yes, Hastings. I believe in these things. You must not
underrate the force of superstition.”

“What are we going to do about it?”

“_Toujours pratique_, the good Hastings! _Eh bien_, to begin with
we are going to cable to New York for fuller details of young Mr.
Bleibner’s death.”

He duly sent off his cable. The reply was full and precise. Young
Rupert Bleibner had been in low water for several years. He had
been a beach-comber and a remittance man in several South Sea
islands, but had returned to New York two years ago, where he had
rapidly sunk lower and lower. The most significant thing, to my
mind, was that he had recently managed to borrow enough money to
take him to Egypt. “I’ve a good friend there I can borrow from,”
he had declared. Here, however, his plans had gone awry. He had
returned to New York cursing his skinflint of an uncle who cared
more for the bones of dead and gone kings than his own flesh and
blood. It was during his sojourn in Egypt that the death of Sir
John Willard occurred. Rupert had plunged once more into his life
of dissipation in New York, and then, without warning, he had
committed suicide, leaving behind him a letter which contained some
curious phrases. It seemed written in a sudden fit of remorse. He
referred to himself as a leper and an outcast, and the letter ended
by declaring that such as he were better dead.

A shadowy theory leapt into my brain. I had never really believed
in the vengeance of a long dead Egyptian king. I saw here a more
modern crime. Supposing this young man had decided to do away with
his uncle—preferably by poison. By mistake, Sir John Willard
receives the fatal dose. The young man returns to New York, haunted
by his crime. The news of his uncle’s death reaches him. He realizes
how unnecessary his crime has been, and stricken with remorse takes
his own life.

I outlined my solution to Poirot. He was interested.

“It is ingenious what you have thought of there—decidedly it is
ingenious. It may even be true. But you leave out of count the
fatal influence of the Tomb.”

I shrugged my shoulders.

“You still think that has something to do with it?”

“So much so, _mon ami_, that we start for Egypt to-morrow.”

“What?” I cried, astonished.

“I have said it.” An expression of conscious heroism spread over
Poirot’s face. Then he groaned. “But, oh,” he lamented, “the sea!
The hateful sea!”

It was a week later. Beneath our feet was the golden sand of the
desert. The hot sun poured down overhead. Poirot, the picture of
misery, wilted by my side. The little man was not a good traveller.
Our four days’ voyage from Marseilles had been one long agony to
him. He had landed at Alexandria the wraith of his former self,
even his usual neatness had deserted him. We had arrived in Cairo
and had driven out at once to the Mena House Hotel, right in the
shadow of the Pyramids.

The charm of Egypt had laid hold of me. Not so Poirot. Dressed
precisely the same as in London, he carried a small clothes-brush
in his pocket and waged an unceasing war on the dust which
accumulated on his dark apparel.

“And my boots,” he wailed. “Regard them, Hastings. My boots, of
the neat patent leather, usually so smart and shining. See, the
sand is inside them, which is painful, and outside them, which
outrages the eyesight. Also the heat, it causes my moustaches to
become limp—but limp!”

“Look at the Sphinx,” I urged. “Even I can feel the mystery and
the charm it exhales.”

Poirot looked at it discontentedly.

“It has not the air happy,” he declared. “How could it, half-buried
in sand in that untidy fashion. Ah, this cursed sand!”

“Come, now, there’s a lot of sand in Belgium,” I reminded him,
mindful of a holiday spent at Knocke-sur-mer in the midst of “_les
dunes impeccables_” as the guide-book had phrased it.

“Not in Brussels,” declared Poirot. He gazed at the Pyramids
thoughtfully. “It is true that they, at least, are of a shape solid
and geometrical, but their surface is of an unevenness most
unpleasing. And the palm-trees I like them not. Not even do they
plant them in rows!”

I cut short his lamentations, by suggesting that we should start
for the camp. We were to ride there on camels, and the beasts were
patiently kneeling, waiting for us to mount, in charge of several
picturesque boys headed by a voluble dragoman.

I pass over the spectacle of Poirot on a camel. He started by
groans and lamentations and ended by shrieks, gesticulations and
invocations to the Virgin Mary and every Saint in the calendar. In
the end, he descended ignominiously and finished the journey on a
diminutive donkey. I must admit that a trotting camel is no joke
for the amateur. I was stiff for several days.

At last we neared the scene of the excavations. A sunburnt man with
a grey beard, in white clothes and wearing a helmet, came to meet
us.

“Monsieur Poirot and Captain Hastings? We received your cable. I’m
sorry that there was no one to meet you in Cairo. An unforeseen
event occurred which completely disorganized our plans.”

Poirot paled. His hand, which had stolen to his clothes-brush,
stayed its course.

“Not another death?” he breathed.

“Yes.”

“Sir Guy Willard?” I cried.

“No, Captain Hastings. My American colleague, Mr. Schneider.”

“And the cause?” demanded Poirot.

“Tetanus.”

I blanched. All around me I seemed to feel an atmosphere of evil,
subtle and menacing. A horrible thought flashed across me. Supposing
I were the next?

“_Mon Dieu_,” said Poirot, in a very low voice, “I do not understand
this. It is horrible. Tell me, monsieur, there is no doubt that it
was tetanus?”

“I believe not. But Dr. Ames will tell you more than I can do.”

“Ah, of course, you are not the doctor.”

“My name is Tosswill.”

This, then, was the British expert described by Lady Willard as
being a minor official at the British Museum. There was something
at once grave and steadfast about him that took my fancy.

“If you will come with me,” continued Dr. Tosswill, “I will take
you to Sir Guy Willard. He was most anxious to be informed as soon
as you should arrive.”

We were taken across the camp to a large tent. Dr. Tosswill lifted
up the flap and we entered. Three men were sitting inside.

“Monsieur Poirot and Captain Hastings have arrived, Sir Guy,” said
Tosswill.

The youngest of the three men jumped up and came forward to greet
us. There was a certain impulsiveness in his manner which reminded
me of his mother. He was not nearly so sunburnt as the others, and
that fact, coupled with a certain haggardness round the eyes, made
him look older than his twenty-two years. He was clearly endeavouring
to bear up under a severe mental strain.

He introduced his two companions, Dr. Ames, a capable looking man
of thirty odd, with a touch of greying hair at the temples, and
Mr. Harper, the secretary, a pleasant lean young man wearing the
national insignia of horn-rimmed spectacles.

After a few minutes’ desultory conversation the latter went out,
and Dr. Tosswill followed him. We were left alone with Sir Guy and
Dr. Ames.

“Please ask any questions you want to ask, Monsieur Poirot,” said
Willard. “We are utterly dumbfounded at this strange series of
disasters, but it isn’t—it can’t be, anything but coincidence.”

There was a nervousness about his manner which rather belied the
words. I saw that Poirot was studying him keenly.

“Your heart is really in this work, Sir Guy?”

“Rather. No matter what happens, or what comes of it, the work is
going on. Make up your mind to that.”

Poirot wheeled round on the other.

“What have you to say to that, _monsieur le docteur_?”

“Well,” drawled the doctor, “I’m not for quitting myself.”

Poirot made one of those expressive grimaces of his.

“Then, _évidemment_, we must find out just how we stand. When did
Mr. Schneider’s death take place?”

“Three days ago.”

“You are sure it was tetanus?”

“Dead sure.”

“It couldn’t have been a case of strychnine poisoning, for
instance?”

“No, Monsieur Poirot. I see what you’re getting at. But it was a
clear case of tetanus.”

“Did you not inject anti-serum?”

“Certainly we did,” said the doctor dryly. “Every conceivable thing
that could be done was tried.”

“Had you the anti-serum with you?”

“No. We procured it from Cairo.”

“Have there been any other cases of tetanus in the camp?”

“No, not one.”

“Are you certain that the death of Mr. Bleibner was not due to
tetanus?”

“Absolutely plumb certain. He had a scratch upon his thumb which
became poisoned, and septicæmia set in. It sounds pretty much the
same to a layman, I dare say, but the two things are entirely
different.”

“Then we have four deaths—all totally dissimilar, one heart failure,
one blood poisoning, one suicide and one tetanus.”

“Exactly, Monsieur Poirot.”

“Are you certain that there is nothing which might link the four
together?”

“I don’t quite understand you?”

“I will put it plainly. Was any act committed by those four men
which might seem to denote disrespect to the spirit of Men-her-Ra?”

The doctor gazed at Poirot in astonishment.

“You’re talking through your hat, Monsieur Poirot. Surely you’ve
not been guyed into believing all that fool talk?”

“Absolute nonsense,” muttered Willard angrily.

Poirot remained placidly immovable, blinking a little out of his
green cat’s eyes.

“So you do not believe it, _monsieur le docteur_?”

“No, sir, I do not,” declared the doctor emphatically. “I am a
scientific man, and I believe only what science teaches.”

“Was there no science then in Ancient Egypt?” asked Poirot softly.
He did not wait for a reply, and indeed Dr. Ames seemed rather at
a loss for the moment. “No, no, do not answer me, but tell me this.
What do the native workmen think?”

“I guess,” said Dr. Ames, “that, where white folk lose their heads,
natives aren’t going to be far behind. I’ll admit that they’re
getting what you might call scared—but they’ve no cause to be.”

“I wonder,” said Poirot non-committally.

Sir Guy leant forward.

“Surely,” he cried incredulously, “you cannot believe in—oh, but
the thing’s absurd! You can know nothing of Ancient Egypt if you
think that.”

For answer Poirot produced a little book from his pocket—an ancient
tattered volume. As he held it out I saw its title, _The Magic of
the Egyptians and Chaldeans_. Then, wheeling round, he strode out
of the tent. The doctor stared at me.

“What is his little idea?”

The phrase, so familiar on Poirot’s lips, made me smile as it came
from another.

“I don’t know exactly,” I confessed. “He’s got some plan of
exorcizing the evil spirits, I believe.”

I went in search of Poirot, and found him talking to the lean-faced
young man who had been the late Mr. Bleibner’s secretary.

“No,” Mr. Harper was saying, “I’ve only been six months with the
expedition. Yes, I knew Mr. Bleibner’s affairs pretty well.”

“Can you recount to me anything concerning his nephew?”

“He turned up here one day, not a bad-looking fellow. I’d never
met him before, but some of the others had—Ames, I think, and
Schneider. The old man wasn’t at all pleased to see him. They were
at it in no time, hammer and tongs. ‘Not a cent,’ the old man
shouted. ‘Not one cent now or when I’m dead. I intend to leave my
money to the furtherance of my life’s work. I’ve been talking it
over with Mr. Schneider to-day.’ And a bit more of the same. Young
Bleibner lit out for Cairo right away.”

“Was he in perfectly good health at the time?”

“The old man?”

“No, the young one.”

“I believe he did mention there was something wrong with him. But
it couldn’t have been anything serious, or I should have remembered.”

“One thing more, has Mr. Bleibner left a will?”

“So far as we know, he has not.”

“Are you remaining with the expedition, Mr. Harper?”

“No, sir, I am not. I’m for New York as soon as I can square up
things here. You may laugh if you like, but I’m not going to be
this blasted old Men-her-Ra’s next victim. He’ll get me if I stop
here.”

The young man wiped the perspiration from his brow.

Poirot turned away. Over his shoulder he said with a peculiar
smile:

“Remember, he got one of his victims in New York.”

“Oh, hell!” said Mr. Harper forcibly.

“That young man is nervous,” said Poirot thoughtfully. “He is on
the edge, but absolutely on the edge.”

I glanced at Poirot curiously, but his enigmatical smile told me
nothing. In company with Sir Guy Willard and Dr. Tosswill we were
taken round the excavations. The principal finds had been removed
to Cairo, but some of the tomb furniture was extremely interesting.
The enthusiasm of the young baronet was obvious, but I fancied that
I detected a shade of nervousness in his manner as though he could
not quite escape from the feeling of menace in the air. As we
entered the tent which had been assigned to us, for a wash before
joining the evening meal, a tall dark figure in white robes stood
aside to let us pass with a graceful gesture and a murmured greeting
in Arabic. Poirot stopped.

“You are Hassan, the late Sir John Willard’s servant?”

“I served my Lord Sir John, now I serve his son.” He took a step
nearer to us and lowered his voice. “You are a wise one, they say,
learned in dealing with evil spirits. Let the young master depart
from here. There is evil in the air around us.”

And with an abrupt gesture, not waiting for a reply, he strode
away.

“Evil in the air,” muttered Poirot. “Yes, I feel it.”

Our meal was hardly a cheerful one. The floor was left to Dr.
Tosswill, who discoursed at length upon Egyptian antiquities. Just
as we were preparing to retire to rest, Sir Guy caught Poirot by
the arm and pointed. A shadowy figure was moving amidst the tents.
It was no human one: I recognized distinctly the dog-headed figure
I had seen carved on the walls of the tomb.

My blood literally froze at the sight.

“_Mon Dieu!_” murmured Poirot, crossing himself vigorously. “Anubis,
the jackal-headed, the god of departing souls.”

“Some one is hoaxing us,” cried Dr. Tosswill, rising indignantly
to his feet.

“It went into your tent, Harper,” muttered Sir Guy, his face
dreadfully pale.

“No,” said Poirot, shaking his head, “into that of the Dr. Ames.”

The doctor stared at him incredulously; then, repeating Dr.
Tosswill’s words, he cried:

“Some one is hoaxing us. Come, we’ll soon catch the fellow.”

He dashed energetically in pursuit of the shadowy apparition. I
followed him, but, search as we would, we could find no trace of
any living soul having passed that way. We returned, somewhat
disturbed in mind, to find Poirot taking energetic measures, in
his own way, to ensure his personal safety. He was busily
surrounding our tent with various diagrams and inscriptions which
he was drawing in the sand. I recognized the five-pointed star or
Pentagon many times repeated. As was his wont, Poirot was at the
same time delivering an impromptu lecture on witchcraft and magic
in general, White Magic as opposed to Black, with various references
to the Ka and the Book of the Dead thrown in.

It appeared to excite the liveliest contempt in Dr. Tosswill, who
drew me aside, literally snorting with rage.

“Balderdash, sir,” he exclaimed angrily. “Pure balderdash. The
man’s an impostor. He doesn’t know the difference between the
superstitions of the Middle Ages and the beliefs of Ancient Egypt.
Never have I heard such a hotch-potch of ignorance and credulity.”

I calmed the excited expert, and joined Poirot in the tent. My
little friend was beaming cheerfully.

“We can now sleep in peace,” he declared happily. “And I can do
with some sleep. My head, it aches abominably. Ah, for a good
_tisane_!”

As though in answer to prayer, the flap of the tent was lifted and
Hassan appeared, bearing a steaming cup which he offered to Poirot.
It proved to be camomile tea, a beverage of which he is inordinately
fond. Having thanked Hassan and refused his offer of another cup
for myself, we were left alone once more. I stood at the door of
the tent some time after undressing, looking out over the desert.

“A wonderful place,” I said aloud, “and a wonderful work. I can
feel the fascination. This desert life, this probing into the heart
of a vanished civilization. Surely, Poirot, you, too, must feel
the charm?”

I got no answer, and I turned, a little annoyed. My annoyance was
quickly changed to concern. Poirot was lying back across the rude
couch, his face horribly convulsed. Beside him was the empty cup.
I rushed to his side, then dashed out and across the camp to Dr.
Ames’s tent.

“Dr. Ames!” I cried. “Come at once.”

“What’s the matter?” said the doctor, appearing in pyjamas.

“My friend. He’s ill. Dying. The camomile tea. Don’t let Hassan
leave the camp.”

Like a flash the doctor ran to our tent. Poirot was lying as I left
him.

“Extraordinary,” cried Ames. “Looks like a seizure—or—what did you
say about something he drank?” He picked up the empty cup.

“Only I did not drink it!” said a placid voice.

We turned in amazement. Poirot was sitting up on the bed. He was
smiling.

“No,” he said gently. “I did not drink it. While my good friend
Hastings was apostrophizing the night, I took the opportunity of
pouring it, not down my throat, but into a little bottle. That
little bottle will go to the analytical chemist. No”—as the doctor
made a sudden movement—“as a sensible man, you will understand that
violence will be of no avail. During Hastings’ brief absence to
fetch you, I have had time to put the bottle in safe keeping. Ah,
quick, Hastings, hold him!”

I misunderstood Poirot’s anxiety. Eager to save my friend, I flung
myself in front of him. But the doctor’s swift movement had another
meaning. His hand went to his mouth, a smell of bitter almonds
filled the air, and he swayed forward and fell.

“Another victim,” said Poirot gravely, “but the last. Perhaps it
is the best way. He has three deaths on his head.”

“Dr. Ames?” I cried, stupefied. “But I thought you believed in some
occult influence?”

“You misunderstood me, Hastings. What I meant was that I believe
in the terrific force of superstition. Once get it firmly
established that a series of deaths are supernatural, and you might
almost stab a man in broad daylight, and it would still be put down
to the curse, so strongly is the instinct of the supernatural
implanted in the human race. I suspected from the first that a man
was taking advantage of that instinct. The idea came to him, I
imagine, with the death of Sir John Willard. A fury of superstition
arose at once. As far as I could see, nobody could derive any
particular profit from Sir John’s death. Mr. Bleibner was a
different case. He was a man of great wealth. The information I
received from New York contained several suggestive points. To
begin with, young Bleibner was reported to have said he had a good
friend in Egypt from whom he could borrow. It was tacitly understood
that he meant his uncle, but it seemed to me that in that case he
would have said so outright. The words suggest some boon companion
of his own. Another thing, he scraped up enough money to take him
to Egypt, his uncle refused outright to advance him a penny, yet
he was able to pay the return passage to New York. Some one must
have lent him the money.”

“All that was very thin,” I objected.

“But there was more. Hastings, there occur often enough words
spoken metaphorically which are taken literally. The opposite can
happen too. In this case, words which were meant literally were
taken metaphorically. Young Bleibner wrote plainly enough: ‘I am
a leper,’ but nobody realized that he shot himself because he
believed that he had contracted the dread disease of leprosy.”

“What?” I ejaculated.

“It was the clever invention of a diabolical mind. Young Bleibner
was suffering from some minor skin trouble, he had lived in the
South Sea Islands, where the disease is common enough. Ames was a
former friend of his, and a well-known medical man, he would never
dream of doubting his word. When I arrived here, my suspicions were
divided between Harper and Dr. Ames, but I soon realized that only
the doctor could have perpetrated and concealed the crimes, and I
learnt from Harper that he was previously acquainted with young
Bleibner. Doubtless the latter at some time or another had made a
will or had insured his life in favour of the doctor. The latter
saw his chance of acquiring wealth. It was easy for him to inoculate
Mr. Bleibner with the deadly germs. Then the nephew, overcome with
despair at the dread news his friend had conveyed to him, shot
himself. Mr. Bleibner, whatever his intentions, had made no will.
His fortune would pass to his nephew and from him to the doctor.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“We cannot be sure. He knew young Bleibner too, remember, and may
have suspected something, or, again, the doctor may have thought
that a further death motiveless and purposeless would strengthen
the coils of superstition. Furthermore, I will tell you an
interesting psychological fact, Hastings. A murderer has always a
strong desire to repeat his successful crime, the performance of
it grows upon him. Hence my fears for young Willard. The figure of
Anubis you saw to-night was Hassan, dressed up by my orders. I
wanted to see if I could frighten the doctor. But it would take
more than the supernatural to frighten him. I could see that he
was not entirely taken in by my pretences of belief in the occult.
The little comedy I played for him did not deceive him. I suspected
that he would endeavour to make me the next victim. Ah, but in
spite of _la mer maudite_, the heat abominable, and the annoyances
of the sand, the little grey cells still functioned!”

Poirot proved to be perfectly right in his premises. Young Bleibner,
some years ago, in a fit of drunken merriment, had made a jocular
will, leaving “my cigarette case you admire so much and everything
else of which I die possessed which will be principally debts to
my good friend Robert Ames who once saved my life from drowning.”

The case was hushed up as far as possible, and, to this day, people
talk of the remarkable series of deaths in connection with the Tomb
of Men-her-Ra as a triumphal proof of the vengeance of a bygone
king upon the desecrators of his tomb—a belief which, as Poirot
pointed out to me, is contrary to all Egyptian belief and thought.

shadowy kings of the Eighth Dynasty, when the Old Kingdom was
falling to decay. Little was known about this period, and the
discoveries were fully reported in the newspapers.

An event soon occurred which took a profound hold on the public
mind. Sir John Willard died quite suddenly of heart failure.

A few weeks later, my friend Hercule Poirot received a letter from Lady Willard, the widow of the dead archaeologist, requesting an urgent consultation. When she arrived at our rooms in her deep mourning weeds, her face was pale and drawn, bearing the unmistakable marks of a recent and terrible anxiety. "It is not for myself that I fear, Monsieur Poirot," she explained in a voice that trembled slightly, "but for my son. Guy is determined to take his father's place in Egypt, and I am convinced that a sinister influence—the Curse of Men-her-Ra—will claim him as its next victim."

A fortnight later, the sensation was further heightened by the news of Mr. Bleibner’s death. He had succumbed to acute blood poisoning, an infection apparently contracted during the excavations. Within a week, a third tragedy followed: Mr. Bleibner’s nephew, a young man in New York, had shot himself, leaving a brief and cryptic note. The "Curse of Men-her-Ra" was no longer a mere journalistic invention; it had become a terrifying reality in the eyes of the public.

A fortnight later, Lady Willard, the widow of the dead archaeologist, called upon my friend. She was a tall, thin woman, dressed in deep mourning, whose face bore the marks of a recent and terrible grief. Poirot greeted her with his usual exquisite politeness, but I could see by the twinkle in his eyes that the mention of the "curse of the Pharaohs" in the morning papers had already piqued his professional curiosity, even if his logical mind rebelled against such occult explanations.

It was a fortnight later that a second blow fell. Mr. Bleibner, the American colleague of Sir John, succumbed to an attack of septicaemia. The newspapers went mad, their headlines screaming of the "Curse of Men-her-Ra." Then came the news from New York that Mr. Bleibner’s nephew, a young man of great promise, had shot himself in a fit of inexplicable depression. It was at this juncture that Lady Willard, the widow of the dead baronet, sought out Hercule Poirot and entreated his assistance on behalf of her son, Guy, who had gone out to Egypt to take his father's place.

It was this atmosphere of superstitious dread that surrounded Lady Willard when she first came to visit Poirot in our rooms at Jermyn Street. Clad in the heavy weeds of her recent widowhood, her face pale and drawn with anxiety, she spoke of the "Curse of the Pharaohs" with a conviction that was chilling. She feared for her son, Guy, who had insisted on returning to Egypt to continue his father’s work. "I am not a superstitious woman," she told us, her voice trembling, "but three deaths, Monsieur Poirot—three deaths in as many weeks! It is more than a coincidence; it is a malevolence that defies the laws of science."

A fortnight later Mr. Bleibner died of acute blood poisoning, and
a few days afterwards a nephew of his shot himself in New York.
The “Curse of Men-her-Ra” was the talk of the day, and the magic
power of dead and gone Egypt was exalted to a fetish point.

It was then that Poirot received a brief note from Lady Willard,
widow of the dead archaeologist, asking him to go and see her at
her house in Kensington Square. I accompanied him.

Lady Willard was a tall, thin woman, dressed in deep mourning. Her
haggard face bore eloquent testimony to her recent grief.

“It is kind of you to have come so promptly, Monsieur Poirot.”

“I am at your service, Lady Willard. You wished to consult me?”

“Let us not quibble at the word, Madame. To me, the ‘supernatural’ is often only the natural which has not yet been explained. But why do you ask? You do not believe, surely, that your husband’s death was caused by the vengeance of a King who has been dust for three thousand years?”

“Let us not misunderstand each other, milady. I do not believe in the magic of the ancients, no. But I believe in the power of the human mind—the force of suggestion. If a man believes himself cursed, he may well die of that belief. However, there are also those who find the mantle of a curse very convenient for more mundane purposes. You fear for your son, is it not so? He has gone out there to continue his father’s work?”

“Let us not scoff, milady. I do not believe in the supernatural as a general rule—no, I am a man of logic, of the little grey cells. But one must admit that there are influences... atmospheres... things that cannot be measured by a ruler or weighed in a balance. However, my experience tells me that it is usually more profitable to look for the human hand before we blame the spirits of the Pharaohs. Is it that you fear your husband’s death was not—natural?”

“Let us not quibble at the word, milady. To me, the supernatural is but the natural of which we have not yet the explanation. But do not believe for one moment that I am a scoffer. I have seen much, and I know that the power of the human spirit is great. But why do you ask me this? You are in fear, is it not so? You fear for the young Sir Guy, your son, who has gone to Egypt to take his father’s place?”

“Believe, milady, that I do not jump to the conclusion of the supernatural. I am a man of logic, of order and method. I use my little grey cells to find the reason that is hidden. Yet, I am also a man of the world, and I know that the mind of man is a strange and powerful thing. If a man believes himself to be cursed, that belief can be more deadly than any poison or dagger. It is the psychology that interests me, the force of an idea that can kill.”

“Let us not misunderstand each other, Lady Willard. It is not a
general question that you are asking me there. It has a personal
application, has it not? You are referring obliquely to the death
of your late husband?”

“That is so,” she admitted.

“You want me to investigate the circumstances of his death?”

“For my son. When the news of his father’s death came, he was in Algiers. He went straight to Egypt to take his place. I have had a letter from him today—and in it there is a suggestion of a new-found gravity, a foreboding that I cannot like. He says that the party is already short-handed. Young Mr. Bleibner’s death has naturally cast a gloom over them all, and they are working in a state of nervous tension that is ill-suited to the climate. If—if anything should happen to Guy, I should never forgive myself for not having taken steps to protect him. I want you to go to Egypt, Monsieur Poirot. Money is no object. If you can only assure me of my son’s safety, I shall be forever in your debt.”

“For my son,” she whispered. “Guy has gone out to Egypt to take his father’s place. He is headstrong, full of the enthusiasm of youth, and he mocks what he calls the ‘tittle-tattle’ of the press. But I, Monsieur Poirot, I am a mother. I feel the cold breath of the Pharaoh’s vengeance. There are others still out there—Dr. Tosswill, the expert from the British Museum; Dr. Ames, who was my husband’s friend and physician; Mr. Harper, the secretary; and even the devoted Hassan. Any one of them might be the next, but it is for my boy that my heart bleeds. If there is a way to protect him, to find the truth behind these tragedies, I beg of you to find it.”

“For my son,” she replied in a hollow voice. “When the news of his father’s death reached him, he was in New York. He started for Egypt at once. He is there now, taking up his father’s work. I am haunted, Monsieur Poirot, by the thought that he will be the next victim. If I could only have him back with me! But he is headstrong, and he will not leave. The shadow of the Pharaoh is over him.”

“For my son,” she replied. “When the news of his father’s death came, he was in New York. He sailed at once for Egypt. He has a passion for Egyptology, and he intends to take his father’s place and carry on the work of the expedition. I have written to him, I have implored him to return, but he will not listen. He is headstrong, like all the Willards. He says it is his duty, and that he does not believe in the curse. But I am afraid—terribly afraid. If I could only feel that someone was there—someone like you, Monsieur Poirot, who would see things that he might not see—then my mind would be at rest.”

“For my son,” she replied, her voice dropping to a whisper. “Guy is out there now. He would go—he felt it his duty to continue his father’s work. But I am haunted, Monsieur Poirot. If there is some malign influence at work—if the dead can indeed strike at the living—then Guy is in peril. I want you to go to Egypt. I want you to protect him.”

“For my son. When the news of my husband’s death came I was ill.
My son, who has just come down from Oxford, went out there. He
brought the—the body home, but now he has gone out again, in spite
of my prayers and entreaties. He is so fascinated by the work that
he intends to take his father’s place and carry on the system of
excavations. You may think me a foolish, credulous woman, but,
Monsieur Poirot, I am afraid. Supposing that the spirit of the dead
King is not yet appeased? Perhaps to you I seem to be talking
nonsense——”

“No, indeed, Lady Willard,” said Poirot quickly. “I, too, believe
in the force of superstition, one of the greatest forces the world
has ever known.”

I looked at him in surprise. I should never have credited Poirot
with being superstitious. But the little man was obviously in
earnest.

“What you really demand is that I shall protect your son? I will
do my utmost to keep him from harm.”

“Yes, in the ordinary way, but against an occult influence?”

“That is so. He was a very wealthy man who found in Egyptology a new interest. It was his money that made the excavations possible. There were others with them, of course. Dr. Tosswill, the great authority from the British Museum; Mr. Harper, who acted as secretary to the expedition; and Dr. Ames, who accompanied them in a medical capacity. And then there were the native servants, including Hassan, who had been with my husband for many years.”

“Oh, quite. He was a very wealthy man who had always been interested in Egyptology, and it was his money that made the excavations possible. He and my husband had been friends for many years. As for the young man, his nephew, he was in New York at the time of his uncle's death. It was a most distressing affair. It is said that he had been in some financial difficulties, but the news of his uncle's sudden death seemed to have affected his mind. He shot himself the following day.”

“Oh, quite. He was a very wealthy man who found in Egyptology a new interest. It was he who provided the funds for the expedition.”

“And the others of the party?” asked Poirot.

“There was Dr. Tosswill, an expert from the British Museum; Dr. Ames, the medical man of the party; and Mr. Harper, who acted as secretary. Then, of course, there were the native servants, including Hassan, who had been with my husband for many years.”

“Oh, quite so,” replied Lady Willard. “He was a very wealthy man who found a late interest in archaeology. He provided much of the necessary capital, but the technical direction was entirely in my husband’s hands. Then there was Dr. Tosswill, the famous expert from the British Museum, and a young man, a Mr. Harper, who acted as secretary to the expedition. And, of course, there was Dr. Ames, who accompanied them in a medical capacity. I believe there was also a native servant, a man named Hassan, who had been with Mr. Bleibner for many years.”

“Oh, yes, Mr. Bleibner was a very wealthy American who provided the financial means for the expedition. He was not himself a scholar, though he had developed a great passion for the subject. My husband was the directing mind. At the site now, there is Dr. Tosswill, a distinguished official from the British Museum, and Dr. Ames, who accompanied the party as a medical man. There is also Mr. Harper, who acted as secretary to Mr. Bleibner. And, of course, the native staff, overseen by a man named Hassan. I believe they are all still at the excavations, despite the tragedies that have occurred.”

“Oh, quite. He was a very wealthy man who dabbled freely in any
subject that happened to take his fancy. My husband managed to
interest him in Egyptology, and it was his money that was so useful
in financing the expedition.”

“And the nephew? What do you know of his tastes? Was he with the
party at all?”

“There is Dr. Tosswill, the eminent expert from the British Museum; Dr. Ames, who accompanies the expedition in a medical capacity; and Mr. Harper, who acted as secretary to Mr. Bleibner. Then, of course, there are the native foremen and laborers, most notably Hassan, my husband's devoted personal servant, who has been with him for many years.”

“There is Dr. Tosswill, the distinguished expert from the British Museum; Dr. Ames, who accompanies the expedition in a medical capacity; and Mr. Harper, the young man who acted as secretary to Mr. Bleibner. Then there are, of course, the various native workmen and the headman, Hassan, who was a most devoted servant to my husband for many years.”

“There is Dr. Tosswill, a very distinguished official from the British Museum; Dr. Ames, who accompanied the party in a medical capacity; and Mr. Harper, who was Mr. Bleibner’s secretary. Then there are the various native workers, and Hassan, my husband’s devoted personal servant who has been in his employment for many years.”

“There is Dr. Tosswill, a minor official from the British Museum; Dr. Ames, who accompanied the expedition in a professional capacity; and Mr. Harper, who was Mr. Bleibner’s secretary. Then there are the native servants, of course, chief among them being Hassan, a very faithful fellow who had been with my husband for many years.”

“There is Dr. Ames, who accompanied the expedition in a professional capacity; and Mr. Harper, the secretary. There is also the Egyptian expert, Dr. Tosswill, of the British Museum; and a young man, Mr. Schneider of the Metropolitan Museum in New York. Then, of course, there is the native staff, overseen by a man named Hassan, who has been with my husband for many years. My son has now joined them at the site, which is why my anxiety is so great.”

“Well, there is Dr. Tosswill, a minor official connected with the
British Museum; Mr. Schneider of the Metropolitan Museum in New
York; a young American secretary; Dr. Ames, who accompanies the
expedition in his professional capacity; and Hassan, my husband’s
devoted native servant.”

“Do you remember the name of the American secretary?”

“Harper, I think, but I cannot be sure. He had not been with Mr.
Bleibner very long, I know. He was a very pleasant young fellow.”

“Thank you, Lady Willard.”

“If there is anything else——?”

“For the moment, nothing. Leave it now in my hands, and be assured
that I will do all that is humanly possible to protect your son.”

The cable was duly dispatched, and the reply, which arrived the following morning, was both full and informative. Rupert Bleibner had been what the world calls a "bad egg." He had been in low water for some time, having a penchant for gambling and a distaste for steady work. He had recently borrowed quite a considerable sum of money. The most significant piece of news, however, was that he had actually been in Egypt at the time of his uncle’s death, but had returned to New York almost immediately afterwards. This seemed to me to strengthen the theory of the curse—a man fleeing from the scene only to be pursued by an inexorable fate across the Atlantic—but Poirot merely hummed a little tune to himself and began to pack his small valise, announcing that our next destination would be the land of the Pharaohs itself.

The cable was duly dispatched, and the reply, when it came, was brief but illuminating. Rupert Bleibner, it appeared, had been in low water for some time. He had been leading a somewhat dissipated life in New York, and had been heard to express himself in the most bitter terms regarding his uncle’s stinginess. He had even gone so far as to hint that he would soon be coming into a large fortune. Then came his uncle’s death, and a few days later, his own suicide. Was it the remorse of a murderer, or the final despair of a ruined man? Poirot’s face grew more thoughtful as he read the message.

The cable reached New York and the reply was not long in coming. It appeared that young Mr. Rupert Bleibner had been in some financial difficulties; he had also been suffering from a strange delusion that he had contracted leprosy. He had shot himself in a fit of depression, leaving a note which said: "I am an outcast. I must follow the others." This news seemed to interest Poirot greatly. He made a few more inquiries, then announced that we were to start for Egypt immediately. A few days later saw us on our way to the East.

The reply was received the following day. It was brief and to the point. Rupert Bleibner had been in the habit of frequenting various New York night-clubs. He had drifted into a fast set, had lost heavily, and had finally put an end to himself after receiving news of his uncle’s death. There appeared to be nothing in that to suggest any weird influence. I told Poirot as much, but he merely shook his head and murmured that it was very strange—very strange indeed.

The reply from New York arrived the following morning. It was brief, stating that Rupert Bleibner had been in financial difficulties and had shot himself after a period of deep depression; curiously, his last letter had contained some rambling references to his being a “leper” and an “outcast.” Poirot sat for a long time in silence, his brow corrugated with thought, as he contemplated this information. Our breakfast was interrupted, however, by the arrival of a second cable, this time from Egypt. It was from Guy Willard, and it contained the news that Mr. Schneider of the Metropolitan Museum had died of tetanus.

He duly sent off his cable. The reply was full and precise. Young
Rupert Bleibner had been in low water for several years. He had
been a beach-comber and a remittance man in several South Sea
islands, but had returned to New York two years ago, where he had
rapidly sunk lower and lower. The most significant thing, to my
mind, was that he had recently managed to borrow enough money to
take him to Egypt. “I’ve a good friend there I can borrow from,”
he had declared. Here, however, his plans had gone awry. He had
returned to New York cursing his skinflint of an uncle who cared
more for the bones of dead and gone kings than his own flesh and
blood. It was during his sojourn in Egypt that the death of Sir
John Willard occurred. Rupert had plunged once more into his life
of dissipation in New York, and then, without warning, he had
committed suicide, leaving behind him a letter which contained some
curious phrases. It seemed written in a sudden fit of remorse. He
referred to himself as a leper and an outcast, and the letter ended
by declaring that such as he were better dead.

The journey was, as Poirot had predicted, a period of unmitigated misery for him; but even the rigours of the sea could not dampen his professional zeal for long. Once we had reached Cairo and transferred to the desert, the dry heat seemed to restore him, though he grumbled incessantly about the dust which "made a disaster of his moustaches." We arrived at the excavation site as the golden glow of the afternoon began to fade. The camp was a scene of quiet but intense activity, dominated by the looming presence of the Pyramids in the distance. A man emerged from one of the larger tents—a man with a lean, bronzed face and a certain professional air that marked him out immediately. This was Dr. Ames, the medical officer of the expedition, who greeted us with a mixture of curiosity and polite restraint.

The journey was every bit as harrowing for Poirot as he had predicted, and it was a very pale and shaken little man who finally set foot upon the sands of Egypt. We travelled by rail and then by camel to the site of the excavations, where the Great Pyramid stood as a silent sentinel over the mysteries of the past. The camp itself consisted of several sturdy tents and a small stone hut used for storage, all shimmering in the pitiless glare of the sun. It was here that we first encountered the survivors of the ill-fated expedition. Dr. Ames, the medical officer, met us with a professional gravity that thinly veiled a profound exhaustion, while nearby, a tall, bronzed young man whom I took to be Mr. Harper, the secretary, watched our arrival with an expression of wary curiosity. The very air seemed thick with a tension that was almost physical, as if the “Curse of Men-her-Ra” were a living entity crouching in the shadows of the tomb.

The journey was, as Poirot had predicted, a period of unmitigated misery for him. He reached Alexandria a mere shadow of his former self, but his spirit remained indomitable. We traveled to Cairo and then onwards to the site of the excavations. The camp was pitched in the desert, not far from the imposing silhouettes of the Pyramids of Gizeh. As we approached, a tall, thin man with a tired, clean-shaven face and a professional manner came out of one of the tents to meet us. This was Dr. Ames, the medical officer of the expedition.

The journey had been a trial for Poirot, whose constitution was ill-suited to the motion of the sea, but once his feet touched the solid, if sandy, earth of Egypt, his spirit revived. We reached the camp near the Pyramids of Gizeh late in the afternoon, finding the excavation party in a state of subdued agitation. Dr. Tosswill received us with a stiff, academic formality that seemed oddly out of place in the wilderness, while Dr. Ames, the expedition's physician, greeted us with a weary kindliness that spoke of many sleepless nights. Standing slightly apart was a young man with a sharp, nervous face whom I took to be Mr. Harper, the secretary, and nearby, the enigmatic figure of Hassan, the native servant, who watched our arrival with an expression of inscrutable melancholy. There was a heavy, expectant silence over the camp, as if everyone were waiting for the next blow from an unseen hand.

The journey was for Poirot a long-drawn-out agony, but at last the day came when we stood upon the burning sands of Egypt. Our arrival at the camp near the Pyramids was marked by a sense of heavy oppression that seemed to hang over the entire party. We were greeted by Sir Guy Willard, a young man whose face was drawn and anxious, and who looked as though he had not slept for weeks. Around him were gathered the survivors of the original expedition: Dr. Tosswill, a dry, pedantic man who appeared to regard the deaths as merely tiresome interruptions to his work; Dr. Ames, the medical officer, a man of middle age with a cynical eye; and Mr. Harper, the secretary, whose hands shook as he offered us refreshment. Even Hassan, the late Sir John's devoted servant, seemed to be watching us with a look of inscrutable suspicion from the shadows of the tents. It was clear that the "Curse of Men-her-Ra" had cast a long shadow over them all.

It was a week later. Beneath our feet was the golden sand of the
desert. The hot sun poured down overhead. Poirot, the picture of
misery, wilted by my side. The little man was not a good traveller.
Our four days’ voyage from Marseilles had been one long agony to
him. He had landed at Alexandria the wraith of his former self,
even his usual neatness had deserted him. We had arrived in Cairo
and had driven out at once to the Mena House Hotel, right in the
shadow of the Pyramids.

"And the dust!" he wailed. "It is everywhere! It penetrates, it permeates, it destroys the very soul of the clothing! My boots, Hastings, look at them—they are no longer of a blackness that is respectable; they are a miserable, dusty grey!" I endeavoured to soothe him, but his mind was set upon his sartorial misfortunes until the moment our car reached the encampment near the tomb. A little knot of men was gathered there, and as we descended, a tall, sunburnt man with a pleasant, professional face stepped forward to meet us. This, as we soon learned, was Dr. Ames. Behind him stood a young man, pale and anxious-looking, whom I correctly guessed to be Sir Guy Willard, and a stouter, older man who watched us with a cold, disinterested eye—Dr. Tosswill, of the British Museum.

"The sand!" moaned Poirot. "It is in the ears, the eyes, the mouth! And the heat—it is an outrage to the intelligence! Why could this King Men-her-Ra not have been buried in a nice, damp climate where the dust does not fly?" We had chartered a car to take us to the site of the excavations, a journey that involved a final, agonizing stretch on camels—a mode of transport that Poirot viewed with the utmost suspicion and loathing. At last, however, we reached the encampment, a cluster of white tents set against the blinding glare of the desert. A tall, thin man with a bronzed face and tired eyes came out to meet us; he introduced himself as Dr. Ames. Beside him stood a thick-set, elderly man with a pedantic expression whom I correctly guessed to be Dr. Tosswill of the British Museum, and a pleasant-looking young American who could be none other than Mr. Harper, the secretary. Standing somewhat apart, a tall, silent figure in native dress, was Hassan, the late Sir John's devoted servant.

"And the sand!" he wailed. "It is everywhere. It gets into the joints of the case, it penetrates the watch, it is even, I fear, in my moustaches! But we must not delay. To the camp, Hastings!" We set out for the excavation site, a journey which Poirot endured with the stoicism of a martyr. As we approached the cluster of white tents pitched in the lee of a rocky ridge, a group of men emerged to meet us. Foremost was a tall, bronzed young man with an air of suppressed strain—Sir Guy Willard. He was accompanied by a lean, dark man with a professional manner who was introduced as Dr. Ames, and a thick-set, elderly man with a pedantic expression—Dr. Tosswill of the British Museum. A few paces behind them stood a pleasant-faced young American, whom I correctly took to be Mr. Harper, the secretary, and a tall, silent figure in native dress, the devoted Hassan.

The following morning saw us on our way to the scene of the excavations. A short journey by camel—an experience which Poirot found even more distressing than the sea—brought us to the encampment. We were met by a young man whose face was burnt a deep brick-red by the Egyptian sun. This was Mr. Harper, the secretary, to whom Poirot had previously sent a telegram. He greeted us with a mixture of surprise and, as it seemed to me, a profound sense of relief.

The following morning found us making our way across the burning sands towards the scene of the excavations. Poirot’s lamentations were piteous to hear. “The sand!” he wailed. “It is in my mouth, it is in my nose, it is in my very soul! And look, Hastings, my boots—they are ruined, absolutely ruined!” We found the camp a scene of quiet but intense activity. A row of white tents stood out sharply against the dazzling blue of the sky. As we approached, a young man with a face tanned a deep mahogany came forward to meet us. This was Sir Guy Willard, and the look of strain about his eyes told its own story of the burden he had inherited.

“And my boots,” he wailed. “Regard them, Hastings. My boots, of
the neat patent leather, usually so smart and shining. See, the
sand is inside them, which is painful, and outside them, which
outrages the eyesight. Also the heat, it causes my moustaches to
become limp—but limp!”

“Look at the Sphinx,” I urged. “Even I can feel the mystery and
the charm it exhales.”

Poirot looked at it discontentedly.

“It has not the air happy,” he declared. “How could it, half-buried
in sand in that untidy fashion. Ah, this cursed sand!”

“Come, now, there’s a lot of sand in Belgium,” I reminded him,
mindful of a holiday spent at Knocke-sur-mer in the midst of “_les
dunes impeccables_” as the guide-book had phrased it.

We took a car out to the camp, which was situated some distance from the hotel. The journey was a short one, but to Poirot it was evidently an eternity of discomfort. As we approached the cluster of white tents that marked the site of the excavations, a young man came forward to meet us. He was tall and thin, with a face that should have been boyish but was instead drawn and haggard. This was Sir Guy Willard, and it was plain to see that his mother’s fears for him were not without foundation. He greeted us with a sort of weary courtesy that was infinitely pathetic.

The expedition camp was situated some distance away, a little cluster of white tents against the vastness of the sands. As we approached, a young man came out to meet us—a tall, clean-cut lad with a face that looked older than his years, marked by the recent strain he had undergone. This was Sir Guy Willard. He greeted us with a sort of desperate eagerness. With him were three other men: a stout, elderly individual with a dry, pedantic manner whom I correctly took to be Dr. Tosswill; a younger, sharp-faced man who was introduced as Mr. Harper; and a tall, thin man with a professional air and a touch of gray at his temples, who was Dr. Ames. In the background, like a silent shadow, stood the figure of Hassan, the late Sir John's devoted servant.

The journey to the excavation site was accomplished the following morning. Poirot’s sufferings on the back of a small and spirited donkey were such that I will not attempt to describe them; his dignity was only preserved by a miracle of balance and a grim determination. At last, the white tents of the camp appeared, nestled against the sun-bleached cliffs where the work was in progress. As we dismounted, a tall, thin man with a tired, clever face and a touch of gray at his temples stepped forward to greet us. This was Dr. Ames, the medical officer of the expedition.

Our journey to the site of the excavations was long and fatiguing. We arrived at last to find a little city of white tents pitched against the background of the rocky hills. As our camels—Poirot's protests during the ride had been heart-rending—groaned and knelt, a tall man with a thin, lugubrious face and a touch of gray at his temples stepped forward to greet us. This was Dr. Ames, the medical man of the expedition. He looked at us with a mixture of weariness and professional interest.

Our journey to the actual site of the excavations was a trial for Poirot, involving as it did a ride upon a camel—an animal for which he conceived an immediate and lasting antipathy. However, we arrived at last at the little cluster of tents which formed the expedition’s headquarters. As we dismounted, a tall man with a thin, clever face and a grey beard came forward to meet us. This was Dr. Ames, the medical man of the party. He greeted us with a quiet courtesy that was very refreshing. Beside him stood a young man whose face, despite its tan, looked strangely haggard. This was Sir Guy Willard, and I could see at once that his mother’s fears were not without foundation; the boy looked as though he were living under a severe nervous strain.

I cut short his lamentations, by suggesting that we should start
for the camp. We were to ride there on camels, and the beasts were
patiently kneeling, waiting for us to mount, in charge of several
picturesque boys headed by a voluble dragoman.

A young man, whose face was haggard and drawn with anxiety, rose to meet us. This was evidently Sir Guy Willard. Beside him were the two other members of the expedition: Dr. Ames, a man of middle age with a thin, clever face and greyish hair; and Mr. Harper, the American secretary, a pleasant-looking young fellow of about thirty. The atmosphere in the tent was one of heavy gloom. It was easy to see that the recent tragedy had shaken them all. Sir Guy’s hand shook as he offered us chairs. “It is good of you to come, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “You find us in a state of great distress. This business of poor Schneider—it’s been the last straw. You have heard, I suppose?”

Sir Guy Willard, a tall, thin lad with a face that was a mask of misery, rose to greet us. He looked as though he had not slept for weeks. Beside him were two other men. One, a young man with a typically alert American face, was introduced as Mr. Harper, the secretary; the other, a man of middle age with a tired, disillusioned expression, was Dr. Ames. They all looked at Poirot with a certain amount of curiosity. It was clear that the atmosphere of the camp was one of deep depression and nervous strain.

Sir Guy Willard rose and came forward to meet us. He was a tall, thin young man, with a face that looked strangely old for his years; there was a haunted, hunted look in his eyes that told of the strain he was undergoing. Beside him sat a man with a quiet, observant face and a professional manner whom I correctly took to be Dr. Ames. The third occupant of the tent was a fair-haired, nervous-looking young man with a slight American accent—Mr. Harper, the secretary. It was easy to see that the nerves of all three men were on edge. The sudden death of Schneider had evidently been the last straw.

A young man rose from a packing case and came forward to meet us. He was a typical specimen of the young Englishman of the upper classes, lean, well-knit, with a face that should have been bronzed and healthy, but was now unnaturally pale. This, then, was Sir Guy Willard. By his side sat a middle-aged man with a thin, clever face and greyish hair, whom I took to be Dr. Ames. The third occupant of the tent was a pleasant-faced young man of about thirty, whose American accent soon proclaimed him to be Mr. Harper, the secretary. They all looked at us with a mixture of curiosity and, I thought, a certain underlying tension.

A tall, thin young man rose to greet us. His face, though youthful, was lined with an expression of grim endurance that was painful to see, and his eyes held a restless, haunted look. This was Sir Guy Willard. He introduced his companions: Dr. Ames, a man of middle age with a thin, professional face and steady, observant eyes, and Mr. Harper, the secretary, a clean-cut young American who seemed to be struggling to maintain his composure in the face of the recent tragedy. The atmosphere in the tent was one of heavy, brooding apprehension; it was as though the "Curse of Men-her-Ra" had a physical weight, pressing down upon the spirits of these men who had dared to disturb the rest of a king. Sir Guy’s voice was steady as he spoke, but I noticed his hands were trembling slightly as he motioned us to be seated.

The youngest of the three men jumped up and came forward to greet
us. There was a certain impulsiveness in his manner which reminded
me of his mother. He was not nearly so sunburnt as the others, and
that fact, coupled with a certain haggardness round the eyes, made
him look older than his twenty-two years. He was clearly endeavouring
to bear up under a severe mental strain.

“No, Monsieur Poirot, it was not. He died of acute blood poisoning.
A small abrasion on the arm became septic and he died of it. It
was a very sad case, but it was just one of those things that
happen in this climate.”

“And Sir John Willard?”

“My father died of heart failure,” put in the young baronet.

“Was his heart weak?”

“Not that I know of.”

“He had not been complaining?”

“No. He had been unusually well.”

Poirot sat silent for a minute or two.

“This young man, Hassan, who was his servant?”

“He is still here,” said Sir Guy. “He is a very good fellow.”

“Would you mind if I had a few minutes’ talk with him?”

“None at all.”

Sir Guy went to the door of the tent and called for Hassan. In a
minute or two he appeared. He was a tall, fine looking fellow with
a dignified bearing. He saluted Poirot with a grave courtesy.

Poirot asked him a few questions in his own language, then dismissed
him.

“Well?” I asked. “What did he say?”

“Nothing. He believes in the Curse. He has seen the spirit of King
Men-her-Ra. He saw him on the night Sir John died. He saw him again
on the night Mr. Bleibner died, and again on the night Mr. Schneider
died. A tall, shadowy figure with the head of a jackal.”

“Anubis!” I cried.

“The God of the Dead,” said Poirot, with a slight shiver. “The curse
of the Tomb is beginning to take a very definite shape.”

“But you don’t believe it, Monsieur Poirot?” cried Sir Guy, a look
of horror in his eyes.

“I believe in the force of superstition, as I told your mother. I
believe that it can be a very potent thing.”

“But how? What can we do?”

“I will tell you,” said Poirot, with sudden energy. “I am going to
spend the night in the Tomb. I shall see if King Men-her-Ra has
any message for me.”

Sir Guy stared at him.

“You are brave, Monsieur Poirot.”

“It is not a question of bravery. It is a question of science. I
wish to test a certain theory of mine.”

I felt a cold chill down my spine. The thought of Poirot, alone in
that grim tomb, with the spirit of the dead king for company, was
anything but pleasant. But Poirot was firm.

“I shall require only a small lamp, and a rug to sit upon. I do
not think the King will find me an intrusive visitor.”

The others were silent. They evidently thought him mad, but they
made no further attempt to dissuade him.

As for me, I spent a sleepless night. I lay awake, listening to
every sound, expecting I knew not what. But nothing happened. The
night passed peacefully.

Early the next morning, we went to the Tomb. Poirot was sitting
on his rug, his lamp still burning. He looked pale and haggard,
but his eyes were bright.

“Well?” we cried. “What happened?”

Poirot rose slowly to his feet.

“The King has spoken,” he said gravely. “He has given me his message.”

“And what is it?”

“He has told me how he died. He was not murdered. He died of a
broken heart. He was a very lonely man, and he was very tired. He
wants to be left in peace.”

Sir Guy looked at him in amazement.

“Is that all?”

“Is it not enough? The King asks for peace. He does not want his
tomb to be disturbed. He has warned us, and we have not listened.
Now he has spoken for the last time. If we do not leave him in
peace, he will strike again.”

“But this is madness!” cried Sir Guy. “We cannot leave the work now.
It is almost finished.”

“The King has spoken,” repeated Poirot. “I can say no more.”

He turned and walked away. I followed him, my head in a whirl. Was
it possible that Poirot, the most logical of men, had really
succumbed to the influence of the Tomb? Or was he merely acting a
part? I could not tell.

For the next two days, Poirot was strangely silent. He spent most
of his time wandering about the camp, or sitting by himself in
deep thought. He seemed to have lost all interest in the
excavations.

But I noticed one thing. He was constantly watching the other members
of the party. His eyes would follow them as they went about their
work, and he seemed to be listening to everything they said.

On the third day, a fresh disaster occurred. Mr. Harper, the
American secretary, was found dead in his bed. He had died,
apparently, of heart failure.

This latest tragedy produced a profound impression on the camp.
Even the most skeptical were shaken. The atmosphere of gloom and
terror was almost palpable.

Sir Guy was in a state of nervous collapse. Dr. Tosswill was grave
and silent. Dr. Ames was the only one who seemed to keep his head.

“This is getting beyond a joke,” he said to me. “If this goes on,
there won’t be one of us left alive. I’m beginning to think Poirot
was right. The place is cursed.”

“What does Poirot say?” I asked.

“He doesn’t say anything. He just sits there and thinks. I wish to
goodness he’d do something.”

I found Poirot in his tent. He was sitting on his bed, his chin in
his hands.

“Well, Poirot?” I said. “Harper is dead.”

“I know,” he said quietly.

“And what are you going to do?”

“I am going to catch the murderer,” said Poirot.

“The murderer? Then you don’t believe in the Curse after all?”

“I believe in the force of superstition, as I have told you many
times. But I also believe in the force of human greed and human
malice. And I think I know who is responsible for these deaths.”

“Who is it?” I cried.

“Wait a little, Hastings. I must be sure. I must have proof. And
for that, I need your help.”

“What do you want me to do?”

“I want you to keep a close watch on Dr. Ames. Do not let him out
of your sight for a moment. And if you see him doing anything
suspicious, let me know at once.”

I was surprised. Dr. Ames seemed the least likely person to be
involved in such a series of crimes. But I had learned by experience
never to doubt Poirot’s judgment.

“I will do as you say,” I said.

For the next twenty-four hours, I followed Dr. Ames like a shadow.
He seemed to be going about his business in the usual way, and I
saw nothing to arouse my suspicions.

Then, on the second night, I saw him go into the small tent where
the medical supplies were kept. I followed him cautiously and
peered through a slit in the canvas.

He was standing by a small table, on which were several bottles and
a hypodermic syringe. He was busily engaged in filling the syringe
from one of the bottles.

I felt a thrill of excitement. Was this the proof Poirot was looking
for?

I waited until he had finished and left the tent. Then I hurried
to Poirot and told him what I had seen.

“Good,” said Poirot. “Now we must act quickly. Come with me.”

We went to Sir Guy’s tent. Dr. Tosswill and Dr. Ames were already
there.

“Sir Guy,” said Poirot, “I have something to tell you. I know who
is responsible for the deaths of your father, Mr. Bleibner, Mr.
Schneider, and Mr. Harper.”

A dead silence followed his words. Every eye was fixed on him.

“It is not the Curse of King Men-her-Ra,” continued Poirot. “It is
something much more modern and much more deadly. It is the curse
of a man’s greed.”

He turned to Dr. Ames.

“Dr. Ames, you are a very clever man. But you have made one fatal
mistake.”

The doctor’s face turned a sickly grey.

“What do you mean?” he stammered.

“I mean that you murdered Sir John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, Mr.
Schneider, and Mr. Harper. And you were about to murder Sir Guy.”

“You are mad!” cried the doctor. “How could I have done such a
thing?”

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “You used your medical knowledge
to kill your victims in such a way that their deaths would appear
natural. You killed Sir John with an injection of digitalis, which
caused heart failure. You killed Mr. Bleibner by infecting a small
wound with virulent bacteria. You killed Mr. Schneider with an
injection of tetanus germs. and you killed Mr. Harper with another
injection of digitalis.”

“But why?” cried Sir Guy. “What possible motive could he have?”

“The motive was money,” said Poirot. “Dr. Ames was in financial
difficulties. He knew that Mr. Bleibner was a very wealthy man,
and he hoped to inherit some of his money. When he found that Mr.
Bleibner had no intention of leaving him anything, he decided to
get rid of him. But he had to make it look as though it were the
work of the Curse, so he started by killing Sir John Willard. Then
he killed Mr. Bleibner, and then Mr. Schneider, to keep up the
illusion. He killed Mr. Harper because he had begun to suspect the
truth. And he was going to kill you, Sir Guy, so that he could
marry your mother and inherit your father’s fortune.”

The doctor made a sudden movement, as if to escape, but I was too
quick for him. I seized him by the arms and held him fast.

“It’s no use, Ames,” I said. “The game is up.”

The doctor sank into a chair, his face buried in his hands. He knew
that he was caught.

“How did you find out?” he asked in a low voice.

“It was the letter from Rupert Bleibner,” said Poirot. “He called
himself a leper and an outcast. I realized that he was not referring
to himself, but to someone else. He had discovered the truth about
his uncle’s death, and he was trying to warn us. But he was too
afraid to speak out, so he took his own life. When I saw you
preparing the hypodermic syringe tonight, I knew that I was right.”

The doctor was led away, and Sir Guy and Dr. Tosswill were left
alone with us.

“I can’t believe it,” said Sir Guy. “Ames—of all people!”

“It is often the person we least suspect who is the guilty one,”
said Poirot. “But now the Curse of Men-her-Ra is at an end. You can
continue your work in peace.”

And so it was. The excavations were completed without further
mishap, and the treasures of the Tomb were safely removed to the
Museum.

As for Poirot, he returned to London, where he was hailed as a
hero. But he remained modest as ever.

“It was nothing,” he would say, with a wave of his hand. “A little
matter of the grey cells, that is all.”

But I knew better. I knew that it was his courage and his
determination that had saved us all from the Curse of the Tomb.

“Yes, quite. That was a clear case of blood-poisoning. A slight
scratch on the hand, which he neglected, and in twenty-four hours
he was dead. And Sir John Willard died of heart failure. He was
not a young man, and the heat and the hard work combined were
too much for him.”

“What about the nephew in New York?”

“That, of course, was a very different thing. It seems he was a
bit of a scamp, and had been in hot water before. It’s a very
curious thing, but I don’t see how we can possibly link it up
with the others.”

“And you, Sir Guy, what do you think of it all?”

“I don’t know what to think. I’m just trying to carry on, as my
father would have wished.”

“You are a brave man, Sir Guy,” said Poirot. “And now I should like
to see the native servant, Hassan.”

“Certainly. I will send for him.”

Hassan was a tall, dignified Arab with a face of bronze. He bowed
low as he entered the tent.

“You were with Sir John Willard at the time of his death?” asked
Poirot.

“I was, _effendi_.”

“And you were with him when he died?”

“Yes, _effendi_.”

“Did he say anything before he died?”

“He spoke only of the work, _effendi_. He was always thinking of
the work.”

“He did not seem—frightened?”

“Frightened? No, _effendi_.”

“He did not mention the Curse of the Tomb?”

“No, _effendi_.”

“Thank you, Hassan. You may go.”

When the servant had left the tent, Poirot turned to Sir Guy.

“And now, if you will be so good, I should like to see the Tomb
itself.”

“Certainly. It is only a few hundred yards from here.”

We all four set out together. The Tomb was situated in a small
rocky valley, and as we approached it I could not help feeling a
sense of awe. The entrance was guarded by two native soldiers.
We passed through a narrow passage into a large chamber. The walls
were covered with beautiful paintings and inscriptions. In the
centre of the room stood a large stone sarcophagus.

“This is where the body of King Men-her-Ra was found,” said Sir
Guy.

Poirot looked round him with interest.

“It is very beautiful,” he murmured. “And the inscriptions? What
do they say?”

“They are mostly prayers and incantations for the soul of the dead
King,” said Sir Guy. “But there is one inscription over the door
which is rather curious. It says: ‘The spirit of Men-her-Ra shall
watch over his resting-place, and woe unto those who disturb his
peace.’”

“Aha!” said Poirot. “The Curse of the Tomb! It is very interesting.”

He spent some time examining the inscriptions and the paintings,
and then we returned to the camp.

As we walked back, I noticed that Dr. Ames seemed to be watching
Poirot with a certain amount of suspicion. I wondered if he, too,
believed in the Curse.

That evening, as Poirot and I were sitting in our tent, he suddenly
said to me:

“Hastings, I have a feeling that we are on the track of something
very strange. Something very strange indeed.”

“You mean the Curse?” I asked.

“Perhaps. But there are other things as well. Other things that I
do not yet understand.”

He was silent for a few minutes, and then he said:

“I think I will go for a little walk. The night air will do me
good.”

“Shall I come with you?” I asked.

“No, thank you, Hastings. I would rather be alone.”

He went out, and I was left to my own reflections. I could not help
feeling a certain amount of uneasiness. The atmosphere of the camp
was thick with mystery and suspicion. And there was always the
Curse—the Curse of Men-her-Ra.

I must have fallen asleep, for the next thing I knew was that
Poirot was shaking me by the shoulder.

“Wake up, Hastings! Wake up!”

“What is it?” I asked, rubbing my eyes.

“There has been another death.”

“Another death?” I cried. “Who is it this time?”

“It is the American secretary, Mr. Harper.”

“Harper? But how? What happened?”

“He was found dead in his tent. It looks like heart failure.”

“Heart failure? Like Sir John Willard?”

“Yes. It is very strange. Very strange indeed.”

I got up and dressed hurriedly. When we reached Mr. Harper’s tent,
we found Sir Guy Willard, Dr. Tosswill, and Dr. Ames already there.

“This is terrible,” said Sir Guy. “Absolutely terrible. What can
it mean?”

“It means that the Curse is still at work,” said Dr. Tosswill
solemnly.

Dr. Ames was examining the body.

“It looks like heart failure, certainly,” he said. “But it’s very
sudden. He was perfectly well last night.”

“He was a very nervous young man,” said Sir Guy. “The strain of the
last few weeks must have been too much for him.”

Poirot was looking round the tent. He seemed to be searching for
something. Suddenly he stooped and picked up a small piece of
paper from the floor. He looked at it for a moment and then put it
in his pocket.

“What is it, Poirot?” I asked.

“Nothing, Hastings. Nothing of importance.”

But I could see by the expression on his face that he was not
telling the truth.

We left the tent and went back to our own. Poirot was very silent.
He seemed to be deep in thought.

“What do you think of it, Poirot?” I asked at last.

“I think, Hastings, that we are dealing with a very clever and
very dangerous person.”

“A person? Then you don’t believe in the Curse?”

“The Curse is a very convenient thing, Hastings. It covers a
multitude of sins.”

“But who could it be? And why?”

“That is what we have to find out. But I think I have a clue.”

“A clue? What is it?”

“The piece of paper I found in Mr. Harper’s tent.”

“What was on it?”

“It was a small piece of paper with some figures on it. I think
they are coordinates.”

“Coordinates? You mean for a map?”

“Yes. I think so.”

“But what does that mean?”

“It means, Hastings, that Mr. Harper was interested in something
else besides Egyptology. Something that he was perhaps trying to
keep secret.”

“And you think that’s why he was killed?”

“It is a possibility.”

He was silent again for a few minutes, and then he said:

“I think I will go and see Dr. Tosswill. I want to ask him some
questions about Mr. Harper.”

He went out, and I was left alone once more. I could not help
feeling that we were getting closer to the truth. But at the same
time, I felt a sense of dread. Whoever was behind these deaths was
not going to stop at anything.

When Poirot returned, he looked even more serious than before.
