“I have spoken to Dr. Tosswill,” he said. “He tells me that Mr.
Harper was a very quiet and unassuming young man. He had been with
Mr. Bleibner for about a year. He seemed to be very interested in
his work, but he never talked much about himself.”

“And the coordinates?” I asked.

“Dr. Tosswill knows nothing about them. He says that Mr. Harper
never mentioned anything of the sort.”

“So what do we do now?”

“We wait, Hastings. We wait and see what happens next.”

But we did not have to wait long. That afternoon, as we were
sitting in our tent, we heard a loud cry from the direction of the
Tomb. We rushed out and saw Hassan running towards us.

“Effendi! Effendi!” he cried. “The Tomb! Something has happened in
the Tomb!”

We followed him to the Tomb. When we got there, we found Sir Guy
Willard and Dr. Ames standing at the entrance. They looked white
and shaken.

“What is it?” I asked. “What has happened?”

“It’s the sarcophagus,” said Sir Guy. “It’s been opened.”

“Opened?” I cried. “But how? It was guarded.”

“The guards were drugged,” said Dr. Ames. “They’re still unconscious.”

We went into the Tomb. The stone lid of the sarcophagus had been
pushed aside. Inside, the mummy of King Men-her-Ra lay undisturbed.
But there was something else in the sarcophagus. Something that
had not been there before.

It was a small, black box.

Poirot stepped forward and picked it up. He opened it carefully.
Inside was a set of maps and some documents.

“What are they?” I asked.

“I think, Hastings, that they are the maps and documents that Mr.
Harper was looking for.”

“But what do they mean?”

“They mean, Hastings, that there is more to this Tomb than we
thought. Much more.”

He turned to Sir Guy.

“Sir Guy, I think it would be wise if we all went back to the camp.
I have something to say to you all.”

We went back to the camp and gathered in the large tent. Poirot
stood in the centre of the room, looking at us all in turn.

“Messieurs,” he said. “I have a very serious announcement to make.
I have discovered the truth about the deaths that have occurred
here.”

There was a sudden silence. We all looked at him, waiting for him
to continue.

“The deaths were not due to a Curse,” he said. “They were the work
of a human hand.”

“A human hand?” cried Sir Guy. “But who? And why?”

“The motive was greed,” said Poirot. “Greed for the treasures that
lie hidden in this Tomb. But not the treasures of King Men-her-Ra.
Something much more valuable.”

“What do you mean?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“I mean, monsieur, that there is oil in this desert. A vast amount
of oil. And the coordinates on the piece of paper I found in Mr.
Harper’s tent show exactly where it is.”

“Oil?” I cried. “But what has that to do with the deaths?”

“Everything, Hastings. Mr. Bleibner had discovered the oil, and
he was planning to exploit it. But he needed money. So he
persuaded Sir John Willard to join him in his excavations. Sir John
thought they were looking for the Tomb of King Men-her-Ra, but Mr.
Bleibner was really looking for the oil.”

“But why were they killed?” asked Sir Guy.

“They were killed because they knew too much. Or because they were
in the way. Mr. Bleibner was killed by someone who wanted the oil
for himself. And Sir John Willard was killed because he was
beginning to suspect the truth.”

“And Mr. Harper?” I asked.

“Mr. Harper was killed because he had found the maps and documents.
He was going to use them to blackmail the killer.”

“But who is the killer?” asked Dr. Ames.

Poirot looked at him steadily.

“The killer, monsieur, is you.”

Dr. Ames started back, his face pale with shock.

“Me? You’re crazy! Why should I kill them?”

“Because you wanted the oil for yourself,” said Poirot. “You knew
that Mr. Bleibner had found it, and you were determined to get
your hands on it. You killed Mr. Bleibner by infecting him with
blood-poisoning. You killed Sir John Willard by giving him a
fatal dose of digitalis. And you killed Mr. Harper because he
knew too much.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Dr. Ames. “You have no proof!”

“I have more proof than you think, monsieur,” said Poirot. “I have
the piece of paper with the coordinates. I have the maps and
documents from the sarcophagus. And I have the testimony of
Hassan, who saw you entering Mr. Harper’s tent last night.”

Hassan stepped forward and nodded his head.

“It is true, _effendi_. I saw the doctor entering the tent of the
young American.”

Dr. Ames looked round him wildly. He saw the grim faces of the
others, and he knew that he was trapped.

“All right,” he said, his voice shaking with rage. “I did it. I
killed them all. And I’d do it again! That oil is worth millions!
Millions, do you hear?”

He made a sudden dash for the door of the tent, but he was seized
by the native soldiers and led away.

There was a long silence after he had gone. Then Sir Guy spoke.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, you have certainly done us a great service.
I don’t know how to thank you.”

“There is no need to thank me, Sir Guy,” said Poirot. “I was only
doing my duty.”

He turned to me.

“And now, Hastings, I think it is time we left this place. This
sand, it is not good for my boots.”

I smiled. Even in the midst of tragedy, Poirot could still think
of his boots.

As we rode away from the camp, I looked back at the Pyramids,
standing silent and mysterious in the desert sun. I thought of the
men who had died, and of the greed that had led to their deaths.
And I thought of Poirot, the little man with the big brain, who
had seen through the mystery and brought the killer to justice.

It was a strange adventure, and one that I shall never forget. But
as I looked at Poirot, sitting primly on his donkey, I knew that
as long as he was with me, there was nothing to fear. Not even the
Curse of Men-her-Ra.

“Absolutely. It was a clear case of blood poisoning. He had a slight
scratch on his thumb, it became septic, and he died of general
septicaemia.”

“Then you don’t think that the Curse of Men-her-Ra had anything to
do with it?”

Dr. Ames shrugged his shoulders.

“Oh, well, as to that——”

“You are not a believer?”

“I’m a doctor, Monsieur Poirot. I don’t believe in anything that
isn’t physiological. But I must admit that the things which have
been happening lately have been rather uncanny.”

“Indeed they have!” cried Willard. “What did the newspapers say?
Three deaths? No, four. My father, then Mr. Bleibner, then his
nephew, and now Schneider. Four deaths—all in the space of a
month!”

“You are forgetting the cat,” said a voice from outside.

The flap of the tent was lifted and a tall, dark man entered. He
was dressed in native costume, and his face was impassive. This,
then, was Hassan, the late Sir John Willard’s servant.

He stood for a moment, his eyes travelling from one to the other
of us. Then he spoke again.

“The cat of the King. It was seen last night. It was seen by me.”

“The cat?” I cried. “What cat?”

“The sacred cat of the temple. It has come to guard its master’s
tomb. It is a sign. Death to the desecrators!”

He turned and went out.

“He is a strange fellow,” said Dr. Tosswill, who had followed him
into the tent. “He is a mystic and a dreamer. He sees things.”

“And what is it he saw?” I asked.

“He saw a cat. A black cat with golden eyes. It is the sacred cat
of the Pharaohs.”

“Rubbish!” said Dr. Ames. “I don’t believe in any such nonsense.”

“Wait,” said Poirot. “Wait and see. It may be that the cat of the
King will have more to say to us before we have finished.”

I felt a cold chill run down my spine. The atmosphere of the camp
was getting on my nerves. I could see that even Poirot was affected
by it. He seemed to be constantly on the alert, as though he
expected something to happen.

The next few days passed quietly enough. We spent our time in
examining the excavations and in talk with the various members of
the party.

Dr. Tosswill was a mine of information. He showed us the various
finds that had been made, and explained their significance. He was
evidently a very learned man, and his enthusiasm for his work was
infectious.

Mr. Harper, the secretary, was also very helpful. He was a bright,
intelligent young man, and he seemed to have a great deal of
knowledge about the excavations.

But it was Dr. Ames who interested me most. He was a man of great
character and intelligence, and he seemed to have a very clear
understanding of the situation. He was not a man to be easily
frightened, and he seemed to be determined to see the thing
through.

One evening, as we were sitting in the tent, Poirot suddenly spoke.

“I have been thinking,” he said. “What is it that we are looking
for? Is it a murderer, or is it a curse?”

“A murderer, of course!” I cried.

“But who could it be?” asked Dr. Ames. “We have all been together
the whole time. There has been no opportunity for anyone to commit
a murder.”

“That is true,” said Poirot. “But there is one person who has not
been with us the whole time.”

“Who is that?” asked Sir Guy.

“Hassan,” said Poirot.

“Hassan!” I cried. “But he is a devoted servant. He would never do
anything to harm Sir John or his family.”

“He is a mystic,” said Poirot. “And mystics are sometimes capable of
very strange things.”

I looked at Hassan, who was standing in the doorway of the tent.
He seemed to be listening to our conversation. His face was
impassive, but I thought I saw a strange light in his eyes.

“Do you think it could be Hassan?” I asked Poirot later, when we
were alone.

“I do not know, Hastings. But we must be careful. We must be very
careful.”

The next morning, we were all shocked to find that Sir Guy Willard
had disappeared. He had not been seen since the previous evening,
and no one knew where he had gone.

We searched the camp and the surrounding desert, but there was no
sign of him.

“He must have been kidnapped!” I cried.

“Or worse,” said Poirot.

We were all very worried. Sir Guy was a young man, and he was not
very experienced in the ways of the desert.

Then, just as we were beginning to lose hope, we saw a figure in
the distance. It was Sir Guy. He was walking towards us, and he
looked very exhausted.

“Where have you been?” I cried, as he reached us.

“I don’t know,” he said. “I was walking in the desert, and then I
suddenly found myself in a strange place. I don’t know how I got
there.”

He seemed to be in a state of shock. We took him back to the camp
and gave him something to eat and drink.

“What happened?” asked Poirot.

“I don’t know,” said Sir Guy. “I was just walking, and then I
suddenly felt a strange sensation. It was as though I were being
drawn towards something. And then I found myself in this strange
place. It was like a tomb, but it was different from any of the
other tombs we have found.”

“A tomb?” said Poirot. “What kind of a tomb?”

“It was very large,” said Sir Guy. “And it was filled with strange
and beautiful things. There were statues and paintings, and there
was a large sarcophagus in the middle of the room.”

“And did you see anything else?” asked Poirot.

“Yes,” said Sir Guy. “I saw a cat. A black cat with golden eyes.
It was sitting on the sarcophagus, and it was looking at me.”

“The cat of the King!” I cried.

“Yes,” said Sir Guy. “I think it was.”

We were all very silent. The story seemed almost too strange to be
true. But Sir Guy was obviously telling the truth.

“What do you think it means, Poirot?” I asked.

“I do not know, Hastings. But I think we are nearing the end of our
investigation.”

The next day, we were all surprised to see a stranger arrive at the
camp. He was a tall, thin man with a very pale face.

“Who is that?” I asked Poirot.

“That,” said Poirot, “is Dr. Tosswill’s assistant.”

“I didn’t know he had an assistant,” I said.

“Neither did I,” said Poirot.

The stranger went straight to Dr. Tosswill’s tent and was seen
talking to him for some time.

Later that evening, Poirot and I were sitting in our tent when
there was a knock at the door. It was Dr. Tosswill.

“I have something to tell you,” he said. “My assistant has just
arrived from London. He has some very important information for
us.”

“What is it?” asked Poirot.

“He has found out that Mr. Bleibner’s nephew did not commit
suicide,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“Not commit suicide?” I cried. “But what happened then?”

“He was murdered,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“Murdered!” I cried. “But by whom?”

“That,” said Dr. Tosswill, “is what we have to find out.”

We were all very shocked. The news of the murder of Mr. Bleibner’s
nephew seemed to change everything.

“But why would anyone want to murder him?” I asked.

“Perhaps he knew something,” said Poirot. “Something that someone
didn’t want him to know.”

“But what could it be?” I asked.

“I do not know, Hastings. But I think we are about to find out.”

The next morning, we were all called to the main tent. Dr. Tosswill
was there, along with Sir Guy, Dr. Ames, Mr. Harper and Hassan.

“I have some very important news for you,” said Dr. Tosswill. “My
assistant has found out who murdered Mr. Bleibner’s nephew.”

“Who was it?” asked Sir Guy.

“It was Mr. Harper,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“Mr. Harper!” I cried. “But why?”

“Because he was in love with Mr. Bleibner’s niece,” said Dr. Tosswill.
“And he wanted to get her uncle’s money.”

“But how did he do it?” asked Sir Guy.

“He used a very clever method,” said Dr. Tosswill. “He poisoned him
with a rare Egyptian poison.”

“A poison?” I cried. “But how did he get it?”

“He got it from the tomb,” said Dr. Tosswill.

We were all very shocked. The news of Mr. Harper’s crime seemed
almost too much to bear.

“But what about the other deaths?” asked Sir Guy. “What about my
father and Mr. Bleibner and Mr. Schneider?”

“Those,” said Dr. Tosswill, “were all accidents.”

“Accidents?” I cried. “But how could they be accidents?”

“Sir John Willard died of heart failure,” said Dr. Tosswill. “Mr.
Bleibner died of blood poisoning. And Mr. Schneider died of
tetanus. They were all very unfortunate accidents.”

“But what about the cat?” asked Sir Guy. “What about the cat of
the King?”

“That,” said Dr. Tosswill, “was just a figment of your imagination.”

“A figment of my imagination?” cried Sir Guy. “But I saw it! I saw
it with my own eyes!”

“You were in a state of shock,” said Dr. Tosswill. “Your mind was
playing tricks on you.”

Sir Guy looked very disappointed. He had really believed in the
cat of the King.

“So it was all just a series of coincidences?” I asked Poirot,
when we were alone.

“Perhaps, Hastings. Perhaps.”

“But what about Mr. Harper?” I asked. “Is he really the murderer?”

“I do not know, Hastings. But I think we should talk to him.”

We went to Mr. Harper’s tent, but it was empty. He had disappeared.

“He must have fled!” I cried.

“Or been murdered,” said Poirot.

We searched the camp, but there was no sign of him.

“This is getting very strange,” I said.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “Very strange indeed.”

The next morning, we were all shocked to find that Dr. Ames had
been murdered. He had been stabbed to death in his tent.

“Another murder!” I cried. “This is getting out of hand!”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is.”

We searched the camp again, but there was no sign of the murderer.

“Who could it be?” I asked.

“I do not know, Hastings. But I think I have an idea.”

Poirot led me to Hassan’s tent. We entered and found Hassan
sitting on the floor, his eyes closed.

“Hassan,” said Poirot. “We know what you have done.”

Hassan opened his eyes and looked at us. His face was impassive.

“What have I done?” he asked.

“You have murdered Dr. Ames,” said Poirot.

“I have not murdered anyone,” said Hassan.

“But we found your knife in his tent,” said Poirot.

“It was not my knife,” said Hassan.

“Then whose was it?” asked Poirot.

“It belonged to the King,” said Hassan.

“The King?” I cried. “What King?”

“King Men-her-Ra,” said Hassan.

“This is nonsense!” I cried.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Let us see.”

He took out a small piece of paper from his pocket.

“This,” he said, “is a letter that I found in Dr. Ames’s tent. It
is written in a very strange language.”

“What does it say?” I asked.

“It says that the King is angry,” said Poirot. “And that he will
not rest until his tomb has been closed.”

“This is unbelievable!” I cried.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is.”

We were all very silent. The story seemed to be getting stranger
and stranger.

“But what about Mr. Harper?” I asked. “What happened to him?”

“I think I know,” said Poirot.

He led us to the tomb of King Men-her-Ra. We entered and found
Mr. Harper’s body lying on the floor. He had been strangled.

“Another murder!” I cried.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is the work of the King.”

“The King?” I cried. “But how could a dead King commit murder?”

“He did not commit murder,” said Poirot. “He used a human agent.”

“A human agent?” I cried. “Who?”

“Dr. Tosswill,” said Poirot.

“Dr. Tosswill!” I cried. “But why?”

“Because he was obsessed with the King,” said Poirot. “He believed
that he was the reincarnation of the King, and he wanted to protect
his tomb.”

“But how did he do it?” I asked.

“He used a very clever method,” said Poirot. “He used the sacred
cat of the King to commit the murders.”

“The cat?” I cried. “But how could a cat commit murder?”

“It was not a real cat,” said Poirot. “It was a mechanical cat,
which Dr. Tosswill had designed himself.”

“A mechanical cat!” I cried. “This is unbelievable!”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “It is.”

We were all very shocked. The news of Dr. Tosswill’s crime seemed
almost too much to bear.

“But what will happen to him?” I asked.

“He will be brought to justice,” said Poirot.

And so, the mystery of the Tomb of King Men-her-Ra was finally
solved. Dr. Tosswill was arrested and brought to trial, and he was
sentenced to life imprisonment.

As for Poirot and me, we returned to London, where we were greeted
as heroes. Our investigation had been a great success, and we were
hailed as the greatest detectives of our time.

But even now, when I think back on that strange and terrible time,
I cannot help but feel a sense of unease. For I know that there are
some things in this world that are beyond our understanding, and
that the power of the past is a force to be reckoned with.

“Quite. Mr. Bleibner died of blood-poisoning. A small scratch on
the thumb, he was a very negligent man, and didn’t take the proper
precautions.”

“A small scratch on the thumb? From what, Monsieur le Docteur?”

“It was said to be from a jagged piece of the sarcophagus itself,”
replied the doctor. “But one cannot be certain.”

“And Sir John Willard?”

“Heart failure, Monsieur Poirot. He had been ailing for some time.”

“He had never complained of his heart before, had he?”

“Not that I’m aware of. But he was over sixty, and the climate here
is trying.”

“I see.” Poirot’s eyes strayed over the tent. “And Hassan?”

“Oh, Hassan is the late Sir John’s native servant. A very faithful
soul. He is quite convinced that his master was killed by the
curse.”

“And you, Sir Guy?”

The young man laughed nervously.

“I? Oh, I don’t know. I’m beginning to believe in it myself.”

“And you, Monsieur le Docteur?”

Dr. Ames shrugged his shoulders.

“It’s a queer business, I’ll grant you that. But as for curses,
well, that’s not in my line.”

“And Mr. Harper?”

“He’s the only one of us who seems to have any sense,” said the
doctor. “He doesn’t believe in anything but his typewriter.”

“And Dr. Tosswill?”

“Oh, Tosswill’s a dry-as-dust old stick. He lives for his work.
I don’t believe he’d notice if the Sphinx itself came to life and
spat at him.”

“_Bien_,” said Poirot. “I think I have the hang of things now. If
you will allow me, I should like to look round a little.”

“By all means. Dr. Ames will show you everything there is to see.”

We went out with the doctor. The excavations were on a large scale.
A number of native labourers were at work, and we were shown the
various chambers that had been opened.

“It’s a wonderful piece of work,” I said.

“It is,” agreed the doctor. “A pity it should have such a sinister
reputation.”

“You don’t believe in that yourself?”

“I don’t say that. But there are more things in heaven and earth,
you know, than are dreamt of in our philosophy.”

He spoke with a certain amount of gravity.

“Is there any one else in the camp besides those I have seen?”
asked Poirot.

“No, that’s the lot. Oh, there’s a young fellow called O’Connor,
an assistant of Tosswill’s, but he’s away in Cairo just now.
Otherwise you’ve seen the whole party.”

“And Hassan?”

“Oh, yes, I forgot Hassan.”

As he spoke, a tall, thin man in native dress approached us. He
had a dark, inscrutable face, and he moved with a curious, silent
tread.

“That is Hassan,” said the doctor.

The man bowed low to Poirot.

“You are the great detective from England?” he said in excellent
English. “My master told me of you. He said that if anything
happened to him, I was to go to you.”

“Your master? You mean Sir John Willard?”

“No, monsieur. Mr. Bleibner. He was a very good master to me.”

“Mr. Bleibner? But I thought you were Sir John Willard’s servant?”

“I was, monsieur. But when Sir John died, Mr. Bleibner took me into
his service.”

“I see.” Poirot’s eyes were fixed on the man’s face. “And what did
Mr. Bleibner tell you?”

“He said: ‘Hassan, if anything happens to me, go to the great
detective, Monsieur Poirot. Tell him that I was afraid.’”

“Afraid? Of what?”

“Of the curse, monsieur. The curse of Men-her-Ra.”

The man bowed again and withdrew.

“A strange fellow,” I remarked.

“Yes,” said the doctor. “They’re all more or less like that.
Superstitious to the core.”

“And you, Monsieur le Docteur? You are not superstitious?”

Dr. Ames laughed.

“I’ve seen too much of life and death for that, Monsieur Poirot.
To me, death is just a biological fact.”

“And yet,” said Poirot softly, “it is a fact that has been occurring
with some frequency lately.”

The doctor did not reply. He led us back to the tent where we had
left Sir Guy Willard.

“If there is nothing more I can do for you?”

“Nothing, thank you, Dr. Ames.”

The doctor nodded and walked away.

“Well, Poirot?” I asked, when we were alone. “What do you think of
it all?”

Poirot was silent for a moment. Then he said:

“I think, Hastings, that we are in the presence of a very clever
and a very cold-blooded murderer.”

“A murderer? But who?”

“That is what we have to find out.”

“But the curse?”

“The curse, _mon ami_, is a very convenient thing. It covers a
multitude of sins.”

“But how could any one have managed it? Sir John Willard died of
heart failure, Mr. Bleibner of blood-poisoning, and Mr. Schneider
of tetanus. You can’t commit murder by heart failure or tetanus.”

“Can you not?” Poirot’s eyes were dark and mysterious. “You would
be surprised, Hastings, at what can be done by a man who has
knowledge and—opportunity.”

“But who is the man?”

“Ah, that is the question. We have four suspects, Hastings. Dr.
Tosswill, Dr. Ames, Mr. Harper and Hassan. One of those four is a
murderer.”

“But what could be the motive?”

“That also we have to find out. But I think, Hastings, that we
shall not have to wait very long. The murderer is not yet satisfied.
He has still more work to do.”

“You mean—Sir Guy Willard?”

“Exactly. Sir Guy Willard is the next on the list.”

“But why? What has he done?”

“He is the owner of the Willard fortune, Hastings. And he is the
son of the man who discovered the Tomb of Men-her-Ra. In the eyes
of the murderer, that is quite enough.”

“But who would benefit by his death?”

“That is what we have to find out. And now, Hastings, if you will
be so good, I should like to have a little talk with Mr. Harper.”

“The secretary?”

“Exactly. The pleasant young man with the horn-rimmed spectacles.”

We found Mr. Harper in a small tent, busily engaged with his
typewriter. He looked up as we entered.

“Oh, hello, Monsieur Poirot. Anything I can do for you?”

“I should like to ask you a few questions, Mr. Harper, if you don’t
mind.”

“Not at all. Fire away.”

“You were with Mr. Bleibner for some time, I believe?”

“About six months. I went to him just before he started for Egypt.”

“And you liked him?”

“Oh, he was all right. A bit eccentric, you know, but a good sort
on the whole.”

“Did he ever speak to you about his nephew?”

“Rupert? Oh, yes, often. He was very fond of him, really, though
he used to pretend he wasn’t. He was always bailing him out of
some scrape or other.”

“So they were on good terms?”

“Oh, yes. Rupert was a bit of a scallywag, but he was a likeable
chap. Mr. Bleibner was very cut up when he heard of his death.”

“He heard of it before he died himself?”

“Oh, yes. The news came about a week before Mr. Bleibner’s own
death.”

“I see.” Poirot was silent for a moment. “And what about Sir John
Willard? Did Mr. Bleibner get on well with him?”

“Not particularly. They were always having rows about the
excavations. Sir John was a bit of a martinet, and Mr. Bleibner
was—well, he liked to have his own way.”

“And Dr. Tosswill?”

“Oh, Tosswill’s all right. He’s a bit of a dry stick, as the doctor
says, but he knows his job.”

“And Dr. Ames?”

“Ames is a top-hole chap. We’re all very fond of him.”

“And Hassan?”

“Hassan? Oh, he’s just a native. He’s a good servant, I believe.”

“Thank you, Mr. Harper.”

As we went out, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you make of Mr. Harper?”

“He seems a very pleasant young man,” I said.

“Yes,” agreed Poirot. “Very pleasant. And very observant. Did you
notice his eyes, Hastings? They are very quick, those eyes behind
the horn-rimmed spectacles.”

“You don’t think——?”

“I think nothing as yet. But I should like to have a look at Mr.
Bleibner’s will.”

“His will?”

“Exactly. It might be interesting to know who inherits his money.”

“But he had no relations, except his nephew, and he’s dead.”

“Precisely. That is why it might be interesting.”

We spent the rest of the day wandering about the camp and talking
to the various members of the party. Poirot seemed particularly
interested in the medical arrangements. He questioned Dr. Ames
closely about the anti-serum he had used for Mr. Schneider.

“You say you got it from Cairo?”

“Yes. It was sent out by special messenger.”

“And you are sure it was all right?”

“Of course it was all right. Why shouldn’t it be?”

“I was only wondering,” said Poirot mildly.

That evening, as we were sitting in our tent, there was a sudden
commotion outside. We rushed out to find a crowd of native labourers
gathered round one of the tents. In the centre of the group was
Sir Guy Willard, looking very pale and shaken.

“What’s the matter?” I cried.

“It’s the curse!” cried one of the natives. “The curse of
Men-her-Ra!”

“Nonsense!” said Dr. Tosswill sternly. “What has happened, Sir
Guy?”

“I—I don’t know,” stammered the young man. “I was sitting in my
tent, when suddenly I felt a sharp prick in my arm. I looked round,
but there was no one there.”

“A sharp prick?” said Dr. Ames, stepping forward. “Let me see.”

He took Sir Guy’s arm and examined it closely.

“There’s a small puncture here,” he said. “It looks like a needle
prick.”

“A needle prick?” said Poirot. “That is very strange.”

“It’s the curse!” cried the native again. “The spirit of the dead
King has struck!”

“Be quiet!” snapped Dr. Tosswill. “Dr. Ames, what do you make of
it?”

“I don’t know,” said the doctor slowly. “It may be nothing. Or it
may be—something very serious.”

“You mean—tetanus?” I whispered.

“It’s possible,” said the doctor. “We must take every precaution.
I’ll give him an injection of anti-serum at once.”

“But you have none,” I reminded him.

“I have a small supply which I kept in case of emergency,” said the
doctor.

He went to his tent and returned a few minutes later with a
hypodermic syringe.

“Now, Sir Guy,” he said. “If you’ll just hold out your arm.”

Sir Guy obeyed, and the doctor skillfully injected the serum.

“There,” he said. “That should make you safe. But you’d better go
to bed and stay there for the present.”

Sir Guy nodded and went into his tent, followed by Dr. Ames.

“Well, Poirot?” I said, when they had gone. “What do you think of
that?”

“I think, Hastings,” said Poirot, “that the murderer has struck
again. But this time, I think he has made a mistake.”

“A mistake? What do you mean?”

“I mean, Hastings, that he has given me the very clue I was looking
for.”

“What clue?”

“The clue of the hypodermic syringe.”

“But Dr. Ames used a hypodermic syringe to give the injection.”

“Exactly, Hastings. Exactly.”

“But surely you don’t think——?”

“I think many things, Hastings. But for the moment, I will say
nothing. I have a little experiment to make.”

“An experiment?”

“Yes. A very simple experiment. If you will come with me to the
tomb, I will show you.”

We walked across the sand to the entrance of the tomb. Poirot
produced a small electric torch and led the way down the narrow
passage. We came at last to the central chamber, where the great
sarcophagus of Men-her-Ra stood.

“Now, Hastings,” said Poirot. “I want you to help me. I am going
to move the lid of the sarcophagus.”

“Move the lid? But it’s tremendously heavy!”

“With your help, I think we can do it. It is already partially
opened, you see.”

We put our shoulders to the heavy stone lid and, after a great
effort, succeeded in moving it a few inches.

“That will do,” said Poirot. “Now, look inside.”

I peered into the dark depths of the sarcophagus. At first I could
see nothing, but as Poirot moved his torch, I saw something lying
at the bottom.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a small glass phial,” said Poirot. “And if I am not mistaken,
it contains the remains of a very powerful poison.”

“Poison? But how did it get there?”

“It was placed there by the murderer, Hastings. To give color to the
story of the curse. You see, the person who was intended to find
it was Mr. Bleibner. And he did find it—to his cost.”

“But what about Sir John Willard? And Mr. Schneider?”

“Sir John Willard died of heart failure, Hastings. A very
convenient death for a murderer. And Mr. Schneider died of
tetanus—or what appeared to be tetanus.”

“But the anti-serum?”

“The anti-serum, Hastings, was also poisoned.”

“But who could have done such a thing?”

“There is only one person who could have done it, Hastings. One
person who had the knowledge and the opportunity.”

“Who?”

“Dr. Ames.”

“Dr. Ames? But he’s a doctor! Why should he want to kill these
people?”

“Because, Hastings, he is a very ambitious man. And he is also a
very poor man. He wanted money, and he saw a way to get it.”

“But how? He doesn’t inherit anything from Mr. Bleibner or Sir John
Willard.”

“No, but he expected to inherit from Rupert Bleibner.”

“Rupert Bleibner? But he’s dead!”

“Exactly, Hastings. He is dead. And he died in very mysterious
circumstances. Do you remember the letter he left behind? The one
in which he called himself a leper and an outcast?”

“Yes.”

“Well, Hastings, I have been thinking about that letter. And I
think I know what it means. Rupert Bleibner was not a leper in the
physical sense. He was a leper in the moral sense. He had
committed a crime—a terrible crime.”

“What crime?”

“The crime of murder, Hastings. He had murdered his uncle, Mr.
Bleibner.”

“But Mr. Bleibner died in Egypt!”

“Exactly. And Rupert Bleibner was in Egypt at the time. He had
come there to borrow money from his uncle, but his uncle had
refused him. So he decided to kill him.”

“But how?”

“By means of the poison in the phial. He placed it in the
sarcophagus, knowing that his uncle would be the first to handle
it. And his plan worked. Mr. Bleibner died of blood-poisoning.”

“But what has that to do with Dr. Ames?”

“Everything, Hastings. You see, Dr. Ames knew what Rupert had
done. He had seen him place the phial in the sarcophagus. And he
used that knowledge to blackmail the young man.”

“Blackmail?”

“Exactly. He forced Rupert to make a will in his favour, leaving
him everything he possessed. And then, he killed him.”

“Killed him? But Rupert committed suicide in New York!”

“So it appeared, Hastings. But I think, if we were to investigate,
we should find that Dr. Ames was in New York at the time. He had
followed the young man there, and he had used his medical knowledge
to make the death look like suicide.”

“But what about the others? Sir John Willard and Mr. Schneider?”

“They were killed because they were in the way, Hastings. Dr. Ames
wanted the excavations to stop, so that he could get away with his
ill-gotten gains. He used the story of the curse to frighten people
away, and when that didn't work, he resorted to murder.”

“But Sir Guy Willard? Why did he try to kill him?”

“Because, Hastings, Sir Guy was becoming suspicious. He was
beginning to realize that there was something wrong. So Dr. Ames
decided to remove him. He used the needle prick to frighten him,
and then he gave him the poisoned anti-serum.”

“But you stopped him!”

“Yes, Hastings. I stopped him. I had already suspected him, and
when I saw him with the hypodermic syringe, I knew I was right.”

“But how did you know the anti-serum was poisoned?”

“I didn’t, Hastings. But I took the precaution of changing the
syringes while the doctor was in his tent. The injection he gave
Sir Guy was perfectly harmless.”

“And what about the doctor?”

“He is now in the hands of the authorities, Hastings. I had him
arrested as soon as we left the tent.”

“Well, Poirot,” I said. “You have certainly excelled yourself this
time.”

“It was a simple case, Hastings,” said Poirot modestly. “A very
simple case. But it just goes to show that you should never
underrate the force of superstition—especially when it is used as
a cloak for murder.”

We walked back to the camp in silence. The moon was rising over the
desert, and the Pyramids stood out like giant ghosts against the
sky. I felt a sudden shiver of dread. The curse of Men-her-Ra might
be a myth, but the evil that men do is very real.

“Positive. It was a clear case of blood poisoning. He was a man
of over seventy and his constitution was not as robust as it might
have been. Sir John Willard’s death followed on an attack of
fever. Of course his heart was not strong, but it was not tetanus.”

“So we have three deaths in three weeks—and each of a different
kind. That is remarkably interesting.”

“It’s more than interesting,” said Sir Guy. “It’s getting on my
nerves.”

Poirot’s eyes wandered to where a tall, dark-skinned man in white
robes stood like a statue at the entrance of the tent.

“Is that the servant Hassan?” he asked.

“Yes, he was my father’s devoted servant. He has been with him for
over twenty years.”

“And he is a believer in the Curse?”

“Absolutely. He spends half his time in prayer and the other half
in some secret ritual of his own. If you want any information
about the superstitions of the country, he’s your man.”

Poirot made a sign to the man to come forward. Hassan did so with
a grave dignity. He spoke English fairly well.

“The spirit of the Great King is angry,” he said. “He will not
allow his rest to be disturbed. Death will come to all who enter
the sacred portals.”

“And you, Hassan?” asked Poirot. “Are you not afraid?”

“I am but a servant, and I do not enter the inner chamber. Also I
have a charm.”

He drew a small amulet from his breast and showed it to us. It was
a curious thing, of green basalt, representing a heart.

“Very interesting,” said Poirot. “And the others, have they no
charms?”

Hassan shook his head.

“The white men believe not in these things. They are fools, and
they will die.”

He withdrew as silently as he had come.

“Absolutely plumb certain. He had a scratch upon his thumb which
became poisoned, and septicæmia set in. It sounds pretty much the
same to a layman, I dare say, but the two things are entirely
different.”

“Then we have four deaths—all totally dissimilar, one heart failure,
one blood poisoning, one suicide and one tetanus.”

“Exactly, Monsieur Poirot.”

“Are you certain that there is nothing which might link the four
together?”

“I don’t quite understand you?”

“I will put it plainly. Was any act committed by those four men
which might seem to denote disrespect to the spirit of Men-her-Ra?”

The doctor gazed at Poirot in astonishment.

“You’re talking through your hat, Monsieur Poirot. Surely you’ve
not been guyed into believing all that fool talk?”

“Absolute nonsense,” muttered Willard angrily.

Poirot remained placidly immovable, blinking a little out of his
green cat’s eyes.

“So you do not believe it, _monsieur le docteur_?”

“No, sir, I do not,” declared the doctor emphatically. “I am a
scientific man, and I believe only what science teaches.”

“Then why is it that you think Mr. Schneider’s death was tetanus?”

“Because the symptoms were identical. No one could have mistaken
it for anything else.”

“I see. And you, Sir Guy?”

“I? Oh, I think it’s just one of those rotten bits of luck that
will happen. We’ve been unlucky, that’s all.”

“Wait, Sir Guy, what are you doing with that small box?”

The young man was playing with a small lacquer box, which was
lying on the table. He turned it over and over.

“It’s nothing. Only a curio I picked up.”

“I see.”

Poirot’s eyes wandered to the corner of the tent where a native
servant was standing with a tray of cups and saucers. He was a
tall, well-built man, with a very dark face and a dignified
bearing.

“Is that Hassan?” he asked.

“Yes, Monsieur Poirot.”

Poirot called the man to him.

“You were with Sir John Willard at the time of his death?”

“I was, monsieur.”

“Tell me, what did you see?”

The man’s face was impassive.

“I saw nothing, monsieur. Sir John was sitting in his tent. He
complained of a sudden pain in his chest. I went for the doctor,
but when I came back he was dead.”

“And you saw no—no one?”

“No one, monsieur.”

The man’s tone was perfectly respectful, but I felt that he was
lying. He seemed to me to be concealing something.

“And you were also present when Mr. Bleibner died?”

“Yes, monsieur. He was very ill for many days. The doctor did all
he could, but it was in vain.”

Poirot dismissed the man with a wave of his hand.

“Well, Sir Guy, I will not keep you any longer. I should like to
have a talk with Dr. Tosswill, if I may.”

“Certainly. You will find him in his own tent.”

We found Dr. Tosswill in a small tent nearby. He was busy cleaning
some small objects of pottery. He looked up as we entered.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot? Have you discovered anything yet?”

“Not yet, Dr. Tosswill. I am still at the stage of collecting
information.”

“I see. Well, if there’s anything I can tell you, I shall be only
too glad.”

“What was your opinion of Mr. Schneider’s death?”

The doctor’s face clouded.

“It was a very tragic affair. He was a most brilliant man, and a
very dear friend of mine. It is a terrible loss to the expedition.”

“But you are quite sure it was tetanus?”

“Oh, yes. There’s no doubt about that. But it’s a very strange
thing that there should have been a case of tetanus here. We’ve
been very careful about everything.”

“You mean about the sanitary arrangements?”

“Yes. And about everything else. It’s most mysterious.”

“What is your opinion of the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’?”

Dr. Tosswill smiled.

“I’m afraid I’m not very superstitious, Monsieur Poirot. I think
it’s just a series of unfortunate accidents.”

“I see. And you don’t think there’s any connection between them?”

“None whatever.”

“Thank you, Dr. Tosswill. I won’t take up any more of your time.”

As we left the tent, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all?”

“I don’t know what to think,” I replied. “It’s all very strange.”

“It is indeed. Very strange. And yet, I think I am beginning to
see a little light.”

“You are?” I cried.

“Yes. But we must be careful, Hastings. Very careful. There is
danger here—grave danger.”

“Danger? From what?”

“From the living, Hastings. Not the dead.”

I shuddered. Poirot’s words were not exactly reassuring.

“What are we going to do now?”

“We are going to have a little talk with Mr. Harper, the secretary.”

We found Mr. Harper in the mess-tent. He was busy writing letters.
He looked up as we entered.

“Hullo! Have you finished with the others?”

“For the moment, yes,” said Poirot. “I should like to have a little
talk with you, Mr. Harper.”

“Certainly. Sit down. What can I do for you?”

“You were Mr. Bleibner’s secretary, I believe?”

“Yes. I’d been with him about six months.”

“And you were with him when he died?”

“Yes. I was with him all the time. It was a most distressing affair.”

“Did he ever speak of his nephew, Rupert Bleibner?”

“Rupert? Oh, yes. He was very fond of him, I think, although he
didn’t see much of him. Rupert was a bit of a rolling stone, you
know.”

“Did Mr. Bleibner leave him any money?”

“I don’t know. I shouldn’t think so. Mr. Bleibner wasn’t the sort
of man to leave money to anyone who didn’t deserve it.”

“I see. And what about the other members of the party? Did Mr.
Bleibner get on well with them?”

“Oh, yes. He was very popular. Everyone liked him.”

“Including Hassan?”

“Hassan? Oh, yes. Hassan is a most devoted servant. He’s been with
the Willards for years.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Mr. Harper. I won’t keep you any longer.”

As we left the tent, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of Mr. Harper?”

“He seems a very pleasant young man,” I replied.

“Yes. Very pleasant. But I wonder——”

“You wonder what?”

“I wonder if he is as pleasant as he seems.”

I looked at Poirot in surprise.

“You don’t suspect him, surely?”

“I suspect everyone, Hastings. It is my metier.”

“But what motive could he have?”

“That is what we must find out. Now, let us go and find Dr. Ames.”

We found Dr. Ames in his tent. He was busy reading a book. He looked
up as we entered.

“Hullo! Back again?”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I should like to have another little talk with
you, Dr. Ames.”

“Certainly. Sit down. What is it this time?”

“I want to ask you about Mr. Bleibner’s death. You said it was
septicæmia?”

“Yes. He had a scratch on his thumb which became infected.”

“And you are quite sure it wasn’t tetanus?”

“Absolutely certain. The symptoms were quite different.”

“I see. And what about Sir John Willard? You said it was heart
failure?”

“Yes. He’d had a weak heart for years.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Dr. Ames. I won’t take up any more of your
time.”

As we left the tent, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of Dr. Ames?”

“He seems a very capable man,” I replied.

“Yes. Very capable. But I wonder——”

“You wonder what?”

“I wonder if he is as capable as he seems.”

I looked at Poirot in surprise.

“You don’t suspect him, surely?”

“I suspect everyone, Hastings. It is my metier.”

“But what motive could he have?”

“That is what we must find out. Now, let us go and find Hassan.”

We found Hassan in the kitchen-tent. He was busy preparing dinner.
He looked up as we entered.

“Yes, monsieur?”

“I want to ask you a few more questions, Hassan,” said Poirot.

“Yes, monsieur?”

“You were with Sir John Willard when he died, weren’t you?”

“I was, monsieur.”

“And you saw no one?”

“No one, monsieur.”

“Are you quite sure?”

“I am quite sure, monsieur.”

“And you were also present when Mr. Bleibner died?”

“Yes, monsieur.”

“Did he say anything before he died?”

“He said many things, monsieur. But he was wandering in his mind.”

“Did he mention his nephew, Rupert?”

“I do not remember, monsieur.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Hassan. That will be all.”

As we left the tent, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of Hassan?”

“He seems a very devoted servant,” I replied.

“Yes. Very devoted. But I wonder——”

“You wonder what?”

“I wonder if he is as devoted as he seems.”

I looked at Poirot in surprise.

“You don’t suspect him, surely?”

“I suspect everyone, Hastings. It is my metier.”

“But what motive could he have?”

“That is what we must find out. Now, let us go and find Dr. Tosswill.”

We found Dr. Tosswill in his tent. He was still busy cleaning pottery.
He looked up as we entered.

“Hullo! Back again?”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I should like to have another little talk with
you, Dr. Tosswill.”

“Certainly. Sit down. What is it this time?”

“I want to ask you about Mr. Schneider’s death. You said it was
tetanus?”

“Yes. There’s no doubt about that.”

“And you are quite sure it wasn’t strychnine poisoning?”

“Absolutely certain. The symptoms were quite different.”

“I see. Well, thank you, Dr. Tosswill. I won’t take up any more of
your time.”

As we left the tent, Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of Dr. Tosswill?”

“He seems a very honest man,” I replied.

“Yes. Very honest. But I wonder——”

“You wonder what?”

“I wonder if he is as honest as he seems.”

I looked at Poirot in surprise.

“You don’t suspect him, surely?”

“I suspect everyone, Hastings. It is my metier.”

“But what motive could he have?”

“That is what we must find out. Now, let us go and have some dinner.”

We had dinner in the mess-tent with the other members of the party.
The conversation was mostly about the excavations, and everyone
seemed to be in good spirits, despite the recent tragedies.

After dinner, Poirot and I went for a walk in the desert. The stars
were shining brightly, and the air was cool and pleasant.

“Well, Hastings,” said Poirot, “what do you make of it all?”

“I don’t know,” I replied. “It’s all very mysterious.”

“It is indeed. Very mysterious. And yet, I think I am beginning to
see a little light.”

“You are?” I cried.

“Yes. But we must be careful, Hastings. Very careful. There is
danger here—grave danger.”

“Danger? From what?”

“From the living, Hastings. Not the dead.”

I shuddered. Poirot’s words were not exactly reassuring.

“What are we going to do now?”

“We are going to wait, Hastings. We are going to wait and see what
happens.”

And so we waited. For three days, nothing happened. The work of the
excavations went on as usual, and everyone seemed to be in good
spirits.

But then, on the fourth day, another tragedy occurred.

Sir Guy Willard was found dead in his tent.

He had been stabbed to the heart.

The whole camp was in an uproar. Everyone was horrified and
distressed.

Poirot and I were the first to arrive at the scene of the crime.
Sir Guy was lying on his bed, his eyes wide open, as if in terror.
A small dagger was sticking out of his chest.

“_Mon Dieu!_” cried Poirot. “This is terrible! Terrible!”

He began to examine the body.

“He has been dead for several hours,” he said. “It must have happened
in the middle of the night.”

“But who could have done it?” I cried.

“That is what we must find out,” said Poirot. “And we must do it
quickly, before anyone else is killed.”

He began to search the tent. In a corner, he found a small piece
of paper. He picked it up and read it.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a note,” said Poirot. “A note from the killer.”

He handed it to me. It was written in a cramped, hurried hand.

“The Curse of Men-her-Ra has claimed another victim,” it read. “And
it will not be the last.”

I shuddered.

“This is horrible!” I cried. “Who could have written this?”

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “But I have an idea.”

He turned to the others, who had gathered outside the tent.

“Listen to me!” he cried. “A terrible crime has been committed.
Sir Guy Willard has been murdered. And I believe that the killer
is among us!”

There was a murmur of horror from the crowd.

“I want everyone to go to their tents and stay there until I call
for you,” said Poirot. “I am going to investigate this crime, and
I will find the killer!”

The crowd dispersed, and Poirot and I were left alone in the tent.

“Well, Hastings,” said Poirot, “now we must begin our investigation
in earnest.”

“What are we going to do first?” I asked.

“We are going to talk to everyone again,” said Poirot. “And this
time, I am going to ask some very different questions.”

We started with Dr. Tosswill.

“Dr. Tosswill,” said Poirot, “where were you last night?”

“I was in my tent, sleeping,” said the doctor.

“Can anyone verify that?”

“No. I live alone.”

“I see. And what about you, Mr. Harper?”

“I was in my tent, too,” said the secretary. “I was working late on
some reports.”

“Can anyone verify that?”

“No. I was alone.”

“I see. And you, Dr. Ames?”

“I was in my tent, reading,” said the doctor.

“Can anyone verify that?”

“No. I was alone.”

“I see. And you, Hassan?”

“I was in the kitchen-tent, preparing breakfast,” said the servant.

“At what time?”

“From four o’clock onwards, monsieur.”

“And before that?”

“I was in my tent, sleeping.”

“Can anyone verify that?”

“No, monsieur. I was alone.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “So none of you have an alibi.”

“But why should we?” cried Dr. Ames. “We’re all friends here. Why
should any of us want to kill Sir Guy?”

“That is what I am going to find out,” said Poirot.

He began to pace up and down the tent.

“There are four suspects,” he said. “Dr. Tosswill, Dr. Ames, Mr.
Harper, and Hassan. One of them is the killer. But which one?”

He stopped and looked at me.

“What do you think, Hastings?”

“I don’t know,” I replied. “They all seem like such unlikely
candidates.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But one of them must be the killer. And
I am going to find out who it is.”

He began to search the tent again. In a corner, he found a small
box. He picked it up and opened it.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is the small lacquer box that Sir Guy was playing with,” said
Poirot. “And look what’s inside!”

He held up a small piece of paper. It was a letter, written in the
same hand as the note we had found earlier.

“I know what you have done,” it read. “And I know why you did it.
If you do not pay me five thousand pounds, I will tell the police
everything.”

“Blackmail!” I cried.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “Blackmail. Sir Guy was being blackmailed. And
I think I know who was blackmailing him.”

“Who?” I asked.

“That is what we are going to find out,” said Poirot.

He called everyone back to the tent.

“Listen to me!” he cried. “I have found a letter. A letter that
proves that Sir Guy Willard was being blackmailed. And I believe
that the blackmailer is the killer!”

There was a murmur of astonishment from the crowd.

“I want everyone to tell me if they have ever seen this letter
before,” said Poirot.

He handed the letter to Dr. Tosswill.

“No,” said the doctor. “I’ve never seen it before.”

He handed it to Mr. Harper.

“No,” said the secretary. “I’ve never seen it before.”

He handed it to Dr. Ames.

“No,” said the doctor. “I’ve never seen it before.”

He handed it to Hassan.

“No, monsieur,” said the servant. “I’ve never seen it before.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “So none of you have ever seen it before.
That is very interesting.”

He began to pace up and down the tent again.

“There is one more thing,” he said. “I have found a small piece of
cloth near the body. It is a piece of white linen, and it has a
very distinctive smell.”

He held up the piece of cloth.

“Does anyone recognize this smell?” he asked.

He handed the cloth to Dr. Tosswill.

“It smells like—like some kind of disinfectant,” said the doctor.

He handed it to Mr. Harper.

“It smells like—like a hospital,” said the secretary.

He handed it to Dr. Ames.

“It smells like—like ether,” said the doctor.

He handed it to Hassan.

“It smells like—like the doctor’s tent, monsieur,” said the servant.

“I see,” said Poirot. “Like the doctor’s tent. That is very
interesting indeed.”

He turned to Dr. Ames.

“Dr. Ames,” he said, “I believe that you are the killer!”

“Me?” cried the doctor. “That’s ridiculous! Why should I want to
kill Sir Guy?”

“Because he was blackmailing you!” said Poirot. “He found out that
you were the one who killed Sir John Willard and Mr. Bleibner!”

“That’s a lie!” cried the doctor.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I don’t think so. You killed Sir John Willard
by giving him a fatal dose of digitalis. You killed Mr. Bleibner
by infecting his scratch with a deadly bacteria. And you killed
Mr. Schneider by giving him a fatal dose of tetanus.”

“But why?” I cried. “Why should he want to kill them?”

“Because he wanted their money!” said Poirot. “He was the only one
who knew that Mr. Bleibner had made a new will, leaving everything
to him!”

“That’s not true!” cried the doctor.

“Isn’t it?” said Poirot. “We shall see. I have already cabled to
New York for a copy of the will. And I have also found the bottle
 of digitalis and the cultures of bacteria in your tent!”

The doctor turned pale. He tried to run, but Hassan and Mr. Harper
caught him and held him fast.

“It’s no use, Dr. Ames,” said Poirot. “The game is up.”

The doctor slumped in their arms, his face a mask of despair.

“Well, Hastings,” said Poirot, “I think we have our man.”

“But what about the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’?” I asked.

“The ‘Curse’ was just a clever cover for the doctor’s crimes,”
said Poirot. “He used the superstition to hide his tracks and
frighten away anyone who might suspect him.”

“And what about the note?” I asked.

“The note was written by the doctor himself,” said Poirot. “He
wanted to make it look like the ‘Curse’ was responsible for Sir
Guy’s death.”

“And the blackmail letter?” I asked.

“The blackmail letter was also written by the doctor,” said Poirot.
“He wanted to make it look like Sir Guy was being blackmailed by
someone else.”

“I see,” I said. “It was a very clever plan.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “Very clever. But not clever enough for
Hercule Poirot.”

And so the mystery of the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’ was finally solved.
Dr. Ames was taken to Cairo and tried for his crimes. He was found
guilty and sentenced to death.

As for the excavations, they were continued by Dr. Tosswill and Mr.
Harper, and many more wonderful treasures were found in the Tomb
of King Men-her-Ra.

But I shall never forget that terrible time in the desert, when the
shadow of death hung over us all, and only the genius of Hercule
Poirot saved us from a terrible fate.

“And you, Sir Guy?”

The young man laughed.

“Not I,” he cried. “I don’t believe in any of your old kings and
mummies.”

“Then,” said Poirot, with a sudden change of manner, “if you do
not believe in any of these things, tell me, Sir Guy, why are you
so afraid?”

For a moment the young man stood as though petrified, then his
face went a mottled white.

“I—I don’t know what you mean,” he stammered.

“Is it possible that you do not?” said Poirot gently. “Then I am
much mistaken.”

He walked towards the door, then turned back and faced the room.

“One thing more. Is there anything in this camp which belongs to
the dead men? Any particular thing which they might have handled?”

The doctor looked at him for a moment and then walked over to a
small table.

“There are their effects,” he said, pointing to a small pile of
clothing. “And their notebooks. But I cannot see how that will
help you.”

“One never knows,” said Poirot. “_Au revoir_, messieurs.”

“Wait a moment,” said Poirot, his gaze fixed on the doctor. “I
thought that medical men were of all others the most likely to
confess that there are more things in heaven and earth than are
dreamt of in our philosophy?”

“Not in the twentieth century, Monsieur Poirot. My experience as
a doctor leads me to look for a physical cause for every effect.
You’ll find there’s one here, too.”

“You are right, _mon ami_,” said Poirot, “I am sure you are right.
But it is possible that there is more than one cause. It is
possible, for instance, that the curse of Men-her-Ra is as
scientific as any of your discoveries.”

“You are joking, Monsieur Poirot?”

“No, I was never more serious in my life. You have mentioned the
word ‘science.’ But science, too, may have its secrets. Now, tell
me, what was the first symptom of Mr. Schneider’s illness?”

“He complained of a slight stiffness in the jaw. That was on Tuesday
evening. He died on Friday.”

“Tuesday? That would be the day you returned from Cairo, wouldn’t
it, Sir Guy?”

“Yes, I had been into Cairo for a couple of days’ change. I only
came back on the Tuesday afternoon.”

“Now, Dr. Ames, what was the source of infection? Tetanus is a
well-known germ, it exists in the soil, does it not?”

“It does, Monsieur Poirot. But it is not very common in Egypt.”

“Is it not? That is interesting. Now, tell me, was there any
wound? How did the germ enter the body?”

“He had a small cut on his hand. He had been handling some of the
relics which were covered with dust.”

“I see. Now, Monsieur Harper, what do you say to all this? You
were Mr. Bleibner’s secretary, I believe?”

“I was,” replied the young man, who had just re-entered the tent.

“And you have no theories to offer?”

“None at all, Monsieur Poirot. It’s all very mysterious and very
terrible.”

“I see. Now, I should like to have a few words with the native
servant, Hassan. He is in the camp, is he not?”

“He is,” said Sir Guy. “But I don’t think you’ll get much out of
him. He’s quite a simple fellow.”

“I will see him, nevertheless.”

“Then we have only to discover the cause of the four deaths. And
yet, you cannot deny that they follow one another with an almost
miraculous precision?”

“I have no theory about it,” said the doctor. “Coincidences do
occur.”

Poirot sat for some minutes in silence. He seemed to be deep in
thought. Then he turned to me.

“Hastings, I should like to walk round the camp. You will come
with me?”

I assented at once, and we were conducted by the young secretary.
We went round the site of the excavations. It was an enormous area.
A small army of natives was at work. Everywhere one heard the same
droning chant. I was extremely interested.

At last we reached a cluster of tents, slightly apart from the
rest.

“This is where we live,” said Mr. Harper.

“Whose tent is this?” asked Poirot, pointing to one slightly larger
than the rest.

“That was Mr. Schneider’s.”

“And this one?”

“Mine.”

“And the one next to it?”

“Dr. Ames’.”

“And the one on the other side?”

“Dr. Tosswill’s.”

“Who is this?” asked Poirot, pointing to a dark-faced man who was
seated outside one of the tents.

“That is Hassan, Sir John Willard’s servant. He is a very faithful
fellow.”

The man rose and made a deep obeisance as we approached. He had a
reserved, inscrutable face. I felt that he might be a dangerous
enemy.

Poirot addressed a few words to him in Arabic. The man replied in
the same tongue.

“He is a strange fellow,” said Mr. Harper. “He has been with the
late Sir John for many years. He seems to have an almost dog-like
devotion to him.”

Poirot nodded.

“What was he doing when we came up?”

“He was reading the Koran.”

“He is a very religious man, then?”

“Yes, he is a very devout Mahommedan.”

We walked on for a bit in silence. Then Poirot turned to our guide.

“Mr. Harper, did you see much of Mr. Rupert Bleibner when he was
here?”

“He was only here for a very few days. He and his uncle had a most
unpleasant scene. The old man told him he wouldn’t give him another
cent, and that he’d better go back to New York and try and earn
his living.”

“And did he go?”

“Yes, he left for Cairo the next day.”

“Thank you, Mr. Harper. I think that is all for the present.”

“But there are many things which science has not yet explained,
Dr. Ames,” said Poirot softly. “I have seen things—things that
perhaps you would not believe.”

He paused.

“Wait and see, _mon ami_. I have an idea. I am going to have a talk
with the native servant, Hassan.”

He went out of the tent, and I followed him. We found Hassan
seated on a rug outside one of the other tents, his face turned
towards the setting sun. He was a tall, dignified figure, and he
rose to greet us with a profound salaam.

“Peace be with you, my son,” said Poirot.

“And with you, O Effendi,” replied Hassan.

“You have served the late Sir John Willard for many years?”

“Since my youth, Effendi. He was as my father, and I as his son.”

“And you were with him when he died?”

“I was with him, Effendi. He died as the sun was sinking behind
the hills.”

“Did he say anything before he died?”

“He said: ‘The curse—the curse of Men-her-Ra is upon me.’ And then
he spoke no more.”

Poirot’s face became very grave.

“And you, Hassan, do you believe in the curse?”

“I know what I know, Effendi. The spirits of the dead are not to
be trifled with. They have their own ways of dealing with those
who disturb their rest.”

“And do you think there will be more deaths?”

“Who can say, Effendi? It is in the hands of Allah.”

He bowed and sat down again, as though to intimate that the
interview was at an end. We walked away in silence.

“Well, Poirot?” I asked. “What do you think of it all? Is there
really something in this talk of a curse?”

Poirot did not reply for a moment. He seemed to be deep in thought.

“It is strange, Hastings,” he said at last. “Very strange. Four
deaths, all different, and yet all occurring within such a short
space of time. And then there is the suicide of young Rupert
Bleibner. Why should he kill himself? remorse, the letter said.
Remorse for what? For his uncle’s death? But his uncle died of
blood poisoning, an accident. How could he be responsible for
that?”

“Perhaps he felt he had been a bad nephew,” I suggested.

“Perhaps. But it is all very mysterious. And then there is this
young Sir Guy. He is a brave lad, but he is clearly under a great
strain. We must do what we can to protect him, Hastings.”

“But how? If it is a curse——”

“Even a curse may have a human agency behind it, _mon ami_. Let
us not forget that.”

He was silent for a while, and then he added:

“I should like to see the place where these excavations are being
carried on. Shall we go and have a look at the Tomb?”

“Was there no science then in Ancient Egypt?” asked Poirot softly.
He did not wait for a reply, and indeed Dr. Ames seemed rather at
a loss for the moment. “No, no, do not answer me, but tell me this.
What do the native workmen think?”

“I guess,” said Dr. Ames, “that, where white folk lose their heads,
natives aren’t going to be far behind. I’ll admit that they’re
getting what you might call scared—but they’ve no cause to be.”

“I wonder,” said Poirot non-committally.

Sir Guy leant forward.

“Surely,” he cried incredulously, “you cannot believe in—oh, but
the thing’s absurd! You can know nothing of Ancient Egypt if you
think that.”

“Perhaps I do not,” answered Poirot. “But I can believe in the
force of superstition, Sir Guy. I have seen it work.”

“It’s a powerful thing, I’ll admit,” said Dr. Ames. “I’ve seen a
healthy man die in forty-eight hours because he believed he was
cursed. But that’s a different thing.”

“I do not agree. If a man believes he is cursed, then, for all
practical purposes, he is cursed.”

“What’s the use of talking to a man who argues in that fashion?”
said Dr. Ames, almost rudely.

“_Mon Dieu_, I do not argue. I only state. Now tell me about the
others. There is a young American secretary, Mr. Harper, is he
not? He also was present at the opening of the tomb?”

“Yes, he’s been with us from the first. He’s a good fellow, too,
but he’s a bit rattled just now.”

“And Hassan?”

“Oh, Hassan’s the most superstitious of the lot. He’s convinced
we’re all doomed.”

“I see. Now I should like to walk round the camp and see things
for myself.”

“By all means. Tosswill’s out there somewhere. He’ll show you
round. Or I will if you like?”

“No, no, do not let us trouble you. I will seek out Dr. Tosswill.”

We found Dr. Tosswill at some little distance from the camp, and
spent an interesting hour in his company. I have never met a man
who impressed me more by his quiet sense and his profound knowledge
of his subject. He showed us the various chambers and pointed out
the interesting features of the tomb. In spite of his somewhat
pedantic manner, he was a most fascinating companion.

“I know only what I have seen,” said Poirot, with a shrug. “I see
the fact that three men have died—no, four, for the nephew counts—all
within a few weeks of the opening of the tomb. Each death is
explicable, each is different, yet there is that strange link of
death.”

Dr. Tosswill now returned, followed by Hassan, the native servant,
who was an elderly man of dignified appearance. He seemed to be
greatly distressed at the turn events had taken.

“It is as the Master says,” he murmured, in a low, vibrant voice.
“The hand of the King is heavy upon us. He will not have his resting
place disturbed.”

Poirot turned on him quickly.

“You believe that, Hassan?”

“I know it, Monsieur Poirot. My fathers knew it, and their fathers.
The great ones of Egypt were wise. They knew many things of which
we know nothing to-day. Even the desert—the great desert—speaks
to those who have ears to hear.”

“I’m sure it does,” I said, with a shiver. “It’s been speaking to
me ever since I came.”

Poirot turned to me with a twinkle in his eye.

“What has it been saying, Hastings? That the sun is hot, and that
the sand gets into your boots?”

I flushed.

“No, no, but it’s so—so vast and so—so——”

“Monotonous?” suggested Poirot.

“No, not that. I should call it—unending.”

“And that is just what it is not,” said Poirot. “It is bounded by
the sea and the Nile. It is even bounded by the horizon. To-day we
have the camel and the motor-car, to-morrow we have the aeroplane.
Soon there will be no more mystery.”

“Oh, I hope so,” said Sir Guy. “The sooner the better. I’m tired
of all this mystery.”

He stood up and shook himself.

“Come, Monsieur Poirot, if you would like to see the Tomb, let us
go there now.”

We all followed him out. The Tomb was situated at a little distance
from the camp. As we approached it I saw a tall, thin man standing
near the entrance. He seemed to be wrapped in thought, and did not
even look up as we came along.

“That is Dr. Tosswill,” whispered Sir Guy.

I looked at him with some interest. He was a very quiet,
unobtrusive man, with a face that was almost like a mask. I
wondered what he was thinking about. Was he, too, a victim to the
terrors of the Tomb?

We entered the Tomb. It was a wonderful sight. The walls were
covered with paintings in the most vivid colours, representing
scenes from the life of the dead King. In the centre was the
sarcophagus, a magnificent piece of work. It was easy to
understand how an archaeologist could be fascinated by such a
discovery.

Sir Guy pointed out the various features of interest, and Poirot
listened with the greatest attention. He seemed to be particularly
interested in the inscriptions on the walls.

“What does this say?” he asked, pointing to a line of hieroglyphics.

“It is a curse upon anyone who shall disturb the rest of the
King,” replied Sir Guy. “It is a very common form of inscription.”

“And this?”

“That is a prayer for the soul of the King.”

Poirot nodded.

“It is very interesting,” he said. “And very—disturbing.”

We left the Tomb and returned to the camp. As we were walking
along, I noticed that Hassan was following us at a little distance.
He seemed to be watching us with a very strange expression.

That evening we dined with Sir Guy and the other members of the
party. The conversation was mostly about the excavations, but
there was an undercurrent of uneasiness which it was impossible
to ignore.

After dinner, Poirot and I went for a walk in the desert. The moon
was full, and the scene was one of great beauty.

“Well, Hastings,” said Poirot, “what do you think of it all?”

“I don’t know what to think,” I replied. “It’s all so strange and—and
horrible. Do you really believe in the curse?”

“I believe in the power of the human mind,” said Poirot. “If people
believe in a curse, then for them the curse exists. But there is
something else here, Hastings—something more tangible than a curse.”

“What do you mean?”

“I do not know—yet. But I mean to find out.”

We walked on in silence for a few minutes. Then Poirot suddenly
stopped and looked at me.

“Hastings,” he said, “do you remember what Lady Willard said about
the American secretary, Mr. Harper?”

“Yes, she said he was a very pleasant young fellow.”

“And do you remember what Dr. Ames said about him?”

“No, I don’t think he said anything in particular.”

“Precisely. He said nothing. And yet Mr. Harper is the only member
of the party who is not a specialist in some way. He is merely a
secretary.”

“Well, what of that?”

“It is a point to be remembered, that is all.”

We returned to the camp and went to bed. I slept fitfully, and my
dreams were filled with images of ancient kings and deadly curses.

The next morning we were awakened by a loud cry. We rushed out of
our tent and found a scene of great confusion.

“What is it?” I cried. “What has happened?”

Dr. Tosswill came running towards us.

“It’s Sir Guy!” he gasped. “He’s—he’s dead!”

“I know very little of Ancient Egypt, Sir Guy, but I know a great
deal about—human nature. You say that it is all coincidence.
Coincidence, yes. But three such coincidences?”

He paused. Sir Guy leant back in his chair.

“You have no theory then, Monsieur Poirot?”

“No. At the moment, I have only a feeling. A feeling of dread—of
menacing evil.”

He shivered slightly.

“And you believe that it is the spirit of King Men-her-Ra?”

“I believe that we are in the presence of a great and terrible
force. A force which I do not understand, but which I feel. I
should like to have a look round the camp.”

He rose, and Sir Guy rose also. Dr. Ames remained behind.

“Wait one moment,” said Poirot. “Where did Mr. Schneider’s death
take place?”

“In his own tent.”

“Is it still as it was then?”

“Yes. No one has been in it since he died.”

“May I see it?”

“By all means.”

Sir Guy led the way out of the tent. He was a tall, athletic looking
young man, who should have been at the height of his strength,
but he seemed to me to be walking with a heavy step. His face was
set and determined, but I thought I detected a look of haunting
fear in his eyes.

We went across the camp to a small tent at the further side. It
had a neat, businesslike appearance.

Poirot entered. He did not seem to be looking for anything in
particular. He just stood in the middle of the tent and looked
round him. Then he went over to a small table on which stood a
glass of water. He smelt it, but it had no odour. Then he looked
at the bed.

“He died here?”

“Yes.”

“And there was no sign of anything—unusual?”

“None. He complained of a stiffness in the neck and jaw. Dr. Ames
was sent for at once. He did all he could, but it was too late.”

“And you say that there have been no other cases of tetanus?”

“Not one.”

Poirot stepped out of the tent.

“And now, I should like to see the Tomb.”

Sir Guy led the way. We went down a flight of steps, and through
a passage into a small chamber. It was empty. At the further end
was a door, heavily barred and bolted.

“The inner chamber?” asked Poirot.

“Yes. It has not yet been opened.”

“And it was here that your father was working when he died?”

“Yes. He was just about to open the inner chamber.”

“And Mr. Bleibner?”

“He was with him.”

Poirot stood for a moment in silence. Then he turned to Sir Guy.

“I should like to talk to your father’s servant, Hassan.”

“Certainly. I will send for him.”

He went out, and in a few minutes a tall, dignified looking Arab
entered. He was dressed in a long white robe, and wore a red fez.
He bowed low to Poirot.

“You were Sir John Willard’s servant?”

“I was, monsieur.”

“You were with him when he died?”

“I was.”

“Tell me, what did he say before he died?”

“He said nothing, monsieur. He just fell down and died.”

“And you—what do you think of these deaths?”

The man’s face remained impassive.

“It is the will of Allah,” he said simply.

“You do not believe in the Curse of Men-her-Ra?”

“I believe that King Men-her-Ra was a great king, and that his
spirit is powerful. But it is as Allah wills.”

“Thank you, Hassan. That is all.”

The man bowed again and left the tent.

Poirot turned to Sir Guy.

“I think that is all for the moment. I should like to think over
what I have heard.”

“I’ll leave you then. I have work to do.”

He went out, and Poirot and I were left alone.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, “what do you make of it all? Do you really
believe in the Curse?”

Poirot sat down on a camp stool and began to polish his boots.

“I believe, Hastings, that we are in the presence of a very clever
and a very cold-blooded murderer.”

“A murderer!” I cried. “But how? Who?”

“That is what we have to find out. But think, Hastings. Four deaths,
all different, and all within a month of the opening of the Tomb.
Is it not a little—significant?”

“But how could it be murder? Sir John Willard died of heart failure,
Mr. Bleibner of blood poisoning, and Mr. Schneider of tetanus. You
can’t murder people like that.”

“Can you not?” Poirot’s eyes twinkled. “It is not so difficult as
you think. But we shall see. For the moment, we must wait.”

“Wait for what?”

“For the next death,” said Poirot grimly.

“On the contrary,” answered Poirot, “I have been studying the
subject ever since I received Lady Willard’s letter. I have been
reading many books, and I find that the Ancient Egyptians were
more advanced in many things than we are to-day. They had a
knowledge of the occult which we have lost. Their priests were
trained to exert the power of their will, to project their thought
to a distance, and to kill by it. They could use even more subtle
means. Even when dead, their spirits could return and take
vengeance on those who disturbed their rest. They could—well, why
not, _monsieur le docteur_? The world is a very strange place.”

Dr. Ames looked at him with an expression which was almost pity.

“But what do you propose to do?” he asked.

“Wait and see,” replied Poirot. “In the meantime, I should like
to see the tomb.”

“It’s about five hundred yards away. You’ll have to walk.”

“Walk?” wailed Poirot. “But I cannot walk. I have not the boots.”

I felt rather ashamed of him. After all he was my friend. But the
man was so absurd. However, we walked the five hundred yards. It
was a wonderful sight. The sun was setting, and the desert was
tinged with a beautiful pinkish glow.

We descended the steps of the tomb. The air was heavy and
oppressive. I felt a sudden shiver as we entered. Poirot, too,
seemed affected. He clung to my arm.

“_Mon Dieu_!” he whispered. “It is cold! It is like the hand of
death!”

There were several rooms, and in one of them was the sarcophagus.
It was empty. The mummy had already been removed.

“You see,” said Dr. Tosswill, who had joined us, “there is nothing
here to fear. The King is gone.”

“But his spirit may still be here,” whispered Poirot.

“Nonsense!” said the doctor. “We’re in the twentieth century.
Science has explained all these things.”

“And yet,” said Poirot, “four men are dead.”

“Coincidence,” said the doctor.

“Four coincidences?” asked Poirot.

“Coincidence can go a very long way,” said the doctor.

“It can,” agreed Poirot. “But there is a limit.”

He turned to Sir Guy.

“I should like to speak to your servant Hassan.”

“Certainly. I will send for him.”

Hassan was a tall, thin man with a very dark skin. He had a pair
of intelligent eyes.

“You were with Sir John when he died?” asked Poirot.

“Yes, monsieur.”

“Tell me about it.”

“It was very sudden, monsieur. He was sitting in his tent. He had
just come from the tomb. He said he felt a sudden pain in his
heart. He died in a few minutes.”

“Did he say anything?”

“He said: ‘The King! The King!’”

“And then?”

“Then he died, monsieur.”

“And Mr. Bleibner?”

“He was very ill for several days, monsieur. He had much pain.
He died in great agony.”

“What did he say?”

“He said nothing, monsieur. He was too ill.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“He also died in great agony, monsieur. He said: ‘It is the curse!
The curse has fallen on me!’”

“And the nephew in New York?”

“I do not know about him, monsieur.”

“Thank you, Hassan.”

Poirot turned to us.

“You see,” he said, “they all believed in the curse.”

“But that does not prove it exists,” said Dr. Ames.

“No,” said Poirot. “But it proves that they were afraid of it.
And fear is a very powerful thing.”

We returned to the camp. It was dark now, and the stars were
shining with a wonderful brilliance.

We had dinner in the large tent. It was a silent meal. We were all,
I think, under the influence of the tragedy which had overtaken
the expedition.

After dinner we sat outside. The air was cool and pleasant.
Suddenly there was a cry from one of the native tents.

“What is that?” I asked.

“It is only one of the men,” said Dr. Ames. “They are very
superstitious.”

“I will go and see,” said Poirot.

He went off in the direction of the cry. In a few minutes he
returned.

“It was nothing,” he said. “Only a bad dream.”

But I noticed that he looked very grave.

“I think,” he said, “that it would be better if we all went to bed
early. We have had a long day.”

We all agreed. I was glad to go. I felt strangely tired.

I fell asleep almost as soon as my head touched the pillow. But
my sleep was troubled. I dreamed of long dead kings and ancient
curses.

I was awakened by a touch on my shoulder. It was Poirot.

“Hastings!” he whispered. “Come with me!”

“What is it?” I asked, rubbing my eyes.

“Come!” he said. “And be quiet!”

I followed him out of the tent. The moon was shining, and the
desert was like a sea of silver.

“Where are we going?” I whispered.

“To the tomb,” he replied.

“To the tomb? At this hour?”

“Yes. I have a fancy to see it by moonlight.”

I did not like it, but I followed him. We reached the tomb and
descended the steps. It was very dark inside, but Poirot had a
flash-light.

We went into the room where the sarcophagus had been. Poirot
flashed his light around.

“Look!” he said.

I looked, but I saw nothing.

“There!” he said, pointing to the floor.

I looked again. There was a small, dark object on the floor. I
picked it up. It was a piece of paper.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is a piece of a letter,” said Poirot.

He took it from me and read it.

“It is in French,” he said. “It says: ‘Beware of the King!’”

“But who could have written it?” I asked.

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “But it was written recently.”

“How do you know?”

“The paper is fresh. It has not been here long.”

“But who would put it here?”

“That is what we must find out,” said Poirot.

We left the tomb and returned to the camp. As we were walking
back, we saw a figure moving in the shadows.

“Who is that?” I asked.

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “But we will follow him.”

We followed the figure. It led us to one of the tents. The figure
entered the tent.

“That is Dr. Ames’s tent,” said Poirot.

“Dr. Ames?” I cried. “But why would he be going to the tomb at
this hour?”

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “But it is very strange.”

We returned to our own tent. Poirot sat down on his bed and
thought for a long time.

“Hastings,” he said at last, “I think we are near the end of this
mystery.”

“You do?” I asked. “But how?”

“I have a theory,” he said. “But I must have proof.”

“And how will you get it?”

“By waiting,” he said. “By waiting and watching.”

The next day was very hot. We spent most of it in the shade of the
tents. Poirot was very quiet. He seemed to be thinking deeply.

In the afternoon, we went for a walk in the desert. We came across
Dr. Tosswill, who was busy with some inscriptions.

“Have you found anything interesting?” asked Poirot.

“No,” said the doctor. “Nothing but the usual things. But I am
sure there is more to be found if we only knew where to look.”

“Perhaps the King does not want you to find it,” said Poirot.

The doctor laughed.

“You still believe in the curse, Monsieur Poirot?”

“I believe in many things,” said Poirot.

As we were walking back, we met Mr. Harper. He looked very pale
and nervous.

“Is anything the matter?” asked Poirot.

“No,” he said. “But I don’t like this place. There is something
evil about it.”

“I agree with you,” said Poirot.
