That evening, after dinner, Poirot asked Sir Guy if he could see
the things that had been found in the tomb.

“Certainly,” said Sir Guy. “They are in the small tent over there.”

We went to the tent. There were many beautiful things—gold
ornaments, pottery, and statues. Poirot looked at them all very
carefully.

“They are very beautiful,” he said. “But they are also very
dangerous.”

“Dangerous?” asked Sir Guy. “How?”

“Because they are the property of a dead King,” said Poirot. “And
he may want them back.”

Sir Guy laughed, but I could see that he was uneasy.

That night, I was awakened again by Poirot.

“Hastings!” he whispered. “Come quickly!”

I followed him out of the tent. He led me to the small tent where
the treasures were kept. We looked inside.

The tent was empty! All the treasures were gone!

“They have been stolen!” I cried.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “But by whom?”

“The natives?” I suggested.

“No,” said Poirot. “I do not think so.”

“Then who?”

“We shall see,” said Poirot.

He went to the door of the tent and looked out.

“Look!” he said.

I looked. In the distance, I could see a figure moving across the
sand. It was carrying a heavy bundle.

“Follow him!” said Poirot.

We followed the figure. It led us to the tomb. The figure
descended the steps.

We followed cautiously. We saw the figure enter the room where the
sarcophagus had been. It put down the bundle and began to unpack
it.

It was Dr. Ames!

“So it was you!” cried Poirot, stepping forward.

Dr. Ames started and turned round. He looked at us with an
expression of defiance.

“Yes,” he said. “It was I. But I had a good reason.”

“And what was that?” asked Poirot.

“I wanted to protect them,” said the doctor. “I knew that if they
stayed in the camp, they would be stolen. So I decided to hide
them in the tomb.”

“In the tomb?” said Poirot. “But that is the last place anyone
would look for them.”

“Exactly,” said the doctor.

“But why didn’t you tell Sir Guy?” asked Poirot.

“Because I didn’t want him to know,” said the doctor. “He would
have insisted on keeping them in the camp.”

Poirot looked at him for a long time.

“I see,” he said at last. “Well, perhaps you were right. But you
should have told me.”

“I didn’t think you would understand,” said the doctor.

“I understand many things,” said Poirot.

We returned to the camp. Dr. Ames went to his tent, and we went to
ours.

“Do you believe him?” I asked Poirot.

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “It is a very strange story.”

The next morning, Sir Guy was informed of the disappearance of the
treasures. He was very angry, but Poirot told him what had
happened.

“Dr. Ames was only trying to protect them,” said Poirot.

Sir Guy was not satisfied, but he agreed to leave the treasures in
the tomb for the time being.

That afternoon, a messenger arrived from Cairo with a letter for
Poirot. He read it and then handed it to me.

It was from the police in New York. It said that they had found
evidence that Rupert Bleibner had been poisoned.

“Poisoned!” I cried. “But how?”

“With a very rare and subtle poison,” said Poirot. “One that
leaves no trace.”

“But who could have poisoned him?” I asked.

“That is what we must find out,” said Poirot.

He turned to Dr. Tosswill.

“Doctor, did you know Rupert Bleibner?”

“No,” said the doctor. “I never met him.”

“And you, Mr. Harper?”

“I knew him slightly,” said Harper. “He was a bit of a scoundrel.”

“And you, Dr. Ames?”

“I knew him well,” said the doctor. “He was a friend of mine.”

“A friend?” asked Poirot. “Then why didn’t you say so before?”

“I didn’t think it was important,” said the doctor.

“It is very important,” said Poirot.

He turned to Hassan.

“Hassan, did you know Rupert Bleibner?”

“Yes, monsieur. He came to the camp many times.”

“And did he have any enemies?”

“Many, monsieur. He was not a good man.”

Poirot thought for a moment.

“I think,” he said, “that I have the answer to this mystery.”

“You do?” I cried. “Who is the murderer?”

“Wait,” said Poirot. “I must have one more piece of evidence.”

He went to his tent and stayed there for a long time. When he came
out, he was carrying a small bottle.

“What is that?” I asked.

“It is the evidence I need,” he said.

He went to the tent where the treasures were kept. He opened the
bottle and poured some of the liquid onto one of the statues.

Suddenly, the statue began to glow with a strange light.

“What is it?” I cried.

“It is a chemical reaction,” said Poirot. “This statue has been
treated with a poison.”

“A poison?” I asked. “But how?”

“Someone has rubbed a poison onto the statues,” said Poirot. “And
anyone who touches them will be poisoned.”

“But who would do such a thing?” I asked.

“Someone who wanted to kill everyone who entered the tomb,” said
Poirot.

He turned to Dr. Ames.

“Dr. Ames, I arrest you for the murder of Sir John Willard, Mr.
Bleibner, Mr. Schneider, and Rupert Bleibner!”

Dr. Ames turned pale.

“You have no proof!” he cried.

“I have all the proof I need,” said Poirot. “I found this bottle
in your tent.”

Dr. Ames looked at the bottle and then at Poirot. He realized that
he was caught.

“Yes,” he said. “I did it. I wanted the treasures for myself. And
I knew that if I killed everyone else, they would be mine.”

“But why did you kill your friend Rupert Bleibner?” I asked.

“Because he knew too much,” said the doctor. “He saw me putting
the poison on the statues, and he tried to blackmail me. So I had
to kill him.”

“And how did you do it?” asked Poirot.

“I sent him a letter,” said the doctor. “And I put the poison on
the paper.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, you will have plenty of time to
think about your crimes in prison.”

The police were sent for, and Dr. Ames was taken away.

The mystery of the Curse of Men-her-Ra was solved. It was not a
curse from the past, but a crime from the present.

As we were leaving Egypt, Poirot looked back at the Pyramids.

“They are very beautiful,” he said. “But I am glad to be going
home.”

“And I,” I said. “I have had enough of ancient kings and curses.”

Poirot smiled.

“But it was a very interesting case, Hastings. A very
interesting case indeed.”

“I know enough to be aware that the ancient Egyptians were a very
wise and a very powerful people. They knew many things of which
we know nothing. They had at their command forces—forces that we
cannot even name, though we can feel their presence. What if they
could project those forces through the centuries?”

“It sounds a lot of poppycock,” I said to myself, and I saw that
the others were of my opinion. They were obviously disillusioned
as to Poirot’s ability. I must say that I myself was a little
puzzled. Was Poirot really in earnest, or was he playing a part?
His face was so serious that I was inclined to believe the former.

He rose now and asked to see the Tomb. We were escorted to the
opening. It was a wonderful sight, and the many treasures that
had been found were being carefully catalogued.

A small, dark man with a keen face was busy at work there. It was
Hassan, Sir John’s servant. He greeted us with a low salaam.

“Peace be with you, effendi,” he said. “The dead King is angry.
The Great One will have his revenge. It is not well to disturb
the sleep of the mighty.”

He looked at us with his dark, smouldering eyes. I felt a sudden
shiver of apprehension. Was there indeed something in it?

“You see,” said Poirot, “even the servant believes it.”

“Hassan is an old fool,” said Sir Guy.

“Maybe,” said Poirot, “but his words have a ring of truth in them.
What say you, Dr. Tosswill?”

The archaeologist shrugged his shoulders.

“It’s not my business,” he said. “My business is to find out all
I can about the Eighth Dynasty. If the King is angry, he must just
get over it.”

“And you, Mr. Harper?”

The young American laughed.

“I guess I’m not losing any sleep over it,” he said. “I’m a
modern, I am.”

“And you, Dr. Ames?”

“I’m with Mr. Harper. Science is enough for me.”

Poirot looked from one to the other.

“So you are all brave men,” he said. “That is well. Now, if you
will excuse me, I will go and walk a little by myself and meditate.
The air of the desert is very pure.”

He moved away. I followed him.

“What is it, Poirot?” I asked. “Do you really believe all this
supernatural stuff?”

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “I believe in the evidence of my senses.
And my senses tell me that there is something very wrong here.
Four deaths, Hastings! Four deaths in one month! And all in
connection with this Tomb. It is not natural.”

“But you don’t think——?”

“I think nothing—as yet. But I observe. I observe many things.”

“What things?”

“I observe, for instance, that Sir Guy Willard is very nervous.
I observe that Dr. Tosswill is very stolid. I observe that Mr.
Harper is very modern. And I observe that Dr. Ames is very
scientific.”

“And Hassan?”

“Hassan? Ah, Hassan is very—Egyptian.”

He said no more, and we walked on in silence for some time. The
sun was beginning to sink, and the desert was bathed in a wonderful
golden light. In the distance, we could see the Pyramids, like
great silent guardians of the past.

Suddenly, Poirot stopped.

“Look, Hastings,” he said, pointing.

I looked in the direction he indicated. A tall, thin figure was
moving towards us across the sand. As it came nearer, I saw that
it was a man dressed in the robes of a Bedouin. He was walking
with a curious, rhythmic gait, and his eyes were fixed on the
ground.

“Who is it?” I asked.

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “But he is not one of the workmen.”

The man passed us without a word, his eyes still fixed on the
ground. He seemed to be in a kind of trance.

“A religious fanatic, perhaps,” I suggested.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But did you see his face, Hastings?”

“No, he was looking down.”

“I saw it. It was the face of a man who has seen a ghost.”

He turned and looked after the retreating figure.

“Come,” he said. “It is time we returned to the camp. The air is
getting cold.”

As we walked back, I couldn't help feeling a sense of unease. The
whole place seemed to be permeated with an atmosphere of mystery
and dread. Was it possible that the “Curse of Men-her-Ra” was
real? Or was there some more human agency at work?

When we reached the camp, we found the others gathered round the
evening meal. The atmosphere was somber, and there was little
conversation.

After dinner, Poirot and I were sitting outside our tent, when
Dr. Ames came over to us.

“I thought you might like to see this,” he said, handing Poirot
a small piece of papyrus. “It was found in the Tomb this morning.”

Poirot took it and examined it by the light of a lantern.

“It is a curse,” he said, his voice low and grave. “A curse on
any who should dare to disturb the sleep of the King.”

“It’s probably just a piece of ancient superstition,” said the
doctor. “But it’s interesting, don't you think?”

“Very interesting,” said Poirot. “Very interesting indeed.”

He handed the papyrus back to the doctor.

“Tell me, Dr. Ames,” he said, “what do you think of the deaths
that have occurred?”

“I've told you already,” said the doctor. “I think they're just
unfortunate coincidences.”

“And the suicide of Mr. Bleibner’s nephew in New York?”

“Well, that's a bit more difficult to explain. But he was a bit of
a rotter, by all accounts. Maybe he just couldn't face life any
longer.”

“And the tetanus of Mr. Schneider?”

“That's more straightforward. He must have got some infected soil
into a cut or scratch.”

“Infected soil?”

“Yes. Tetanus spores are often found in the soil, especially in
places like this.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And Sir John Willard’s heart failure?”

“He was an old man, and he’d been working too hard. It’s not
altogether surprising.”

“And Mr. Bleibner’s blood poisoning?”

“As I said, he had a scratch on his thumb that became septic.”

Poirot nodded.

“It all seems very simple,” he said. “Very simple indeed.”

“It is simple,” said the doctor. “If you look at it scientifically.”

“And if you don't look at it scientifically?”

“Then you get all sorts of crazy ideas about curses and ghosts.”

The doctor laughed and walked away.

Poirot sat for a long time in silence, staring out into the
darkness.

“What are you thinking, Poirot?” I asked.

“I am thinking, Hastings, that science is a very wonderful thing.
But it does not explain everything.”

“You mean you still believe in the curse?”

“I mean, Hastings, that there are more things in heaven and earth
than are dreamt of in your philosophy.”

He rose and went into the tent. I followed him, feeling more
uneasy than ever.

The next morning, we were woken by a commotion outside. We rushed
out to find the workmen in a state of great excitement.

“What is it?” asked Poirot.

“It’s the King!” cried one of them. “The King has spoken!”

“What do you mean?”

“The Tomb! Something has happened in the Tomb!”

We hurried to the Tomb, followed by the others. When we got there,
we found the entrance blocked by a large stone.

“It was not like this last night,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“Someone must have moved it,” said Mr. Harper.

“But who? And why?”

We all looked at each other in silence. The atmosphere was thick
with suspicion and fear.

“Let us move it,” said Sir Guy.

We all lent a hand, and after some effort, we managed to move the
stone. When we entered the Tomb, we found that everything was
in a state of confusion. The treasures had been tossed about, and
the sarcophagus of the King had been opened.

“This is sacrilege!” cried Dr. Tosswill.

“It’s more than that,” said Poirot. “It’s a warning.”

He pointed to a wall of the Tomb. There, written in large, crude
letters, were the words:

“BEWARE THE WRATH OF MEN-HER-RA.”

“Who could have done this?” asked Sir Guy.

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “But whoever did it, did it with
a purpose.”

“And what is that purpose?”

“To frighten us. To make us leave this place.”

“Well, it’s not going to work,” said Sir Guy. “I’m not going to
be frightened away by a few words on a wall.”

“Nor am I,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“Me neither,” said Mr. Harper.

“I’m with you,” said Dr. Ames.

Poirot looked at them all for a moment, then he turned and walked
out of the Tomb.

“What now, Poirot?” I asked.

“Now, Hastings, we must wait. We must wait and see what happens
next.”

We didn't have to wait long. That afternoon, Mr. Harper was found
dead in his tent. The cause of death appeared to be a snake bite.

“This is getting beyond a joke,” said Dr. Ames, as we stood round
the body.

“It was never a joke,” said Poirot.

“But a snake bite! In his own tent!”

“It is not impossible,” said Poirot. “There are many snakes in the
desert.”

“But to be bitten in his sleep!”

“Perhaps he was not asleep,” said Poirot.

He looked at the body for a long time, then he turned to Dr. Ames.

“Tell me, doctor, was there any sign of a struggle?”

“No, none at all. He seems to have died quite peacefully.”

“And the snake? Was it found?”

“No, it must have got away.”

Poirot nodded.

“I see,” he said.

He turned and walked away, his face more serious than ever.

That evening, as we were sitting round the camp fire, Hassan
approached us.

“The King is not yet appeased,” he said. “More deaths will follow
unless you leave this place.”

“Go away, Hassan!” cried Sir Guy. “We've had enough of your
superstitious nonsense.”

Hassan looked at him for a moment, then he turned and walked away.

“He’s right, you know,” said Dr. Tosswill. “Something is very wrong
here.”

“We can’t leave now,” said Sir Guy. “We’re so close to finding
the inner chamber.”

“Is it worth it?” asked Dr. Tosswill. “Is it worth the lives of
more men?”

“I don’t know,” said Sir Guy. “I just don't know.”

He buried his face in his hands.

Poirot rose and walked over to him.

“Sir Guy,” he said, “I think it is time we had a little talk.”

“About what?”

“About the deaths that have occurred. About the ‘Curse of
Men-her-Ra’. And about the true culprit.”

We all looked at Poirot in astonishment.

“The true culprit?” asked Dr. Ames. “You mean you think someone
is behind all this?”

“I am sure of it,” said Poirot.

“But who?”

“That is what I am going to tell you.”

He looked from one to the other, his green eyes flashing in the
firelight.

“The true culprit,” he said, “is one of you.”

There was a stunned silence. No one spoke.

“One of us?” asked Dr. Tosswill at last. “But that’s impossible!”

“It is not impossible,” said Poirot. “It is the only explanation.”

“But how? And why?”

“That is what I am going to explain.”

He sat down and began to speak.

“Let us look at the facts,” he said. “Four deaths, all in connection
with the Tomb. All seemingly due to different causes. But are
they?”

He paused for a moment, then he continued.

“Sir John Willard died of heart failure. Mr. Bleibner died of
blood poisoning. Mr. Bleibner’s nephew committed suicide. And
Mr. Schneider died of tetanus. Now, we have a fifth death, Mr.
Harper, who died of a snake bite.”

“But they're all different!” cried Dr. Ames.

“Are they?” asked Poirot. “Let us look a little closer.”

“Sir John Willard’s heart failure. Could it have been caused by
something else? A sudden shock, perhaps? Or a drug?”

“Mr. Bleibner’s blood poisoning. Could it have been caused by
something other than a scratch on his thumb? An injection,
perhaps?”

“Mr. Bleibner’s nephew’s suicide. Could he have been driven to it?
Or could it have been murder disguised as suicide?”

“Mr. Schneider’s tetanus. Could the spores have been introduced
deliberately?”

“And Mr. Harper’s snake bite. Could the snake have been placed
in his tent?”

“But who would do such a thing?” asked Dr. Tosswill. “And why?”

“The motive,” said Poirot, “is simple. It is money. A great deal
of money.”

“Money?” asked Sir Guy. “But whose money?”

“Mr. Bleibner’s money,” said Poirot. “He was a very wealthy man.
And who would inherit his money if his nephew were dead?”

We all looked at each other.

“The nephew was his only relation,” said Dr. Ames. “If he died,
the money would go to—to someone else.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And who is that someone else?”

He looked at Dr. Ames.

“You, Dr. Ames,” he said. “You were Mr. Bleibner’s doctor. You
knew about his will. You knew that if his nephew were dead, you
would inherit his fortune.”

Dr. Ames went pale.

“That’s a lie!” he cried. “I didn't even know he’d made a will.”

“I think you did,” said Poirot. “And I think you saw an opportunity
to get your hands on his money. You knew about the ‘Curse of
Men-her-Ra’. You knew that people would be ready to believe in
supernatural deaths. So you decided to use the curse as a cover
for your crimes.”

“You killed Sir John Willard to create an atmosphere of fear. You
killed Mr. Bleibner to get his money. You drove his nephew to
suicide. You killed Mr. Schneider because he was getting too close
to the truth. And you killed Mr. Harper because he saw you doing
something you shouldn't have been doing.”

“That’s not true!” cried Dr. Ames. “You have no proof!”

“I have more than proof,” said Poirot. “I have the evidence of
my own eyes. I saw you last night, Dr. Ames. I saw you going into
Mr. Harper’s tent with a small box. A box that contained a snake.”

Dr. Ames looked at Poirot in horror.

“You—you saw me?”

“I did,” said Poirot. “And I saw you writing those words on the
wall of the Tomb. You wanted to make us think the King was angry,
so that we would leave and you could escape with your ill-gotten
gains.”

Dr. Ames slumped in his chair.

“It’s over, Ames,” said Poirot. “The game is up.”

The doctor didn't say anything. He just sat there, staring into the
fire.

“But what about the tetanus?” asked Dr. Tosswill. “How did he
manage that?”

“Simple,” said Poirot. “He had a supply of tetanus spores with
him. He used them to infect a small scratch on Mr. Schneider’s
arm.”

“And the blood poisoning?”

“An injection of septic matter. It was easy for him, as a doctor.”

“And Sir John Willard?”

“A drug that causes heart failure. Again, easy for a doctor.”

“It’s incredible,” said Sir Guy. “To think that he could do such
a thing.”

“The love of money,” said Poirot, “is the root of all evil.”

He turned to Dr. Ames.

“Come, monsieur,” he said. “The police are on their way. It is
time for you to leave this place.”

Dr. Ames rose and walked away, followed by two of the workmen.

Poirot turned to us and smiled.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “it was an interesting case, was it
not?”

“It was indeed, Poirot. But how did you know it was Dr. Ames?”

“It was the letter, Hastings. The letter that Mr. Bleibner’s
nephew wrote before he died. He referred to himself as a leper.
Now, why would he do that?”

“I don't know.”

“Because he believed he had a disease. A disease that Dr. Ames
had told him he had. Dr. Ames had convinced him that he was
suffering from leprosy, in order to drive him to suicide. It was
a cruel and heartless plan, but it worked.”

“But how did you know that Dr. Ames had told him that?”

“I didn't, not for sure. But it was the only thing that made
sense. And once I began to suspect Dr. Ames, everything else fell
into place.”

“And the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’?”

“As I said, Hastings, the force of superstition is a very powerful
thing. Dr. Ames used it to his advantage, but in the end, it was
his undoing. He forgot that even the most powerful curse cannot
protect a murderer from the truth.”

We sat in silence for a while, looking out over the desert. The
stars were beginning to come out, and the air was still and cool.

“It is a beautiful place, is it not, Hastings?”

“It is, Poirot. A beautiful and mysterious place.”

“And now,” said Poirot, rising, “it is time for us to leave. The
dead King can rest in peace at last.”

We walked back to our tent, the sound of our footsteps muffled by
the soft, golden sand.

The next day, we left the camp and began our journey back to
Cairo. As we rode away on our camels, I looked back one last time
at the Tomb of Men-her-Ra. It stood there, silent and inscrutable,
a testament to a civilization that had long since passed away.

And as I looked, I couldn't help wondering if, somewhere deep
inside that tomb, the spirit of the old King was finally at rest.

Poirot, of course, was already busy brushing the dust off his coat.

“Ah, Hastings,” he said, “the sand! It is everywhere! I shall be
glad to get back to civilization.”

I laughed and turned my camel towards the horizon. It had been an
adventure I would never forget. And as for Hercule Poirot, he had
once again proved that, no matter how powerful the curse, the
truth will always prevail.

THE END.

For answer Poirot produced a little book from his pocket—an ancient
tattered volume. As he held it out I saw its title, _The Magic of
the Egyptians and Chaldeans_. Then, wheeling round, he strode out
of the tent. The doctor stared at me.

“What is his little idea?”

The phrase, so familiar on Poirot’s lips, made me smile as it came
from another.

“I don’t know exactly,” I confessed. “He’s got some plan of
exorcizing the evil spirits, I believe.”

I went in search of Poirot, and found him talking to the lean-faced
young man who had been the late Mr. Bleibner’s secretary.

“No,” Mr. Harper was saying, “I’ve only been six months with the
expedition. Yes, I knew Mr. Bleibner’s affairs pretty well.”

“Can you recount to me anything concerning his nephew?”

“Rupert? Oh, a young ne’er-do-well. His uncle couldn’t stand him
at any price. It wasn’t a case of love lost between them. Why,
only last year——”

“You are referring to something that occurred?”

“Yes. Rupert came out here, into the camp. He hadn’t a cent to his
name, and his uncle had just had a stroke of luck—the discovery of
the Tomb, you know. He hoped for a share, but his uncle would have
nothing to say to him. He was for kicking him out of the camp
forthwith. However, the others pleaded for him, and so he stayed
on for a bit. But he was a sulky sort of chap, and he made no
secret of his dislike for the old man. I was sorry for him myself,
because I know what it is to be down on one’s luck. I gave him a
bit myself, in a small way, to help him on. But it was no use.
When Sir John died he got the idea into his head that his uncle
had had something to do with it—some sort of black magic, he
called it—and he started a regular row. After that, of course,
there was nothing for it but for him to go. He went off to New
York, and the next we heard was that he’d shot himself. Poor
fellow, he’d always been a bit of a failure.”

“He was not at all an Egyptologist, then?”

“Lord, no! He knew no more about it than—well, than I do myself.”

“Then why should he have had these ideas about black magic?”

Harper shrugged his shoulders.

“Oh, I don’t know. He was a queer fish altogether. He had a theory
that his uncle was a sort of reincarnation of an old Egyptian
priest, or something of that kind.”

Poirot’s eyes gleamed for a moment. He thanked the young man and
turned away. I joined him.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all? A strange case,
_n’est-ce pas_? This young Rupert Bleibner, now, he interests me.
Yes, he interests me very much.”

“He seems to have been a very unpleasant young man,” I remarked.

“Possibly, possibly. But his death, Hastings, his death. You
remember what he wrote in that last letter of his—that he was a
leper and an outcast? A strange choice of words, was it not? A
leper! Why a leper?”

“It was just a way of speaking, I suppose,” I suggested.

“Perhaps, perhaps. But I should like to know more about this young
Rupert. Tell me, Hastings, what did you think of the others?”

“Dr. Tosswill seems a very capable man,” I said. “And Dr. Ames
is a very pleasant fellow.”

“And Mr. Harper?”

“He’s a very ordinary type of young American, I should say.”

Poirot nodded.

“Yes, an ordinary young man. Not at all the sort of person to be
mixed up in anything—well, unusual. And yet—and yet——”

He broke off and stood looking out over the desert. The sun was
setting in a glory of gold and crimson. For a moment the vast
expanse of sand seemed to be drenched in blood.

“It is beautiful, is it not?” said a voice behind us.

It was Dr. Ames. He had come up unobserved.

“But it is also terrible,” he added. “There is something about
Egypt—something old and evil—that gets into one’s blood. I shall
be glad to be back in London, I can tell you.”

“You are going back soon, then?” asked Poirot.

“As soon as I can be spared. Sir Guy is better now—he’s got over
the first shock of his father’s death—and I don’t think there’s
much more for me to do here. I’m a Londoner, Monsieur Poirot, and
I don’t breathe freely when I’m away from the sound of Big Ben.”

He laughed, but it seemed to me that there was a certain lack of
sincerity in his mirth. He looked tired and overstrained.

“Well, I must be getting back to the camp,” he said. “Good-night
to you both.”

He turned and walked away. Poirot stood looking after him for a
moment.

“A very pleasant fellow, as you say, Hastings. But he is not happy.
No, he is not happy at all.”

“I suppose it’s the effect of all these deaths,” I suggested. “It
must be very trying for a medical man.”

“Perhaps, perhaps. But there is something else—something that I
do not yet understand. Tell me, Hastings, did you notice anything
peculiar about his manner?”

“No, I can’t say I did.”

“Ah! Well, perhaps it is only my imagination. But I have a feeling,
Hastings, a very strong feeling, that we are on the eve of some
great discovery.”

He would say no more, and we returned to the camp in silence.

“He didn’t mention him. The old man was a regular old crab, you
know, and I never thought he had a relation in the world until
I saw of this fellow’s death in the papers. He was a bad lot,
wasn’t he?”

“He was—unlucky,” said Poirot softly. “He had spent all his money
and was at the end of his tether. Was there no one else whom Mr.
Bleibner would be likely to leave his money to?”

“He left a large sum to various museums, but the bulk of it went
to his son. He had a son, you know.”

“No, I did not know.”

“Oh, yes. But they had a regular break-up about ten years ago.
The boy was—well, he was a bit of a handful, I believe. He went
off to Australia, and no one’s heard of him since.”

“_Tiens_!” said Poirot, “that is interesting. Very interesting
indeed.”

He stood for a moment, lost in thought.

“Did Mr. Bleibner ever mention this son?”

“Never. He was a very close-mouthed old man.”

“Then it is possible that he was dead?”

“Oh, yes, it’s quite likely. I don’t think he’d have been mentioned
in the will in any case.”

Poirot’s face had become very grave.

“One more thing, Mr. Harper. Was there anything about this tomb
which struck you as being particularly unusual? Any—well, any
supernatural manifestations?”

The young man laughed.

“Not a sign of one, Monsieur Poirot. I’m not at all a superstitious
person. I’m a hard-headed New Yorker, and I don’t believe in
spooks.”

“You are a very sensible young man,” said Poirot, nodding his
head. “Now I want to have a talk with Hassan.”

Hassan was the native servant of Sir John Willard. He was a tall,
stately man with a fine presence. He spoke English fairly well,
but with a strong accent.

“Yes, my master was a good man. He was very kind to me. It is a
great grief to me that he is dead.”

“You have been with him a long time?”

“Many years, Monsieur Poirot. Since I was a boy.”

“And you think that his death was—due to the Curse of Men-her-Ra?”

The man’s face became very solemn.

“It is not for me to say, monsieur. But the Great King was a powerful
magician, and those who disturb his rest must pay the penalty.”

“You believe that?”

“I know it, monsieur.”

“Then you are not surprised at these other deaths?”

“No, monsieur. They were to be expected. The Great King will not
be denied.”

“And what of Sir Guy Willard? Is he also in danger?”

“I cannot say, monsieur. But I fear for him—I fear for him
greatly.”

He moved away with a dignified gesture.

Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of it all?”

“I don’t know what to think. It’s a most extraordinary business.
But you—you don’t really believe in this curse, do you?”

Poirot’s eyes twinkled.

“My dear Hastings, I believe in everything—until it is proved to
be untrue. That is my method. Now let us go and find Dr. Tosswill.”

We found the British expert in one of the smaller tents. He was
busy over some pottery fragments.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot, have you found out anything yet?”

“I have found out that you are a very skeptical man, Dr. Tosswill.”

The doctor laughed.

“I’m a man of science, Monsieur Poirot. I don’t believe in anything
that can’t be explained by natural causes.”

“And yet,” said Poirot softly, “there are many things in this world
which cannot be explained by natural causes.”

“Perhaps. But the death of Sir John Willard was not one of them.
He was an old man, and his heart was not strong. The heat and the
excitement were too much for him. As for Mr. Bleibner, septicæmia
is a very common thing in this country. And the nephew in New
York—well, that was just a coincidence.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“Tetanus is also not uncommon. The soil here is full of the
bacillus.”

“But it is a very strange coincidence that all these deaths should
have occurred just at this time.”

“Coincidences do happen, Monsieur Poirot.”

“I agree with you. They do. But when they happen too often, one
begins to wonder.”

He paused for a moment, and then went on.

“Tell me, Dr. Tosswill, was there anything unusual about the
opening of the tomb? Anything—well, anything that might be
interpreted as a bad omen?”

The doctor looked at him curiously.

“I see you’ve been talking to the natives, Monsieur Poirot. They’re
full of all sorts of stories. No, there was nothing unusual—except,
perhaps, for the fact that a jackal was seen near the entrance
just before we went in.”

“A jackal? That is the symbol of Anubis, the god of the dead.”

“Exactly. The natives made a great deal of it, of course. But it
was probably just a common jackal.”

“Perhaps. And yet—it is a strange coincidence, is it not?”

Poirot turned away and we walked back towards the main camp.

“Well, Hastings,” he said, “what do you make of Dr. Tosswill?”

“He seems a very sensible, level-headed man,” I replied.

“Yes. A very sensible man. Too sensible, perhaps.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, _mon ami_, that sometimes it is the most sensible people
who are the most easily deceived.”

I looked at him in surprise, but he would say no more.

That evening we dined with Sir Guy Willard and Dr. Ames. The
conversation was mostly about the excavations and the wonderful
treasures that had been found in the tomb. But under it all there
was a sense of uneasiness, a feeling that something was wrong.

After dinner, Poirot and I went for a stroll in the desert. The
moon was full, and the Pyramids looked like giant ghosts in the
pale light.

“It is a beautiful night, Hastings,” said Poirot. “A night for
dreams—and for nightmares.”

He was silent for a long time, looking out over the sand.

“Do you know, Hastings,” he said at last, “I am beginning to have
an idea. A very strange idea.”

“What is it?” I asked eagerly.

“I cannot tell you yet. I must think it over. But if I am right—if
I am right, then we are in the presence of a very clever and a
very cold-blooded murderer.”

“A murderer? But who——?”

“That is what I have to find out. But I think—I think I know where
to look.”

He would say no more, and we returned to the camp in silence.

The next morning, Poirot was up early. He spent most of the day
talking to the workmen and the various members of the expedition.
He seemed particularly interested in Mr. Harper, the secretary.

“A very pleasant young man,” he said to me later. “Very pleasant
and very efficient. But he is a little—how shall I say?—a little
too anxious to please.”

“I didn't notice it,” I said.

“No, Hastings, you would not. You are too honest yourself to
suspect others of being anything else. But I—I have a suspicious
nature. It is my profession.”

In the afternoon, we went with Sir Guy Willard to the tomb itself.
It was a wonderful sight, the walls covered with beautiful
paintings and the chambers filled with priceless treasures.

“It is magnificent, Sir Guy,” said Poirot. “Truly magnificent.”

“It is the work of my life, Monsieur Poirot,” said the young man.
“I will not let anything—not even the fear of death—stop me from
completing it.”

As we were leaving the tomb, Poirot stopped and looked back.

“The Great King Men-her-Ra,” he murmured. “He has slept here for
thousands of years. And now we have disturbed his rest. Is it any
wonder that he is angry?”

Sir Guy laughed, but it was a nervous laugh.

“You still believe in that, Monsieur Poirot?”

“I believe in the power of the past, Sir Guy. It is a power that
we should not underestimate.”

That night, as I was falling asleep, I heard a sound outside my
tent. It was a low, mournful cry, like the howl of a wolf. Or a
jackal.

I shivered and drew the blankets closer around me.

The next day, the blow fell.

We were sitting at lunch when a workman came running into the tent.
He was breathless and his face was grey with fear.

“The master!” he cried. “The master! He is dead!”

We all jumped up and followed him. In one of the smaller excavation
chambers, we found Dr. Tosswill. He was lying on his face, his
hands clenched in the sand.

Dr. Ames knelt down beside him and turned him over. He felt his
pulse and listened to his heart. Then he looked up at us, his face
grave.

“He is dead,” he said.

“What was it?” asked Sir Guy in a whisper. “Another heart attack?”

Dr. Ames shook his head.

“No. Look.”

He pointed to a small red mark on the back of the doctor’s neck.

“It looks like a sting,” he said. “A scorpion sting, perhaps. Or
a snake bite.”

“But there are no scorpions or snakes in this chamber,” said Sir
Guy. “We searched it thoroughly only yesterday.”

“Then how did it happen?” I asked.

Poirot, who had been standing silently by, stepped forward.

“It happened, _mon ami_, because someone wanted him dead.”

He looked round at the little group of men.

“This is not the work of a ghost, or a curse. it is the work of
a man. A very clever and a very dangerous man.”

“But who?” cried Sir Guy. “Who would want to kill Dr. Tosswill? He
was the most harmless man in the world.”

“That is what I intend to find out,” said Poirot. “And I think I
know where to begin.”

He turned to Mr. Harper.

“Mr. Harper, I would like to have another talk with you. In private.”

The young man looked surprised, but he followed Poirot out of the
chamber.

I stayed behind with Sir Guy and Dr. Ames. We were all stunned by
this latest tragedy.

“I can’t believe it,” said Sir Guy. “First my father, then Mr.
Bleibner, then Mr. Schneider, and now Dr. Tosswill. It’s—it’s
incredible.”

“It is more than incredible, Sir Guy,” said Dr. Ames. “It is
diabolical.”

A few minutes later, Poirot returned. He looked very grave.

“Well?” I asked. “Did you find out anything?”

“I found out several things, Hastings. Several very interesting
things.”

“Tell us!” cried Sir Guy.

“Not yet. I must make certain of one or two points first. But I
can tell you this: the murderer is here, in this camp. And I know
who he is.”

We all stared at him in amazement.

“You know who he is?” said Dr. Ames. “Then why don't you arrest
him?”

“Because I have no proof. Not yet. But I shall have it. I shall
have it very soon.”

He turned to me.

“Hastings, I want you to do something for me.”

“Anything,” I said.

“I want you to go to Cairo. I have a list of things I want you to
find out. It is very important.”

“I'll go at once,” I said.

“Good. Here is the list. And be careful, Hastings. Be very
careful.”

I took the list and left the camp. It was a long and tiring journey,
but I was determined to do what Poirot had asked.

In Cairo, I spent several days visiting various officials and
making enquiries. It was not easy, but slowly the pieces of the
puzzle began to fall into place.

When I returned to the camp, Poirot was waiting for me.

“Well, Hastings? What have you found out?”

I told him everything I had learned. He listened intently, nodding
his head from time to time.

“Excellent, Hastings! Excellent! You have done well. Now I have
all the information I need.”

“Then you know who the murderer is?” I asked.

“Yes, Hastings. I know.”

He gathered everyone together in the main tent. Sir Guy, Dr. Ames,
Mr. Harper and Hassan were all there.

“Messieurs,” said Poirot, “I have called you here to tell you the
truth about the deaths that have occurred in this camp.”

He paused for a moment, looking at each of them in turn.

“For a long time, we have been led to believe that these deaths
were the result of a curse—the Curse of Men-her-Ra. It was a very
clever idea, a very effective way of covering up a series of cold-blooded
murders.”

“Murders?” cried Sir Guy. “But how? And why?”

“The why is simple, Sir Guy. It is the oldest motive in the world:
money.”

He turned to Mr. Harper.

“Mr. Harper, you told me that Mr. Bleibner had a son who went to
Australia and was never heard of again. That was not quite true,
was it?”

The young man turned pale.

“I—I don’t know what you mean.”

“I think you do. You see, Hastings has been busy in Cairo. He has
found out that Mr. Bleibner’s son did indeed go to Australia. But
he did not stay there. He returned to England, under a different
name. A name that you know very well.”

He turned to Dr. Ames.

“That name, monsieur le docteur, was yours.”

There was a moment of stunned silence. Then Dr. Ames laughed.

“This is ridiculous! Are you suggesting that I am Mr. Bleibner’s
son?”

“I am not suggesting it, Dr. Ames. I am stating it as a fact.
You are the son who was disinherited by his father. And when you
heard that your father was financing this expedition, you saw your
chance. You joined the expedition as a doctor, waiting for the
right moment to strike.”

“But my father died of blood poisoning!” cried Dr. Ames.

“A blood poisoning that was very easily induced, was it not? A
simple scratch, a little infected material... it was all very easy
for a doctor.”

“And Sir John Willard?” asked Sir Guy.

“His death was an accident. But it served Dr. Ames’s purpose very
well. It gave him the idea of the curse. He knew that if he could
make people believe in the curse, no one would suspect him of
murder.”

“And the nephew in New York?” I asked.

“That was also part of the plan. Dr. Ames knew that if the nephew
were to die, he would be the sole heir to his father’s fortune.
So he sent him a letter—a letter that drove the young man to
suicide. It was a very clever piece of psychological murder.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“He was beginning to get suspicious. He had noticed something—I
don’t know what—that made him think that Mr. Bleibner’s death was
not accidental. So he had to be removed. Tetanus is a very painful
way to die, is it not, Dr. Ames?”

The doctor said nothing. He just stared at Poirot with a look of
pure hatred.

“And finally, Dr. Tosswill,” continued Poirot. “He was also
becoming a danger. He was a man of science, and he was beginning
to look for a natural explanation for these deaths. He had noticed the
mark on Mr. Schneider’s neck, and he was starting to make
connections. So he, too, had to be killed.”

“But how?” asked Sir Guy. “How did he do it?”

“It was very simple. He used a small, poisoned needle. A needle
that left a mark like a sting. He could easily have used it while
he was examining Dr. Tosswill, or even while they were just talking.”

Poirot turned to Dr. Ames.

“Well, Dr. Ames? What have you to say for yourself?”

The doctor did not answer. Instead, he suddenly reached into his
pocket and pulled out a small glass phial. Before anyone could
stop him, he had swallowed the contents.

He fell to the floor, his body convulsed with pain. Within minutes,
he was dead.

“Cyanide,” said Poirot, looking down at the body. “A quick and
painless death. More than he deserved.”

He turned to Sir Guy.

“I am sorry, Sir Guy. I know this is a great shock to you.”

The young man shook his head.

“It’s alright, Monsieur Poirot. I—I just can’t believe that someone
could be so evil.”

“The human heart is a dark and mysterious place, Sir Guy,” said
Poirot. “And sometimes, the most dangerous monsters are the ones
that look the most human.”

We left the camp the next day. As we rode away on our camels, I
looked back at the tomb of King Men-her-Ra.

“Do you think the curse is really over now, Poirot?” I asked.

Poirot smiled.

“The only curse, Hastings, is the curse of human greed. And as
long as there is money in the world, that curse will never be over.”

He adjusted his hat and looked out over the desert.

“And now, _mon ami_, let us go home. I have had quite enough of
the sand.”

“Not much. I only met him once, and he didn’t make a good
impression on me. He struck me as a young man who was more than
usually ‘down and out.’ He had a way of being very mysterious
about his prospects—always expecting a windfall.”

“He had been here, then?”

“Oh, yes, he was with us for a week or so, just before his uncle
died.”

“And what about this Dr. Tosswill?”

“Oh, he was a very old friend of Sir John’s. He’s a first-rate
Egyptologist, and he’s been with the expedition from the very
beginning.”

“I see. Now, will you please tell me, was there any talk of
interrupting the excavations after Sir John’s death?”

“None. It was decided to carry on as before.”

“By whom?”

“By Mr. Bleibner.”

“I see. Thank you.”

Poirot turned away, and I followed him.

“What’s your game, Poirot?” I asked.

“My game, Hastings? It is to examine everything, that is all. It
is more than ever mysterious.”

“What is?”

“The variety of these deaths! They are so diverse that they would
seem to be the result of a chance—or else of a very cunningly
contrived plan. But how could any one man have brought them all
about? And why?”

He was walking along in a brown study. Suddenly he looked up at me.

“Hastings, I must go and speak with Hassan. You go back to the
tent.”

I found Sir Guy and the doctor together.

“What’s your friend doing?” asked Dr. Ames.

“I haven’t the least idea,” I admitted.

“I’m sure I don’t want to be disrespectful,” said the doctor,
with a smile, “but it’s my belief that your friend’s a bit of an
ass. Or else he’s trying to pull our legs.”

“I shouldn’t be too sure of that,” I said.

Just then Poirot came into the tent. He looked quite excited.

“Listen, Sir Guy, I have a request to make. Will you give me
permission to spend the night in the Tomb of Men-her-Ra?”

“What?” cried Sir Guy.

“It is my wish.”

Sir Guy shrugged his shoulders.

“Certainly, if you wish it. But I should have thought that, after
all you’ve said about the supernatural——”

“It is because of that that I wish to be there. I will go now and
make my preparations.”

He was gone again. He would not allow me to accompany him.

“No, no, Hastings. I must be alone. You stay here with the others.”

The evening passed slowly. Sir Guy was moody and silent. Dr. Ames
was inclined to be talkative, but his remarks were mostly of a
sarcastic nature. Dr. Tosswill sat apart, deep in a book. Mr.
Harper was also present.

It was about ten o’clock when a sudden cry from outside the tent
startled us. We all sprang to our feet.

“What was that?” cried Sir Guy.

We rushed out. Standing near the entrance to the tomb was the figure
of a man, his arms raised to heaven. It was Hassan. He was gabbling
incoherent Arabic.

“What is it?” I asked.

He pointed towards the tomb.

“The spirit! The spirit of the King! It has come!”

We all looked in the direction he pointed. For a moment I thought
I saw a shadowy figure flitting among the rocks, but it might have
been only a trick of the moonlight.

“Nonsense,” said Dr. Ames. “There’s nothing there. The man’s
frightened out of his wits.”

He went up to Hassan and took him by the arm.

“Come, come, my man, pull yourself together. There’s nothing to be
afraid of.”

But Hassan continued to tremble and point.

“I saw it,” he whispered. “I saw the spirit of the King. It was
clothed in white, and its face was the face of a dead man.”

I felt a cold shiver run down my spine.

“I’m going to see if Poirot is all right,” I said.

I ran towards the tomb. As I reached the entrance I saw Poirot
coming out. He looked pale and shaken.

“What is it?” I cried. “Did you see anything?”

He shook his head.

“I saw nothing, Hastings. But I heard—I heard a sound that I shall
never forget.”

“What was it?”

“It was the sound of a woman weeping.”

“A woman?”

“Yes. A woman’s voice, full of such unutterable sorrow that it
seemed to come from the very depths of the earth.”

We all stood silent for a moment. Then Dr. Ames spoke.

“It was the wind, Monsieur Poirot. The wind often makes strange
noises among these rocks.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “Perhaps you are right.”

But I could see that he was not convinced.

We went back to the tent. Poirot refused to say anything more about
his experience in the tomb. He seemed to be sunk in a deep
meditation.

The next morning he was up early. He seemed to have recovered his
spirits.

“_Eh bien_, Hastings,” he said, as we sat at breakfast. “I have
arrived at a conclusion.”

“Already?”

“But yes. It is quite simple, when one has the—how do you say
it?—the ‘flair.’ Everything points to one person.”

“Who is it?” I asked eagerly.

He shook his head.

“Not yet, Hastings. I must have one more piece of evidence. And
for that I must go to Cairo.”

“Can I come with you?”

“No, no. You stay here and keep an eye on things. I shall be back
this evening.”

He was as good as his word. He arrived back just as we were sitting
down to dinner. He looked tired but satisfied.

“I have it!” he whispered to me, as we went into the tent. “The
last link in the chain.”

Dinner was a silent meal. We were all thinking of the events of the
previous night. After dinner, Poirot stood up.

“Messieurs,” he said, “I have a few words to say to you. As you
know, I came here to investigate the deaths that have occurred in
connection with this expedition. I have now completed my
investigation.”

There was a sudden stir among the company.

“You know who the murderer is?” asked Sir Guy.

“I do.”

“Then why don’t you tell us?” cried Dr. Ames.

Poirot looked at him steadily.

“Because, _monsieur le docteur_, I wish to give the murderer one
last chance.”

“A chance for what?”

“To confess. It will be better for him in the end.”

There was a long silence. No one spoke.

“Very well,” said Poirot. “Since no one will speak, I must name the
guilty person. The person who is responsible for the deaths of Sir
John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, and Mr. Schneider—and also for the
suicide of young Rupert Bleibner.”

He paused for a moment, his eyes travelling round the circle of
faces. Then he pointed a finger.

“The murderer,” he said, “is——”

At that moment, there was a sudden commotion outside the tent. A
native servant rushed in, his face grey with terror.

“The spirit!” he cried. “The spirit of the King! It is here again!”

We all rushed out. The scene was the same as on the previous night.
Hassan was standing near the tomb, his arms raised, his face
convulsed with fear.

“There!” he cried. “There!”

We looked in the direction he pointed. This time there was no
mistake. A tall, white figure was standing by the entrance to the
tomb. Its face was masked, but its eyes seemed to glow with an unearthly
light.

“Stop!” cried Poirot. “I know who you are!”

The figure turned and fled into the darkness. We all started in
pursuit. But the figure was too quick for us. It vanished among the
rocks.

“It is no use,” said Poirot. “We shall never catch it now. But it
does not matter. I know who it was.”

We went back to the tent.

“Who was it?” asked Sir Guy.

“It was the murderer,” said Poirot. “And now, messieurs, I will
tell you his name.”

He looked at each of us in turn.

“The murderer,” he said, “is Dr. Tosswill.”

There was a gasp of astonishment.

“Dr. Tosswill!” I cried. “But why? How?”

“It is very simple,” said Poirot. “Dr. Tosswill is a great
Egyptologist, as we all know. But he is also a man of great
ambition. He wanted the glory of this discovery all for himself.
He knew that Sir John Willard and Mr. Bleibner would never allow
him to take the credit. So he decided to get rid of them.”

“But how did he do it?” asked Sir Guy.

“He used his knowledge of Ancient Egypt to create the impression
of a curse. He knew that if he could make people believe in the
vengeance of the King, he would be able to commit his crimes with
impunity. He killed Sir John Willard by injecting him with a rare
and deadly poison which leaves no trace. He did the same with Mr.
Bleibner. And he killed Mr. Schneider by infecting him with
tetanus.”

“And young Rupert Bleibner?” I asked.

“He was the one who nearly ruined everything. He had seen Dr.
Tosswill doing something suspicious, and he had tried to blackmail
him. Dr. Tosswill realized that he had to get rid of him too. He
persuaded him that he was under the curse of the King, and that the
only way he could escape it was by taking his own life. The poor
young man, already weakened by his life of dissipation, believed
him.”

“But what about the spirit?” I asked. “Who was that?”

“That was Dr. Tosswill himself,” said Poirot. “He used a mask and
a white robe to frighten the natives and to keep up the illusion
of the curse. He was trying to frighten us away when he appeared
to-night.”

Dr. Tosswill stood up. He looked pale, but he was quite calm.

“You are a very clever man, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “But you
have no proof.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot. “I have all the proof I need. I
found the poison in your medicine chest, and I have a witness who
saw you entering Mr. Schneider’s tent on the night he died.”

Dr. Tosswill’s face changed. He realized that the game was up.

“Very well,” he said. “I confess. I did it all. But I would do it
again. I am the greatest Egyptologist in the world, and I deserve
all the credit for this discovery.”

He was led away by the guards.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we sat in our tent later that night.
“You’ve done it again. But tell me, how did you know it was Dr.
Tosswill?”

“It was the clothes-brush, Hastings,” said Poirot, with a smile.

“The clothes-brush?”

“Yes. You remember how I was always brushing my clothes? Well, I
noticed that Dr. Tosswill was never doing so. And yet his clothes
were always clean. That could only mean one thing—he was not
spending his time in the desert like the rest of us. He was
spending it in the tomb, where there is no dust. And that is where
he was keeping his poisons and his disguises.”

I looked at Poirot in admiration.

“You are a genius, Poirot,” I said.

“I know,” said Poirot. “It is a great responsibility.”

“Rupert? Oh, he was a bad egg, right enough. He’d run through a
couple of fortunes in New York, and had been a general bad lot for
years. He came out here about three months ago, but his uncle
wouldn’t have anything to do with him.”

“Did he ever speak to you of his uncle’s death?”

“No. I don’t think he’d heard of it then. He was in New York, you
see.”

“I mean, after his return to New York?”

“I haven’t seen him since.”

“He did not write to you?”

“No.”

“You are quite sure of that?”

“Quite sure.”

“And you were with Mr. Bleibner when he died?”

“No. I was in Cairo at the time.”

“I see.”

Poirot turned away, and I followed him.

“Well,” he said, when we were alone, “the story seems to be a very
pretty one, and no one would wish to see it simplified. But I like
simplicity, Hastings. The _crime passionnel_ is so much more
artistic.”

“The _crime passionnel_!” I cried. “You don’t mean that you think
this is a crime of passion?”

“I didn’t say so, Hastings. I merely said that I liked it.”

The little man was in one of his most aggravating moods. We were
sitting on the sand, and he was carefully building a little pyramid
out of five of the smaller stones.

“_Tiens_,” he exclaimed, as he added the fifth. “The shape is at
least correct. Now, why did Rupert Bleibner kill himself? That is
a thing which does not interest our friends. It was not because
of remorse for having killed his uncle—his uncle died of septicæmia,
not poison. Then what was it? He was a young man who had no
conscience, remember. Why then should he kill himself?”

I suggested that he might have been in even greater difficulties
than we knew.

“It is possible,” said Poirot, “but it does not satisfy me. There
is something else. Something we do not know.”

“You think there is more behind it?”

“Yes. There is a great deal behind it. But we shall see, Hastings.
We shall see.”

He began to hum a little tune to himself, and his eyes had that
faraway look which I knew so well. I felt that he was on the track
of something.

The next few days passed quietly enough. We spent most of our time
at the excavations, where the work was proceeding steadily. The
excitement of the discovery of the Tomb of King Men-her-Ra was now
over, and the more prosaic work of clearing and cataloguing the
contents of the chambers was in progress.

One afternoon, we were sitting in the shade of a rock, when we
were joined by Dr. Ames.

“I’m glad to find you here,” he said. “I wanted to have a talk with
you. You’ve been here some days now, Monsieur Poirot. What do you
think of the situation?”

Poirot looked at him thoughtfully.

“It is a strange one,” he said. “A very strange one.”

“You’ve heard the latest?”

“No. What is it?”

“One of the native workmen has been taken ill. He’s got all the
symptoms of—well, I don’t like to say what I suspect.”

“Not tetanus?” I cried.

“No, not tetanus. It’s more like—bubonic plague.”

I felt a cold shiver run down my spine.

“Bubonic plague!” I exclaimed. “But that’s impossible! There hasn’t
been a case of it in this part of the country for years.”

“I know,” said the doctor. “That’s what makes it so strange. But
the symptoms are unmistakable.”

“And the man?” asked Poirot.

“He’s very ill. I don’t think he’ll recover.”

“Is there any chance of it spreading?”

“I hope not. We’ve isolated him, of course, but you never can tell
with these things.”

He was silent for a moment, and then he added:

“It’s a queer business, Monsieur Poirot. First one thing, then
another. It’s almost as if—as if there were something in this story
of the Curse, after all.”

Poirot did not answer, and the doctor, after a few more words,
left us.

“What do you think of it, Poirot?” I asked.

“I think,” said Poirot, “that it is very interesting. Very
interesting indeed.”

“But the plague!” I cried. “Surely you don’t think that the Curse
could—could cause that?”

“The Curse can cause many things, Hastings. But we must wait. We
must wait and see.”

That evening, as we were sitting at dinner in the mess-tent, there
was a sudden commotion outside. One of the native boys rushed in,
crying out in Arabic.

“What is it?” asked Sir Guy, who had some knowledge of the language.

“He says,” translated Dr. Tosswill, “that the man is dead.”

“Which man?”

“The one who was taken ill this afternoon.”

A hush fell upon the little party. We all looked at each other in
consternation.

“This is getting serious,” said Sir Guy. “If this gets out, we
shall have a panic among the men.”

“It’s out already,” said Dr. Ames. “You can’t keep things from
them. They’ve got it into their heads that the King is angry, and
that they’re all going to die.”

“We must do something,” said Sir Guy. “We must show them that
there’s nothing to be afraid of.”

“How?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“I don’t know. But we must do something.”

The rest of the evening was spent in anxious discussion. It was
decided that Sir Guy should speak to the men the next morning,
and try to reassure them.

But the next morning brought fresh disaster. When the men went to
their work, they found that one of their number was missing. He
was a man who had been particularly loud in his expressions of
fear the night before.

A search was made, and his body was found at the bottom of one of
the excavation shafts. He had evidently fallen down in the dark,
and his neck was broken.

This was the finishing touch. The men refused to work any longer.
They declared that the Tomb was cursed, and that they would have
nothing more to do with it.

In vain Sir Guy and Dr. Tosswill argued with them. They were
adamant. They packed up their belongings and started off across
the desert.

By midday, the camp was almost deserted. Only Sir Guy, Dr. Tosswill,
Dr. Ames, Mr. Harper, Hassan, Poirot and myself were left.

“Well,” said Sir Guy, with a grim smile, “it looks as if we’re
beaten. We can’t go on without the men.”

“We must wait,” said Poirot. “We must wait and see.”

“Wait for what?” asked Sir Guy. “For another of us to die?”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot.

I looked at him in horror. He seemed to be perfectly serious.

The afternoon passed in a state of tension. We were all on edge,
watching each other, wondering who would be the next victim.

As the sun began to set, Poirot called us all together in the
mess-tent.

“Messieurs,” he said, “we are in a very grave position. Five deaths
have already occurred, and there may be more. It is time that we
looked the facts in the face.”

“What do you mean?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that we must find out the truth. Is it
the Curse of Men-her-Ra, or is it something else?”

“What else could it be?” asked Sir Guy.

“That is what we have to find out. And to do that, we must use our
intelligence. We must use our little grey cells.”

He paused, and looked round at us.

“I have been thinking,” he continued. “I have been thinking very
much. And I have come to a conclusion.”

“And what is that?” asked Dr. Ames.

“I will tell you,” said Poirot. “But first, I must ask you all a
question. Where were you on the night that Mr. Bleibner died?”

We all looked at him in surprise.

“I was in Cairo,” said Mr. Harper.

“I was in my tent,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“I was with Mr. Bleibner,” said Dr. Ames.

“I was with my father,” said Sir Guy.

“And you, Hassan?” asked Poirot.

The native servant, who was standing by the door, replied in
Arabic.

“He says,” translated Sir Guy, “that he was outside the tent of
his master.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And where were you on the night that Sir
John Willard died?”

“I was in Cairo,” said Mr. Harper.

“I was in my tent,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“I was with Sir John,” said Dr. Ames.

“I was in England,” said Sir Guy.

“And you, Hassan?”

“He says,” translated Sir Guy, “that he was with his master.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. “And where were you on the night that
Mr. Schneider died?”

“I was in Cairo,” said Mr. Harper.

“I was in my tent,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“I was with Mr. Schneider,” said Dr. Ames.

“I was in my tent,” said Sir Guy.

“And you, Hassan?”

“He says,” translated Sir Guy, “that he was in the camp.”

“I see,” said Poirot for the third time.

“And what do you see?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“I see,” said Poirot, “that Dr. Ames was present at all three
deaths.”

There was a moment of dead silence. Then Dr. Ames spoke.

“Are you suggesting,” he said, in a low, dangerous voice, “that I
had something to do with those deaths?”

“I am suggesting nothing,” said Poirot. “I am merely stating a
fact.”

“It’s a fact that I’m the doctor to the expedition!” cried Ames.
“Of course I was present! It was my duty to be present!”

“Precisely,” said Poirot. “And it was also your duty to see that
they did not die. But they did die.”

“You’re mad!” cried Ames. “You’re absolutely mad!”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But let us go on. There is another death
to be considered—the death of Rupert Bleibner.”

“But he was in New York!” cried Mr. Harper.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “He was in New York. And yet, he died.
And he died because he was a ‘leper and an outcast’. Those were
his own words, remember.”

“What of it?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“This,” said Poirot. “Rupert Bleibner was not a leper. He was a
man who had been told that he was a leper. And he was told so by
someone he trusted—someone who had a reason for wanting him out
of the way.”

“And who was that?” asked Sir Guy.

“That,” said Poirot, “was the person who stood to gain by his
death. The person who would inherit Mr. Bleibner’s fortune if
Rupert were dead.”

“But Mr. Bleibner left his money to his nephew!” cried Mr. Harper.

“I know,” said Poirot. “But if the nephew were dead, who would
inherit then?”

“I don’t know,” said Mr. Harper. “I suppose it would go to his
next of kin.”

“And who is his next of kin?”

“I don’t think he had any. He was an only child, and his parents
are both dead.”

“Then,” said Poirot, “the money would go to the person named in
his will as his residuary legatee.”

“And who is that?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I have been trying to find out. And
I think I have found out.”

He looked at Dr. Ames.

“Dr. Ames,” he said, “is it not a fact that you were a close friend
of Mr. Bleibner?”

“Yes,” said the doctor. “We were very close friends.”

“And is it not a fact that he had a great deal of confidence in
you?”

“I believe so.”

“And is it not a fact that he made a will shortly before his death,
in which he left you a very large sum of money?”

The doctor paled.

“I—I don’t know,” he stammered.

“I think you do,” said Poirot. “And I think you also knew that
if Rupert Bleibner were dead, you would inherit even more.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Ames. “A damnable lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “We shall see. I have cabled to New York
for a copy of the will. It should be here at any moment.”

Even as he spoke, one of the native boys came in with a cablegram.
Poirot took it, tore it open, and read it.

“Yes,” he said, “it is as I thought. Dr. Ames is the residuary
legatee.”

There was another moment of silence. Then the doctor made a sudden
movement. But before he could do anything, Poirot had produced a
revolver from his pocket.

“Stay where you are, monsieur,” he said. “I have no wish to kill
you, but I will if I have to.”

The doctor sank back into his chair, his face a ghastly grey.

“And now,” said Poirot, “I will tell you how it was done. It was
not the Curse of Men-her-Ra. It was a much more modern curse—the
curse of greed.”

“Mr. Bleibner was a wealthy man. Dr. Ames wanted that wealth. He
knew that Mr. Bleibner was not a young man, and that he might not
live many more years. But he wanted the money now. So he decided
to hasten matters.”

“He knew that Sir John Willard was also in a precarious state of
health. He had a weak heart. It would not take much to kill him.
A little fright—a little suggestion of the supernatural—and the
work would be done.”

“So he started the story of the Curse. He used the death of Sir
John to give it colour. Then he turned his attention to Mr.
Bleibner. He poisoned him—not with a common poison that could be
easily detected, but with something much more subtle. He used the
germs of septicæmia.”

“He knew that Mr. Bleibner had a scratch on his thumb. It was the
work of a moment to infect it. And the result was exactly what he
had expected.”

“Then came the nephew. He was a difficulty. He was in New York,
and it was not easy to get at him. But the doctor was resourceful.
He wrote to him—he told him that he had contracted leprosy during
his visit to Egypt. He knew that the young man was already in a
state of nervous depression. The news was the final blow. He took
his own life.”

“Then there was Mr. Schneider. He was beginning to be suspicious.
He had to be removed. And what could be more natural than that he
should die of tetanus—a common enough disease in this part of
the world?”

“But the doctor made one mistake. He used a culture of tetanus
germs that he had brought with him from England. He did not
realize that the symptoms of tetanus are very similar to those of
strychnine poisoning. And that was what first put me on the
track.”

“As for the native workman, that was a stroke of luck for the
doctor. The man really did have a touch of the plague, and his
death served to further the idea of the Curse.”

“But the doctor was not satisfied. He wanted to make sure that the
excavations would be stopped, so that no more questions would be
asked. So he killed the second workman—not with the plague, but
by pushing him down the shaft in the dark.”

“It was a clever plan, monsieur le docteur, but it did not work.
You forgot one thing—the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot!”

The doctor did not answer. He sat staring at Poirot with eyes full
of hate.

“And now,” said Poirot, “we will go back to Cairo. There are some
gentlemen there who will be very interested to meet you.”

He turned to Sir Guy.

“Sir Guy,” he said, “I think you can go on with your work now.
The Curse of Men-her-Ra is at an end.”

The young man looked at him with eyes full of gratitude.

“I don’t know how to thank you, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “You’ve
saved my life—and my father’s work.”

“It was nothing,” said Poirot, with a modest wave of his hand.
“It was just a matter of the little grey cells.”

As we rode away across the desert, I looked back at the Tomb of
King Men-her-Ra. The sun was setting, and the ancient monument
was bathed in a golden light.

“You know, Poirot,” I said, “I’m still not quite sure about that
Curse. After all, five men died.”

Poirot smiled.

“My dear Hastings,” he said, “there are many things in this world
that we do not understand. But one thing I do know—the greatest
force in the world is not the supernatural. It is the human
intelligence.”

And with that, he turned his donkey towards Cairo, and we rode on
into the gathering night.

“Not much. I only met him once. I don’t think he had much of a
character. He’d be what you’d call a weakling—but he was a good-looking
chap in a way.”

“And Mr. Bleibner? Did he seem to take an interest in his nephew’s
affairs?”

“Not a bit. In fact, he never mentioned him. I only heard of him
after the poor chap’s suicide. Mr. Bleibner had no other relations.”

“Did he leave any will?”

“Everything goes to Sir John Willard’s excavations. He had a great
belief in the work, and I think he wanted to make sure it was
continued.”

“You knew he was going to make a will to that effect?”

“I knew he had made it.”

“It would have been better for his nephew if he had not done so,
_hein_?”

The young secretary laughed.

“Much better. In fact, if there had been no will, he’d have come
into a very tidy little fortune. But there was a will—and there’s
no doubt about that.”

I could see Poirot was thinking. He stood looking out over the
stretch of sand. Then he asked:

“Where did Sir John Willard die?”

“In his tent.”

“Is that his tent?”

“No. It was pulled down after his death. That one belongs to Dr.
Tosswill.”

“And Mr. Bleibner’s?”

“That is it—the one next to it.”

“Thank you, Mr. Harper. I will go and pay my respects to Dr.
Tosswill.”

He found the doctor in his tent, surrounded by a mass of pottery
shards. He seemed busy.

“Good morning, Dr. Tosswill.”

“Good morning, Monsieur Poirot.”

The doctor did not look as though he wanted to be interrupted.

“I have come to ask you if you can tell me something about Hassan.”

“Hassan? What should I know about him? He’s a first-class servant,
one of the best.”

“How long had he been with Sir John Willard?”

“Oh, for years. He was most devoted to him.”

“Did he believe in the Curse of Men-her-Ra?”

“He’s an Arab,” said Dr. Tosswill shortly. “They’re all
superstitious.”

“And you, monsieur le docteur?”

“I? Certainly not.”

“You are a man of science, are you not? Then you can tell me this.
How was it that Mr. Schneider died of tetanus, while no one else
was affected?”

“I can’t tell you,” snapped Dr. Tosswill. “But it was tetanus.
Ames will tell you the same.”

“Ah, yes, Dr. Ames. A very capable man, I should say.”

“Ames is a very good fellow,” said Dr. Tosswill, more cordially.
“I’ve a great respect for him.”

“He is the medical officer to the expedition?”

“Yes.”

“And he was with it from the beginning?”

“Yes.”

“Thank you, Dr. Tosswill.”

Poirot walked away. As we went towards our own tent he remarked:

“A very interesting man, Dr. Tosswill. And he has a very high
opinion of Dr. Ames.”

“He seems a very capable fellow,” I agreed.

“And Hassan? What did you think of him?”

“I have not seen him yet.”

“Ah, I forgot. He was not in the tent with Sir Guy Willard.”

He said no more, but I could see that his mind was busy. That
evening, after a dinner of tinned meat and biscuits, Poirot
suggested a walk.

“It is a beautiful night, Hastings. Let us enjoy the moonlight.”

We wandered out into the desert. The Pyramids stood out, vast and
silent, against the sky. Poirot seemed to have forgotten his
dislike of the sand. He walked along with a light, springy step.

“Tell me, Hastings,” he said suddenly. “What do you think of Dr.
Ames?”

“I liked him,” I said. “He seemed a very straightforward, capable
fellow.”

“And Mr. Harper?”

“A very pleasant young man.”

“And Dr. Tosswill?”

“A bit of a bear, I should say, but a clever one.”

“And Sir Guy Willard?”

“A nice boy, but very high-strung. I’m afraid this business is
going to be too much for him.”

“It is a strange business, Hastings. Four deaths—and all so
different. And yet, if there is a common factor——?”

“The Curse of Men-her-Ra!” I suggested.

Poirot smiled.

“Perhaps. But I do not think so.”

“Then what is it?”

“That is what I am here to find out. But see, who is this?”

A tall figure in white robes was coming towards us. As it drew
near, I saw that it was a native. He bowed low as he approached.

“Peace be with you,” he said in a deep, sonorous voice.

“And with you be peace,” replied Poirot. “You are Hassan?”

“I am Hassan, the servant of the dead master.”

“You were with him when he died?”

“I was with him. He died in my arms.”

“And he said—what did he say?”

“He said: ‘Hassan, the King is angry. I have disturbed his rest,
and he is taking his revenge.’ Those were his last words.”

“And you believe him, Hassan?”

“I believe him. Did not the great King Men-her-Ra say: ‘Whosoever
shall disturb my rest, upon him shall fall the shadow of my
vengeance’?”

“It is written in the Tomb,” said Poirot.

“It is written. And it is true. Already four have died. There will
be more.”

“Who will be the next, Hassan?”

“That I cannot say. But the shadow is over the camp.”

He bowed again, and passed on into the darkness.

“A strange man,” I said, with a shiver.

“He is a man of the East,” said Poirot. “He believes what he
says.”

“And you, Poirot? Do you believe it?”

“I believe that there is a very clever and a very cold-blooded
murderer at work, Hastings.”

“A murderer? But how? There have been four deaths—all from
different causes.”

“That is the cleverness of it. But I have a little idea. A very
little idea. We shall see if I am right.”

He would say no more, and we returned to the camp.

The next day was one of intense heat. We spent most of it in the
shade of our tent. Poirot seemed to be dozing, but I noticed that
his eyes were always open, and that he was watching everything
that went on in the camp.

In the afternoon, Dr. Ames came to see us. He looked tired and
worried.

“This is a nightmare,” he said, sitting down and wiping his
forehead. “I’ve just been seeing Sir Guy. He’s in a state of
collapse.”

“Is it the Curse?” asked Poirot.

“It’s nerves,” said the doctor. “But it’s just as bad. If he doesn’t
pull himself together, he’ll be the next victim.”

“Can you do nothing for him?”

“I’ve given him a sedative. But it’s the mental strain that’s the
trouble. He’s got it into his head that he’s doomed.”

“And you, doctor? Do you not feel the shadow?”

“I’m too busy to think about it,” said Dr. Ames. “But I’ll admit
the atmosphere of this place is getting on my nerves. I’ll be glad
when the whole thing is over.”

“It will be over soon,” said Poirot quietly.

The doctor looked at him.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that I have found the common factor.”

“The common factor? What is it?”

“The desire for money,” said Poirot.

“Money? But who——?”

“That we shall see. But tell me, doctor, have you any strychnine in
your medicine chest?”

“Strychnine? Yes, of course. Why?”

“I should like to see it.”

The doctor looked surprised, but he rose and led the way to his
tent. He opened his medicine chest and pointed to a small bottle.

“There it is,” he said.

Poirot took the bottle and examined it.

“It is nearly full,” he remarked.

“I’ve had no occasion to use it,” said the doctor.

“And the tetanus anti-serum? You said you had none?”

“No. I had to send to Cairo for it.”

“I see.” Poirot replaced the bottle of strychnine. “Thank you,
doctor.”

As we left the tent, we met Mr. Harper. He looked pale and
agitated.

“Have you heard?” he cried. “Dr. Tosswill—he’s been taken ill!”

“What?” cried Dr. Ames. “Where is he?”

“In his tent. He was working there, and suddenly he collapsed.”

We all hurried to Dr. Tosswill’s tent. The doctor was lying on his
camp bed. He was conscious, but he seemed to be in great pain. His
face was contorted, and his breathing was laboured.

Dr. Ames knelt beside him and made a quick examination.

“It’s the same thing,” he whispered. “Tetanus!”

“Tetanus?” I cried. “But how? He hasn’t had any wound!”

“It must be the same as Schneider,” said the doctor. “A scratch
that he didn’t notice.”

“But it is impossible!” I cried. “Two cases of tetanus in one week,
in a camp where there have been none before!”

“It is the Curse,” said a voice behind us.

It was Hassan. He was standing in the doorway of the tent, his
dark eyes fixed on the dying man.

“The King is not yet appeased,” he said.

“Get out of here!” cried Dr. Ames.

Hassan bowed and withdrew.

“Can you do nothing for him?” asked Poirot.

“I’ll do what I can,” said the doctor. “But I fear it’s too late. I’ll
send for more anti-serum at once.”

But it was too late. Two hours later, Dr. Tosswill died.

The camp was now in a state of panic. The native workmen refused
to go near the Tomb, and even the Europeans were visibly shaken.
Sir Guy Willard was in a state of collapse, and Mr. Harper was
hardly better.

Only Poirot seemed unmoved. He spent the evening in our tent,
reading his little book on Egyptian magic.

“Poirot,” I said, “this is horrible. Another death—and such a
death!”

“It is very sad,” said Poirot. “Dr. Tosswill was a great expert. His
loss will be felt.”

“But don’t you see? It’s the Curse! It must be!”

“No, Hastings, it is not the Curse. It is something much more
human—and much more deadly.”

“But who could have done it? And how?”

“The ‘how’ is simple. As for the ‘who’—well, I have my
suspicions.”

“Tell me!”

“Not yet, Hastings. I must be sure. But to-morrow, I think, we
shall have the answer.”

The next morning, Poirot asked to see Sir Guy Willard. We found
him in his tent, looking like a ghost.

“Sir Guy,” said Poirot, “I have a request to make. I wish to
examine the Tomb of Men-her-Ra. Alone.”

Sir Guy stared at him.

“Alone? But why?”

“I have a theory,” said Poirot. “And I must test it. I believe that
the secret of these deaths is to be found in the Tomb.”

“But it’s dangerous!” cried Sir Guy. “The Curse——!”

“I am not afraid of the Curse,” said Poirot. “I have my own
charms.” He smiled and patted his little book.

Sir Guy hesitated, but at last he gave his consent.

“Very well,” he said. “But I wash my hands of the consequences.”

“I accept the responsibility,” said Poirot.

He asked me to accompany him as far as the entrance to the Tomb.
When we reached it, he turned to me.

“Stay here, Hastings. And do not let anyone enter.”

“But Poirot——!”

“Do as I say, _mon ami_. It is important.”

He disappeared into the darkness of the Tomb. I waited outside, my
heart beating fast. The sun was hot, and the silence of the desert
was oppressive.

Half an hour passed. Then, suddenly, I heard a cry from the Tomb.
It was a cry of terror.

I rushed inside, forgetting Poirot’s instructions. I found myself
in a narrow passage, lit by the torches that had been placed there
by the excavators. I followed the passage to the main chamber.

There I saw a sight that froze my blood. Poirot was standing in the
centre of the chamber, his face pale with horror. Before him, on the
altar, lay a figure in white robes. It was Hassan. He was dead.

“Poirot!” I cried. “What has happened?”

“The Curse, Hastings!” he whispered. “The Curse of Men-her-Ra!”

“But Hassan—how did he die?”

“I do not know. I found him here, like this.”

I looked at the dead man. His face was distorted, as though in his
last moments he had seen something too horrible for human eyes to
behold.

“This is awful,” I said. “The Curse is real, Poirot! It must be!”

“Wait!” said Poirot. He was looking at the dead man’s hand. He
picked something up from the floor.

“What is it?” I asked.

“A small piece of glass,” said Poirot. “It looks like a fragment of
a bottle.”

He looked around the chamber. His eyes fell on a small niche in the
wall. He went over to it and looked inside.

“Ah!” he cried. “What have we here?”

He reached into the niche and pulled out a small, dark object. It
was a bottle.

“A bottle of strychnine!” I cried. “The same as in the doctor’s
chest!”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And it is empty.”

“Then Hassan——?”

“Hassan was poisoned,” said Poirot. “But not by the Curse.”

He looked at the dead man again.

“Tell me, Hastings, do you see anything strange about this body?”

I looked closely.

“No,” I said. “Except that he looks—well, terrified.”

“Look at his feet,” said Poirot.

I looked. Hassan was wearing the usual native sandals.

“I see nothing strange,” I said.

“Look again. His feet are bare.”

I looked more closely. It was true. The sandals were lying on the
floor beside him.

“Why should he have taken off his sandals?” I asked.

“Because he was told to,” said Poirot. “By someone he trusted.”

“But who?”

“The person who killed him, Hastings. The person who has killed
all the others.”

“But why?”
