“To protect themselves. Hassan knew too much.”

“What did he know?”

“He knew the truth about the death of Sir John Willard.”

“And what was that truth?”

“That Sir John Willard did not die of heart failure. He was
murdered.”

“Murdered? But how?”

“By a very simple and very deadly method. A method that was also
used to kill Mr. Schneider and Dr. Tosswill.”

“But they died of tetanus!”

“Did they, Hastings? Did they really?”

Poirot looked at me, his eyes shining with a strange light.

“Come,” he said. “We must go back to the camp. I have something to
say to Sir Guy Willard and the others.”

We returned to the camp. Poirot asked Sir Guy, Dr. Ames and Mr.
Harper to meet us in the main tent.

When they were all assembled, Poirot began to speak.

“Messieurs,” he said, “I have a confession to make. I did not come
here to investigate a Curse. I came here to investigate a murder.”

“A murder?” cried Sir Guy. “But who has been murdered?”

“Sir John Willard,” said Poirot. “And Mr. Schneider. And Dr.
Tosswill. And now, Hassan.”

“But this is madness!” cried Dr. Ames. “They died of natural
causes—except for Hassan, and we don’t know yet how he died.”

“They died of what appeared to be natural causes,” said Poirot.
“But it was not so. They were all killed by the same hand.”

“And whose hand was it?” asked Mr. Harper, his voice trembling.

“It was the hand of someone who had a very good reason for
wanting them out of the way,” said Poirot. “Someone who stood to
gain a great deal of money by their deaths.”

“Money?” said Sir Guy. “But who would gain by their deaths?”

“You would, Sir Guy,” said Poirot. “You inherited your father’s
title and his fortune.”

Sir Guy turned pale.

“Are you suggesting that I killed my father?”

“No,” said Poirot. “I am not. Because you would not have gained by
the deaths of the others.”

“Then who?”

“There is someone else who stood to gain,” said Poirot. “Someone
who was in financial difficulties, and who saw a way to clear his
debts and make a fortune.”

“You mean—Rupert Bleibner?” I asked.

“No,” said Poirot. “Rupert Bleibner was a victim, not a murderer.
He was driven to suicide by the man who killed his uncle.”

“But who killed Mr. Bleibner?” I asked.

“The same person who killed the others,” said Poirot. “And he did
it for the same reason—money. Mr. Bleibner had made a will leaving
everything to the excavations. If he died, the money would go to
the expedition. And who was in charge of the expedition’s finances?”

All eyes turned to Mr. Harper. He turned white and began to
stammer.

“But—but I didn’t—I couldn’t——!”

“No, Mr. Harper,” said Poirot. “It was not you. You are a very
pleasant young man, but you have not the brains for such a
crime.”

“Then who?” I cried.

Poirot turned to Dr. Ames.

“Dr. Ames,” he said, “will you be so good as to tell us what you
were doing in the Tomb of Men-her-Ra this morning?”

The doctor stared at him.

“In the Tomb? I wasn’t in the Tomb this morning!”

“Oh, but you were,” said Poirot. “I saw you.”

“You saw me? But you were in the Tomb yourself!”

“Exactly. And I saw you enter after I did. You did not see me,
because I was hiding. But I saw you. I saw you go to the altar,
where Hassan was lying. And I saw you place something in his
hand.”

“It’s a lie!” cried the doctor.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain why your
fingerprints are on the bottle of strychnine I found in the niche?”

The doctor was silent. His face was a mask of fury.

“You see, messieurs,” said Poirot, “Dr. Ames was in financial
difficulties. He had lost a great deal of money in speculation. He
needed a large sum, and he saw a way to get it. He knew that Mr.
Bleibner had made a will leaving everything to the excavations.
He also knew that Sir John Willard was the head of the
expedition. If Sir John died, the money would be under the
control of his successor. And who was that successor? Sir Guy
Willard—a young man who knew nothing of finance, and who would be
easily led by his medical adviser.”

“But why kill the others?” I asked.

“To make it look like the Curse,” said Poirot. “If everyone who was
connected with the opening of the Tomb died, no one would suspect
murder. It would all be blamed on the spirit of Men-her-Ra.”

“But how did he kill them?” I asked.

“By a very simple method,” said Poirot. “He used his position as a
doctor to inject them with a deadly culture. In the case of Mr.
Bleibner, it was a septicæmia culture. In the cases of Mr.
Schneider and Dr. Tosswill, it was tetanus. It was easy for him
to do—a small scratch, an injection while he was ‘examining’
them—and the deed was done.”

“And Sir John Willard?”

“Heart failure. A common enough end for a man of his age, and one
that can easily be induced by the right drug.”

“And Hassan?”

“Hassan had seen the doctor injecting Mr. Schneider. He didn’t
understand what it meant at the time, but later he began to
suspect. He told the doctor what he had seen, and the doctor
realized he had to be silenced. He told Hassan to meet him in the
Tomb, and there he gave him a ‘protective’ injection. It was, of
course, a fatal dose of strychnine.”

Dr. Ames suddenly sprang to his feet.

“You think you’re very clever, don’t you, Poirot?” he snarled.
“But you can’t prove anything! My fingerprints on a bottle? That’s
nothing! I’m a doctor—I handle bottles all the time!”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But you do not handle bottles of
strychnine and then hide them in the Tomb of an Egyptian king.
Unless, of course, you are trying to make it look like a suicide.”

“It _was_ a suicide!” cried the doctor. “Hassan killed himself
because he was afraid of the Curse!”

“Then why did he take off his sandals?” asked Poirot.

“What does that matter?”

“It matters a great deal. In Ancient Egypt, it was the custom to
remove one’s shoes before entering a holy place. Hassan was a
devoted servant, and he would have done so if he had been told to
by someone he respected. But he would not have done so if he were
about to commit suicide.”

The doctor let out a yell of rage and lunged at Poirot. But I was
ready for him. I caught him by the arms and held him until the
others could come to my aid.

“It is no use, Dr. Ames,” said Poirot. “The game is up. I have
already cabled the police in Cairo. They will be here shortly.”

The doctor slumped in his chair, his face a mask of despair.

“The Curse of Men-her-Ra,” whispered Sir Guy. “It was not the King
after all.”

“No,” said Poirot. “It was the curse of greed—a much more modern,
and a much more deadly, spirit.”

He turned to me.

“Come, Hastings. Let us leave this place. I have had enough of the
sand—and of the dead.”

As we walked away from the tent, I looked back at the Pyramids.
They stood silent and inscrutable, as they had stood for
thousands of years.

“Do you think the King is satisfied now, Poirot?” I asked.

Poirot smiled.

“Who knows, Hastings? Who knows?”

“He turned up here one day, not a bad-looking fellow. I’d never
met him before, but some of the others had—Ames, I think, and
Schneider. The old man wasn’t at all pleased to see him. They were
at it in no time, hammer and tongs. ‘Not a cent,’ the old man
shouted. ‘Not one cent now or when I’m dead. I intend to leave my
money to the furtherance of my life’s work. I’ve been talking it
over with Mr. Schneider to-day.’ And a bit more of the same. Young
Bleibner lit out for Cairo right away.”

“Was he in perfectly good health at the time?”

“The old man?”

“No, the young one.”

“I believe he did mention there was something wrong with him. But
it couldn’t have been anything serious, or I should have remembered.”

“One thing more, has Mr. Bleibner left a will?”

“So far as we know, he has not.”

“Are you remaining with the expedition, Mr. Harper?”

“Only for a little longer. Then I’m off. I had a bit of a row with
Dr. Tosswill, and I’m going. I don’t mind confessing I’m a bit
jumpy too. It’s got on my nerves.”

“You do not believe in the curse?”

“I don’t know what I believe. This is a queer place, Monsieur
Poirot. I’ve never seen anything like it. It’s enough to make any
man lose his nerve.”

“There is something here which I cannot understand,” Poirot told
me as we walked towards our tent. “The air is heavy with it. It is
as if the old world were closing in on us, and we were struggling
against it. Look at that man there!”

He pointed to a native who was standing at some little distance,
his eyes fixed on us with a strange and brooding expression. I
felt a sudden shiver.

“That is Hassan,” I said. “He is very devoted to his late master.”

“I do not like the look of him,” said Poirot. “He has a look of
fanaticism. I should not like to meet him on a dark night.”

I laughed.

“You’re getting as superstitious as anyone else, Poirot.”

“I’ve lived too long in the East, Hastings,” he said, with a queer
look. “And I’ve seen too many strange things.”

I was about to reply when we were interrupted by the arrival of
Sir Guy Willard.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said, and his face was very grave, “I’ve just
had a talk with Dr. Ames. He’s of the same opinion as I am. We
want you to leave the camp at once.”

“What?” Poirot cried, in amazement.

“It’s for your own safety,” Willard went on. “We can’t have anything
happening to you. The curse—or whatever it is—is evidently after
the party, and you might be the next victim.”

“I see,” said Poirot slowly. “You wish to protect me. But I am not
afraid. I have my own methods of protection.”

“But it’s more than that,” Willard said. “The men are getting
restless. They think your presence here is a bad omen. They’re
ready for anything.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. “So I am to be sacrificed to the
superstitions of the workmen?”

“It’s not quite that, Monsieur Poirot. But we must have peace in
the camp if the work is to go on.”

“I understand,” said Poirot. “And if I refuse to go?”

“Then I’m afraid I shall have to ask you to go,” said Willard, with
a touch of his old-time manner. “I am the head of the expedition,
and I must be obeyed.”

Poirot bowed.

“I understand. We will leave at once.”

I was speechless with indignation as we walked away.

“To think of it!” I cried. “After all you’ve done!”

“Do not be so upset, Hastings,” Poirot said. “It is as I expected.
The powers of darkness are at work. But they shall not triumph.”

He was silent for a moment, and then he added:

“We will go to Cairo, and there we will wait. The end is not yet.”

  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

“Well, for the moment. There’s a certain amount of correspondence
to be dealt with, and then I’m going to stay on for a little while,
until some one else is appointed to take my place. But it’s
heart-breaking work.”

“How is that?”

“Well, you know, we’ve found so much, and yet we can’t bring it
home. It seems to have a curse on it. All the things we’ve
found—wonderful, they are—and yet what’s the good if no one ever
sees them? It’s enough to make a man superstitious, I can tell
you.”

“You are not yet so?”

“Well, I’m not sure. I don’t like it, Monsieur Poirot. I tell you
straight. I don’t like it.”

“That is very interesting,” said Poirot. “And Dr. Tosswill, what
does he think?”

“Oh, Tosswill’s a dry-as-dust old fellow. He’s no imagination. He
only thinks of his work.”

“And Hassan?”

“Hassan? He’s a queer old card. But he doesn’t say much. He’s been
with Sir John for years, and he’s very much cut up about his death.
He’s a very good fellow, though.”

“You would not call him a man of imagination, then?”

“No, I wouldn’t. He’s a solid, matter-of-fact sort of chap. He’s
not the sort to go into heroics, you know.”

“Thank you, Mr. Harper. You have been most kind.”

“Well, I’m wondering about that. You see, I was only with Mr.
Bleibner. Since his death I’ve been staying on to help Sir Guy,
but now my work’s nearly finished.”

“Are you an Egyptologist?”

“Lord, no! I’m a secretary, pure and simple. I’ve a good deal to
do with the administration and the accounts, as you can imagine.”

“Quite so. Now, tell me, Mr. Harper, have you seen anything—_extraordinary_
about the camp?”

“I don’t know what you mean by that, Monsieur Poirot.”

“I mean—well, anything—supernatural? Anything to make you
uncomfortable?”

“No,” said Harper slowly, “nothing of that sort. But I can tell
you this—there’s an atmosphere of—of dread, if you understand me.
It’s like—like a weight on one’s chest. We’re all—jumpy.”

“Except the doctor, of course?”

“Oh, Ames is all right. He’s got no nerves. But the others—well,
even Tosswill is not himself.”

“I see.”

Poirot stood for a moment, looking out over the desert. Then he
turned and walked back to our tent. He did not speak a word until
we reached it.

“What are you going to do?” I asked.

“I am going to consult my little grey cells, Hastings. They are
the only thing that can help me now.”

“I’m going for a stroll,” I said.

I wandered about the camp for some time. There was an air of
restlessness everywhere. The native workmen were gathered in little
groups, whispering together. I saw Hassan, the late Sir John
Willard’s servant, and spoke to him. He was a tall, dignified
man with a grave face.

“The Curse is upon us, _sitt_,” he said. “It is written. Who shall
escape the wrath of the dead?”

I shivered, in spite of the blazing sun. It was an uncanny
experience, this—as if one were back in the days of the Old
Kingdom.

As I turned to go back to the tent, I saw Dr. Ames. He was standing
by his tent door, looking out over the desert. There was an
expression on his face that I did not quite understand. It was
not fear—rather, it was a kind of—of calculation.

I joined Poirot in the tent. He was sitting with his eyes closed,
his hands folded on his knee. He did not move as I entered. I sat
down and waited. At last he opened his eyes.

“Hastings,” he said, “I have been thinking. It is all very
strange—very strange indeed.”

“You mean the deaths?”

“Precisely. Four deaths—and all different. It is not—logical.”

“But if it is a curse——?”

“A curse, _mon ami_, should be more—how shall I say it?—more
consistent. A curse that kills by heart failure, blood poisoning,
suicide and tetanus—it is a very versatile curse, is it not?”

“Then you don’t believe in it?”

“I did not say that. But I say that it is—strange.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I have a little plan. I want you to help me.”

“Of course. What is it?”

“To-night, Hastings, we will watch.”

“Watch? Where?”

“By the Tomb.”

“But—but why?”

“Because, _mon ami_, I have a feeling—a very strong feeling—that
something is going to happen to-night.”

I did not like the idea, I must confess. The thought of spending
the night by that lonely, haunted Tomb was not a pleasant one.
But I could not refuse.

“Very well,” I said. “I will come.”

“Good. We will meet here at ten o’clock.”

The rest of the day passed slowly. There was a sense of
expectation in the air. We dined with Sir Guy and the others.
The conversation was fitful and constrained. Only Dr. Ames seemed
his usual self. He talked of his experiences in different parts
of the world, and his stories were both interesting and amusing.
But even he seemed to be under a certain strain.

At ten o’clock Poirot and I met in our tent. He had provided
himself with a large electric torch.

“Come,” he said.

We stole out into the night. The desert was bathed in moonlight.
The Pyramids stood out, vast and mysterious, against the sky.
We made our way towards the Tomb. As we neared it, I felt a
sudden shiver of fear. The place seemed—evil.

We reached the entrance to the Tomb. Poirot signalled to me to
remain quiet. We sat down in the shadow of a large rock.

The hours passed slowly. The only sound was the occasional cry
of a jackal in the distance. The moonlight was so bright that
I could see the entrance to the Tomb quite clearly.

Suddenly Poirot gripped my arm.

“Look!” he whispered.

I looked. A figure was emerging from the Tomb. It was a tall,
shrouded figure, and it seemed to glide rather than walk. It
moved slowly away from the Tomb and disappeared into the
shadows.

“What was it?” I breathed.

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “But we will follow.”

We followed the figure as it made its way across the desert. It
seemed to be heading towards the camp. We kept at a safe
distance, taking advantage of every bit of cover.

Suddenly the figure stopped. It was standing by one of the
tents. I recognized it as Dr. Ames’s tent.

The figure stood there for a moment, then it turned and walked
away. It disappeared into the darkness.

“What does it mean?” I asked.

“I do not know,” said Poirot again. “But I think we have seen
enough for to-night.”

We returned to our tent. Poirot was very silent. I could see
that he was thinking deeply.

The next morning we were awakened by a loud outcry. I rushed
out of the tent. A crowd of native workmen was gathered round
Sir Guy Willard’s tent.

“What is it?” I asked one of them.

“The Curse!” he cried. “The Curse has struck again!”

I pushed my way through the crowd and entered the tent. Sir
Guy was lying on his bed. He was dead.

Dr. Ames was bending over him. He looked up as I entered.

“Heart failure,” he said briefly. “Just like his father.”

I turned and saw Poirot standing behind me. His face was very
grave.

“Heart failure?” he said. “Are you sure, _monsieur le docteur_?”

“Quite sure,” said Ames.

Poirot walked over to the bed and looked at the dead man. Then
he turned to Ames.

“Tell me, doctor,” he said, “did Sir Guy have any—enemies?”

“Enemies? Here? Of course not. Everyone liked him.”

“I see.”

Poirot turned and walked out of the tent. I followed him.

“What are you going to do now?” I asked.

“I am going to talk to Hassan,” he said.

We found Hassan sitting by himself. He looked even more
melancholy than usual.

“Hassan,” said Poirot, “you were with Sir John Willard when he
died, were you not?”

“I was, _sitt_.”

“And you were with Sir Guy last night?”

“I was not, _sitt_. He sent me away. He said he wanted to be
alone.”

“I see. And did you see anything—unusual—last night?”

Hassan hesitated.

“I saw—the Spirit of the King,” he said at last.

“The Spirit of the King?”

“Yes, _sitt_. It came out of the Tomb and walked across the
desert.”

“I see. Thank you, Hassan.”

Poirot turned to me.

“Well, Hastings, what do you think of that?”

“It’s—it’s incredible,” I said.

“Is it? I wonder.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I want to see Mr. Harper.”

We found Harper in his tent. He looked very white and shaken.

“This is terrible,” he said. “First Sir John, then Mr. Bleibner,
then Mr. Schneider, and now Sir Guy. Who will be next?”

“That is what I am wondering,” said Poirot. “Tell me, Mr.
Harper, do you know anything about Sir Guy’s—affairs?”

“His affairs? You mean his money?”

“Yes.”

“I believe he was quite well off. But I don’t know much about
it.”

“I see. And what about Mr. Bleibner’s money? Who will inherit
that now that his nephew is dead?”

“I don’t know. I suppose it will go to some distant relative.”

“I see. Thank you, Mr. Harper.”

As we walked away, Poirot said:

“Hastings, I want you to go to Cairo.”

“To Cairo? Why?”

“I want you to find out everything you can about Mr. Bleibner’s
will. And also about the nephew—Rupert Bleibner.”

“But I thought we knew all about him.”

“We know what the cable told us. I want more details.”

“Very well. I will go.”

I spent two days in Cairo. I found out that Mr. Bleibner had
not left a will, and that his money would indeed go to a
distant relative—a cousin in America. As for Rupert Bleibner,
I found out that he had been in Cairo just before he died,
and that he had been seen in the company of a certain—Dr.
Ames.

I returned to the camp and told Poirot what I had found out.
He listened with great interest.

“Ah,” he said. “Dr. Ames. That is very interesting.”

“Do you think he—?”

“I think nothing—yet. But I have a little plan.”

“Another plan?”

“Yes. This time, Hastings, we will—how shall I say it?—we will
lay a trap.”

“A trap? For whom?”

“For the murderer, _mon ami_.”

“The murderer? But you said it was a curse.”

“I said I believed in the force of superstition. I did not say
I believed in the Curse of Men-her-Ra.”

“Then you think—?”

“I think, Hastings, that we shall see some developments
to-night.”

That evening, Poirot invited all the members of the expedition
to our tent. Dr. Tosswill, Dr. Ames, Mr. Harper and Hassan
were all there.

“Gentlemen,” said Poirot, “I have asked you here because I
believe I can explain the mystery of the deaths that have
occurred.”

There was a sudden silence. Everyone looked at Poirot.

“As you know,” he continued, “there have been five deaths. Sir
John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, Rupert Bleibner, Mr. Schneider and
Sir Guy Willard. All of them, it would seem, victims of the
Curse of Men-her-Ra.”

He paused, then went on:

“But is it a curse? Or is it something—more human?”

“What do you mean?” asked Dr. Ames.

“I mean, _monsieur le docteur_, that I have found evidence of—
murder.”

A murmur of astonishment ran through the room.

“Murder?” said Dr. Tosswill. “But how? The deaths were all so
different.”

“Exactly. That was the cleverness of it. But they all had one
thing in common. They all served the purpose of one man.”

“And who is that man?” asked Harper.

Poirot looked round the room. His eyes rested on each of the
men in turn. Then he spoke.

“The man who killed Sir John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, Rupert
Bleibner, Mr. Schneider and Sir Guy Willard is—Dr. Ames!”

For a moment there was a stunned silence. Then Ames broke out
into a laugh.

“You’re mad!” he cried. “Quite mad! Why on earth should I
kill them?”

“For money, _monsieur le docteur_. For a very large sum of
money.”

“Money? What money?”

“The money of Mr. Bleibner. You see, you knew that Rupert
Bleibner was the heir to his uncle’s fortune. You also knew
that Rupert was—ill. In fact, he was dying. You met him in
Cairo and you made him a proposal. You would help him to
get his uncle’s money, and in return he would make a will
leaving everything to you.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Ames.

“Is it? I think not. You killed Sir John Willard to make Mr.
Bleibner the head of the expedition. Then you killed Mr.
Bleibner. Then you persuaded Rupert to commit suicide—perhaps
by telling him that he had a fatal disease. Then you killed
Mr. Schneider because he suspected something. And finally,
you killed Sir Guy Willard because he was the only one left
who might interfere with your plans.”

Ames was white with rage.

“You have no proof!” he shouted.

“Have I not?” said Poirot. He reached into his pocket and
produced a small bottle. “This was found in your tent, Dr.
Ames. It contains—tetanus spores. The same spores that killed
Mr. Schneider.”

Ames stared at the bottle. Then, with a sudden movement, he
snatched a small phial from his pocket and swallowed its
contents.

He collapsed onto the floor. Dr. Tosswill rushed to his side,
but it was too late. Ames was dead.

“Cyanide,” said Tosswill. “He must have had it ready.”

Poirot nodded.

“It is better so,” he said.

Later, as we sat in our tent, I asked Poirot:

“But how did you know? And what about the figure we saw coming
out of the Tomb?”

“The figure, _mon ami_, was Dr. Ames himself. He was trying to
keep up the superstition of the Curse. As for how I knew—it
was the dissimilar nature of the deaths that gave me the clue.
A curse, as I said, would have been more consistent. It was
only a human mind that would have thought of such a variety
of means.”

“And the bottle of tetanus spores?”

“A little bluff, Hastings. It was actually a bottle of
hair-wash. But it served its purpose.”

I looked at Poirot in admiration.

“You are a truly remarkable man, Poirot,” I said.

“I know,” he replied. “I am.”

“Until the end of the season. I owe it to Mr. Bleibner’s memory.
I am very much interested in the work, too.”

“You do not believe in the curse, then?”

“It would take more than that to frighten me away.”

“What about the others?”

“The others?”

“Yes, Dr. Tosswill, for instance.”

“Oh, Tosswill’s too much of a dry-as-dust to have any imagination.”

“And Hassan?”

A look of fear came into the young man’s eyes.

“Hassan? Ah, he is different. He is more of an Oriental than the
rest. I believe he is terrified. He spends half his time in
muttering prayers.”

“Thank you, Mr. Harper.”

Poirot rejoined me. He seemed to have been satisfied with his
talk.

“Well, Hastings, what do you make of it?”

“I don’t know what to make of it. It’s all very mysterious. What
have you been doing?”

“I have been looking into the question of the native workmen. I
have had several interesting talks with them.”

“What did they tell you?”

“A good deal. For instance, that many of them have been seen by
Hassan in a sort of trance, and that during these trances they
have spoken in strange tongues.”

“You mean,” I cried, “that Hassan is a—a medium?”

“Something of that kind, I suppose. And now I must consult my
little book. It is a mine of information.”

“But, Poirot, you’re not surely—serious?”

Poirot looked at me with a grave face.

“I was never more serious in my life, Hastings. You see, I am an
expert in the psychology of the human mind, and I know its power.
Do you know that many a man has died of a broken heart? Then why
should not a man die of a curse?”

“I don’t believe it,” I said stoutly.

“Nevertheless, it is a possibility to be considered. We must
examine every aspect of the case.”

“And what about the anti-serum?”

“Ah, yes, the anti-serum. That was a very curious point, was it
not? The serum was sent for from Cairo. It was presumably quite
all right. Yet Mr. Schneider died.”

“You think it may have been tampered with?”

“It is possible. But it would be a very difficult thing to prove.”

“What are you going to do now?”

“I am going to have a talk with Hassan.”

We found Hassan in his own quarters. He was a tall, dark man with
an inscrutable face. He seemed to be expecting us.

“The Effendi wishes to speak with me?”

“Yes, Hassan. I want to ask you a few questions about the late Sir
John Willard.”

“The Effendi was a great man. He is now with the gods.”

“You think he was killed by the curse of Men-her-Ra?”

“It is as the gods will.”

“And Mr. Bleibner?”

“He also. It is written.”

“And the nephew in New York?”

“The hand of the King is long.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“The King was angry. He has taken his revenge.”

“And who will be the next, Hassan?”

The man looked at him with a strange expression.

“Who can say? It may be the young Effendi, it may be the doctor,
it may be the secretary—it may be you, or it may be I.”

He turned away with a dignified gesture.

“Well, what do you think of him?” I asked as we walked away.

“He is a very interesting study, Hastings. He is a man of great
character and power. I should not like to have him for an enemy.”

“You think he may have had something to do with the deaths?”

“It is a possibility. But he has no motive.”

“Except, of course, a religious one.”

“Yes, but that would hardly apply to the nephew in New York.”

“True. I had forgotten that.”

“And now, Hastings, I have a little experiment to make. I want
your assistance.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to help me to—to watch.”

“To watch? What for?”

“To watch for—the spirit of Men-her-Ra.”

I looked at him in amazement.

“You’re joking, Poirot.”

“I was never more serious. I want you to come with me to the Tomb
to-night.”

“To the Tomb? At night?”

“Yes. I have reason to believe that something may happen there.”

“But what?”

“That I cannot tell you. But I want you to be with me.”

I could see that he was in earnest, so I agreed to go with him.

The night was dark and still. We made our way to the Tomb. Poirot
had a small electric torch with him. We entered the funeral
chamber. It was a strange, eerie place. The walls were covered with
hieroglyphics and strange figures. In the centre was the sarcophagus
of the King.

“Now,” said Poirot, “we must wait.”

We sat down in a corner of the chamber and waited. The minutes
passed slowly. The silence was absolute. I found myself listening
for every sound.

Suddenly, I heard a low, chanting sound. It seemed to come from
the direction of the sarcophagus. I felt a cold shiver run down my
spine.

“What is it?” I whispered.

“Hush!” said Poirot.

The chanting grew louder. It was a strange, rhythmic sound, unlike
anything I had ever heard before. Then, slowly, a figure began to
emerge from the sarcophagus. It was a tall, shadowy figure,
shrouded in white.

I felt a thrill of horror. Was it possible? Could this be the
spirit of Men-her-Ra?

The figure moved slowly towards us. Its arms were outstretched. It
seemed to be chanting a prayer or a curse.

I felt a sudden impulse to flee. But I restrained myself. I must
see this thing through.

The figure was now only a few feet away from us. I could see its
face. It was a dark, inscrutable face, like that of the Sphinx.

Suddenly, Poirot sprang forward. He seized the figure by the arm.

“Now, Hastings!” he cried.

I rushed to his assistance. Together, we managed to overpower the
figure. As we did so, its shroud fell away, and we saw—Hassan!

“So it was you, Hassan!” I cried.

The man looked at us with a sullen expression.

“I was only doing my duty,” he said. “The King must be protected.”

“And how did you manage to get into the sarcophagus?” asked Poirot.

“There is a secret passage,” said Hassan. “I have known of it for
a long time.”

“And the deaths?” I asked. “Did you have anything to do with
them?”

“I have already told you,” said Hassan. “It was the will of the
gods.”

“We shall see about that,” said Poirot. “In the meantime, we must
take you to Sir Guy Willard.”

We led Hassan out of the Tomb and back to the camp. Sir Guy was
waiting for us.

“What is the meaning of this?” he asked.

“We have found the ‘spirit’ of Men-her-Ra,” said Poirot. “It was
Hassan.”

Sir Guy looked at the man in amazement.

“Hassan? But why?”

“He says he was protecting the Tomb,” said Poirot. “But I think
there is more to it than that.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that Hassan may have been used as a tool by someone else.”

“By whom?”

“That is what I intend to find out.”

Poirot turned to Hassan.

“Now, Hassan, tell us the truth. Who told you to do this?”

The man remained silent.

“Very well,” said Poirot. “If you will not speak, we must find out
for ourselves.”

He turned to Sir Guy.

“I think it would be as well if you were to keep Hassan under
supervision for the time being.”

“Certainly,” said Sir Guy. “I will see to it at once.”

As we walked away, I asked Poirot what he intended to do next.

“I am going to have another talk with Dr. Ames,” he said. “I have
a feeling that he may be able to throw some light on the matter.”

“Dr. Ames? But what could he have to do with it?”

“That is what I want to find out.”

We found Dr. Ames in his tent. He was busy with some papers.

“Ah, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “What can I do for you?”

“I want to ask you a few more questions about Mr. Schneider’s
death,” said Poirot.

“Certainly. What is it you want to know?”

“You said that you had the anti-serum sent for from Cairo?”

“Yes, that is so.”

“And you are certain that it was the correct serum?”

“Absolutely certain. I checked it myself.”

“And yet Mr. Schneider died?”

“Yes. As I told you, it was a very severe case of tetanus.”

“I see. And now, tell me about Mr. Bleibner’s death.”

“I have already told you. It was a case of septicæmia.”

“And you are certain of that, too?”

“Of course I am certain. I am a doctor, Monsieur Poirot.”

“Yes, I know you are. And a very clever one, too, I have no doubt.”

Poirot looked at the doctor for a moment in silence. Then he said:

“Tell me, Dr. Ames, have you ever heard of a drug called curare?”

The doctor’s face paled.

“Curare? Yes, of course I have heard of it. It is a very powerful
poison.”

“And its effects are very similar to those of tetanus, are they
not?”

“In some ways, yes. But there are differences.”

“What differences?”

“Well, for one thing, curare causes paralysis of the respiratory
muscles, whereas tetanus causes spasms.”

“I see. And would it be possible to mistake one for the other?”

“It might be possible for a layman, but not for a doctor.”

“I see. Thank you, Dr. Ames. That is all I wanted to know.”

As we walked away, I asked Poirot what he made of the doctor’s
answers.

“He is a very clever man, Hastings. Very clever indeed.”

“You think he’s the murderer?”

“I didn’t say that. But I think he knows more than he is telling.”

“But what could be his motive?”

“That is the question. What could be his motive?”

Poirot was silent for a moment. Then he said:

“I think I have the answer, Hastings. But I must be sure.”

“How can you be sure?”

“I am going to make another experiment.”

“What kind of experiment?”

“I am going to catch the murderer in his own trap.”

“How?”

“You will see, Hastings. You will see.”

The next day, Poirot announced that he was going to hold a meeting
of all the members of the expedition.

“I have discovered the truth about the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’,” he
declared. “And I want you all to be present when I reveal it.”

The meeting was held in the large tent. All the members of the
expedition were there—Sir Guy Willard, Dr. Tosswill, Dr. Ames, Mr.
Harper and Hassan.

Poirot began by recounting the events that had led up to the present
situation. He spoke of the deaths of Sir John Willard, Mr.
Bleibner, the nephew in New York, and Mr. Schneider. He then turned
to the question of the curse.

“Many people believe in the power of the curse,” he said. “And I
must admit that there is some evidence to support this view. The
deaths have all been very strange, and they have all occurred
shortly after the opening of the Tomb.”

“But,” he continued, “there is another possibility. A possibility
that is far more sinister.”

He paused for a moment, then went on:

“I believe that the deaths were not the result of a curse, but the
work of a very clever and cold-blooded murderer.”

There was a murmur of astonishment from the audience.

“A murderer?” cried Sir Guy. “But who?”

“That is what I am about to tell you,” said Poirot.

He looked around the room, his eyes resting on each of the suspects
in turn.

“First, let us consider Dr. Tosswill. He is a very learned man, and
he has a great deal of knowledge of Ancient Egypt. Could he have
used this knowledge to commit the murders?”

Dr. Tosswill looked at Poirot in amazement.

“Me? But why should I want to kill anyone?”

“That is the question,” said Poirot. “What could be your motive?”

He turned to Mr. Harper.

“And what about you, Mr. Harper? You were the late Mr. Bleibner’s
secretary. You knew all about his affairs. Could you have killed
him in order to inherit his money?”

Mr. Harper’s face paled.

“Me? But I didn’t inherit any money. Mr. Bleibner didn’t leave a
will.”

“That is true,” said Poirot. “But perhaps you didn’t know that at
the time.”

He turned to Hassan.

“And then there is Hassan. He is a very devout man, and he
believes in the power of the gods. Could he have killed the others
in order to protect the Tomb?”

Hassan remained silent, his face inscrutable.

“And finally,” said Poirot, “there is Dr. Ames.”

The doctor looked at Poirot with a look of defiance.

“And what about me, Monsieur Poirot? What motive could I have for
killing anyone?”

“I think I have the answer to that,” said Poirot.

He turned to the audience.

“As you all know, Mr. Bleibner was a very wealthy man. He had no
children, and his only relative was his nephew in New York.”

“When Mr. Bleibner died, his money would naturally have gone to
his nephew. But the nephew was also dead.”

“So the question is, who would inherit the money now?”

“I have made some inquiries, and I have found that Mr. Bleibner
did, in fact, leave a will. He left all his money to—Dr. Ames!”

There was a gasp of horror from the audience.

Dr. Ames’s face went white.

“It’s a lie!” he cried. “I never knew anything about a will!”

“Oh, I think you did,” said Poirot. “In fact, I think you were the
one who persuaded Mr. Bleibner to make it.”

“And when he had made it, you decided to do away with him. You
poisoned him, and then you poisoned the others to make it look
like the work of a curse.”

“And the nephew in New York?” asked Sir Guy. “How did he die?”

“That was the most ingenious part of the whole plan,” said Poirot.
“Dr. Ames knew that the nephew was in low water, and that he was
desperate for money. He suggested that the nephew should come to
Egypt and try to borrow money from his uncle.”

“When the nephew arrived, Dr. Ames told him that his uncle was
refusing to see him. He then gave the nephew a letter to take back
to New York—a letter which he claimed was from Mr. Bleibner.”

“But the letter was actually a forgery. It told the nephew that he
was a leper and an outcast, and that he would never receive a cent
of his uncle’s money.”

“The nephew was so distraught that he committed suicide.”

“And Mr. Schneider?” asked Dr. Tosswill. “Why did he have to die?”

“Because he knew too much,” said Poirot. “He was present when Mr.
Bleibner made his will, and he knew that Dr. Ames was the
beneficiary.”

“And Sir John Willard?” asked Sir Guy. “Was he also murdered?”

“No,” said Poirot. “Sir John Willard died of natural causes. But
his death gave Dr. Ames the idea for the curse.”

“And how did you find all this out?” asked Mr. Harper.

“It was very simple,” said Poirot. “I merely followed the clues.
The anti-serum that was sent for from Cairo was, in fact, perfectly
all right. But Dr. Ames replaced it with a dose of curare.”

“And Hassan?” asked Sir Guy. “What was his part in all this?”

“Hassan was merely a tool,” said Poirot. “Dr. Ames knew that he was
very superstitious, and he used this to his advantage. He
persuaded Hassan that the deaths were the result of a curse, and
he encouraged him to dress up as the spirit of Men-her-Ra and haunt
the Tomb.”

“But why did he do that?” asked Mr. Harper.

“To keep people away from the Tomb, of course,” said Poirot. “He
didn’t want anyone to discover the truth.”

Dr. Ames stood up, his face contorted with rage.

“You’ll never prove it!” he cried. “You have no evidence!”

“Oh, I think I have,” said Poirot.

He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small glass vial.

“This,” he said, “is the vial of curare that you used to kill Mr.
Schneider. I found it in your tent.”

Dr. Ames’s face went pale. He knew he was trapped.

“It’s over, Dr. Ames,” said Poirot. “You have no where to run.”

The doctor looked around the room, his eyes wild. Then, suddenly,
he pulled a small bottle from his pocket and swallowed its
contents.

He collapsed to the floor, dead.

“Well, Hastings,” said Poirot, as we walked away. “What do you
think of my little experiment?”

“It was brilliant, Poirot. Absolutely brilliant.”

“It was merely a matter of using the little grey cells, Hastings.
The little grey cells.”

And so the mystery of the Curse of Men-her-Ra was solved. But I
still sometimes think of that dark and eerie Tomb, and the
shadowy figure of the King, and I wonder... was it really all just
the work of a clever murderer? Or was there something else? Something
that we moderns, with all our boasted science, can never truly
understand?

“Well, I guess I’m pretty nearly through. I don’t think there’s
much for me to do here now. I’ve just been helping Sir Guy as much
as possible, but I think I’ll go home to-day. My heart’s not in
this digging anyway.”

“_Très bien_, monsieur, then I will say goodbye to you. We shall
no doubt meet again before you leave.”

He left us, and Poirot turned to me.

“I was looking for some one, Hastings. Did you see that native
with the very fierce cast of countenance—Hassan?”

“I have seen him, but why him?”

“Hassan was Sir John’s servant, and he was with his master at the
moment of his death. If there is any occult influence at work here,
he would be likely to know more about it than any of these
cold-blooded scientific men.”

I went with him. He soon found Hassan, and for half an hour they
talked together in Arabic. I could not understand a word of it,
but Poirot seemed satisfied.

“He is a strange fellow, Hastings. But what is he saying? There
is no doubt that he is thoroughly frightened. He thinks that the
spirit of the Pharaoh is abroad and is taking his revenge.”

“Is that all he can tell us?”

“No, no, he tells me of a strange thing—of a secret that his late
master shared with him.”

“What sort of a secret?”

“I will tell you later. For the moment, we must proceed with our
investigation.”

I followed him to the tent where Dr. Tosswill was at work. He was
bending over some fragments of pottery.

“Ah, Monsieur Poirot, you have been talking to Hassan, I see. He
is a mine of information for those who can understand him.”

“He is very much afraid,” said Poirot.

Dr. Tosswill shrugged his shoulders.

“That is only natural. These people are very superstitious. But
there is no cause for alarm, I assure you.”

“None the less, monsieur, there have been four deaths.”

“I know, I know. But they are all perfectly explicable. My own
health is excellent. I have no fear.”

Poirot looked at him thoughtfully.

“You are a brave man, Dr. Tosswill. And Mr. Schneider, what of
him?”

“He was an able man, a very able man. It is a great loss to
science.”

“Was he also a believer in the supernatural?”

“Schneider? Good heavens, no! He was as hard-headed a Yankee as
ever lived.”

“And yet he is dead,” said Poirot softly.

Dr. Tosswill did not answer. He turned back to his pottery.

Poirot and I went out into the sunshine.

“It is a strange business, Hastings,” he said. “Four deaths, and
each one different. Heart failure, blood poisoning, suicide and
tetanus. It is very confusing. But there is one thing that links
them all together.”

“What is that?”

“They were all members of the expedition. And they all died within
a month of the opening of the tomb.”

“But Rupert Bleibner was not a member of the expedition.”

“No, but he visited it. And he died within the month.”

“Do you think there will be another death, Poirot?”

“I hope not, Hastings. But we must be on our guard. There is an
evil influence at work here, and we do not know where it will
strike next.”

He was silent for a moment, and then he added:

“We must watch, Hastings. We must watch and wait.”

But we had not long to wait. That very night, a strange and
terrible thing happened.

We were sitting in our tent, for the night was cold, when we heard
a sudden cry. It was a long, low wail, like the cry of a lost soul.

“What was that?” I cried, starting up.

“It is the voice of the desert,” said Poirot.

But it was not the voice of the desert. It was the voice of a
human being in agony.

We rushed out of the tent. The camp was in an uproar. Men were
running to and fro, and there was a sound of wailing and
lamentation.

“What is it?” I asked of a passing native.

“The spirit!” he cried. “The spirit of the Pharaoh! He has come!”

We pushed our way through the crowd to the tent of Sir Guy Willard.
Inside, we found a scene of confusion. Dr. Ames and Mr. Harper
were bending over a prostrate figure. It was Sir Guy Willard.

“What has happened?” asked Poirot.

“He has had a seizure,” said Dr. Ames. “I don’t know what it is.
It looks like some kind of a fit.”

Sir Guy was lying on the ground, his face contorted and his limbs
twitching. He was moaning piteously.

“Is he—is he going to die?” I asked.

“I don’t know,” said the doctor. “We must get him to Cairo at
once.”

But it was too late. Even as he spoke, the twitching ceased and
Sir Guy Willard lay still.

Dr. Ames bent over him for a moment, and then he stood up.

“He is dead,” he said.

A gasp of horror went up from the onlookers.

“Another death!” I cried. “That makes five!”

“And the cause?” asked Poirot.

“I don’t know,” said the doctor. “It looks like some kind of a
cerebral hemorrhage. But I can’t be sure without an autopsy.”

Poirot turned away. His face was very grave.

“The curse of Men-her-Ra,” he said. “It is no longer a matter of
superstition, Hastings. It is a matter of fact.”

I felt a cold shiver run down my spine. The atmosphere of the camp
seemed to be thick with evil. I felt as if we were being watched
by unseen eyes.

“What are we going to do, Poirot?” I asked.

“We must find out the truth, Hastings. We must find out the truth
before it is too late.”

But how were we to find out the truth? The deaths were all so
different, and there seemed to be no link between them.

And yet, as I looked at Poirot, I saw a strange look in his eyes.
It was a look of determination, of resolve.

“I have an idea, Hastings,” he said. “A very strange idea. But it
is the only way.”

“What is it?” I asked.

“We must consult the dead,” he said.

“The dead?” I cried. “What do you mean?”

“I mean that we must go into the Tomb of Men-her-Ra,” he said.
“We must go into the tomb and speak to the spirit of the Pharaoh.”

I stared at him in amazement.

“But that’s madness!” I cried. “You can’t do that!”

“I must do it, Hastings. It is the only way.”

And so, late that night, when the camp was still, Poirot and I
stole out of our tent and made our way to the Tomb of Men-her-Ra.

The entrance to the tomb was guarded by two native sentries, but
they were fast asleep. We slipped past them and entered the
darkness of the tomb.

It was a strange and eerie place. The walls were covered with
hieroglyphics, and the air was thick with the smell of age and
decay.

We made our way deep into the tomb, until we reached the central
chamber. There, in the middle of the room, was the sarcophagus of
the Pharaoh.

Poirot approached the sarcophagus and knelt down. He began to
mutter something in a low voice. I could not hear what he was
saying, but it sounded like an incantation.

Suddenly, a strange thing happened. The air in the tomb seemed to
grow cold, and a faint light began to glow around the sarcophagus.

I felt a sense of terror such as I have never felt before. I
wanted to turn and run, but I was rooted to the spot.

And then, a voice spoke. It was a deep, hollow voice, and it
seemed to come from the very depths of the tomb.

“Who disturbs the sleep of Men-her-Ra?” it said.

Poirot stood up. He was pale, but he did not flinch.

“I am Hercule Poirot,” he said. “I have come to ask for your
help.”

“Help?” said the voice. “Why should I help you?”

“Because there is a murderer among us,” said Poirot. “A murderer
who is using your name to hide his crimes.”

There was a long silence. And then, the voice spoke again.

“A murderer?” it said. “Who is this murderer?”

“That is what I want to find out,” said Poirot.

“I will tell you,” said the voice. “But you must be prepared for
the truth.”

“I am prepared,” said Poirot.

“Then listen,” said the voice.

And then, the voice began to speak. It told a story of greed, of
jealousy and of murder. It told of how one man had killed another,
and then another, in order to gain possession of the treasures of
the tomb.

As I listened, I felt a sense of horror and amazement. The story
was so strange, so unbelievable, and yet it had the ring of truth.

When the voice had finished speaking, the light around the
sarcophagus faded and the air in the tomb grew warm again.

Poirot turned to me.

“You heard, Hastings?” he said.

“Yes,” I said. “I heard.”

“And you know who the murderer is?”

“Yes,” I said. “I know.”

“Then let us go,” said Poirot. “We have work to do.”

We left the tomb and made our way back to the camp. The sun was
just beginning to rise, and the camp was beginning to wake up.

Poirot went straight to the tent of Dr. Ames. I followed him.

Inside, we found the doctor sitting at his desk, writing. He
looked up as we entered.

“Ah, Monsieur Poirot,” he said. “What can I do for you?”

Poirot did not answer. He simply looked at the doctor with his
steady, green eyes.

“What is it?” asked the doctor, looking uncomfortable. “Why are
you looking at me like that?”

“I know the truth, Dr. Ames,” said Poirot.

The doctor’s face went pale.

“The truth?” he said. “What truth?”

“I know that you are the murderer,” said Poirot.

The doctor started to laugh.

“The murderer?” he said. “Don’t be ridiculous, Monsieur Poirot.
I’m a doctor. Why should I want to kill anyone?”

“Because you wanted the money,” said Poirot. “The money that Mr.
Bleibner was going to leave to the expedition. You knew that if
the members of the expedition died, the money would eventually
come to you.”

“That’s nonsense!” cried the doctor. “I didn’t even know Mr.
Bleibner.”

“But you did,” said Poirot. “You knew him very well. You were his
nephew’s doctor in New York.”

The doctor’s face went white.

“How did you find that out?” he whispered.

“I cabled to New York,” said Poirot. “And I found out that you
were the one who advised Rupert Bleibner to go to Egypt. You knew
that his uncle would not give him any money, and you knew that he
would eventually commit suicide. And you were right.”

The doctor was silent for a moment. And then, he spoke.

“It’s true,” he said. “I did it. I killed them all.”

“But how?” I asked.

“It was easy,” said the doctor. “I used the cultures of tetanus
and septicæmia that I brought with me. And for Sir John Willard,
I used a drug that causes heart failure.”

“And Sir Guy Willard?” I asked.

“I used the same drug,” said the doctor. “It’s undetectable in an
autopsy.”

“And why did you do it?” I asked.

“For the money,” said the doctor. “I wanted the money. I’ve
always wanted money. And I thought I could get away with it. I
thought the curse of the Pharaoh would protect me.”

“But you were wrong,” said Poirot. “The curse of the Pharaoh does
not protect murderers. It only protects the dead.”

The doctor was silent for a long time. And then, he stood up.

“I suppose you’re going to hand me over to the police,” he said.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “That is my duty.”

The doctor looked at us for a moment, and then he walked out of
the tent.

We followed him, but he was too fast for us. He ran towards the
Tomb of Men-her-Ra.

“Stop him!” I cried.

But it was too late. Before we could reach him, the doctor had
entered the tomb.

We followed him inside, but he was nowhere to be seen. We
searched the entire tomb, but we could find no trace of him.

It was as if he had vanished into thin air.

“What has happened to him?” I asked.

“I do not know, Hastings,” said Poirot. “Perhaps the spirit of
the Pharaoh has taken him.”

And that was the end of the mystery of the Tomb of Men-her-Ra.
The deaths ceased, and the work of excavation continued.

But I have never forgotten that night in the tomb, and the voice
that spoke from the darkness.

And I have never forgotten the look in the eyes of Dr. Ames as he
confessed to his crimes.

It was a strange and terrible adventure, and one that I shall
never forget.

“No, sir, I am not. I’m for New York as soon as I can square up
things here. You may laugh if you like, but I’m not going to be
this blasted old Men-her-Ra’s next victim. He’ll get me if I stop
here.”

The young man wiped the perspiration from his brow.

Poirot turned away. Over his shoulder he said with a peculiar
smile:

“Remember, he got one of his victims in New York.”

“Oh, hell!” said Mr. Harper forcibly.

“That young man is nervous,” said Poirot thoughtfully. “He is on
the edge, but absolutely on the edge.”

We then encountered Hassan, the late Sir John’s devoted servant. He was a tall, lean Egyptian of middle age, with a face like a mask. He prostrated himself before Poirot with a rhythmic wailing, invoking the names of Allah and the ancient gods in one breath. He spoke of the "Shadow of the King" and how it walked the sands at night. Poirot listened with an air of profound respect, even asking the man if he had seen anything unusual on the night of Mr. Schneider's seizure. Hassan’s eyes rolled in his head as he described a tall figure in the vestments of a Pharaoh that had vanished into the darkness of the tomb. When he had left us, Poirot stood looking after him for some time.

We went towards the excavation itself. Near the entrance to the tomb, a tall, thin figure was standing like a statue. It was Hassan, the late Sir John’s servant. He was a man of middle age, with a face like a mask, and eyes that seemed to see things far beyond our ken. As we approached, he made a deep obeisance, but there was something in his gaze that was not entirely subservient. It was as though he looked upon us—the intruders—with a mixture of pity and a dark, secret knowledge. I felt a shiver pass over me. Here, in the shadow of these ancient monuments, the "Curse of Men-her-Ra" felt less like a newspaper headline and more like a living, breathing presence.

We traversed the camp as the sun began to set, casting long, distorted shadows across the sand. Near the entrance of the tomb, we encountered Hassan, the late Sir John’s servant. He stood like a figure carved in stone, his eyes fixed upon the darkening horizon. Poirot addressed him in a few words of Arabic, and the man replied with a sudden, passionate gesture towards the excavation. “He says,” translated Poirot softly, “that the King is not yet satisfied. That the secrets of the dead have been violated, and that the price must be paid in full. There is a grim sincerity about him, Hastings, that one cannot ignore. Whether it be the curse of a Pharaoh or the madness of a man, the danger is very real.”

We encountered Hassan a few minutes later, standing near the
entrance of the newly discovered tomb. He was a tall, impressive
figure, his face an impenetrable mask. Poirot engaged him in a
brief conversation in Arabic, which I could not follow. When he
joined me again, his face was more troubled than ever. “He
speaks, Hastings, of the ‘Guardian of the Threshold,’ of a
figure seen at night that is not of this world. He says that
Sir John was warned in a dream, but would not listen. For Hassan,
the matter is simple: the King has awakened, and he strikes at
the intruders one by one. It is a primitive belief, perhaps,
but it has its own dark logic.”

We walked on toward the actual site of the excavations. Near the dark opening that led down into the bowels of the earth, a tall, thin figure was standing. It was Hassan, the late Sir John’s devoted native servant. He stood with folded arms, his eyes fixed on the horizon, seemingly oblivious to our presence. As we drew near, he made a deep salaam, but his expression remained inscrutable. Poirot spoke to him briefly in Arabic, and the man replied in a low, sonorous voice. Then, with another obeisance, he moved away. Poirot looked after him thoughtfully. “That man,” he murmured, “is a devotee. He does not fear the King Men-her-Ra; he respects him. And in that respect, there is a very great danger for those whom the King may consider his enemies.”

I glanced at Poirot curiously, but his enigmatical smile told me
nothing. In company with Sir Guy Willard and Dr. Tosswill we were
taken round the excavations. The principal finds had been removed
to Cairo, but some of the tomb furniture was extremely interesting.
The enthusiasm of the young baronet was obvious, but I fancied that
I detected a shade of nervousness in his manner as though he could
not quite escape from the feeling of menace in the air. As we
entered the tent which had been assigned to us, for a wash before
joining the evening meal, a tall dark figure in white robes stood
aside to let us pass with a graceful gesture and a murmured greeting
in Arabic. Poirot stopped.

“You are Hassan, the late Sir John Willard’s servant?”

“I am he, effendi.”

“How long did you serve your late master?”

“Ten years, effendi.”

“You are a faithful servant?”

“He was my father and my mother, effendi.”

“The spirit of Men-her-Ra is restless, Hassan,” said Poirot
softly.

The man’s dark eyes flashed.

“The Curse is on the house, effendi. The spirits of the dead
kings are powerful.”

Poirot did not speak again, and after another low-voiced greeting
the man passed on.

We were dining in the largest tent of the camp. The evening was
strangely still, even the jackals were silent. The moon had risen,
and its cold light was silvering the desert sand.

Suddenly, a wild cry, a long, drawn-out wail of agony, rang through
the night.

“What’s that?” I cried, jumping to my feet.

Dr. Ames, who was sitting next to me, laid his hand on my arm.

“It’s only a jackal,” he said. “You’ll get used to them. It’s an
eerie sound, I’ll admit, but you’ll soon find it’s nothing more.”

I sank back into my seat, a little ashamed. I felt my nerves were
all on edge.

“I’m sorry,” I said. “I’m a bit jumpy to-night.”

“We all are,” said Sir Guy. “The events of the last few weeks
have been enough to shake anyone’s nerves.”

“You are not going to be the next victim, Sir Guy,” said Poirot
confidently. “I have my little book here, you see. I have
consulted the ancient Egyptian magic, and I think I can promise
you that you will be safe.”

A little smile of amusement went round the table.

“Well, let’s hope you’re right, Monsieur Poirot,” said Dr.
Tosswill. “I’m a sceptic myself, but I’d be glad to think you’re
right.”

“You have your little book, Poirot,” I said, “but I’m afraid I’m
not so lucky. I haven’t even a scrap of paper.”

“You have your common-sense, Hastings,” said Poirot with a smile.
“That is even better than a little book.”

We were just finishing our meal when a sudden commotion arose
outside the tent. A native came running in, his face grey with
terror.

“Effendi! Effendi!” he cried. “The Curse! The Curse of Men-her-Ra!”

We all jumped to our feet.

“What is it?” cried Sir Guy.

“The secretary! The American effendi! He is dead!”

“Dead?” cried Dr. Ames. “Harper dead? But he was all right half
an hour ago!”

We all rushed out of the tent. In the secretary’s tent, Mr. Harper
was lying across his table. A small glass was clutched in his hand.
Dr. Ames bent over him.

“Prussic acid,” he said briefly. “Suicide. The poor fellow’s
nerves must have given way.”

“Another victim!” whispered Sir Guy, his face white.

“The fifth!” I added, my heart sinking.

Poirot was bending over the dead man. He picked up a small scrap of
paper which was lying on the table.

“Listen to this,” he said. “‘I cannot bear it any longer. The
Curse is on me. I am the next. It is better to end it now.’”

“Poor fellow!” said Dr. Ames. “He was always a bit of a coward.”

“But why should he think he was the next?” I asked.

“Who knows?” said Dr. Tosswill. “The atmosphere of this place is
enough to turn anyone’s brain.”

We turned away, our hearts heavy with the tragedy. As we walked
back to our tent, Poirot was strangely silent.

“What is it, Poirot?” I asked. “What are you thinking?”

“I am thinking, Hastings, that there is something very strange
about these deaths. Five deaths, all dissimilar, yet all
connected with the Tomb of Men-her-Ra. It is a problem, my
friend, a very pretty problem.”

“But surely you don’t believe in the Curse now?” I cried.

“I believe in the power of the mind, Hastings. And I believe that
someone is using that power for a very sinister purpose.”

“You mean—it’s murder?”

“I mean, Hastings, that we must be very careful. Very careful
indeed.”

The man bowed. He had a fine face, and he seemed more intelligent
than the majority of his class.

“I was his servant, and I will be his son’s.”

“You are from the Fayum, aren’t you?”

“Yes, from near the Lake Karun.”

“I have heard of your family. You are of the old breed.”

“We are of the pure blood, _effendi_.”

“And you know much of the old wisdom?”

The man’s eyes flashed.

“I know what I know,” he said, in a low voice. “I have seen things
in my time.”

“What did you see in the Tomb?”

“Things that I do not care to speak of, _effendi_.”

“Do you know what killed your late master?”

“The spirit of the dead King, _effendi_.”

“And Mr. Bleibner?”

“He, too.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“Truly, and I think he will be the last.”

“You are sure of that?”

“I have said it, _effendi_.”

“And why do you think so?”

“Because the King is satisfied. He has had four victims.”

“Four? But Sir John was only the first!”

“There were four, _effendi_. One—two—three—four!”

He told them off on his fingers.

“But who was the fourth?”

The man hesitated.

“Rupert Bleibner, in New York.”

“How did you know of his death?”

“It was in the air, _effendi_.”

“But he died in New York, thousands of miles away!”

“Distance is nothing to the spirits, _effendi_.”

He bowed again and passed on.

Poirot stood for a moment looking after him. Then he turned to me.

“What do you think of that, Hastings?”

“I think he is a very impressive person,” I said. “He seems to
be quite sure of himself.”

“Yes, he is very sure of himself. Now let us see what Dr. Ames
can give us for dinner.”

“I am, monsieur. I serve now my master’s son.”

The man was a fine specimen of his race, with a certain dignity
which I always find impressive.

“And you believe in the Curse of Men-her-Ra?”

“He who offends the gods, monsieur, he will pay. The Ancient ones
should not be disturbed. Their rest should be sacred.”

“You are not afraid yourself, then?”

“It is as Allah wills, monsieur. I am his servant. Also, my late
master, the great Effendi, had his secrets. It may be that I, too,
know them.”

“That is all, thank you, Hassan.”

As the man moved away, Poirot turned to me.

“Did you notice that, Hastings? He knows his master’s secrets.
What were those secrets? I wonder.”

“You think they might throw some light on the mystery?”

“I do not know. But I am convinced that there is a mystery.
Ames, the doctor, is a hard-headed man, he will not admit it.
Tosswill, the scientist, is also sceptical. Harper, the secretary,
is frankly terrified. And Sir Guy, he is torn between his passion
for the work and his fears for himself.”

“And you, Poirot?”

“I, Hastings, I am what you call ‘open to conviction.’ But I am
going to have a little talk with Dr. Tosswill.”

I did not see Poirot again until we met for dinner in the mess
tent. The conversation was mainly on Egyptology. Dr. Tosswill
proved to be a mine of information. He spoke of the different
dynasties with an ease that was amazing. After dinner, Poirot and
I sat outside for a little while, under the brilliant starlight.
The silence of the desert was almost oppressive.

“To-morrow, Hastings,” said Poirot, “I am going to begin my
investigations in earnest. I have a feeling that we are on the
threshold of a very strange discovery.”

“In what direction?”

“That I cannot say as yet. But I have certain ideas—certain ideas.
Now, let us go to bed. I am tired.”

The next morning, Poirot was up early. I found him talking to one
of the native workmen. He seemed to be making inquiries about the
finds that had been made. Later, he had a long conversation with
Dr. Ames. I joined them just as they were finishing.

“So you see, Monsieur Poirot,” the doctor was saying, “there is
absolutely no evidence of anything but natural causes. It’s just
a run of bad luck, that’s all.”

“Perhaps, perhaps,” said Poirot. “But what about the nephew in
New York? His death was not due to natural causes.”

“That’s true. But then, he was a bit of a rotter, anyway. He may
have had his own reasons for doing what he did.”

“Quite so. But it’s a curious coincidence, isn’t it? Four deaths,
all connected with the same expedition.”

“I’ll grant you it’s curious. But I don’t see how you can link
them together, unless you believe in the Curse.”

“I do not say that I believe in it, but I do not say that I
disbelieve in it either. There are more things in heaven and earth,
_mon ami_, than are dreamt of in your philosophy.”

The doctor laughed.

“Well, I’ll leave you to your theories, Monsieur Poirot. I’ve
got work to do.”

As he walked away, Poirot turned to me.

“He is a very self-confident man, that Dr. Ames. Too
self-confident, perhaps.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that he is so sure of his own opinions that he may be
blind to other possibilities. Now, Hastings, I want you to do
something for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to find out all you can about Mr. Harper. He seems
to be a very nervous young man. I want to know why.”

I spent the rest of the morning talking to Harper. He was, as
Poirot had said, extremely nervous. He seemed to be constantly
on the watch, as though he expected something to happen at any
moment.

“I tell you, Captain Hastings,” he said, “there’s something wrong
about this place. I can feel it. It’s as though someone—or
something—is watching us all the time.”

“You mean the spirit of Men-her-Ra?”

“I don’t know what I mean. All I know is that I’ll be glad to
get away from here. If I could leave to-morrow, I would.”

“But surely you don’t really believe in the Curse?”

“I don’t know what to believe. All I know is that three men are
dead, and a fourth has killed himself. That’s enough for me.”

I reported my conversation to Poirot. He nodded thoughtfully.

“He is certainly very much afraid. But is he afraid of the
Curse, or is he afraid of something else?”

“What else could he be afraid of?”

“That is what we must find out. Now, let us have another talk with
Dr. Tosswill.”

We found Dr. Tosswill in one of the burial chambers. He was
examining some inscriptions on the wall.

“Fascinating, isn’t it?” he said, as we approached. “This is the
history of the reign of Men-her-Ra. It’s a pity so much of it is
damaged.”

“Dr. Tosswill,” said Poirot, “I want to ask you a question. Was
there anything unusual about the opening of the Tomb? Anything
that might have—shall we say—disturbed the spirits of the
departed?”

Dr. Tosswill smiled.

“Nothing more than usual, Monsieur Poirot. Of course, the
natives were a bit jumpy, but that’s always the case. They don’t
like disturbing the dead.”

“And was there anything found in the Tomb that was not reported?”

Dr. Tosswill looked at him sharply.

“What do you mean?”

“I mean, was there anything—any object of value—that might have
been—removed?”

“Certainly not. Everything that was found was carefully
catalogued and sent to Cairo.”

“I see. Thank you, Dr. Tosswill.”

As we walked away, Poirot whispered to me:

“He was very quick to deny it, was he not? I wonder if there is
any truth in the rumours I have heard.”

“What rumours?”

“Rumours that certain objects of great value were found in the
Tomb, but were never accounted for.”

“But who would have taken them?”

“That is the question, Hastings. That is the question.”

That evening, we were sitting in the mess tent when Hassan
entered. He looked agitated.

“Effendi,” he said, addressing Sir Guy, “there is trouble among
the workmen. They say they will not work any longer. They say
the Curse is upon us, and they are afraid.”

Sir Guy stood up.

“Nonsense! Tell them I will double their wages if they stay.”

“It is not a matter of money, Effendi. They are afraid for their
lives.”

“I will go and talk to them,” said Sir Guy.

He hurried out, followed by Dr. Tosswill and Mr. Harper.
Poirot and I were left alone with Dr. Ames.

“This is getting serious,” said the doctor. “If the workmen leave,
the excavations will have to stop.”

“Perhaps it would be for the best,” said Poirot quietly.

The doctor stared at him.

“You really believe that?”

“I believe that there is a very real danger here, Dr. Ames. A
danger that we do not yet fully understand.”

At that moment, a piercing scream rang out from the direction of
the excavations. We all rushed out. In the moonlight, we could
see a crowd of workmen gathered round one of the shafts. As we
approached, they fell back, revealing a figure lying on the
ground. It was Sir Guy Willard. He was clutching his chest, and
his face was contorted with pain.

Dr. Ames knelt down beside him.

“Heart failure,” he muttered, after a moment. “Just like his
father.”

He looked up at Poirot.

“The Curse, Monsieur Poirot. It has claimed another victim.”

Poirot did not answer. He was looking at the ground near where
Sir Guy had fallen. He stooped and picked something up. It was
a small, dark object. He slipped it into his pocket.

“We must get him back to the camp,” said Dr. Ames.

As they carried Sir Guy away, Poirot turned to me.

“The plot thickens, Hastings. The plot thickens.”

“But what did you find on the ground?” I asked.

Poirot produced the object from his pocket. It was a small
talisman, carved in the shape of a scarab.

“A scarab,” I said. “What does it mean?”

“It means, Hastings, that we are dealing with a very clever and
very dangerous opponent. An opponent who knows how to use the
forces of superstition to his own advantage.”

“You mean—it wasn’t the Curse?”

“I mean, Hastings, that Sir Guy Willard did not die of heart
failure. He was murdered.”

I gasped.

“Murdered? But how?”

“That is what we are going to find out. But first, we must have
a talk with Hassan.”

We found Hassan in his tent. He seemed to be expecting us.

“You knew this would happen, Hassan?” asked Poirot.

“I knew that the Curse would not be stayed, monsieur. The gods
are not to be trifled with.”

“Tell me, Hassan, what did you mean when you said your late
master had his secrets?”

Hassan hesitated.

“He found something, monsieur. Something that was not in the
Tomb of Men-her-Ra. Something that belonged to an even older
and more powerful king.”

“And what was this—something?”

“It was a papyrus, monsieur. A papyrus that contained the secret
of life and death.”

“And where is this papyrus now?”

“I do not know, monsieur. After my master’s death, it
disappeared.”

“I see. Thank you, Hassan.”

As we walked away, Poirot was very thoughtful.

“A papyrus that contains the secret of life and death. A very
interesting idea, Hastings. Very interesting indeed.”

“But you don’t really believe that, do you?”

“I believe that someone wants us to believe it. And that someone
is the person who murdered Sir Guy Willard.”

The next day, Poirot was busy making inquiries. He talked to
the workmen, to Dr. Tosswill, to Mr. Harper, and to Dr. Ames.
He seemed to be looking for something, but I didn’t know what.

In the afternoon, he called us all together in the mess tent.

“Messieurs,” he said, “I have come to a conclusion. The deaths
that have occurred here are not the result of a Curse. They are
the result of a very human—and very cold-blooded—plan.”

There was a murmur of astonishment.

“A plan?” said Dr. Ames. “What kind of a plan?”

“A plan to acquire a great fortune,” said Poirot. “A fortune
that was found in the Tomb of Men-her-Ra, but was never
reported.”

“But who would do such a thing?” asked Mr. Harper.

“That is what I am about to tell you,” said Poirot. “But first,
let us look at the facts. Sir John Willard died of heart
failure. Mr. Bleibner died of blood poisoning. His nephew
committed suicide. Mr. Schneider died of tetanus. And now,
Sir Guy Willard has died of heart failure. All these deaths
seem to be natural, or at least explicable. But they are
not.”

“Then how did they die?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“They were murdered,” said Poirot. “All of them. Except perhaps
the nephew, whose death was a necessary part of the plan.”

“But how were they murdered?” asked Dr. Ames. “I examined them
myself, and I found no evidence of foul play.”

“That is because you were looking for the wrong thing,” said
Poirot. “You were looking for signs of poison, or of violence.
But the murderer used a much more subtle method. He used the
power of suggestion—and a very dangerous drug.”

“What drug?” asked Dr. Ames.

“A drug that is known only to a few,” said Poirot. “A drug that
can cause heart failure, or blood poisoning, or tetanus,
depending on how it is administered.”

“I’ve never heard of such a drug,” said Dr. Ames.

“Neither had I, until I began my investigations,” said Poirot.
“But I found a reference to it in an old papyrus—the same
papyrus that Hassan mentioned.”

“But where is this papyrus?” asked Mr. Harper.

“It is in the possession of the murderer,” said Poirot. “And
that murderer is—Dr. Tosswill!”

Dr. Tosswill stood up, his face pale with anger.

“This is an outrage! How dare you accuse me of such a thing!”

“I have the evidence, Dr. Tosswill,” said Poirot. “I found the
scarab that you dropped near Sir Guy’s body. And I found the
remains of the drug in your tent.”

Dr. Tosswill sank back into his chair, his face a mask of
despair.

“It’s true,” he whispered. “I did it. I wanted the treasure for
myself. I thought I could use the Curse as a cover.”

“But why did you kill the nephew?” asked Mr. Harper.

“I didn’t kill him,” said Dr. Tosswill. “He killed himself
because he thought he was responsible for his uncle’s death.
I had managed to convince him of that.”

“And Sir Guy?” asked Poirot.

“He was getting too close to the truth. I had to get rid of him.”

“And the others?”

“They were in my way. I wanted the treasure all for myself.”

“Well, Dr. Tosswill,” said Poirot, “I’m afraid your plan has
failed. The police are on their way from Cairo.”

As Dr. Tosswill was led away, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings, the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’ was nothing but
a clever smokescreen. But it was no match for the ‘little grey
cells’ of Hercule Poirot.”

“But Poirot,” I said, “what about the papyrus? Does it really
contain the secret of life and death?”

Poirot smiled.

“That, Hastings, is a mystery that even I cannot solve. But
I suspect that the only ‘secret’ it contains is the secret of
human greed.”

And with that, we left the desert and the Tomb of Men-her-Ra
behind us, and set off on our journey home.

The man’s eyes met his with a proud and steady gaze.

“I am, monsieur.”

“Your late master was a good man, Hassan?”

“He was a very good man, monsieur.”

“Tell me, what do you know of his death?”

“It was the will of Allah, monsieur.”

“You do not believe it was any other thing?”

“Allah is all-powerful, monsieur. His hand is in everything.”

“You do not believe that the curse of the dead and gone king can
reach across the centuries?”

The man’s face was expressionless.

“The past is with the past, monsieur. It is the will of Allah.”

He turned away with a certain dignity.

“There is no doubt,” said Poirot as we were washing our hands,
“that the man is a fanatic. He believes in the occult—and he
certainly does not like me. He knows that I am here to find a
natural cause for these deaths.”

“I’m not so sure,” I said. “He seemed to me to be simply a devout
Moslem who believes that everything is the will of Allah.”

“_Tiens_! I should not be surprised if he were the one who had
done it.”

“How?”

“By some subtle poison known to the East for centuries. But why
should he?”

“That is what we have to find out.”

I did not see any more of Poirot until the next morning. He was
very silent and preoccupied. But as we were sitting at our
breakfast in the cool of the day, he suddenly turned to me.

“Hastings,” he said, “did you notice that Dr. Tosswill was not at
dinner last night?”

“No, I didn’t. Where was he?”

“He had a touch of sun, apparently. He’s all right this morning,
though.”

I was about to make some comment when Sir Guy Willard came into
the tent. He looked pale and worried.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’ve been thinking over what you said
about the curse. I don’t believe in it, but—but I can’t help
feeling that there’s something wrong. I wish you’d look into
things as quickly as you can.”

“I will do my best, Sir Guy.”

“And there’s another thing. Mr. Harper, the secretary, has
suddenly decided to leave us. He’s going to Cairo this morning.”

“Indeed?” said Poirot. “That is very interesting. I should like
to have a word with him before he goes.”

But Mr. Harper had already left. We saw his car disappearing in
the distance as we came out of the tent.

“That is a pity,” said Poirot. “I wanted to ask him a few more
questions.”

“What about?” I asked.

“About the late Mr. Bleibner’s affairs. He was his secretary, you
know.”

“But he told you all he knew yesterday,” I reminded him.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But I have been thinking. It is a very
strange thing that Mr. Bleibner should have died of blood
poisoning from a scratch on his thumb. A very strange thing
indeed.”

“But Dr. Ames said it was septicæmia,” I pointed out.

“So he did,” said Poirot. “But septicæmia can be produced in more
ways than one.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“I think I will go and have a talk with Dr. Ames.”

We found the doctor in his tent. He was busy with some medical
reports. He looked up as we entered.

“Morning, Monsieur Poirot. Anything I can do for you?”

“I was wondering, doctor,” said Poirot, “if you could tell me
exactly where Mr. Bleibner had that scratch on his thumb?”

“Why, let me see. It was on the right thumb, near the nail.”

“And it was a very slight scratch?”

“Oh, yes, just a mere nothing. He probably got it when he was
handling some of the finds. You know how sharp some of those old
things are.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And how long was it before he died?”

“About four days. He didn't think anything of it at first, but it
soon began to look ugly, and he had a high temperature. We did all
we could, but it was no use.”

“I see,” said Poirot again. “And Sir John Willard—you were with
him when he died?”

“No, I wasn’t. He died quite suddenly in the night. Dr. Tosswill
found him in the morning.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “And Mr. Schneider? You were with him?”

“Yes, I was. It was a very painful death. Tetanus is a horrible
thing.”

“And you are quite sure it was tetanus?”

“Oh, absolutely. There’s no doubt about it.”

“Thank you, doctor,” said Poirot. “That is all I wanted to know.”

As we walked away from the tent, Poirot was very thoughtful.

“Hastings,” he said, “I am beginning to see light. But it is a
very strange light—a very strange light indeed.”

“What do you mean?” I asked.

“I mean,” said Poirot, “that there is a very clever brain at work
here. A very clever brain indeed.”

“But who?” I asked.

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He was silent for the rest of the morning. In the afternoon he
announced that he was going to Cairo for a few hours.

“I have some inquiries to make,” he explained. “I shall be back
this evening.”

He returned about seven o’clock, looking very pleased with himself.

“I have found out several things,” he announced. “Several very
interesting things.”

“What are they?” I asked.

“I will tell you later,” he said. “For the moment, I want to have
another talk with Sir Guy Willard.”

We found Sir Guy in his tent, looking even more worried than
before.

“Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “I’m glad you’re back. Something else
has happened.”

“What is it?” asked Poirot.

“Hassan, my father’s servant, has disappeared.”

“Disappeared?” cried Poirot. “When?”

“This afternoon. No one has seen him since about three o’clock.”

“That is very strange,” said Poirot. “Very strange indeed.”

He was silent for a moment, then he said:

“Sir Guy, I think I can tell you now what is going on here. But
first, I must ask you to call everyone together—Dr. Tosswill and
Dr. Ames. I have something to say to you all.”

Sir Guy looked surprised, but he did as Poirot requested. In a few
minutes we were all assembled in the large tent.

Poirot stood in the middle of the group, his eyes sparkling with
excitement.

“Messieurs,” he said, “I have been investigating the deaths which
have occurred here, and I have come to a very interesting
conclusion. You have all been talking about the curse of
Men-her-Ra. But I can tell you that there is no curse—at least,
not in the way you think.”

He paused for a moment, then he continued:

“The deaths of Sir John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, and Mr. Schneider
were all murders.”

There was a gasp of astonishment from everyone.

“Murders?” cried Sir Guy. “But how? And who?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am going to tell you. But first,
let us look at the facts. Sir John Willard died of heart failure.
Mr. Bleibner died of blood poisoning. Mr. Schneider died of
