tetanus. All three deaths were apparently from natural causes. But
were they? I think not.”

He turned to Dr. Ames.

“Doctor,” he said, “you were the one who diagnosed these cases.
Is it not possible that you were mistaken?”

Dr. Ames looked at him in surprise.

“Mistaken? No, Monsieur Poirot, I was not mistaken. I am a
medical man, and I know what I am talking about.”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But let us look at the case of Mr.
Bleibner. You said he died of blood poisoning from a scratch on
his thumb. But I have found out that Mr. Bleibner was a very
wealthy man, and that he had no will. His money would go to his
nearest relative—his nephew, Rupert Bleibner. And we know that
Rupert Bleibner was in great need of money.”

“But Rupert Bleibner is dead,” said Sir Guy. “He committed
suicide in New York.”

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And why did he commit suicide? Because
he was haunted by the thought that he had killed his uncle. He
believed that he had sent him some poisoned object which had
caused his death. But he was wrong. He did not kill his uncle.”

“Then who did?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“The person who had the most to gain from Mr. Bleibner’s death,”
said Poirot. “And that person was not Rupert Bleibner.”

He turned to Dr. Ames again.

“Doctor,” he said, “I have been to Cairo this afternoon, and I
have found out some very interesting things about you. I have
found out that you were in great financial difficulties before you
joined this expedition. In fact, you were on the verge of ruin.”

Dr. Ames went very pale.

“That’s a lie!” he cried.

“It is not a lie,” said Poirot. “I have proof. And I also have
proof that you were the one who killed Mr. Bleibner. You
injected him with a culture of deadly bacteria, and you made it
look like blood poisoning from a scratch on his thumb.”

Dr. Ames started to say something, but Poirot silenced him with a
gesture.

“And that is not all,” he continued. “You also killed Sir John
Willard. You gave him a drug which caused heart failure. And you
killed Mr. Schneider with a culture of tetanus.”

“But why?” cried Sir Guy. “Why should he do such a thing?”

“Because,” said Poirot, “he wanted to get control of the
expedition’s funds. He knew that if the leaders of the expedition
were out of the way, he would be in a position of authority. And
he hoped that the talk of the curse would cover up his crimes.”

Dr. Ames suddenly made a dash for the door of the tent, but he was
intercepted by Hassan, who had suddenly appeared from behind a
curtain.

“No, doctor,” said Poirot. “You will not escape. Hassan has been
watching you for some time. He suspected that you were up to no
good, and he has been helping me with my inquiries.”

Dr. Ames saw that the game was up. He slumped down into a chair,
his face a mask of despair.

“It’s no use,” he muttered. “You’ve got me.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “I have got you. And now, Sir Guy, I think we
can safely say that the curse of Men-her-Ra is at an end.”

He turned to me with a smile.

“You see, Hastings,” he said, “there is always a natural cause for
everything—if you only know where to look for it.”

And so the mystery of the Tomb of King Men-her-Ra was solved, and
Hercule Poirot once again proved that his ‘little grey cells’ were
more than a match for any curse, ancient or modern.

“Yes, effendi, I have been his shadow for many years. Now I serve
the young master. His father was a great and wise man.”

“Did he ever speak of the Curse?”

“He did not, effendi, but it is there. Why else do the great ones
die? It is because they have disturbed the rest of the King.”

Hassan’s dark eyes were fixed on Poirot.

“What then will be the end?”

“The end? Who can say? But let the young master beware. The hand
of the dead is strong.”

He passed on, leaving us alone.

“A creepy sort of fellow,” I said.

“I find him interesting,” said Poirot. “I think he knows more than
he will tell.”

The meal that night was not exactly a cheerful one. Every one seemed
to be more or less under a cloud. Even Dr. Tosswill’s dry
unemotionalism seemed to have vanished, and he sat silent, wrapped
in his own thoughts. Dr. Ames was the only one who showed any sign
of his usual talkative self.

“I say, monsieur,” he cried, “have you really any theory about
this?”

“I have a theory,” Poirot replied, “but I am not yet sure if it is
the right one.”

“And it is——?”

“That these deaths are not due to coincidence.”

“Then you think they are due to——?”

“A supernatural cause? Perhaps. Who can say? We do not know what
may have been the powers of the ancient Egyptians.”

“Well, anyway,” said Dr. Ames, “I’m for keeping an eye on things.
I’ve a hunch there’s more to come.”

“And you, Sir Guy?” Poirot turned to him.

“I? Oh, I’m sticking it out. It’s for my father’s sake. He would
have wished it.”

“I see. And you, Mr. Harper?”

The secretary looked up with a start.

“I’m for home as soon as I can manage it,” he declared. “It’s too
much for my nerves.”

“And you, Dr. Tosswill?”

“I shall stay here until my work is done,” said the archaeologist
stolidly.

“Then we shall see what we shall see,” said Poirot.

I slept but fitfully that night. The heavy silence of the desert
seemed to wrap us round. Once I thought I heard a cry, but it was
only the howl of a jackal. Then, quite suddenly, I heard someone
moving in the tent next to ours. I sat up. It was Poirot. I heard
him strike a match. Then all was silent again.

In the morning we were early afoot. Poirot seemed to be in the
best of spirits.

“To-day,” he announced, “we shall visit the Tomb of King Men-her-Ra.
I am anxious to see it for myself.”

It was a most interesting experience. The funeral chambers were
still in a state of wonderful preservation. The wall paintings
were as fresh as the day they were painted.

“And it was here,” said Poirot, “that the body of the King was
found?”

“In that inner chamber,” replied Dr. Tosswill.

“And what is that?” Poirot pointed to a small niche in the wall.

“That is the place where the ‘_Ka_’ or spirit of the dead man was
supposed to dwell. There were always offerings of food and drink
left there for its refreshment.”

“How very interesting. And—hullo, what is this?”

Poirot had picked up something from the floor. It was a small
shrivelled object.

“Only a piece of some ancient fruit,” said Dr. Tosswill. “The
excavators must have overlooked it.”

Poirot put it in his pocket.

“I will keep it as a souvenir,” he said.

We spent the rest of the morning in the Tomb. Just as we were leaving,
Poirot turned to Hassan, who was standing at the entrance.

“You are a faithful servant, Hassan,” he said. “You would do
anything for your master, would you not?”

“Anything, effendi.”

“Even if it were something—shall we say—unusual?”

“If it were his wish, effendi.”

“I see.”

Poirot walked on in silence for some minutes. Then he turned to
me.

“Hastings, I have a little commission for you. Will you go to Cairo
for me? I want you to find out one or two things.”

“Certainly,” I said. “What are they?”

Poirot gave me his instructions. They were simple enough, and I
saw no reason for his mystery. However, I followed his directions
to the letter. I was back in the camp by the following afternoon.

“Well?” asked Poirot.

“I have done what you asked.”

“And the result?”

“It is as you thought.”

“Ah!” Poirot’s eyes gleamed. “Then we are on the right track.”

“But what does it mean?” I asked.

“It means, my friend, that the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’ is more potent
than I thought.”

That evening, as we sat in the mess tent, the conversation turned
once more on the supernatural.

“It is strange,” said Dr. Ames, “how people will believe in such
things. Now, I’m a man of science, and I can’t see any reason for
it.”

“And yet,” said Poirot, “there are things which science cannot
explain.”

“Such as?”

“Such as the power of the human mind. The power of suggestion is
a very real thing.”

“I grant you that. But it doesn’t explain three deaths from heart
failure, blood poisoning and tetanus.”

“Doesn’t it?” said Poirot. “I’m not so sure.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that if a man believes he is going to die, he very often
does.”

“That may be. But it doesn’t explain how he dies.”

“Does it not?” Poirot’s eyes were fixed on the doctor. “Supposing
someone wanted to kill these men. How would they go about it? Not
by any ordinary means. That would be too dangerous. But by using
the power of suggestion. By making them believe that they were the
victims of a curse.”

“But how could they do that?”

“In many ways. By a word here, a hint there. By playing on their
fears and superstitions. Until at last the victim is ready for the
final stroke.”

“And what is that?”

“The death itself. A death that can be explained by natural causes,
but which is in reality a murder.”

“A murder?” Dr. Ames laughed. “That’s a bit far-fetched, isn’t it?”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Let us see. Sir John Willard dies of heart
failure. A very common cause of death in a man of his age. But
supposing his heart was already weak? And supposing he was subjected
to a series of shocks, of subtle hints and suggestions, until his
nerves were on edge? Then, one day, he sees something—something
that to him is the final proof of the Curse. His heart fails, and
he dies.”

“And Mr. Bleibner?”

“Septicæmia. A scratch on the thumb. A very simple thing. But
suppose that scratch was not accidental? Suppose it was made by
something—something that was already infected with the germs of
death?”

“And the nephew?”

“Remorse. The hardest of all things to bear. Especially when one
believes that one’s crime has been discovered.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“Tetanus. A horrible death. But again, a death that could be
produced by—shall we say—a simple injection?”

“You’re suggesting that someone in this camp is a murderer?”

“I am suggesting it, Dr. Ames.”

“And who is it?”

“That is what I am here to find out.”

There was a moment of tense silence. Then Dr. Ames laughed again.

“Well, I hope you find your murderer, Monsieur Poirot. But I think
you’ll find it’s the old King after all.”

“We shall see,” said Poirot.

As we went to our tent that night, I asked Poirot if he really
believed what he had said.

“I believe it is possible, Hastings. But we have no proof. Not
yet.”

“And the piece of fruit you found in the Tomb?”

“That, my friend, is a very important clue. It was not a piece of
fruit at all.”

“Then what was it?”

“It was a piece of—but no, I will not tell you yet. You would only
laugh.”

I was about to protest when a sudden cry rang out through the
stillness of the night. It came from the direction of Sir Guy
Willard’s tent.

We rushed out. Sir Guy was standing in the entrance of his tent,
his face white and shaken.

“What is it?” I cried.

“The—the spirit!” he gasped. “I saw it! A tall, shadowy figure—it
passed close to me—and then it vanished!”

“Which way did it go?” asked Poirot.

“Towards the Tomb. Oh, it was horrible! The face—it was the face
of the King!”

Poirot did not wait for more. He dashed off in the direction of
the Tomb. I followed him.

As we neared the entrance, we saw a figure standing there. It was
Hassan.

“Did you see anything, Hassan?” asked Poirot.

“I saw nothing, effendi. But the spirit of the King is abroad
to-night. I feel its presence.”

Poirot looked at him for a moment. Then he turned to the Tomb.

“We will go inside,” he said.

I hesitated. The thought of entering that dark, silent place at
night was not a pleasant one. But Poirot was already inside. I
followed him, my heart beating fast.

We made our way to the inner chamber. All was silent. Then, quite
suddenly, Poirot stopped.

“Listen!” he whispered.

I listened. At first I heard nothing. Then, very faintly, I heard
a sound. It was like a low, rhythmic chanting.

“Where is it coming from?” I breathed.

“From behind that wall,” said Poirot.

He pointed to the wall where the ‘_Ka_’ niche was situated. He
pressed his ear against the stone.

“It is a secret passage,” he whispered. “I thought as much.”

He began to feel along the edge of the wall. Suddenly, a portion
of the masonry swung back. A dark opening appeared.

“Come,” said Poirot.

We entered the passage. It was narrow and winding. The chanting
grew louder as we went on. At last we came to a small chamber. In
the center was a stone altar. And standing before it, his back to
us, was a man in white robes.

He was chanting in a strange, rhythmic tongue. As we watched, he
raised his hands above his head. In one hand he held a small,
glittering object.

“Halt!” cried Poirot.

The man turned. It was Hassan. But it was not the Hassan we knew.
His face was transformed by a look of wild, fanatical devotion.

“What are you doing here?” demanded Poirot.

“I am serving my master,” said Hassan. “The King has spoken. He
demands a sacrifice.”

“A sacrifice?” I cried. “What do you mean?”

“The young master,” said Hassan. “He must die. Only then will the
King be appeased.”

“You’re mad!” I said.

“No, not mad,” said Poirot. “Only a very faithful servant. Is it
not so, Hassan?”

Hassan did not answer. He was staring at Poirot with a look of
intense hatred.

“You have interfered for the last time, effendi,” he said. “The
King will deal with you.”

He raised the glittering object in his hand. It was a long, thin
needle.

“I shouldn’t do that if I were you, Hassan,” said Poirot calmly.
“You see, I have the piece of ‘fruit’ in my pocket.”

Hassan’s face went white. He lowered the needle.

“How—how did you know?” he gasped.

“It was simple,” said Poirot. “The ‘fruit’ was not fruit at all.
It was a piece of cotton wool, soaked in a very powerful poison.
The same poison that killed Mr. Bleibner. And the needle—that is
what you used to kill Mr. Schneider. A simple injection of tetanus
germs.”

“But why?” I asked. “Why did he do it?”

“Because he believed he was serving his master,” said Poirot. “He
thought that by killing those who had disturbed the Tomb, he was
carrying out the will of the King.”

“But Sir John Willard? How did he die?”

“Heart failure, as we thought. But it was a heart failure brought
on by fear. Hassan saw to that. He played on Sir John’s
superstitions, until the poor man was in a state of constant
terror. Then, one night, Hassan appeared to him in the guise of
the King’s spirit. The shock was too much for Sir John’s weak
heart.”

“And the nephew?”

“He was the only one who really was a victim of the Curse—but not
the Curse of Men-her-Ra. The Curse of his own conscience. He had
come to Egypt to borrow money from his uncle. When his uncle
refused, he had, in a fit of rage, threatened him. When Sir John
died so soon afterwards, the young man believed he was responsible.
He thought his threats had somehow brought about his uncle’s death.
The remorse was more than he could bear.”

“And Sir Guy? Why did you want to kill him, Hassan?”

“Because he is the last,” said Hassan. “Once he is dead, the Tomb
will be sealed forever. The King will rest in peace.”

“I think not,” said Poirot. “You see, Hassan, there is one thing
you have forgotten.”

“What is that?”

“That I, Hercule Poirot, do not believe in curses. I believe only
in the little grey cells of the brain.”

He turned to me.

“Come, Hastings. I think we have seen enough. We will take Hassan
back to the camp. The authorities in Cairo will know how to deal
with him.”

As we led Hassan away, I couldn’t help feeling a certain pity for
him. He was a fanatic, it was true, but he had acted out of a
misguided sense of loyalty.

“Well, Poirot,” I said, as we walked back to our tent, “you’ve done
it again. But tell me, how did you know about the secret passage?”

“I didn’t, Hastings. But I knew there must be one. How else could
the ‘spirit’ appear and disappear so suddenly? And the chanting—that
was a very clever touch. It added just the right atmosphere of
mystery and dread.”

“And the piece of cotton wool?”

“Ah, that was the final proof. I found it in the Tomb, near the
‘_Ka_’ niche. Hassan must have dropped it when he was preparing his
last ‘sacrifice’. It was a very small thing, but it was enough to
hang a man.”

“And what about the anti-serum?”

“That was the only thing I wasn’t sure about. But when you told me
that the doctor had to send to Cairo for it, I knew that Hassan
must have had plenty of time to substitute a harmless liquid for
the real thing.”

“So Dr. Ames was innocent after all?”

“Quite innocent, Hastings. He was just a man of science, who
couldn’t see beyond the facts. He didn’t realize that the most
powerful force in the world is not science, but the human mind.”

I looked at Poirot. He was busy brushing some invisible speck of
dust from his sleeve.

“You know, Poirot,” I said, “I think you’re right. The ‘Curse of
Men-her-Ra’ was a very real thing—but only because people believed
in it.”

“Exactly, Hastings. And now, if you don’t mind, I think I will go
to bed. It has been a very long day, and my boots—they are still
full of that cursed sand!”

I watched him as he went into his tent. He was a strange little
man, but there was no denying his genius. As for me, I lay down
on my bed and was soon fast asleep. For the first time in many
nights, I did not dream of Egyptian kings or ancient curses. I
dreamt of London, and the cool, grey mists of the Thames. And I
knew that, whatever dangers might lie ahead, I was safe in the
hands of Hercule Poirot.

THE END

“I served my Lord Sir John, now I serve his son.” He took a step
nearer to us and lowered his voice. “You are a wise one, they say,
learned in dealing with evil spirits. Let the young master depart
from here. There is evil in the air around us.”

And with an abrupt gesture, not waiting for a reply, he strode
away.

“Evil in the air,” muttered Poirot. “Yes, I feel it.”

Sir Guy Willard, Dr. Tosswill, Dr. Ames and Mr. Harper were
already in the mess-tent when we joined them. Poirot sat at my
right.

I remember that dinner as a weird and almost uncanny experience.
The flickering light of the candles, the dark shadows that danced
on the tent walls, the sense of the desert all around us. The
conversation was fitful and spasmodic. Dr. Tosswill and Sir Guy
did most of the talking, while Poirot and Dr. Ames were mostly
silent. As for the young American, he sat there, his head on his
hand, his eyes starting from his head as though he expected every
moment to see some grisly phantom appear from the shadows.

After dinner, we sat out in the starlight. The night was cold and
very still. Suddenly from the darkness there came a long-drawn cry,
piercingly sweet and infinitely sad.

“What’s that?” I cried.

“The jackal,” said Dr. Tosswill calmly. “They often howl at night.”

“To me,” said Poirot, “it sounded like the cry of some lost spirit.”

He got up and went towards his tent. I followed him.

“What are you going to do?” I asked.

“I am going to consult my little book,” he replied.

He took out the tattered volume and began to turn the pages.

“_Ecoutez, Hastings_,” he said, “this is very curious.”

He read me a passage from the book. It was an account of the
punishment of those who violated the tombs of the Pharaohs.

“It is interesting, is it not?” he said. “I think I will sleep
well to-night.”

But I did not sleep well. All night long I seemed to hear that
weird, unearthly cry. Was it a jackal, or was it indeed some
restless spirit of the past? I wondered if Poirot was sleeping
peacefully, and then I remembered his words about the little book.
Surely he could not really believe in such things?

The next morning, Poirot was early astir. He seemed to have
recovered his spirits.

“I have had a most interesting night, Hastings,” he said. “I have
been communing with the spirits.”

I looked at him in surprise.

“You don’t really mean that?”

“But certainly. They have told me many things.”

“What things?”

“That remains to be seen.”

He would say no more, and we went to join the others at breakfast.

After breakfast, we went to the excavations. Sir Guy was already
there, and he seemed more cheerful than he had been the night
before.

“We’ve found something very interesting this morning,” he said.
“Come and see.”

He took us to one of the funeral chambers. On the wall was a series
of paintings.

“These are very rare,” said Sir Guy. “They represent the journey
of the soul after death.”

Poirot looked at them with interest.

“They are very beautiful,” he said. “But what is this?”

He pointed to a small figure in one of the paintings.

“That,” said Sir Guy, “is the jackal-headed god, Anubis. He is the
guardian of the dead.”

“Ah,” said Poirot. “The jackal-headed god. That is very
interesting.”

He turned away and began to talk to Dr. Tosswill.

I stayed behind for a moment, looking at the paintings. As I turned
to follow the others, I saw a figure standing in the shadows. It
was Hassan, the servant. He was watching Poirot with a strange
expression on his face.

“What is it, Hassan?” I asked.

He did not answer, but turned and walked away.

I followed the others back to the camp.

As we approached the mess-tent, we saw a man running towards us.
It was Mr. Harper. He looked as though he had seen a ghost.

“He’s dead!” he cried. “He’s dead!”

“Who is dead?” asked Sir Guy.

“Dr. Ames! He’s in his tent. He’s been murdered!”

We all ran to Dr. Ames’s tent. He was lying on his bed, his face
contorted in an expression of agony. There was a small wound in
his neck.

“It’s the curse!” cried Mr. Harper. “The curse of Men-her-Ra!”

Poirot went over to the body and examined it.

“It is not the curse,” he said quietly. “It is murder.”

“Murder?” cried Sir Guy. “But who would want to murder Dr. Ames?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we must find out.”

He looked around the tent. On the table was a small bottle of
anti-serum.

“What is this?” he asked.

“It’s the anti-serum for tetanus,” said Dr. Tosswill. “Dr. Ames
must have been about to use it.”

“But he didn’t use it,” said Poirot. “He was murdered before he
could.”

He looked at the wound in Dr. Ames’s neck.

“It was done with a very sharp instrument,” he said. “A needle,
perhaps.”

He turned to Mr. Harper.

“Where were you when this happened?”

“I was in my tent,” said Mr. Harper. “I heard a cry and I ran
here.”

“And you, Dr. Tosswill?”

“I was at the excavations,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“And Sir Guy?”

“I was with Dr. Tosswill,” said Sir Guy.

“And Hassan?”

“I do not know where Hassan was,” said Poirot.

He looked at the body of Dr. Ames.

“This is a very clever murder,” he said. “The murderer knew exactly
where to strike.”

He turned to us.

“I must think,” he said. “I must think very carefully.”

He went back to his tent, and I followed him.

“What do you think, Poirot?” I asked.

“I think,” he said, “that we are dealing with a very dangerous
person.”

“But who?”

“That is what I must find out.”

He took out his little book and began to read.

“What are you looking for?” I asked.

“I am looking for the answer,” he said.

He read for a few minutes, then he closed the book.

“I think I have it,” he said.

“What?”

“The answer.”

He got up and went out of the tent. I followed him.

We went to the mess-tent, where the others were waiting for us.

“I have something to say to you all,” said Poirot.

He looked around the room.

“Dr. Ames was murdered,” he said. “He was murdered because he knew
too much.”

“Too much about what?” asked Sir Guy.

“About the deaths of Sir John Willard and Mr. Bleibner,” said
Poirot.

“But they died of natural causes,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“No,” said Poirot. “They were murdered.”

“Murdered?” cried Sir Guy. “But how?”

“They were murdered by someone who wanted to get their money,” said
Poirot.

“But who would want their money?” asked Mr. Harper.

“Someone who knew that they had no wills,” said Poirot.

He looked at Mr. Harper.

“You, Mr. Harper, were Mr. Bleibner’s secretary. You knew that he
had no will.”

“But I didn’t murder him!” cried Mr. Harper.

“No,” said Poirot. “You didn’t.”

He turned to Dr. Tosswill.

“You, Dr. Tosswill, were a friend of Sir John Willard. You knew
that he had no will.”

“But I didn’t murder him!” cried Dr. Tosswill.

“No,” said Poirot. “You didn’t.”

He turned to Sir Guy.

“You, Sir Guy, are the son of Sir John Willard. You would inherit
his money if he died without a will.”

“But I didn’t murder my father!” cried Sir Guy.

“No,” said Poirot. “You didn’t.”

He looked around the room.

“There is only one person left,” he said.

He looked at Hassan.

“You, Hassan, were the servant of Sir John Willard. You knew all
his secrets.”

“But I did not murder my master!” cried Hassan.

“No,” said Poirot. “You didn't.”

He paused for a moment, then he said:

“The murderer is Dr. Tosswill.”

There was a moment of silence. Then Dr. Tosswill spoke.

“That is a very serious accusation, Monsieur Poirot. Do you have
any proof?”

“I have the proof in my hand,” said Poirot.

He held up a small needle.

“This needle,” he said, “was used to kill Dr. Ames. It was covered
with a very deadly poison.”

“But how do you know it was Dr. Tosswill?” asked Sir Guy.

“Because,” said Poirot, “he was the only one who had access to the
poison.”

“What poison?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“The poison of the Ancient Egyptians,” said Poirot.

He looked at Dr. Tosswill.

“You found it in the tomb, did you not?”

Dr. Tosswill didn’t answer.

“You used it to kill Sir John Willard and Mr. Bleibner,” said
Poirot. “And then you used it to kill Dr. Ames because he
suspected you.”

Dr. Tosswill suddenly pulled out a small bottle and drank from it.

“You will never take me alive!” he cried.

He fell to the floor, dead.

“He has committed suicide,” said Poirot.

He looked at the body of Dr. Tosswill.

“He was a very clever man,” he said. “But he was not as clever as
Hercule Poirot.”

He turned to us.

“And now,” he said, “I think it is time for us to leave this place.
The curse of Men-her-Ra is over.”

We left the camp the next day. As we rode away on our camels, I
looked back at the pyramids. They seemed more mysterious than ever.

“Do you really believe in the curse, Poirot?” I asked.

“I believe in the power of the human mind, Hastings,” he said.
“And that is the greatest curse of all.”

As we sat round our evening meal in the mess tent I felt the
shadow of death hanging over us. Dr. Ames, it is true, was
cheerful enough. He was a man with a wide experience of life,
and he talked pleasantly enough, though with a certain cynical
vein. Dr. Tosswill, however, was silent and preoccupied. As for
Sir Guy, he seemed to have caught the infection of the general
mood. His young face looked drawn and haggard. Mr. Harper, the
secretary, sat with his head in his hands, hardly speaking.

I must say that I was glad to be able to leave the tent and get
out into the night air. The moon was at the full and it was a
marvellous sight, the great Pyramids standing out against the
darkness of the sky.

Suddenly a figure came from between the tents. I saw its outline
clearly. It was the figure of a man with the head of a jackal!

I let out a cry of horror. Poirot and the others came running
out of the tent.

“There!” I cried, pointing into the distance. “The spirit of the
God Anubis!”

“He’s seen it,” muttered the secretary. “I saw it last night!”

“Where did it go?” demanded Sir Guy.

“Into the desert there,” I replied, still trembling.

“Let us follow!” cried Sir Guy. “There’s some devilry here!”

We set off in pursuit, but we had not gone far before we realized
the hopelessness of our task. The figure had disappeared into
the labyrinth of rocks and sand.

“It is gone,” said Sir Guy. “But what can it be?”

“The spirit of the Tomb,” whispered the secretary. “It is the
end for us all!”

“Nonsense!” said Dr. Ames sharply. “Some native playing a trick.
We’ll have a guard set to-morrow.”

But as we walked back to the camp I could see that even he was
shaken.

Poirot alone seemed unmoved. He had remained silent throughout
 the whole scene, but now he spoke.

“It was a very interesting sight, Hastings. Decidedly, it was most
instructive.”

“Instructive!” I cried. “It was horrible!”

“To you, perhaps, _mon ami_, but to me—ah, that is another matter.”

And he would say no more.

Next morning I found him early at work. He had been out since
daybreak, and I found him talking to one of the native boys.

“What have you been doing?” I asked.

“Collecting information, Hastings. One must always collect
information. It is the basis of all sound deduction.”

“And have you found out anything?”

“I have found out that the figure of Anubis was seen by several
of the natives last night. They are in a state of terror.”

“And what do you deduce from that?”

“That the person who played the part of Anubis is a very clever
actor, Hastings. Also, that he has a very good reason for wanting
to frighten the camp.”

“You think it was a man, then?”

“But certainly, _mon ami_. Spirits do not wear sandals, and the
figure I saw had very substantial footwear.”

“I didn’t see its feet,” I admitted.

“No, you were too busy looking at its head. But I—I always look
at the feet first. It is a habit of mine.”

“Then you know who it was?”

“Not yet, Hastings. But I have my suspicions.”

And again he would say no more.

The day passed without incident, but the atmosphere of the camp
was one of suppressed excitement. The natives were sullen and
unwilling to work, and it was only with the greatest difficulty
that Dr. Tosswill could get anything done.

That night we were all on the alert. Sir Guy had insisted on
having a guard of four men, and we ourselves were prepared to
take it in turns to keep watch.

It was about two o’clock in the morning when the alarm was
given. I was in my tent when I heard a shout from the direction
of Sir Guy’s quarters. I rushed out, to find Poirot already there.

“What is it?” I cried.

“Sir Guy!” gasped the secretary, who was standing by the door
of the tent. “He’s been attacked!”

We rushed inside. Sir Guy was lying on his bed, his face pale
and his eyes closed. Dr. Ames was bending over him.

“He’s fainted,” said the doctor. “He says he saw the figure
of Anubis again, and that it struck him a blow on the head.”

“Is he badly hurt?” asked Poirot.

“No, it’s only a slight concussion. He’ll be all right in a day
or two.”

“And the figure? Did anyone see it?”

“I saw it,” said the secretary. “It went out of the back of the
tent. I tried to follow it, but it was too quick for me.”

“And the guards?”

“They were at the front of the tent. They didn’t see anything.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “A very clever figure, this Anubis. He
seems to know exactly where to go.”

He turned to the doctor.

“You will stay with him, monsieur le docteur?”

“Certainly. I shall not leave him for a moment.”

“Good. Then we can leave him in your hands.”

As we went out of the tent, Poirot turned to me.

“The plot thickens, Hastings. It thickens very much.”

“What do you mean?”

“I mean that the time has come for me to take a hand in the
game. I have seen enough.”

“What are you going to do?”

“I am going to exorcize the evil spirit, Hastings. And I am
going to do it now.”

He led the way to the center of the camp, where a large fire
had been lit. The natives were huddled around it, their faces
pale with terror.

Poirot stepped into the circle of light.

“Listen to me!” he cried, in a voice that rang through the
silence of the night. “The spirit of Men-her-Ra is troubled.
He seeks for vengeance on those who have disturbed his rest.
But he is a just king, and he will not strike the innocent.
Only the guilty shall suffer!”

He paused, and a low murmur rose from the crowd.

“I have the power to call upon the spirit,” continued Poirot.
“I will ask him to show us the face of the one who has brought
this evil upon us!”

He took a small bottle from his pocket and poured its contents
onto the fire. A thick cloud of white smoke rose into the air,
filling the camp with a strange, pungent odor.

“Men-her-Ra!” cried Poirot. “Spirit of the Great King! Show
us the face of the murderer!”

The smoke began to swirl and eddy, and for a moment it seemed
to take the shape of a human figure. Then, with a sudden
movement, Poirot pointed his finger at one of the men standing
by the fire.

“There!” he cried. “There is the man!”

It was the secretary, Mr. Harper!

For a moment there was a dead silence. Then Harper broke into
a discordant laugh.

“You’re mad!” he cried. “Quite mad! Why should I want to kill
anyone?”

“Because,” said Poirot, his voice cold and steady, “you are
not Mr. Harper at all. You are Rupert Bleibner!”

The man’s face went white. He made a movement as though to
flee, but the guards were too quick for him. They seized him
and held him fast.

“It is true,” said Poirot. “The real Mr. Harper died in New
York two months ago. You took his place, knowing that your
uncle would not recognize you after so many years. You wanted
his money, and you knew that he intended to leave it to the
expedition. So you decided to eliminate the members of the
party, one by one, until only you were left.”

“But the deaths!” I cried. “How did he manage them?”

“It was very simple, Hastings. He used his knowledge of
medicine—for he was a medical student before he went to the
South Seas—to induce the various diseases. He poisoned the
scratch on his uncle’s thumb, and he injected the tetanus
germs into Mr. Schneider’s arm. As for Sir John Willard, he
died of a heart attack, it is true, but it was an attack
brought on by a drug which Harper—or Bleibner—had
administered.”

“And the figure of Anubis?”

“A clever trick to frighten the others and to provide a
supernatural explanation for the deaths. He used a mask and
a costume which he had secreted in his luggage.”

“And Sir Guy?”

“A final attempt to clear the way for his inheritance. But
he failed, thanks to the quickness of our friend the doctor.”

Bleibner looked at Poirot with a gaze of baffled fury.

“You’re a clever devil,” he hissed. “But you’ll never prove
it!”

“I think I can,” said Poirot quietly. “You see, I have your
luggage in my tent. And in it I found the mask of Anubis and
a supply of the drugs you used.”

The man’s face collapsed. He knew that the game was up.

“It was the money,” he muttered. “I had to have it.”

“The love of money is the root of all evil,” said Poirot
solemnly. “And now, if you will excuse me, I think I will go
and have a little sleep. This night air is not good for the
constitution.”

And with a little bow he turned and walked away, leaving us
all staring after him in amazement.

The Mystery of the Tomb of Men-her-Ra was solved. It was not
the curse of a dead king that had brought death to the camp,
but the greed and cunning of a living man. And as I looked
at Poirot’s retreating figure, I realized once again that
there is no mystery too deep for the little Belgian detective
to solve.

Dinner was a silent meal. Dr. Ames and Mr. Harper were both
preoccupied, and Sir Guy Willard seemed too exhausted to talk.
The meal was almost over when Poirot suddenly turned to Dr. Ames
and asked:

“I suppose you’ve no doubt that Mr. Schneider’s death was
legitimate? That he hadn’t any enemies?”

The doctor stared.

“He hadn’t an enemy in the world. He was a most popular man.”

“Then it must have been the curse,” said Poirot, with a slight
shiver.

He was silent for a few moments, then he added:

“Is it true that the native workmen have been deserting?”

“Some of them have,” admitted Dr. Ames. “They’re a superstitious
lot.”

“And you, Hassan? You are not afraid?”

The Egyptian shook his head.

“I have my charms, Monsieur Poirot.”

“Ah,” said Poirot, with a touch of interest. “What charms?”

The man reached into his robes and produced a small amulet. Poirot
examined it with curiosity.

“Very interesting,” he murmured. “And do you really believe in its
power?”

“It has never failed me yet,” said the man simply.

I saw a faint smile on Dr. Ames’s face.

“Superstition again,” he murmured.

“Perhaps,” said Poirot. “But what if it is the only thing that
can save us?”

He rose from the table.

“I am tired,” he said. “I think I will go to bed. Captain Hastings,
will you come with me?”

I followed him to our tent.

“Poirot,” I said, as soon as we were alone, “what are you going to
do? You don’t really believe in all this, do you?”

Poirot looked at me.

“My friend, I do not know. But I am going to find out. There is
something here—something that I do not understand.”

He was silent for a moment, then he added:

“I have a feeling that we are not yet at the end of the deaths.
There is another to come.”

“Who?” I asked, with a shiver.

“I do not know. But I am going to watch.”

He sat down on his bed and began to take off his boots.

“I have a plan,” he said. “But I must be careful. I do not want to
alarm the murderer—if there is a murderer.”

“Then you do believe it’s a human agency?”

“I did not say so. But it is possible. And if it is, I must be
prepared.”

He looked at me with a strange expression.

“Captain Hastings, I want you to do something for me.”

“What is it?”

“I want you to stay awake to-night. I want you to watch the tent
of Sir Guy Willard.”

“Why?”

“Because I believe he is in danger.”

“But why his tent particularly?”

“Because he is the head of the expedition now. And if the curse
is really at work, he will be the next victim.”

“But what am I to watch for?”

“Anything. Any movement, any sound. And if you see or hear anything,
let me know at once.”

“I’ll do my best,” I said.

“Good. Now, I am going to sleep. I am very tired.”

He lay down on his bed and was soon fast asleep. I sat by the
opening of the tent and watched.

The night was very still. The only sound was the occasional cry
of a jackal in the distance. The moon was high in the heavens,
and its light turned the desert into a silver sea.

I watched for what seemed like hours. Nothing happened. Sir Guy’s
tent was about twenty yards away, and I could see it clearly in
the moonlight.

Suddenly I saw something. A figure was moving stealthily towards
the tent. It was a man, dressed in white robes. I could not see
his face, but I knew who it was. It was Hassan.

He reached the tent and disappeared inside. I waited for a few
moments, then I went to wake Poirot.

“Poirot!” I whispered. “Hassan has just gone into Sir Guy’s tent.”

Poirot was awake in an instant.

“Hassan? Are you sure?”

“Yes. I saw him.”

“Come,” said Poirot.

We crept out of our tent and made our way towards Sir Guy’s. As
we reached it, we heard a muffled cry from inside.

Poirot pushed aside the flap and we rushed in.

The scene that met our eyes was a strange one. Sir Guy was sitting
up in bed, his face pale with terror. Hassan was standing over
him, his hand raised as if to strike.

But it was not a weapon that he held. It was the amulet that he
had shown us at dinner.

“What is the meaning of this?” demanded Poirot.

Hassan turned to us, his eyes flashing.

“I was but protecting my master,” he said. “The evil spirit was
here—I felt its presence. I came to drive it away.”

“An evil spirit?” said Poirot. “In what form?”

“I know not. But it was here. I felt it.”

He turned back to Sir Guy.

“Fear not, my master. The spirit has gone. You are safe now.”

Sir Guy sank back onto his pillows, his breath coming in short
gasps.

“Thank you, Hassan,” he whispered.

Hassan bowed and left the tent.

Poirot looked at Sir Guy.

“Are you all right, Sir Guy?”

“Yes—yes, I think so. It was just—I had a nightmare, I suppose.
And then I saw Hassan standing there, and I—I was frightened.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Well, try to get some sleep now. We will
be near if you need us.”

We left the tent and went back to our own.

“What do you make of that, Poirot?” I asked.

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “It is very strange. But one thing
is certain—Hassan believes in his amulets.”

“Or he wants us to believe he does,” I suggested.

“Perhaps. But we shall see. We shall see.”

He lay down again and was soon asleep. But I could not sleep. I
sat by the opening of the tent and watched until the sun rose
over the desert.

It was a strange dinner that night. In the middle of it a loud
noise of weeping and wailing came to our ears.

“What is that?” I cried, startled.

“One of the workmen,” answered Dr. Tosswill briefly. “They are
given to it.”

Poirot’s eyes, large and luminous, were fixed on the door of the
tent.

“The sound of death,” he said softly.

Sir Guy Willard turned pale.

“I—I think I’ll just go and see what is the matter,” he said,
rising to his feet.

“Do so,” said Poirot. “I will go with you.”

I followed them. Outside a group of natives were gathered round a
prostrate form. One of them was weeping loudly. Sir Guy went up to
the group and questioned them in Arabic. He came back to us.

“A young lad has just died of some kind of fit,” he explained.

“Heart failure?” suggested Poirot.

“I suppose so.”

“Wait,” said Poirot. He went into the group and I saw him bending
over the body. When he came back his face was very grave.

“There are more ways of killing than one,” he said.

“What do you mean?” I asked.

“I mean that the power of suggestion is a very great one. He
believed that he was going to die, and so he died.”

“But why did he believe it?”

“Because he saw a spirit.”

“A spirit?”

“The spirit of Men-her-Ra.”

Sir Guy Willard laughed.

“Oh, come, Monsieur Poirot, you’re pulling my leg.”

“I am not. I’m speaking in all seriousness. The boy told his
comrades that he had seen a figure in the royal robes of Ancient
Egypt, and that it had beckoned to him. He went into a fit and
died.”

Sir Guy’s face was white.

“I—I don’t know what to think,” he muttered. “This is getting
beyond me.”

The dinner that night was a gloomy meal. Sir Guy was clearly in
no spirits for conversation, and the others were little better.
Ames and Tosswill seemed to be on terms of some intimacy, but they
had little to say to us. The evening was hot and the air was very
still. I noticed that Sir Guy’s hand shook as he poured out some
wine. I thought it better to try and lead the conversation into
channels that might be more cheerful. But I met with little success.
We were all glad when the meal was over.

“What’s that?” asked Dr. Ames suddenly.

We all listened. From a distance came a long drawn-out wail, eerie
and mournful.

“The jackals,” said Sir Guy.

“No, that’s not a jackal,” said the doctor. “What’s that, Tosswill?”

“It was a human voice,” said Tosswill.

The cry was repeated, and then we heard running footsteps. A
frightened-looking native appeared in the doorway of the tent.

“My Lord! My Lord!” he gasped. “The Spirit of the Dead! It is there,
by the Tomb!”

Sir Guy sprang up.

“What nonsense are you talking?” he cried.

The man pointed a trembling finger.

“It is there, my Lord. It is there. A tall figure, in the robes
of a King, with a crown upon its head!”

Sir Guy rushed out, followed by the rest of us. The moon was
shining brightly, and in the distance we could see a white figure
flitting among the excavations. As we watched it, it seemed to
vanish into the darkness.

“Wait here,” cried Sir Guy, and he started to run.

We followed him, but we had not gone far before we saw him stumble
and fall. When we reached him he was unconscious.

“Sunstroke,” said Dr. Ames, who was the first to reach him. “We
must get him back to the tent at once.”

We carried him back and laid him on his bed. He was breathing
heavily, and his face was flushed.

“He’ll be all right,” said the doctor, after he had examined him.
“It’s just a touch of the sun. He’s been overdoing it lately.”

But I noticed that Poirot was looking very grave.

“You think it was sunstroke, _monsieur le docteur_?” he asked.

“What else could it be?” said the doctor.

“I do not know,” said Poirot. “But I do not like it. I do not like
it at all.”

We left Sir Guy in the care of his servant, and went back to our
own tent.

“What do you make of it, Poirot?” I asked.

“I do not like it, Hastings,” he repeated. “There is something
wrong here. Something very wrong indeed.”

“You don’t believe in the Spirit of the Dead?” I asked.

“I believe in the power of the human mind,” said Poirot. “And I
believe that there is someone here who is using that power for
evil purposes.”

“But who?” I asked.

“That is what we have to find out,” said Poirot. “And we must find
out quickly, or there will be more deaths.”

He sat down and began to study his little book of Egyptian magic.

“I must think,” he said. “I must think.”

I left him to his meditations and went to bed. But I did not sleep
well. I was haunted by the vision of that white figure flitting
among the excavations, and by the thought of the deaths that had
already occurred. Was it possible that there was some truth in
the story of the Curse of Men-her-Ra? Or was it all the work of
some human agency?

I fell into a troubled sleep at last, only to be awakened by a cry.

“Hastings! Hastings! Come quickly!”

It was Poirot’s voice. I sprang out of bed and rushed into the
next room. Poirot was standing by the window, looking out into
the night.

“Look!” he cried, pointing.

I looked out and saw a figure in white robes standing by the
entrance to the Tomb. It was the same figure we had seen earlier,
but this time it was not flitting away. It was standing quite
still, as if it were waiting for something.

“What is it?” I whispered.

“It is the Spirit of the Dead,” said Poirot. “And it has come for
another victim.”

As he spoke, the figure turned and began to walk towards us. I felt
a cold shiver run down my spine.

“What are we going to do?” I asked.

“We must wait,” said Poirot. “We must wait and see what happens.”

The figure came closer and closer, until it was right outside our
tent. Then it stopped and began to chant in a low, monotonous
voice.

I could not understand the words, but they seemed to be filled
with a terrible menace.

Suddenly, the figure turned and vanished into the darkness.

“It is gone,” I said.

“For the moment,” said Poirot. “But it will return. It will return
until it has achieved its purpose.”

“And what is its purpose?” I asked.

“To kill,” said Poirot. “To kill everyone who has dared to disturb
the rest of King Men-her-Ra.”

He turned away from the window and began to pace the room.

“We must act,” he said. “We must act at once.”

“But what can we do?” I asked.

“We must find out who is behind this,” said Poirot. “We must find
out who is using the legend of the Curse to cover up their crimes.”

“But how?” I asked.

“I have a plan,” said Poirot. “But it is a dangerous one. Are you
willing to help me, Hastings?”

“Of course,” I said.

“Then listen carefully,” said Poirot.

He began to outline his plan, and as I listened, I felt a sense
of dread stealing over me. It was indeed a dangerous plan, but it
seemed to be our only hope of catching the killer.

“Are you ready?” asked Poirot.

“Yes,” I said.

“Then let us go,” he said.

We left the tent and made our way towards the excavations. The
moon was still shining brightly, and the desert was bathed in a
silver light.

As we neared the Tomb, we saw a figure standing by the entrance.
It was the same figure we had seen before, but this time it was
not alone. There was another figure with it, a man in modern
clothes.

We crept closer, until we were close enough to hear what they were
saying.

“You have done well,” said the man in modern clothes. “The work
is almost complete.”

“The Spirit of the Dead is pleased,” said the figure in white
robes. “The intruders will be punished.”

“And then the treasure will be ours,” said the man.

“Yes,” said the figure. “The treasure will be ours.”

They turned and entered the Tomb.

“Now!” whispered Poirot.

We followed them into the Tomb, our hearts pounding in our breasts.
The air inside was cold and damp, and there was a strange, sickly
smell.

We made our way through the narrow passages, guided by the sound
of their voices. At last we reached a large chamber, and there we
saw them.

The man in modern clothes was standing by a large stone sarcophagus,
while the figure in white robes was chanting over it.

“Stop!” cried Poirot.

They both turned round, startled. The man in modern clothes was
Dr. Ames. The figure in white robes was Hassan.

“What is the meaning of this?” demanded Poirot.

“We are only doing what the Spirit of the Dead commands,” said
Hassan.

“Nonsense,” said Poirot. “You are using the legend of the Curse
to cover up your crimes. You killed Sir John Willard, and Mr.
Bleibner, and Mr. Schneider. And you were going to kill Sir Guy
Willard too.”

“You have no proof,” said Dr. Ames.

“I have all the proof I need,” said Poirot. “I know how you did
it. You used a rare poison, one that leaves no trace. And you
used Hassan to play the part of the Spirit of the Dead, to frighten
everyone away.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Dr. Ames.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain why you have
this in your pocket.”

He reached into Dr. Ames’s pocket and pulled out a small glass
vial.

“It is the poison,” said Poirot. “The same poison you used to kill
the others.”

Dr. Ames turned pale. He knew that he was caught.

“You’ll never prove it,” he muttered.

“Oh, yes I will,” said Poirot. “The police are on their way here
now. They will find all the evidence they need.”

Dr. Ames and Hassan were taken away by the police, and Sir Guy
Willard recovered from his “sunstroke.”

“You were right, Poirot,” I said, as we were driving back to Cairo.
“It was all the work of human agency.”

“Of course it was,” said Poirot. “The Spirit of the Dead does not
kill. Only the living do that.”

“But how did you know it was Dr. Ames?” I asked.

“It was simple, Hastings,” said Poirot. “He was the only one who
had the knowledge and the opportunity to use the poison. And he
was the only one who had a motive.”

“A motive?” I asked.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “He wanted the treasure for himself. He knew
that if he could get rid of the others, he would be able to claim
it all.”

“And Hassan?” I asked.

“Hassan was his accomplice,” said Poirot. “He was easily persuaded
to help, for he believed in the Curse himself.”

“It was a narrow escape for Sir Guy,” I said.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “But he is safe now. And the Curse of Men-her-Ra
is no more.”

He sat back and closed his eyes.

“And now, Hastings,” he said. “If you don’t mind, I think I will
have a little sleep. It has been a long and tiring day.”

I smiled. Poirot was himself again.

The mystery of the Tomb of King Men-her-Ra was solved, and once
again, the little Belgian detective had proved that his “little
grey cells” were a match for any criminal, even one who tried to
use the power of the supernatural to cover up his crimes.

We returned to London a few days later, and Poirot was greeted
as a hero. Lady Willard was overjoyed to have her son back safe
and sound, and she thanked Poirot from the bottom of her heart.

As for me, I shall never forget the adventure of the Tomb of King
Men-her-Ra, and the lesson it taught me—that things are not always
what they seem, and that even the most supernatural of mysteries
can have a very human explanation.

Poirot, of course, took it all in his stride. He was already
thinking about his next case.

“What will it be, Poirot?” I asked him one morning as we were
sitting in our rooms in Baker Street.

“I do not know, Hastings,” he said. “But I am sure it will be
something interesting. It always is.”

And with that, he turned back to his breakfast, a contented look
upon his face.

The end.

Our meal was hardly a cheerful one. The floor was left to Dr.
Tosswill, who discoursed at length upon Egyptian antiquities. Just
as we were preparing to retire to rest, Sir Guy caught Poirot by
the arm and pointed. A shadowy figure was moving amidst the tents.
It was no human one: I recognized distinctly the dog-headed figure
I had seen carved on the walls of the tomb.

My blood literally froze at the sight.

“_Mon Dieu!_” murmured Poirot, crossing himself vigorously. “Anubis,
the jackal-headed, the god of departing souls.”

“Some one is hoaxing us,” cried Dr. Tosswill, rising indignantly
to his feet.

“It went into your tent, Harper,” muttered Sir Guy, his face
dreadfully pale.

“No,” said Poirot, shaking his head, “into that of the Dr. Ames.”

The doctor stared at him incredulously; then, repeating Dr.
Tosswill’s words, he cried:

“Some one is hoaxing us. Come, we’ll soon catch the fellow.”

We dashed across the intervening space, Dr. Ames leading the way with an agility that surprised me. He flung back the flap of his tent and we crowded in behind him. The interior was lit by a single oil lamp, casting long, wavering shadows against the canvas walls, but of the jackal-headed figure there was no sign. The tent appeared exactly as it had been left, with the doctor’s medical chest and a few books neatly arranged. “Empty!” cried Tosswill, his voice echoing our own bafflement. “But we saw him enter—there is no other way out!” Poirot, who had followed more slowly, stood in the doorway, his eyes travelling searchingly over the sandy floor. He said nothing, but I noticed him bend down for a moment, his gloved finger tracing a light mark in the dust that might have been the print of a foot—or something far more ancient and sinister.

We dashed across the sand, Dr. Ames leading the way with surprising agility. He wrenched back the flap of his own tent and we crowded in behind him, our breath coming in short, sharp gasps. The interior was illuminated by a single oil lamp, casting long, wavering shadows against the canvas, but of the jackal-headed apparition there was no sign. The tent was empty. A small opening at the rear, where the canvas had been left unfastened, fluttered slightly in the evening breeze, suggesting a hurried exit. Dr. Tosswill let out a snort of frustrated indignation, while Mr. Harper, who had followed us at a distance, stood trembling in the doorway. Poirot, however, did not search; he stood in the center of the tent, his eyes fixed on the ground, murmuring prayers in a low, rhythmic tone that sent a chill down my spine.

He broke into a run, his face set in lines of grim determination. We followed close at his heels, stumbling over the uneven ground in the darkness. Ames reached his tent first and flung back the flap, his electric torch swinging in a wide arc. The interior was small and sparsely furnished: a camp bed, a folding table, and a few medical chests. There was no sign of the jackal-headed visitor. The canvas walls were taut and undisturbed, and no hidden exit offered itself to our frantic inspection. Dr. Ames turned to us, his breath coming in short, sharp gasps, the light of his torch trembling slightly in his hand.

He led the way, we following close at his heels. But the tent was empty. There was no sign of any human intruder, nor any place where such a one could have concealed himself. Dr. Ames looked around him, bewildered. Dr. Tosswill, meanwhile, was conducting a vigorous search outside, but he returned a few minutes later, shaking his head. “Not a trace,” he declared. “The fellow must have been as fleet of foot as a gazelle to have vanished so completely. It’s a most extraordinary thing.” Poirot, however, was not looking for footmarks; his eyes were fixed upon a small, dark object that lay upon the floor of the tent. He picked it up and held it out to us. It was a small, strangely shaped piece of flint.

We rushed after the retreating figure, Dr. Ames leading the way with a heavy torch in his hand. We burst into his tent, our hearts hammering against our ribs, but the interior was silent and, to all appearances, empty. There was no sign of the strange, jackal-headed visitant. Dr. Ames flung aside the flap of his sleeping compartment, then turned back to us, his face a mask of bewilderment. “Nothing,” he ejaculated. “The place is as empty as a drum. If that was a man, he’s got the vanishing trick down to a fine art.” Poirot, however, did not seem surprised; he was down on his knees, examining the sandy floor with a minute attention that appeared to me entirely wasted in the shadows.

He dashed energetically in pursuit of the shadowy apparition. I
followed him, but, search as we would, we could find no trace of
any living soul having passed that way. We returned, somewhat
disturbed in mind, to find Poirot taking energetic measures, in
his own way, to ensure his personal safety. He was busily
surrounding our tent with various diagrams and inscriptions which
he was drawing in the sand. I recognized the five-pointed star or
Pentagon many times repeated. As was his wont, Poirot was at the
same time delivering an impromptu lecture on witchcraft and magic
in general, White Magic as opposed to Black, with various references
to the Ka and the Book of the Dead thrown in.

It appeared to excite the liveliest contempt in Dr. Tosswill, who
drew me aside, literally snorting with rage.

“I have always heard that this Monsieur Poirot was a man of sense,
but he’s nothing but a superstitious fool. I never heard such
stuff as he’s talking in my life. One might as well be back in
the Middle Ages.”

I agreed with him. Poirot’s behaviour was certainly most peculiar.
Yet I could not help wondering what his purpose could be. I could
hardly believe that he was as credulous as he seemed. Was it
merely to impress the others? Or was it some subtle plan of his
own?

We were all glad when at last we could seek our beds. The day had
been a trying one. I think we all felt that the atmosphere of
mystery and dread which hung over the camp was beginning to get on
our nerves. As I lay in my bed I could hear the wind moaning over
the desert. It was a most eerie sound. In spite of my fatigue I
could not sleep. I was haunted by the memory of that strange,
dog-headed figure which we had seen flitting among the tents. Was
it indeed a ghost from the past? Or was it some living man playing
a part for his own purposes? And if so, what were those purposes?
The four deaths—were they all due to natural causes, or was there
some sinister connection between them?

My thoughts were interrupted by a low voice from the other bed.

“Hastings, are you awake?”

“Yes,” I replied.

“I have much fear,” whispered Poirot. “There is something here,
something that I do not understand. I feel it in the air. We must
be on our guard, Hastings. We must be on our guard.”

I fell asleep at last, but my dreams were troubled. I was back in
the tomb of King Men-her-Ra, and the dog-headed god was standing
over me, his eyes glowing with an unearthly light. I woke with a
start to find the sun streaming into the tent. Poirot was already
up and dressed. He looked pale and anxious.

“Come, Hastings,” he said, “we must go and see how the others have
fared during the night.”

We found the camp in a state of great excitement. Dr. Ames had
been found dead in his tent. He had apparently died in his sleep.
There were no signs of a struggle. The cause of death appeared to
be heart failure.

This fifth death, following so closely on the others, had a
profound effect on everyone. Even Dr. Tosswill seemed shaken. Sir
Guy Willard was in a state of collapse. Mr. Harper was openly
terrified.

“It’s the curse!” he cried. “The curse of Men-her-Ra! We’re all
doomed! None of us will leave this place alive!”

Poirot said nothing. He stood looking down at the body of the
dead doctor. His face was grave and inscrutable.

“What do you make of it, Monsieur Poirot?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“It is very strange,” said Poirot slowly. “Very strange indeed.”

He turned away and walked out of the tent. I followed him.

“What are you going to do now?” I asked.

“I am going to talk to Hassan,” he replied.

We found the native servant sitting outside his tent, his head
bowed in his hands. He looked up as we approached.

“The spirit of the King is angry,” he said. “He will not be
appeased until we are all dead.”

“Tell me, Hassan,” said Poirot, “did you see anything last night?”

The man hesitated.

“I saw the dog-headed one,” he said at last. “He passed by my tent.”

“In which direction was he going?”

“Towards the tent of the doctor.”

Poirot nodded.

“I thought as much,” he muttered.

He turned back towards the center of the camp.

“Hastings,” he said, “I must think. I must think very carefully.
There is something here that I have missed. Something very simple,
and yet very subtle.”

He spent the rest of the morning pacing up and down the sand, his
brows knit in thought. I left him to his meditations and went to
talk to Sir Guy Willard. I found him in a state of great distress.

“This is terrible, Hastings,” he said. “Ames was a good friend of
mine. I can’t believe he’s gone.”

“It’s very mysterious,” I agreed.

“Do you think Monsieur Poirot will be able to find out what’s
behind all this?”

“I hope so,” I said. “He’s a very clever man.”

“I hope he’s clever enough to deal with the spirit of an ancient
Egyptian king,” said Sir Guy with a wan smile.

The afternoon passed slowly. The heat was intense. We all felt the
strain of the situation. Every shadow seemed to hold a threat.
Every sound made us jump.

As the sun began to set, Poirot called us all together in the
main tent.

“Messieurs,” he said, “I have something to tell you.”

We all looked at him expectantly.

“I have discovered the truth,” he continued. “The deaths of Sir
John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, and Mr. Schneider were not due to the
curse of Men-her-Ra. They were due to a much more modern agency.”

He paused for a moment, then went on.

“They were all murdered.”

A gasp of astonishment went round the group.

“Murdered!” cried Sir Guy. “But how? And by whom?”

“I will tell you,” said Poirot. “But first, I must tell you about
the death of young Rupert Bleibner in New York.”

He then proceeded to explain his theory about Rupert Bleibner’s
suicide.

“He killed himself out of remorse,” said Poirot. “Remorse for a
crime he had committed here in Egypt.”

“What crime?” asked Mr. Harper.

“The murder of Sir John Willard,” said Poirot. “He intended to
kill his uncle, Mr. Bleibner, but by mistake he killed Sir John
instead.”

“But how did he do it?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“He used a very subtle poison,” said Poirot. “A poison that leaves
no trace.”

“And what about the other deaths?” asked Sir Guy.

“They were also murders,” said Poirot. “But they were committed by
someone else. Someone who wanted to cover up the first murder.”

“Who?” we all cried together.

Poirot’s eyes swept round the group. Finally they rested on one
man.

“The murderer,” he said, “is Mr. Harper.”

The young secretary started back, his face turning a sickly grey.

“Me?” he gasped. “You’re crazy! Why should I kill anyone?”

“Because you knew,” said Poirot. “You knew that Rupert Bleibner
had killed Sir John Willard. You saw him do it. And you blackmailed
him.”

“That’s a lie!” cried Harper.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then why did Rupert Bleibner send you money
from New York? We found the record of the transfers in his bank
account.”

Harper was silent.

“He sent you money to keep your mouth shut,” continued Poirot.
“But it wasn’t enough. You wanted more. You wanted Mr. Bleibner’s
fortune for yourself. So you killed him. And then you killed Mr.
Schneider because he suspecting something. And finally you killed
Dr. Ames because he had found out the truth.”

“But how?” I asked. “How did he do it?”

“He used the same poison that Rupert Bleibner had used,” said
Poirot. “He had stolen it from him before he left for New York.”

“And the dog-headed figure?” asked Sir Guy.

“That was also Mr. Harper,” said Poirot. “He used it to frighten
us, to make us believe in the curse.”

Harper suddenly made a dash for the door of the tent, but Dr.
Tosswill and I were too quick for him. We grabbed him and held him
fast.

“It’s no use, Harper,” said Poirot. “The game is up.”

And so the mystery of the Tomb of King Men-her-Ra was solved. It
was not the curse of an ancient king that had caused the deaths,
but the greed and wickedness of a modern man.

As we rode back to Cairo on our camels, Poirot was unusually
silent.

“What is it, Poirot?” I asked. “Are you thinking about the case?”

“No, Hastings,” he replied. “I am thinking about the sea. The
hateful sea!”

I laughed. Poirot might be a great detective, but he would never
be a good sailor.

“If that little idiot is going to do that sort of thing here, he’d
much better have stayed at home. The natives are scared enough
already, without having his superstitious nonsense added to their
terrors. I shall have a talk with Sir Guy and get him sent away.
It’s really too much.”

I could not but agree with him. Poirot’s conduct seemed to me to
be most uncharacteristic. He appeared to have lost his head
completely.

I was restless and unhappy. Not for anything would I have admitted
it, but the uncanny atmosphere of the place was getting on my
nerves. I felt that some tragedy was pending.

The next morning I was early astir. It was a beautiful morning,
cool and fresh, with the light of the rising sun just beginning
to tip the summits of the Pyramids. I strolled towards the diggings.
To my surprise I saw Poirot already there, talking to a group of
excited-looking natives. As I approached, they scattered, and
Poirot came towards me.

“Well, Hastings, I have been making inquiries. Our jackal-headed
friend has not been seen by any of the workmen. That is
satisfactory.”

“What have you been doing?” I asked.

“I have been playing a part, _mon ami_, a part that is not
altogether a part. I have been frightening these poor people. To
frighten is often a way to get at the truth. Also I have been
making a little test.”

“What sort of test?”

“A very simple one. I have been testing the courage of our friends
the Europeans. Dr. Tosswill, as you saw, was merely angry. Sir Guy
was terrified. Mr. Harper was—well, he was what I should call
comfortably scared. And Dr. Ames—did you notice Dr. Ames,
Hastings?”

“He seemed as much in earnest as anyone,” I said.

“He was very much in earnest,” agreed Poirot. “He was even more
earnest than I was myself. Now, let us go to breakfast.”

“Look at him!” he cried, pointing at Poirot. “A man of his
reputation, his standing, behave in such a manner! It’s
unprecedented! It’s positively indecent!”

I could only shrug my shoulders. I felt as though the whole world
were out of gear. It was after midnight when we finally settled
ourselves to rest. In spite of the excitement of the evening I
slept soundly, and was only awakened by the sound of some one
knocking on the tent pole.

I started up, and Poirot, who appeared to be wide awake, followed
my example.

It was Dr. Ames. His face was white and drawn.

“It’s happened,” he gasped. “Sir Guy Willard. He’s dead.”

“Dead!” I cried. “The Curse of Men-her-Ra! It’s claimed another
victim.”

“Wait,” said Poirot, “how did he die?”

“Heart failure. I suppose. I don’t know. I was called to his tent
ten minutes ago. He was already dead.”

“Heart failure,” said Poirot, “like his father.”

He was already dressing with his accustomed care. I followed suit,
my hands shaking with a strange dread. Together we went to the
tent of the dead boy. He lay on his side, his face very pale. He
had evidently died in his sleep.

Dr. Tosswill and Mr. Harper were already there. They looked scared
and miserable.

“It’s the Curse,” muttered the latter. “I’m for New York by the
first boat. I’m not going to wait for my turn.”

“Wait,” said Poirot, “I must see if anything has been disturbed.”

He began a systematic search of the tent. On a small table by the
bedside was a glass of water. Poirot sniffed it, then tasted it
cautiously.

“Ah!” he said, “what have we here?”

He held up a small bottle of tablets.

“These,” said Dr. Ames, “are some that I prescribed for him myself.
They are merely a mild sedative.”

Poirot nodded.

“And this?” he asked, pointing to a small dish on the table.

“That,” said Dr. Tosswill, “is a native dish of some kind. Hassan
brought it to him last night.”

Poirot’s eyes met mine for a second.

“Hassan?” he murmured.

“Yes,” said Sir Guy’s servant, stepping forward from the shadow.
“I brought it to my master. It is a dish that he loved.”

“And you?” said Poirot, turning to Dr. Ames. “You have no doubt
as to the cause of death?”

“None whatever. Heart failure, as I said.”

“Then there will be no need for an autopsy?”

“Hardly, I should say. There are no suspicious circumstances.”

“I see,” said Poirot. He turned to me. “Come, Hastings.”

I followed him out of the tent. The sun was just rising, and the
desert was bathed in a wonderful rose-red light.

“Well,” I said, “what do you think of it?”

“I think,” said Poirot, “that we have a very interesting case.”

“But the Curse?” I cried. “Surely you believe in that now?”

“I believe in many things, Hastings. But most of all I believe in
the little grey cells of the brain.”

“Then you think——?”

“I think that we shall find the murderer before the day is out.”

“The murderer? Then you don’t think it was the Curse?”

“The Curse may have been the instrument, Hastings, but the hand
that wielded it was a human one.”

“But who?” I cried. “Who could have had any motive for killing
Sir Guy Willard?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what we have to find out.”

He walked on in silence for a few minutes. Then he turned to me.

“Hastings, I want you to go to Cairo.”

“To Cairo?” I cried in astonishment.

“Yes. I want you to find out all you can about Mr. Bleibner’s
financial affairs.”

“But what has that to do with Sir Guy Willard’s death?”

“Everything, my friend. Everything.”

I saw that it was useless to argue with him. When Poirot has that
look in his eyes, there is no moving him.

“Very well,” I said, “I will go. But what are you going to do?”

“I,” said Poirot, “am going to have a little talk with Hassan.”

I left him then, and made my way back to the camp to prepare for
my journey. I felt a strange sense of excitement. Poirot was on the
trail, and I knew that he would not rest until he had found the
truth.

It was late in the evening when I returned from Cairo. I had found
out much that was interesting, but I could see no connection between
Mr. Bleibner’s money and the death of Sir Guy Willard.

Poirot was waiting for me in our tent. He looked tired but
triumphant.

“Well?” I asked. “What have you found out?”

“Much, my friend. Much. But first, tell me what you have learned
in Cairo.”

I told him all that I had discovered. Mr. Bleibner had been a very
wealthy man, but he had left no will. His fortune would go to his
nearest relative, who was, as far as could be ascertained, a
distant cousin in America.

“A distant cousin,” said Poirot thoughtfully. “That is interesting.
Very interesting.”

“But what about Hassan?” I asked. “What did he tell you?”

“He told me much, Hastings. He told me of the love he bore his late
master, and of his fear for the young Sir Guy. He told me also of
the strange things he had seen and heard in the night.”

“The dog-headed figure?” I asked.

“Yes, the dog-headed figure. Hassan saw it too. But he saw
something else, Hastings. Something that we did not see.”

“What was it?” I cried.

“He saw the hand that killed Sir Guy Willard.”

“The hand? You mean you know who the murderer is?”

“I think so, Hastings. I think so.”

He rose and walked to the door of the tent.

“Come,” he said, “it is time for us to join the others.”

We found the members of the expedition assembled in the main tent.
They looked a dismal party. Dr. Tosswill was silent and morose,
Mr. Harper was visibly nervous, and Dr. Ames looked worn and
haggard.

Poirot took his seat at the table. For a few minutes he sat in
silence, his eyes moving from one face to another. Then he began
to speak.

“Messieurs,” he said, “we are faced with a very grave situation.
Five deaths have occurred in connection with this expedition. To
the world at large they are the result of a Curse—the Curse of
Men-her-Ra. But to me, they are something very different.”

He paused, and a pin might have been heard to drop in the tent.

“I have investigated these deaths,” Poirot continued, “and I have
come to a very definite conclusion. They are not the work of a
dead king, but of a living man.”

A gasp of astonishment went round the table.

“A living man?” cried Mr. Harper. “But who? Who could have done
such a thing?”

“That,” said Poirot, “is what I am about to tell you. But first, let
us look at the facts. Sir John Willard died of heart failure. Mr.
Bleibner died of blood poisoning. His nephew committed suicide in
New York. Mr. Schneider died of tetanus. And now, Sir Guy Willard
has died of heart failure. Five deaths, all seemingly unrelated.
And yet, there is a link—a very definite link—that binds them all
together.”

“And what is 그 link?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“The link,” said Poirot, “is money. The money of Mr. Bleibner.”

“But what has that to do with Sir John Willard or his son?” asked
Dr. Ames.

“Everything,” said Poirot. “You see, Mr. Bleibner was a very wealthy
man. He had no children, and his only near relative was his nephew,
Rupert. If Rupert were to die, the money would go to—whom? That is
the question I asked myself. And the answer, messieurs, is very
simple. The money would go to the person who had the greatest
influence over Mr. Bleibner—the person who had persuaded him to
finance this expedition—the person who, in short, stood to gain
the most by his death.”

He paused, and his eyes rested on one of the men at the table.

“That person,” said Poirot, “is you, Dr. Ames.”

The doctor started to his feet, his face livid.

“It’s a lie!” he cried. “A damned lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot calmly. “Let us see. You were Mr. Bleibner’s
medical adviser. You knew that he had no will. You knew that if his
nephew were to die, you would be his principal heir. You had already
persuaded him to leave a large sum of money to the expedition, of
which you were a leading member. But that was not enough for you.
You wanted it all. And so, you began your systematic campaign of
murder.”

“You killed Sir John Willard—not because you had anything against
him, but because his death would lend colour to the story of the
Curse. You killed Mr. Bleibner by infecting a scratch on his thumb
with a deadly culture. You drove his nephew to suicide by making
him believe that he was a leper—a simple matter for a doctor who
knew his history. You killed Mr. Schneider with tetanus. And
finally, you killed Sir Guy Willard, again to keep up the illusion
of the Curse.”

“But how?” I cried. “How did he kill Sir Guy Willard?”

“By a very simple method, Hastings. He substituted a deadly poison
for the sedative he had prescribed. A poison that would leave no
trace, and would simulate the symptoms of heart failure.”

“It’s a lie!” shouted Dr. Ames. “You have no proof!”

“Proof?” said Poirot. “I have the proof of Hassan’s eyes. He saw
you enter Sir Guy’s tent last night. He saw you change the bottles.
And I have another proof—the bottle of tablets itself. I have had
it analyzed, and it contains a deadly alkaloid.”

For a moment there was a dead silence. Then, with a sudden cry of
rage, Dr. Ames whipped out a revolver. But before he could fire,
Hassan had sprung upon him from behind, and the weapon was
wrested from his hand.

“It is over, monsieur,” said Poirot. “The Curse of Men-her-Ra is
at an end.”

And so it was. Dr. Ames was taken to Cairo, where he eventually
confessed to his crimes. He had indeed been the principal heir to
Mr. Bleibner’s fortune, and had planned the whole series of
murders with cold-blooded calculation.

As for the Curse, it was never heard of again. The excavations
were continued under the direction of Dr. Tosswill, and many
wonderful discoveries were made. But for me, the most wonderful
discovery of all was the genius of Hercule Poirot, who had seen
through the mists of superstition to the truth that lay behind.

“He’s a charlatan, your friend, Captain Hastings. It’s a
disgrace—nothing more nor less. Pentagrams and such rubbish! How
can a man of his standing talk such rank, unadulterated nonsense!
It’s enough to make a cat laugh!”

“Well,” I admitted, “it does seem a bit thick, I must say. But
Poirot always has some reason for what he does.”

“Fiddlesticks!” he snapped.

I was rather inclined to agree with him, but nevertheless I slept
none the less soundly for Poirot’s precautions.

But next morning we were awakened early by a clamour.

Sir Guy Willard was found dead in his tent. It was another case
of heart failure. His face wore a look of the most intense and
ghastly terror.

The news spread like wildfire through the camp. Panic was the only
word for the state of mind of the natives. They were preparing to
leave in a body.

“You see,” said Poirot to me. “The spirit of Men-her-Ra is not yet
appeased. One more victim! Who will be the next?”

I felt a sudden, sickening qualm.

“For Heaven’s sake, Poirot, don’t talk like that! It’s
ghastly—ghastly!”

“You are right, Hastings. It is ghastly.”

He turned away.

“Where are you going?”

“To have a talk with Dr. Ames.”

The doctor was in his tent, looking very shaken and miserable.

“This is a terrible business,” he said, as we entered. “I’m
absolutely bowled over. I can’t understand it. Both father and
son—it’s—it’s beyond everything.”

“Are you certain it was heart failure?”

“Absolutely. There’s not a mark on him. He just died—of fright,
it looks like.”

“_Tiens!_” said Poirot. “That is a very interesting theory. He
died of fright! Have you ever known a case of the kind before?”

“No, I can’t say I have. But it’s the only possible explanation.”

Poirot nodded thoughtfully.

“Yes, it is possible. But it is not scientific, is it, _monsieur
le docteur_?”

“In the face of these events, science has to take a back seat,”
said the doctor shortly.

“There I agree with you,” said Poirot. “But we must not abandon our
efforts to find the truth. I have a little plan.”

“What is it?”

“I am going to spend the night in the Tomb.”

I uttered a cry of protest.

“Poirot, you mustn’t! It’s—it’s madness!”

“_Au contraire_, it is the only way. To-morrow I shall have much
to tell you.”

Dr. Ames looked at him curiously.

“You’re a brave man, Monsieur Poirot. I shouldn’t care to do it
myself for a good deal.”

“It is my duty,” said Poirot simply. “I have promised Lady Willard
to protect her son. I have failed. Now I must find the murderer.”

“The murderer?” I cried. “Then you don’t believe in the curse after
all?”

Poirot smiled.

“I believe in everything—and in nothing. We shall see.”

I tried in vain to dissuade him from his purpose. He was quite
immovable. At sunset he entered the Tomb, and the heavy door was
closed behind him.

I spent a night of the most agonizing anxiety. What might be
happening in that dark, silent chamber? Every now and then I
fancied I heard a sound—a cry—a groan. I was on the point of
breaking in the door a dozen times.

But at last the morning dawned. The door was opened, and Poirot
stepped out. He looked pale and exhausted, but his eyes were
shining with a strange light.

“Well?” I cried.

“I have seen him,” he said in a low voice. “I have seen the spirit
of Men-her-Ra.”

“Poirot!”

“It is true. He appeared to me in the likeness of a man, with the
head of a jackal. He spoke to me.”

“What did he say?”

“He told me many things. He told me the name of the murderer.”

“And who is it?”

“That I cannot tell you yet. I must have proof—proof that will
stand in a court of law. But I know—I know!”

He refused to say any more, and spent the rest of the day in a
state of suppressed excitement. He was continually looking at his
watch, as though he were waiting for something.

At last, towards evening, a messenger arrived from Cairo with a
large package for Poirot. He tore it open with trembling fingers.
It contained a number of legal-looking documents.

He scanned them quickly, and a cry of triumph escaped him.

“_Enfin!_ I have it! The last link in the chain!”

He turned to me, his face alight with professional pride.
