“And now, Hastings, we will have a little talk with our friends.”

He summoned Dr. Tosswill, Dr. Ames, and Mr. Harper to the mess
tent. Hassan also was present, standing like a statue in the
shadows.

Poirot took his place at the head of the table. He looked more
like a judge than a detective.

“Messieurs,” he began, “I have asked you to come here because I
have at last discovered the truth about the deaths that have
occurred in this camp.”

There was a tense silence. Every eye was fixed on Poirot.

“You have all believed,” he continued, “in the curse of
Men-her-Ra. You have believed that a long-dead king was taking his
vengeance on those who disturbed his rest. It was a very
ingenious theory—very ingenious indeed. It provided a perfect
screen for a very modern and very cold-blooded murderer.”

He paused, as though to let his words sink in.

“The first death, that of Sir John Willard, was indeed due to
natural causes—heart failure. But it was that death which gave the
murderer his idea. He saw how the public mind was affected by the
superstitious stories in the newspapers, and he decided to turn
that superstition to his own advantage.”

“The second death, that of Mr. Bleibner, was not an accident. It
was murder. He was deliberately infected with a deadly culture of
bacteria. The same was true of Mr. Schneider. He did not die of
tetanus contracted naturally. He was poisoned—poisoned by a man who
had the means and the knowledge to do so.”

“And the nephew in New York?” I asked.

“He also was a victim. He was driven to suicide by the same
remorseless hand. He was made to believe that he had committed a
terrible crime, and in his despair he took his own life.”

“And Sir Guy?” cried Dr. Tosswill. “What of him?”

“Sir Guy Willard did not die of heart failure,” said Poirot
gravely. “He was murdered, like the others.”

“But how?” asked Dr. Ames. “There was not a mark on him.”

“There are many ways of killing a man without leaving a mark,
_monsieur le docteur_,” said Poirot. “Ways that are known to
science—and to those who have studied the secrets of the past.”

He leaned forward, his eyes fixed on one of the men at the table.

“The murderer is amongst us now. He is a man of great intelligence,
of great daring, and of no pity. He has played a desperate game,
and he has nearly won. But he made one mistake. He forgot that
Hercule Poirot does not believe in ghosts.”

He stood up, pointing a dramatic finger.

“The murderer of Sir John Willard’s son, of Mr. Bleibner, and of
Mr. Schneider, is you—Dr. Tosswill!”

The archaeologist started back, his face a mask of fury.

“You’re mad!” he cried. “Stark, staring mad! What motive could I
possibly have for these crimes?”

“The motive was simple,” said Poirot. “Mr. Bleibner was a very
wealthy man. He had no heirs—or so it was thought. But you, Dr.
Tosswill, had discovered a secret. You had discovered that you
were, in fact, his nearest living relative. If he died intestate,
his vast fortune would come to you. You decided to hasten his
end, and to remove any others who might stand in your way.”

“It’s a lie!” shouted Tosswill. “A pack of lies!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “I have here the proofs—the records of your
birth and parentage, which I obtained from London and New York.
They show clearly that you are the son of Mr. Bleibner’s elder
brother, who disappeared many years ago.”

Tosswill made a sudden movement, as though to escape, but Hassan
was too quick for him. The powerful Arab seized him by the arms
and held him fast.

“It is no use, monsieur,” said Poirot. “The game is up. The
police are on their way from Cairo.”

The doctor’s face collapsed. He knew that he was beaten.

“Yes,” he muttered, “I did it. And I would do it again. That
money should have been mine—mine to carry on my work. Why should it
be wasted on a pack of fools who know nothing of the glories of
the past?”

He was led away, still muttering to himself.

Poirot turned to me with a tired smile.

“So, Hastings, the mystery is solved. The curse of Men-her-Ra was
nothing but a shadow—a shadow cast by the greed and ambition of a
man.”

“But the figure we saw?” I asked. “The jackal-headed god?”

“A very simple trick, _mon ami_. A mask and a piece of gauze.
Dr. Tosswill played the part himself, to increase the terror of
his victims.”

“And your night in the Tomb?”

“A little piece of theatre, Hastings. I knew that the murderer
would be watching me, and I wanted to lead him on. I saw nothing
in the Tomb but the dust of centuries.”

He sighed and picked up his clothes-brush.

“And now, let us leave this place. I have a great desire to see
once more the streets of London—and to have a pair of boots that
are truly clean!”

“If I were you, Captain Hastings, I should strongly advise your
friend to—well, I’ll be plain—to go home. The man’s as mad as a
Hatter. He’s talking the most infernal nonsense I ever heard. Let
him go home before he makes a fool of himself. He doesn’t
understand the first thing about the subject he’s talking of.”

I agreed with him. I could not understand this new development
of Poirot’s character. I was indeed much distressed. It was not
at all like the little man I knew and loved.

We retired at last to our beds. I fell into a heavy, dreamless
sleep. Then, suddenly, I was awakened by a touch on the shoulder.
It was Poirot. He was sitting on his bed, his face was white and
he was trembling in every limb.

“Hastings,” he whispered, “I am afraid. There is a presence here.
I can feel it. It is as though the very air were thick with evil.
Let us get out of this—let us get away at once.”

“My dear Poirot,” I began, but he interrupted me.

“No, no, I am right. There is something here, something that is
not of this world.”

He pointed with a shaking finger. I followed the direction of his
hand. In the dim light I saw something which I should never have
believed possible. A shadowy, dog-headed figure was standing by
the door of the tent. It was the god Anubis, come to claim his
next victim.

I admit that for a moment I was paralyzed with fear. Then,
collecting my scattered senses, I sprang from my bed and dashed
towards the apparition. It had vanished. I rushed out of the tent.
The moon was shining brightly, and I could see for some distance.
Not a soul was in sight.

I returned to Poirot. He was still sitting on his bed, his teeth
chattering with fear.

“It is the end,” he moaned. “The end of us all.”

“Nonsense,” I said, as stoutly as I could. “It’s someone playing
a trick on us. We’ll catch him yet.”

“No, no,” Poirot shook his head. “It was no human being. I know
it—I feel it. The curse is on us. We shall never leave this place
alive.”

I spent a miserable night. Poirot’s terror was infectious, and
I found myself starting at every shadow. In the morning I felt
tired and unrefreshed. Poirot, too, looked haggard and worn.
He seemed to have aged ten years in a single night.

As we were finishing our breakfast, Dr. Ames came into the tent.
He looked grave and anxious.

“I’m sorry to have to tell you,” he said, “that there has been
another death. Hassan, the native servant, was found dead in his
bed this morning.”

“Hassan!” I cried. “But he seemed perfectly well last night.”

“He was,” said the doctor. “It’s a most mysterious business.
I can’t find any cause of death. It looks almost like—like
fright.”

Poirot groaned.

“I knew it,” he said. “The curse—the curse of Men-her-Ra!”

Dr. Ames looked at him curiously.

“You seem to be taking this very much to heart, Monsieur Poirot,”
he said.

“I am afraid,” Poirot confessed. “Horribly afraid. I want to
leave this place—to leave it at once.”

The doctor’s eyes narrowed.

“I’m afraid that won’t be possible,” he said. “In view of these
mysterious deaths, the authorities will insist on an inquiry.
We must all remain here until it is over.”

Poirot sank back on his bed with a groan. I felt a sudden surge
of anger.

“This is intolerable,” I cried. “We can’t be kept here like
prisoners.”

“I’m afraid you have no choice,” said the doctor. “I’ve already
notified the police.”

He turned and left the tent. I looked at Poirot. He was staring
into vacancy, his face a mask of terror. I realized then that
the little man’s nerve had completely gone. He was no longer the
great Hercule Poirot, the master of his craft. He was just a
frightened, superstitious old man.

I felt a sudden sense of responsibility. It was up to me to
unravel this mystery, to find out the truth behind these
mysterious deaths. I knew that there must be a human agency at
work, and I was determined to find out who it was.

I spent the rest of the morning wandering around the camp,
talking to the various members of the party. Dr. Tosswill was
still snorting with rage at Poirot’s “nonsense,” but he seemed
genuinely distressed by Hassan’s death. Mr. Harper was more
nervous than ever, and he was already making preparations for
his departure. Sir Guy Willard was in a state of nervous
collapse, and he refused to leave his tent.

As I was walking past Dr. Ames’s tent, I saw him talking to
one of the native workmen. They seemed to be in earnest
conversation, and I caught the words “Men-her-Ra” and “curse.”
I decided to keep an eye on the doctor. There was something
about him that I didn’t quite trust.

That evening, as we were sitting around the dinner table, the
atmosphere was tense and strained. No one seemed to have any
appetite, and the conversation was fitful and uneasy. Suddenly,
Poirot stood up.

“I have something to say,” he said, his voice trembling. “I have
been thinking—thinking very deeply. I believe I know the truth
behind these mysterious deaths.”

We all stared at him in astonishment. Was it possible that the
little man had regained his senses?

“The curse of Men-her-Ra is no mere superstition,” Poirot
continued. “It is a real and potent force. But it is not the
spirit of the dead king that is at work. It is a human agency—a
human being who is using the legend of the curse to cover his
own crimes.”

He paused, and his eyes swept round the table.

“And I know who that human being is.”

There was a moment of stunned silence. Then Dr. Ames spoke.

“And who is it, Monsieur Poirot?” he asked, his voice cold and
steady.

Poirot pointed a shaking finger at him.

“It is you, Dr. Ames!” he cried. “You are the murderer of
Sir John Willard, of Mr. Bleibner, of Mr. Schneider, and of
Hassan!”

The doctor laughed—a short, contemptuous laugh.

“You’re mad, Poirot,” he said. “Completely mad. What possible
motive could I have for these crimes?”

“The motive of greed,” Poirot replied. “You knew that
Mr. Bleibner was a wealthy man, and you knew that he had no
near relatives—except for his nephew in New York. You also
knew that he was interested in Egyptology, and you saw an
opportunity to enrich yourself at his expense.”

“And how did I do that?” the doctor asked, his eyes narrowing.

“You persuaded him to finance this expedition,” Poirot said.
“And then you set about getting rid of the other members of the
party. Sir John Willard was the first. You knew that he had a
weak heart, and you used your medical knowledge to bring about
his death in a way that would seem natural.”

“And Mr. Bleibner?”

“You poisoned him,” Poirot said. “You used a slow-acting
poison that would produce the symptoms of septicæmia. And then
you turned your attention to his nephew in New York. You knew
that he was in financial difficulties, and you sent him a letter,
purporting to come from his uncle, in which you offered him a
large sum of money if he would come to Egypt. When he arrived,
you met him in Cairo and—well, we know what happened then.
You drove him to suicide.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“He was becoming suspicious,” Poirot said. “He had noticed
certain things—certain discrepancies in your accounts. You
knew that you had to get rid of him, and you chose a method that
would further the legend of the curse. Tetanus—a disease that
can be easily contracted in the desert.”

“And Hassan?”

“He knew too much,” Poirot said. “He had seen you—seen you
playing the part of Anubis. You knew that he would speak, and
so you silenced him forever.”

The doctor stood up, his face white with rage.

“This is monstrous!” he cried. “A pack of lies! You have no
proof—no proof at all!”

“But I have,” Poirot said, his voice suddenly calm and steady.
“I have the proof in my pocket.”

He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small glass phial.

“This,” he said, “is the poison you used to kill Mr. Bleibner.
I found it in your tent this morning.”

The doctor’s face went ghastly. He made a sudden dash for the
door, but I was too quick for him. I tripped him up, and he
fell heavily to the ground.

“Got him!” I cried.

At that moment, the tent flap was pushed aside and two men
entered. They were the police officers who had been summoned
by the doctor.

“Take him away,” Poirot said, pointing to the prostrate figure
on the floor. “He is the man you want.”

As the doctor was led away, I turned to Poirot.

“How did you do it?” I asked, full of admiration. “I thought
you’d lost your nerve.”

Poirot smiled—the old, familiar smile.

“It was a little play-acting, Hastings,” he said. “I wanted the
murderer to think that I was a frightened, superstitious old
man. It’s a trick I’ve used before—to lul the criminal into a
false sense of security.”

“And the Anubis figure?”

“That was Hassan,” Poirot said. “I’d persuaded him to play the
part—to see if we could provoke a reaction from the murderer.
Unfortunately, Dr. Ames saw through the trick and killed poor
Hassan before he could speak.”

“And the phial of poison?”

“A little invention of my own,” Poirot confessed. “It was
actually a bottle of my favourite stomach medicine. But it
served its purpose.”

I looked at him in amazement.

“You’re a marvel, Poirot,” I said. “A positive marvel.”

“No, no,” Poirot said, modestly. “It was just a matter of
using the little grey cells. And now, if you don’t mind, I think
I’ll go and have a wash. This sand—it is really most unpleasing.”

I watched him as he walked away, his head held high, his
moustaches bristling with pride. Hercule Poirot had done it
again. The mystery of the Egyptian tomb was solved, and the
curse of Men-her-Ra was laid to rest forever.

“Balderdash, sir,” he exclaimed angrily. “Pure balderdash. The
man’s an impostor. He doesn’t know the difference between the
superstitions of the Middle Ages and the beliefs of Ancient Egypt.
Never have I heard such a hotch-potch of ignorance and credulity.”

I calmed the excited expert, and joined Poirot in the tent. My
little friend was beaming cheerfully.

“We can now sleep in peace,” he declared happily. “And I can do
with some sleep. My head, it aches abominably. Ah, for a good
_tisane_!”

The morning dawned with a relentless brilliance that seemed to mock the shadows of the previous night. I found Poirot already astir, his face unusually grave as he watched the camp begin its daily routine. Dr. Ames was the first to join us, looking weary and grey in the harsh sunlight; he inquired after Poirot’s headache and, upon hearing it still lingered, produced a small box of cachets from his pocket. “Take one of these, Monsieur Poirot,” he urged. “They’re a specific of my own—guaranteed to settle the nerves as well as the head.” Poirot accepted the gift with a flourish of gratitude, yet as the doctor turned away to speak with Sir Guy, I saw my friend’s eyes narrow with a sudden, sharp intensity. He did not swallow the medicine, but instead slipped it into his waistcoat pocket with a surreptitiousness that immediately alerted my curiosity, though he said nothing to me of his intentions.

The next morning found the camp in a state of suppressed agitation. Sir Guy was reported to be suffering from a severe headache and was remaining in his tent under the care of Dr. Ames. Poirot, on the other hand, appeared to be in the best of spirits. He spent the early hours of the morning in a long conversation with Hassan, the native servant, a proceeding which seemed to afford him a good deal of satisfaction. I found him later, sitting on a campstool, watching the entrance to the tomb with a singular expression on his face.

The night passed without further manifestations of the supernatural, but the morning air felt heavy with an indefinable dread. Poirot, usually the first to rise and perform his meticulous toilette, remained in his bunk, complaining of a “migraine of the most devastating.” When Dr. Ames entered our tent to inquire after our health, he found the little man wrapped in blankets, despite the growing heat. The doctor, with a professional air of sympathy, suggested a sedative, but Poirot merely groaned and asked for more of the herbal infusion that Hassan had prepared. I noticed Dr. Ames’s eyes linger for a moment on the diagrams Poirot had traced in the sand outside our door—a look of thinly veiled contempt passing over his face before he turned to leave, promising to check on us again before the noon hour.

“But your _tisane_, Poirot,” I said, “how are you to get it in this
wilderness?”
“It is simple. I have asked the good Dr. Ames to prepare me a
little something. He is a man of medicine, he will understand the
requirements of the nervous system.”
Even as he spoke, the flap of the tent was pushed aside and Dr.
Ames entered, carrying a steaming cup.
“Here you are, Monsieur Poirot,” he said with a slightly mocking
smile. “This should settle your nerves and ensure those dreams of
yours are not haunted by Ancient Egyptian deities.”
Poirot thanked him effusively, and the doctor, after a brief nod
to me, went out again into the night.

Hardly had the words left his lips when a shadow fell across the opening of our tent. It was Dr. Ames. He carried a small glass containing a brownish liquid. “I overheard your request for a *tisane*, Monsieur Poirot,” he said with a slightly ironic smile. “As we are short of the genuine article in the desert, I have compounded a little sedative that will serve the purpose just as well. It will ensure you a good night’s rest.” Poirot was profuse in his thanks. He took the glass and set it down on the small table by his bed.

As though in answer to prayer, the flap of the tent was lifted and
Hassan appeared, bearing a steaming cup which he offered to Poirot.
It proved to be camomile tea, a beverage of which he is inordinately
fond. Having thanked Hassan and refused his offer of another cup
for myself, we were left alone once more. I stood at the door of
the tent some time after undressing, looking out over the desert.

The moon was nearly full, and its silver rays made of the camp a
fairyland of white and black. I had been standing there for some
ten minutes, when I heard a low moan from Poirot. I hurried to
his side. He was sitting up on his bed, his face ashen, gasping
for breath.

“The tea!” he gasped. “The tea!”

I seized the cup and smelled it. It was cold now, and gave off a
faint, sickly odour. I had seen enough of its effect in my time
to recognize the smell of cyanide.

The horror of the thing for a moment paralyzed me. Then, realizing
the urgency of the case, I dashed out of the tent in search of
Dr. Ames. He was already at the door of his tent, and I panted
out my news.

“Cyanide!” he cried. “Good heavens! How could it have got there?
Wait, I’ll bring some stuff.”

He was back in a few seconds, with a bottle in his hand. Together
we hurried to Poirot’s side. He seemed to be in a state of
collapse. The doctor made a rapid examination, and then forced a
few drops of the liquid he had brought between the grey lips.

He stayed with me for an hour, watching the patient, who gradually
showed signs of recovery. At last the doctor rose, a look of
infinite relief upon his face.

“He’ll pull through now. But it was a narrow squeak. I’ve seen
some queer things in my time, but never anything quite like this.”

He looked at me with a questioning expression.

“It was in the tea?”

“Yes.”

“How did it get there?”

“That is what I mean to find out.”

He nodded.

“There’s something very wrong here, Captain Hastings. This isn’t
the work of any spirit from the past. It’s a very modern and a
very deadly human brain that’s at work.”

“I agree with you,” I said emphatically. “And I think I know whose
hand it was that gave the cup to Monsieur Poirot.”

“You mean Hassan?”

“I do.”

“Well, it’s possible. But I can’t see the motive.”

“Nor I,” I admitted. “But Poirot may have found out more than we
know.”

He nodded again.

“Well, I’ll leave you now. If he shows any signs of a relapse,
come and fetch me at once.”

“How silent it is, Poirot,” I said. “No sound but the occasional
cry of a jackal—and the rustling of the sand. It’s almost as though
Nature itself were waiting for something to happen.”

“_Nature_,” said Poirot, “she is a very large and impressive person.
Do not let us speak of her. Let us rather speak of my little stomach.
I am convinced it is about to misbehave. Oh, that camomile! I have
drunk it too hot. It is burning me—burning me horribly!”

I turned round in alarm. Poirot’s face was distorted with pain.
He was gasping for breath.

“Water—water,” he choked.

I poured out a glass and held it to his lips. He drank it greedily,
then his head fell back on the pillow and he lay quite still.

“Poirot!” I cried in terror.

There was no answer. He was unconscious. For a moment I stood
paralyzed. Then I dashed out of the tent in search of Dr. Ames.
I found him at last in the mess tent. He was alone, smoking a
solitary pipe.

“Come at once,” I panted. “Poirot—he’s ill—dying, I think.”

The doctor jumped to his feet.

“What? What’s that you say?”

“He’s been poisoned—some thing he drank—Hassan brought it to him.”

The doctor didn’t wait for another word. He snatched up his bag
and followed me at a run to our tent. Poirot was still lying as
I had left him. Dr. Ames bent over him.

“Is he—dead?” I whispered.

The doctor shook his head.

“No, but he’s in a bad way. It looks to me like—it looks like—a
poison of some kind.”

He was busily engaged in making a rapid examination. Suddenly he
looked up.

“What was it he drank?”

“Camomile tea—Hassan brought it.”

“Hassan? Where is the cup?”

I pointed to it. It was still half full of the liquid. The doctor
took it up and smelt it.

“Ah! This is it. I thought as much. Look here, Hastings, stay
with him. I must get my stomach-pump. There’s no time to lose.”

He dashed out of the tent, and I was left alone with my friend.
He seemed to be breathing more easily now, but I was still
horribly anxious. Supposing the doctor was too late?

I looked round the tent. My eyes fell on the cup of tea. If it
contained poison, it was vital that it should be analyzed. I
carefully poured the remaining liquid into a small bottle which I
happened to have in my bag. Then I waited for the doctor’s return.

He came at last, and for the next hour we were both busily engaged
in various unpleasant but necessary tasks. At last Poirot opened
his eyes and looked round.

“Where—where am I?” he murmured.

“It’s all right, Poirot,” I said soothingly. “You’ve been ill, but
you’re better now.”

He seemed to be trying to remember something.

“The tea,” he whispered. “The tea—Hassan——”

“Don’t talk now,” said the doctor. “You must rest. I’ll give you
something to make you sleep.”

He administered a small dose of some sedative, and in a few
minutes Poirot was sleeping peacefully.

The doctor turned to me.

“He’ll do now. It was a narrow squeak, though. If you hadn’t
called me when you did——”

He didn’t finish the sentence, but I understood his meaning.

“What was it?” I asked.

“Cyanide of potassium, I should say, from the smell. A deadly
poison. Someone evidently wanted to get rid of your friend.”

“But who? Hassan?”

“It looks like it. He brought the tea, you say? We must find him
at once.”

But search as we would, no trace of Hassan was to be found. He
had vanished as completely as though the desert had swallowed
him up.

“He’s probably halfway to Cairo by now,” said Dr. Tosswill, who
had joined us in our search. “We must notify the police at once.”

But Poirot, when he woke the next morning, was of a different
opinion.

“No, no,” he said, shaking his head. “Do not notify the police.
It is not necessary.”

“Not necessary?” I cried. “But the man tried to murder you!”

“Perhaps,” said Poirot enigmatically. “But all the same, I do not
wish the police to be called in. I have my own reasons.”

He refused to say more, and I was forced to leave it at that.
But I could see that he was thinking deeply. His eyes were
continually fixed on the door of the tent, as though he were
expecting someone.

It was about eleven o’clock when Mr. Harper, the secretary,
entered. He looked even more nervous than he had done the
previous day.

“I’ve come to say good-bye,” he said. “I’m off to Cairo this
afternoon. I can’t stand this place a minute longer.”

“I do not blame you,” said Poirot. “It is not a healthy spot. By
the way, Mr. Harper, you were with Mr. Bleibner when he died,
were you not?”

“Yes, I was. Why?”

“Did he say anything—anything at all—before he died?”

The young man hesitated.

“Well, he was light-headed, you know. He kept talking about
somebody—somebody who had robbed him.”

“Did he mention a name?”

“No. He just kept saying, ‘He’s robbed me—he’s robbed me of
everything.’ I thought he was just rambling.”

“I see,” said Poirot. “Thank you, Mr. Harper. I wish you a
pleasant journey.”

When he had gone, Poirot turned to me.

“You see, Hastings? The plot thickens.”

“What do you mean?”

“Mr. Bleibner was robbed. By whom? His nephew? Or someone else?”

“But what has that to do with the deaths?”

“Everything, my friend. Everything.”

He relapsed into silence, and for the rest of the day he refused
to discuss the matter further. He spent most of his time sitting
in the sun, staring out over the desert with a far-away look in
his eyes.

It was not until the following evening that he finally spoke.
We were sitting in the mess tent, with Sir Guy, Dr. Tosswill,
and Dr. Ames.

“Messieurs,” said Poirot, “the time has come for me to speak. I
have discovered the truth.”

We all stared at him in astonishment.

“The truth?” cried Sir Guy. “You mean—about the deaths?”

“Precisely. It is a very simple story, but a very terrible one.”

He paused for a moment, as though to collect his thoughts.

“It begins,” he said, “with Mr. Bleibner’s nephew, Rupert. You
will remember that he came here to ask his uncle for money, and
was refused. He returned to New York, and shortly afterwards
he committed suicide. But before he died, he wrote a letter in
which he called himself a leper and an outcast.”

“Yes,” I said. “I remember.”

“That letter,” said Poirot, “was the key to the whole mystery.
Rupert Bleibner did not commit suicide because he was remorseful.
He committed suicide because he believed he had leprosy.”

“Leprosy?” cried Dr. Ames. “But that’s ridiculous! He didn't
have leprosy.”

“I know he didn’t,” said Poirot. “But he _thought_ he had. And
he thought so because someone had told him so—someone who had
deliberately infected him with the idea.”

“But who?” asked Sir Guy.

“The same person,” said Poirot, “who murdered Sir John Willard,
Mr. Bleibner, and Mr. Schneider. The same person who tried to
murder me.”

He turned his eyes slowly round the circle of faces.

“That person,” he said, “is Dr. Ames.”

The doctor jumped to his feet, his face livid with rage.

“You’re mad!” he shouted. “Utterly mad! Why should I want to
murder these men?”

“For a very simple reason,” said Poirot. “For money. You were
Mr. Bleibner’s medical adviser. You knew that he was a very
wealthy man, and that he had no near relations except his
nephew. You also knew that he had not made a will. If he and
his nephew both died, you, as his friend and companion, might
hope to inherit a large portion of his estate.”

“It’s a lie!” cried the doctor. “A damnable lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Let us see. You first turned your
attention to Rupert Bleibner. You told him he had leprosy—a
disease which, in its early stages, is easily mimicked by
certain skin irritants. You convinced him that he was an
outcast, and he, in despair, took his own life. That left only
Mr. Bleibner. But there was a difficulty. Sir John Willard was
also a member of the party. He was a man of great intelligence
and observation. He might have suspected something. So he had
to be removed. A little digitalin in his food, perhaps? It
would produce all the symptoms of heart failure.”

The doctor was trembling with rage, but he said nothing.

“Then came Mr. Bleibner,” continued Poirot. “A scratch on the
thumb—a little septic matter introduced—and the work was done.
But there was still Mr. Schneider. He, too, was beginning to
ask questions. So he had to go. Tetanus is a very convenient
disease, is it not, doctor? Especially when one has the
necessary cultures at hand.”

“And what about the attempt on your life?” I asked.

“Ah,” said Poirot. “That was a master-stroke. The doctor knew
that I was suspicious. So he decided to get rid of me. He
used Hassan to bring me the poisoned tea, knowing that
suspicion would naturally fall on the native servant. But he
made one mistake. He didn't know that I had already suspected
him, and that I was prepared.”

“Prepared?” said Dr. Ames, with a sneer. “You were nearly
dead when I got to you.”

“Was I?” said Poirot, with a smile. “Or was I merely acting?
I knew that Hassan was honest, and that the tea he brought
me was harmless. But I also knew that you were watching me.
So I pretended to be poisoned, in order to see what you would
do. And you did exactly what I expected. You pretended to
find poison in the cup, and you even went so far as to
suggest that Hassan was the culprit.”

He turned to me.

“The bottle of tea you have in your bag, Hastings—I think you
will find, if it is analyzed, that it contains nothing more
deadly than camomile.”

The doctor made a sudden movement towards his pocket, but
before he could reach it, Poirot’s hand was on his arm.

“It is no use, doctor,” he said. “The camp is surrounded by
the police. You cannot escape.”

For a moment the doctor stood at bay, his eyes flashing
defiant. Then, with a sudden gesture of despair, he sank
back into his chair.

“You’re too clever for me, Poirot,” he muttered. “Too clever
by half.”

“It was the letter of Rupert Bleibner that gave you away,”
said Poirot. “A man who is about to commit suicide because
of remorse does not call himself a leper. He calls himself a
murderer. But a man who thinks he has leprosy—ah, that is a
different matter.”

He turned to Sir Guy.

“And now, my friend, I think you can continue your excavations
in peace. The curse of Men-her-Ra is at an end.”

As we walked back to our tent, I looked at Poirot with
undisguised admiration.

“You’re a wonderful man, Poirot,” I said. “How did you
ever suspect him?”

“My friend,” said Poirot, “when a man is too anxious to
prove that he is a man of science, and that he does not
believe in the supernatural, I always begin to wonder what
he is trying to hide. And when I find that he is the only
person who has everything to gain by the deaths of his
companions—well, then I am sure.”

He paused and looked out over the desert.

“The sand,” he said. “It is very untidy. But it has its
uses. It hides many things. But it cannot hide the truth.”

“The Sphinx,” I said aloud, “how wonderful it is!”

“How can you look at it? To me it is only a nightmare—a hideous
nightmare!”

Poirot had joined me. His voice was strangely altered. He was
trembling in every limb.

“It is the air—the air of this place. It is evil, Hastings, evil.”

“Yes, I feel it,” I admitted.

“Hark! what was that?”

“I heard nothing.”

“Listen!”

I listened, and for a long time I heard nothing but the desert
sounds. Then, far away, I caught a long, low, wailing cry. It died
away, then it was repeated. My hair rose on my head.

“_C’est lui_,” whispered Poirot. “It is Anubis, the God of the
Underworld.”

“Nonsense,” I cried. “It’s only some wild animal.”

“No, no, it is the spirit of Men-her-Ra. Oh, I feel it, Hastings,
it is here. My brain—it feels as though a weight were being
pressed upon it.”

He was shaking from head to foot. I was getting seriously alarmed.
I got him into bed, and stayed with him until he had fallen into
a deep sleep. Then, myself, I went to bed and was soon in the same
condition.

I woke with a start. Some one was shaking me by the shoulder. It
was Poirot. He was fully dressed, and looked as if he had not been
to bed at all.

“Quick, Hastings, come.”

“What is it?”

“Sir Guy Willard—he is ill.”

I hurried after him. We found Sir Guy in a state of high fever.
Dr. Ames was with him, and was doing what he could.

“He’ll pull through,” he said as we entered. “It’s a touch of the
sun, nothing more.”

But I could see that the doctor was himself more than a little
anxious. Sir Guy was delirious, and was babbling about the curse
of the Tomb and the jackal-headed god.

“He’s got it on the brain,” said the doctor, with a short, uneasy
laugh. “I’ll give him a sedative.”

He did so, and Sir Guy soon became quieter. We left him in the
doctor’s care, and went out.

“What do you think of it, Poirot?”

“I think that we are in the presence of a very powerful and
malignant influence.”

“You mean the Curse?”

“I mean something which I do not yet understand, Hastings. But we
must act, and act quickly.”

“What are you going to do?”

“I am going to Cairo.”

“To Cairo?”

“Yes, I have certain inquiries to make there.”

“But Sir Guy?”

“I have left him in good hands. Dr. Ames will do all that is
necessary.”

“And what about the Anubis?”

“Ah, the Anubis! I have an idea about the Anubis, Hastings. I think
that we shall see him again before very long.”

With which enigmatical remark Poirot departed. I spent a very
miserable day. Dr. Tosswill was in a state of suppressed fury,
and Mr. Harper was openly terrified. Sir Guy continued to be very
ill, and Dr. Ames did not leave him for a moment.

Poirot returned late in the evening. He looked tired but
satisfied.

“Well?” I asked.

“I have found out what I wanted to know, Hastings. To-morrow we
shall have the answer to our problem.”

“You have found out who is the murderer?”

“There is no murderer, Hastings. There is only a Curse.”

I looked at him in amazement. Was he really serious?

“But the deaths?”

“Wait until to-morrow, Hastings. Then you shall know everything.”

I was far from satisfied, but I knew from experience that it was
useless to try and get anything more out of Poirot when he was in
one of his mysterious moods.

The next morning broke clear and bright. Sir Guy was much better,
the fever having left him during the night. We were all assembled
in the large tent for breakfast, with the exception of the young
baronet.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said Dr. Ames, “and have you found your
murderer?”

“I have found something more important than a murderer, _monsieur
le docteur_,” replied Poirot. “I have found the truth.”

“And what is the truth?”

“The truth is that there is no Curse of Men-her-Ra.”

“I could have told you that myself,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“But there is something else,” continued Poirot. “There is a human
agency at work—a very clever and a very unscrupulous human agency.”

“What do you mean?” asked Mr. Harper, his voice shaking.

“I mean that the deaths of Sir John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, and Mr.
Schneider were all murders.”

“Murders!” cried Dr. Tosswill. “But they were all due to natural
causes.”

“So it appeared,” said Poirot. “But let us examine the facts. Sir
John Willard died of heart failure. A very natural death for a
man of his age. But supposing his heart was already weak, and
supposing he was subjected to a sudden and violent shock? Would
not that be enough to cause his death?”

“It might,” admitted Dr. Ames. “But what shock could he have
received?”

“The shock of seeing something which he believed to be
supernatural,” said Poirot. “The shock of seeing the god Anubis in
his own tent.”

“But that is impossible!” cried Sir Guy, who had just entered.

“Is it?” said Poirot. “We have all seen it ourselves. Why should
not Sir John Willard have seen it also? And if he believed in the
Curse, as we know he did, the shock might well have been fatal.”

“But what about the others?” asked Mr. Harper. “Mr. Bleibner died
of blood poisoning, and Mr. Schneider of tetanus.”

“Both very easy deaths to bring about,” said Poirot. “A little
poison on a thumb-trough, a few tetanus bacilli in a hypodermic
needle—nothing could be simpler.”

“But who could have done such a thing?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“Only one person,” said Poirot. “Some one who had access to the
victims at all times, some one who was trusted by them, some one
who had a motive for their deaths.”

“And who was that?”

“The person who is at this moment trying to escape,” said Poirot,
pointing to the door of the tent.

We all turned round. Mr. Harper was standing there, his face
ghastly pale.

“It’s a lie!” he shouted. “It’s a damned lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain why you were
seen leaving Mr. Schneider’s tent just before he was taken ill?
And perhaps you can explain why you have been in communication
with a firm of moneylenders in New York?”

Harper did not wait to hear any more. He turned and fled from the
tent.

“After him!” cried Dr. Tosswill.

We all joined in the pursuit, but Harper was too quick for us. He
had a horse waiting, and was soon galloping away across the
desert.

“Let him go,” said Poirot. “He will not get far. I have already
informed the police in Cairo.”

“But what was his motive?” I asked.

“Money, Hastings. Always money. He was in debt, and he hoped to
inherit Mr. Bleibner’s fortune. But when he found that the old man
intended to leave his money to the excavations, he decided to get
rid of him and anyone else who stood in his way.”

“But the nephew?” I asked. “Why did he kill himself?”

“He didn’t,” said Poirot. “He was murdered too. Harper followed
him to New York and poisoned him, making it look like suicide. He
even wrote the letter which was found beside the body.”

“It’s incredible,” said Dr. Tosswill. “To think that such a thing
could happen in the twentieth century.”

“The human heart does not change with the centuries, _monsieur_,”
said Poirot. “It is always the same.”

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” said Sir Guy, “I cannot thank you enough
for what you have done. You have saved my life, and you have
cleared up a very dark mystery.”

“It was nothing,” said Poirot modestly. “A little use of the grey
cells, that is all.”

As we were leaving the camp, I turned to Poirot.

“There’s one thing I don’t understand,” I said. “How did you know
it was Harper?”

“I didn’t, Hastings. I only suspected him. But when I went to
Cairo, I found out about his debts and his communication with the
moneylenders. After that, it was easy.”

“And the Anubis?”

“Ah, the Anubis! That was Hassan. He wanted to frighten Sir Guy
away from the camp, and he thought that by dressing up as the god
he could do so. He did not know that he was playing into the
murderer’s hands.”

“I see,” I said. “It was all very simple, after all.”

“Everything is simple, Hastings—once you know the answer.”

And with a little smile, Poirot led the way towards the waiting
donkeys.

The night was intensely still. To my surprise I saw Sir Guy
strolling along the sand, and I noticed that his hands were
clasping and unclasping in a restless fashion. Then, a few minutes
later, he was joined by the doctor.

“Are you not going to bed yet?” I called to them.

“No, I can’t sleep,” Sir Guy replied, while Dr. Ames added that
he was staying with him for a while to keep him company.

I saw them move away into the distance together. Turning to look
at Poirot I found him peacefully asleep, his mouth wide open and
his chest heaving with the most regular of snores. The camomile
tea had certainly had its effect. The next thing I knew was being
shaken by the shoulder. It was broad daylight and Poirot stood by
my side.

“Hastings, wake up! There has been another tragedy.”

I sat up.

“What is it? Not Sir Guy?”

“No, no, thank God! It is the little Harper.”

“The secretary?”

“Yes. He was found dead in his bed. Dr. Ames is with him now.”

“What did he die of?” I asked, as I pulled on my clothes.

“That is what the doctor is trying to find out. There is no sign
of violence—no mark of any kind. It is as though he had died in
his sleep.”

I hurried out. There was an air of suppressed excitement throughout
the camp. The native workmen were huddling together and whispering
eagerly. Dr. Tosswill looked more indignant than ever.

“It is simply incredible!” he exclaimed. “This man was in perfect
health last night.”

“And now he is dead,” said Poirot quietly. “It is a very strange
coincidence, is it not?”

The expert turned away with a snort of disgust.

“Wait here for me, Hastings,” said Poirot. “I am going to speak to
Dr. Ames.”

He was away some little time. When he returned his face was very
grave.

“Well?” I asked.

“The doctor is unable to find any cause of death. He can only
suggest some obscure heart trouble. It is very unsatisfactory—most
unsatisfactory.”

“You mean that you suspect——?”

“I suspect everything and everyone, Hastings. This is a very
wicked world.”

The sand was white and wonderful in the moonlight. I could see
Poirot’s diagrams quite clearly. My head felt a little heavy and
my throat was dry. I felt as if I were about to be ill, and I
decided that I should not be sorry when we should be safely home
again. The desert was certainly most impressive, and there was a
feeling of mystery about it which was rather overawing. All
at once I gave a start. Was that a figure I saw moving over the
sand? I looked again. Yes, it was moving towards the Tomb of
Men-her-Ra. A tall, white-clad figure, it might be a ghost. No,
it was more likely to be one of the native boys. I felt a sudden
impulse to go and see what was happening. I put on my dressing-gown
and stepped out into the night. It was quite cold. My heart beat
a little faster as I neared the Tomb. All at once the figure I
was following seemed to vanish into the ground. I had just reached
the spot where it had disappeared when a hand was laid upon my
shoulder. I let out a cry of terror. Turning, I found myself
face to face with Dr. Ames. He was looking at me with some
surprise.

“What is it, Hastings?” he asked.

“I—I thought I saw someone,” I stammered.

“A native, I expect. They’re a bit restless to-night. You’d better
get back to your tent. It’s not a very healthy spot just now.”

I followed his advice, and found Poirot fast asleep. His breathing
was heavy and regular. I myself did not fall asleep for some time.
When I did so, my dreams were disturbed by the most fantastic
nightmares. It was early when I woke. Poirot was already up.
He was busy brushing his clothes, and I had never seen him more
full of energy.

“_Bon jour_, Hastings! You have slept well?”

“No,” I answered. “I’ve had most horrible dreams.”

“Ah! It is the influence of the Tomb. It is very powerful. I myself
have been dreaming—but dreaming to some purpose.”

“You have?”

“But yes. I have seen the face of the murderer.”

“The murderer?” I cried. “You mean——?”

“I mean that there has been a murderer. Come, Hastings, let us
lose no time. I wish to see the Dr. Tosswill.”

“A wonderful place,” I said aloud, “and a wonderful work. I can
feel the fascination. This desert life, this probing into the heart
of a vanished civilization. Surely, Poirot, you, too, must feel
the charm?”

I turned for an answer, but Poirot had already fallen into a heavy
slumber. I was surprised at the suddenness of it, for it was only
a few minutes since he had taken his cup of camomile tea. I
attributed it to the fatigue of his journey, and was soon as fast
asleep as he was.

I woke up with a start. The sun was shining into the tent. Poirot
was still sleeping, and his breathing was strangely heavy. I
shook him by the shoulder, but he did not wake.

With a sudden sense of dread I realized that he was unconscious.
I hurried out of the tent. No one seemed to be about. At last I
encountered Hassan.

“Where is the doctor?” I demanded.

“He is in his tent, my Lord.”

I ran there and found Dr. Ames asleep. He sat up with a start as
I entered.

“Doctor, come at once. My friend Poirot is ill.”

“Ill? What’s the matter with him?”

“He’s unconscious, and his breathing is very heavy. I can’t wake
him.”

The doctor reached for his bag and followed me. He was soon
bending over Poirot.

“He’s been drugged,” he said at last. “Opium, I should say.
Has he had anything to drink?”

“Only a cup of camomile tea which Hassan brought him.”

“Hassan? I’ll have a word with that fellow.”

He strode out of the tent. I remained by Poirot’s side, full of
anxious thoughts. If Poirot were to be the next victim——!

I heard voices outside, and then the doctor returned, followed
by Hassan. The latter looked sullen and defiant.

“I know nothing,” he declared. “I brought the tea as the little
one had asked. If there was anything in it, I did not put it there.”

“We’ll see about that,” said the doctor grimly.

He turned back to Poirot and began to apply restoratives. For
a long time they seemed to have no effect, but at last the little
man’s eyes opened. He looked round him in a dazed fashion.

“_Qu’est-ce qu’il y a?_” he murmured.

“You’ve been drugged, Poirot,” I said. “But you’re all right now.”

He sat up, his memory evidently returning.

“Ah!” he said. “The camomile tea! It had a strange taste. I
should have known.”

“Hassan brought it to you,” I said.

Poirot looked at the native servant, who was still standing by
the door of the tent.

“So,” he said softly. “It was you, Hassan. And why did you do
it?”

“I did not do it, my Lord. I know nothing of what was in the
tea.”

“We shall see,” said Poirot. “For the moment, I am still a little
confused. Leave me, I pray of you, all of you.”

The doctor and Hassan went out. I remained.

“You, too, Hastings. I wish to be alone.”

I went out, but I did not go far. I was determined to keep a
watchful eye on my friend’s tent. I felt that he was in danger.

A few minutes later I saw Poirot come out of his tent. He was
walking with a firm step, and he seemed to have quite recovered
from the effects of the drug. He went straight to the tent of
Mr. Harper, the secretary. I followed at a distance.

I saw him enter, and a few minutes later he came out again,
looking very grave. He then went to the tent of Dr. Tosswill, and
after that to the tent of Sir Guy Willard. Finally, he returned
to our own tent.

I joined him there.

“Well, Poirot?” I asked. “What have you discovered?”

“I have discovered many things, Hastings. But first, tell me.
What did you think of the apparition of Anubis last night?”

“I thought it was a hoax,” I said. “Someone trying to frighten
us.”

“And who do you think it was?”

“I don’t know. Perhaps one of the native workmen.”

“Or perhaps one of the members of the expedition?”

“But why should any of them do such a thing?”

“To create an atmosphere of superstitious fear. To make us
believe in the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’.”

“But who would want us to believe that?”

“Someone who had a very good reason for doing so. Someone who
had committed a crime and wanted to hide it under the cloak of the
supernatural.”

“A crime? You mean—murder?”

“Yes, Hastings. Murder. Or rather, murders.”

“But who? And how?”

“Wait a moment. I have something to show you.”

He reached into his pocket and pulled out a small piece of
paper. It was a letter, written in a cramped, scholarly hand.

“I found this in the tent of Mr. Harper,” he said. “It is a
letter from Mr. Bleibner to his nephew, Rupert.”

I took the letter and read it. It was a cold, hard letter,
refusing to give the young man any money and telling him that
he was a disgrace to the family.

“But this only confirms what we already knew,” I said.

“Wait,” said Poirot. “Read the postscript.”

I turned the page and read the postscript. It was short and to
the point.

“‘I have decided to change my will. I am leaving everything to
the Foundation for Egyptian Research. Mr. Schneider and I have
already discussed the details.’”

“You see, Hastings? If Mr. Bleibner died before he could change
his will, his money would go to his next of kin. And who was his
next of kin?”

“His nephew, Rupert!” I cried.

“Exactly. But Rupert is dead. He committed suicide in New York.”

“Yes,” said Poirot. “But when did he die? He died _after_ his
uncle.”

“So the money would have gone to him, and then to his heirs?”

“Yes. But Rupert had no heirs. He was a lonely man, with no
friends and no relations.”

“Then who would get the money?”

“That is what I am going to find out.”

He went to the door of the tent and called for Hassan.

“Hassan,” he said, when the servant appeared. “I want you to
bring everyone to this tent. Sir Guy, Dr. Tosswill, Dr. Ames,
and Mr. Harper. I have something to say to them.”

Hassan bowed and went off to do his bidding.

A few minutes later they were all assembled in our tent. They
looked at Poirot with curiosity and some apprehension.

“Messieurs,” said Poirot, “I have asked you here because I have
discovered the truth about the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’.”

He paused for a moment, enjoying the effect of his words.

“There is no curse,” he continued. “There are only crimes.
Crimes committed by a very clever and a very ruthless man.”

“And who is this man?” demanded Dr. Tosswill.

“He is one of you,” said Poirot. “He is the man who killed Sir
John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, and Mr. Schneider. He is the man who
drove Rupert Bleibner to suicide. And he is the man who tried
to drug me last night.”

He turned to Dr. Ames.

“Dr. Ames,” he said, “you are a very clever man. But you have
made one mistake.”

The doctor’s face went pale.

“What are you talking about?” he demanded. “I have made no
mistake.”

“Oh, yes, you have,” said Poirot. “You thought that by creating
an atmosphere of superstitious fear, you could hide your crimes.
But you forgot one thing. You forgot that Hercule Poirot is not
a superstitious man.”

“This is preposterous!” cried the doctor. “What proof have you?”

“I have plenty of proof,” said Poirot. “First, there is the
death of Sir John Willard. You said it was heart failure. But it
was not heart failure. It was a poison that leaves no trace—a
poison that you, as a doctor, would have no difficulty in
obtaining.”

“That’s a lie!” shouted Ames.

“Then there is the death of Mr. Bleibner,” Poirot continued,
unperturbed. “You said it was blood poisoning from a scratch
on his thumb. But it was not. You injected him with a deadly
culture of bacteria—a culture that you had prepared yourself.”

“And Mr. Schneider?” I asked. “What about him?”

“Mr. Schneider died of tetanus,” said Poirot. “But it was not
accidental tetanus. It was tetanus that was deliberately
introduced into his system by Dr. Ames.”

“But why?” I cried. “Why did he do it?”

“For money, Hastings. For a great deal of money. You see, Dr.
Ames was Rupert Bleibner’s only friend. In fact, he was more
than a friend. He was his creditor. Rupert owed him a large
sum of money—money that he had borrowed to pay for his
dissipations in New York.”

“When Rupert came to Egypt, he went to see his uncle, hoping to
get some money from him. But his uncle refused. He told him
that he was changing his will and leaving everything to the
Foundation.”

“Rupert was desperate. He told his friend Dr. Ames about his
troubles. And the doctor saw his opportunity. If Mr. Bleibner
were to die before he changed his will, the money would go to
Rupert. And if Rupert were then to die—or to commit suicide—the
money would go to his only friend and creditor, Dr. Ames.”

“So you see, it was a very simple plan. All the doctor had to
do was to get rid of anyone who might stand in his way. Sir
John Willard was the first. Then Mr. Bleibner. And then Mr.
Schneider, who knew about the change in the will.”

“As for Rupert, the doctor worked on his feelings of remorse
and despair until he was driven to take his own life. It was a
cruel and a heartless plan, but it almost worked.”

“Wait a minute,” said Mr. Harper. “What about the apparition of
Anubis? And the drug in Poirot’s tea?”

“The apparition of Anubis was the doctor himself,” said Poirot.
“He wanted to keep up the illusion of the curse. And the drug
in my tea—well, that was a mistake on his part. He thought that
by drugging me, he could prevent me from investigating his
crimes. But he didn’t know that I have a very strong
constitution—and a very suspicious nature.”

He turned back to Dr. Ames.

“Well, doctor? What have you to say for yourself?”

The doctor did not answer. He stood there, his face white and
drawn, his eyes full of hatred. Suddenly, he made a movement
towards his pocket.

“Look out!” I cried.

But Poirot was too quick for him. He grabbed the doctor’s arm
and twisted it behind his back. A small glass phial fell to the
ground and shattered.

“A quick and easy death, eh, doctor?” said Poirot. “But not
for you. For you, there will be the justice of the law.”

He turned to the others.

“Hassan, go and fetch the police. Sir Guy, Dr. Tosswill, Mr.
Harper—I think we have seen the end of the ‘Curse of
Men-her-Ra’.”

And so it was. Dr. Ames was arrested and tried for the murders
of Sir John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, and Mr. Schneider. He was
found guilty and sentenced to death.

As for the Tomb of Men-her-Ra, the excavations were continued
by Sir Guy Willard, and many more wonderful discoveries were
made. But there were no more deaths, and no more talk of a
curse.

The magic of Ancient Egypt remained, but the evil that had
haunted the camp was gone forever.

“You see, Hastings,” said Poirot, as we sat on the balcony of
the Mena House Hotel, watching the sun set over the Pyramids.
“It is as I said. The force of superstition is a great force.
But the force of the human mind is greater still. And the
‘little grey cells’—they are the greatest force of all!”

A snore was the only answer I received. My friend was already
wrapped in the deepest sleep.

The night seemed incredibly long. I woke from a doze to find Poirot
beside me, his face drawn and haggard.

“_Mon ami_,” he said in a low, trembling voice, “it has begun. It
has begun.”

“What has begun?” I cried, sitting up.

“The death. Look!”

I followed the direction of his pointing finger. Dr. Ames was
standing at the door of his tent, his face ghastly pale.

“Sir Guy Willard is dead,” he said huskily. “My God, I can’t go
on like this. I can’t—I tell you!”

“Sir Guy Willard dead?” I gasped. “Then it—it must be true!”

“He died in his sleep,” said the doctor. “Heart failure.”

“Heart failure!” I cried. “Just like his father?”

“Just like his father.”

“No,” said Poirot, in a low, vibrant voice. “Not just like his
father. Sir John Willard’s death was natural, but this—this is
murder.”

“Murder!” cried Dr. Tosswill, who had joined us. “What do you
mean?”

Poirot turned on him with an unexpected flash of anger.

“I mean what I say, monsieur. Sir Guy Willard has been murdered.
And I know the murderer.”

“You know the murderer?”

“I do. It is one of four men—Dr. Tosswill, Dr. Ames, Mr. Harper,
or Hassan.”

A dead silence followed his words. Then Dr. Tosswill spoke.

“This is a very serious charge, Monsieur Poirot. Have you any
proofs?”

“I have my eyes, monsieur, and my brain. And I have something
better still—I have my little grey cells. Follow me.”

He led the way to the tent where Sir Guy lay. The body was as I
had seen it once before in a dream—cold, still, with a look of
horror on the dead face. Poirot bent over it for a moment, then
he turned to us.

“You see?” he said. “The same look that was on his father’s face.
But there is a difference. On Sir John’s face it was the look of
one who sees a ghost. On this face it is the look of one who sees
his murderer.”

“But who is it?” I cried.

“Wait,” said Poirot. “First let us examine the room.”

He began to search the tent with a minute care that was almost
painful to witness. Nothing seemed to escape his eyes. At last
he stopped.

“Ah!” he exclaimed, with a little cry of triumph. “Look!”

He held up a small, white object. It was a tiny piece of cotton
wool.

“What of it?” asked Dr. Tosswill.

“This,” said Poirot, “is the instrument of death.”

“The instrument of death?” I cried. “A piece of cotton wool?”

“Exactly, Hastings. A piece of cotton wool soaked in a certain
poison—a poison so deadly that a single drop is enough to cause
instant death. It leaves no trace—none. But it has one
peculiarity—it must be inhaled. And it can only be inhaled if the
victim is asleep.”

“But how was it administered?” asked Dr. Ames.

“In a very simple way,” said Poirot. “The murderer waited until
his victim was asleep. Then he crept into the tent, held the
cotton wool to his nose, and in a few seconds all was over.”

“But who could have done such a thing?” I cried.

“The person who had the best opportunity,” said Poirot. “The
person who could come and go as he liked without exciting
suspicion. The person who had access to the medical stores. Dr.
Ames, I arrest you for the murder of Sir Guy Willard!”

The doctor fell back, his face livid.

“It’s a lie!” he cried. “A damnable lie!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you will explain how this
piece of cotton wool came to be in your pocket?”

He reached forward and drew a small, white object from the doctor’s
pocket. It was identical with the one he had found on the floor.

“I—I don’t know,” stammered the doctor. “I must have picked it
up.”

“I think not,” said Poirot. “You used it to kill Sir Guy Willard,
just as you used another piece to kill Mr. Schneider. And you
would have used a third piece to kill me, if I had not been on my
guard.”

“To kill you?” I gasped.

“Yes, Hastings. That cup of camomile tea which Hassan brought me
last night—it was drugged. If I had drunk it, I should have
fallen into a deep sleep, and I should never have waked again.
But I did not drink it. I poured it away, and I pretended to be
asleep. And I saw Dr. Ames creep into my tent with a piece of
cotton wool in his hand. But when he saw that I was awake, he
fled.”

“But why?” I cried. “Why should he want to kill Sir Guy?”

“For the same reason that he killed the others,” said Poirot.
“For money. He knew that Mr. Bleibner was a very wealthy man, and
he knew that he had no near relations except his nephew. If the
nephew died, the money would go to the next of kin—who happened
to be Dr. Ames himself.”

“Dr. Ames!” I cried. “Is he Mr. Bleibner’s next of kin?”

“He is,” said Poirot. “He is Mr. Bleibner’s cousin. I found that
out from the cable I received from New York. And he knew that
if Sir John Willard and his son were out of the way, he would be
left in sole charge of the excavations—and of Mr. Bleibner’s
money.”

The doctor made a sudden dash for the door, but Poirot was too
quick for him. He tripped him up, and in a moment he was
struggling in the arms of the two Arab guards who had appeared at
Poirot’s signal.

“Take him away,” said Poirot. “And see that he does not escape.”

As the doctor was led away, Poirot turned to us with a smile.

“And now, messieurs,” he said, “I think we may all have some
breakfast. I am—how you say?—famished.”

No answer came from the bed. I turned and was surprised to find
Poirot fast asleep. My own eyes were heavy with sleep, and I soon
found myself back in bed. When I awoke it was broad daylight.
Poirot was still asleep, but as I touched his arm, he sat up with
a groan.

“_Mon Dieu!_” he lamented, “how my head it thumps! It is the
sun—the sun of the desert—is it not?”

I suggested a little breakfast, but Poirot shook his head.

“Not for me, Hastings. Not for me. I am not well. The heat has
overcome me.”

I went out and joined the others. It appeared that Mr. Harper had
left for Cairo in the early hours of the morning. Sir Guy looked
depressed and anxious. Dr. Tosswill, on the other hand, was in
excellent spirits.

“Poor fellow,” he said of Poirot, “he’s not a good traveller. Not
surprising, when you come to think of it. The desert—the sand——”

He shrugged his shoulders.

I was rather concerned about Poirot, and hurried back to the tent
to see how he was getting on. To my surprise he was sitting up in
bed, looking quite his usual self.

“Wait!” he said, as I was about to speak. “Hastings, did you drink
any of that camomile tea last night?”

“No,” I answered. “I didn’t.”

“I thought not. Well, neither did I. For some reason, I felt it
was not—quite—as usual. I have kept it for analysis.”

“Poirot!” I cried. “You don’t mean to say——?”

“I mean to say that I should not have been surprised if I had not
woken up this morning.”

I gazed at him in horror.

“But who? Not Hassan?”

“Why not Hassan? He is a native, is he not?”

“But he has been with the family for years.”

“That is true. But the call of his race—the call of the desert——”

Poirot broke off. Then he added:

“There is more in this than meets the eye, Hastings. Much more.
The Curse of Men-her-Ra is a very potent one.”

I felt a shiver run down my spine.

“What are you going to do?”

“We must watch, Hastings. We must watch. There is something—something
very strange about this camp. I cannot quite put my finger on it
as yet.”

“Yes, Hastings,” he answered from his bed. “Yes, it is a truly
magnificent field for a—for a man of my type.”

He seemed to be drifting off to sleep as he spoke.

The sun rose next morning on a scene of wild confusion. It was
Hassan who brought us the news. Sir Guy Willard was dead.

I was stunned. The thing was too horrible. Was there to be no end
to the list of victims? Were we to be mown down one by one, like
the grass in the field?

Hassan was trembling with fear.

“It is the curse!” he whispered. “The spirit of the dead king is
abroad, and it has claimed yet another victim.”

We dressed hurriedly. Sir Guy’s tent was some fifty yards from
our own. A group was already assembled there, including Dr.
Tosswill, Dr. Ames and Mr. Harper.

“What’s the cause?” I asked of Dr. Tosswill.

“The same as before. Heart failure.”

“Heart failure!” I cried. “At twenty-two? Impossible!”

Dr. Ames looked up. His face was set and grey.

“Everything is possible in this cursed place,” he said.

“Wait,” said Poirot. “I must see the body.”

He passed into the tent. We followed him. Sir Guy lay on his back,
his face composed, his eyes wide open. He looked as though he had
died in his sleep.

Poirot bent over him.

“Is there no possibility of foul play?” he asked in a low voice.

“None,” said Dr. Ames. “I have made a careful examination. There
is no sign of violence of any kind.”

Poirot’s eyes wandered round the tent.

“Is there anything here?” he asked.

“Nothing,” replied Dr. Ames. “The tent is exactly as he left it
last night.”

“And there was no one with him?”

“No one.”

“Where is Hassan?” asked Poirot suddenly.

“He is outside, I think,” said Dr. Tosswill.

“Bring him in.”

Hassan was brought in. He was still trembling.

“What do you know of this, Hassan?” asked Poirot.

“Nothing, my Lord. I heard a cry in the night, a long, low cry,
and then all was still. I was too afraid to move. I thought it
was the spirit of the dead King.”

“A cry?” said Poirot. “You heard a cry?”

“Yes, my Lord.”

“Did anyone else hear a cry?” asked Poirot.

No one had heard anything.

“It is strange,” said Poirot. “Very strange.”

He turned to Dr. Ames.

“You are sure of your diagnosis, Doctor?”

“Perfectly. Heart failure, as I said.”

“And you, Dr. Tosswill, you agree?”

“I am not a medical man,” said Dr. Tosswill, “but it seems to me
that there can be no doubt.”

Poirot sighed.

“It is very sad,” he said. “A young life cut short. And now, I
think, we had better inform the authorities in Cairo.”

“I have already done so,” said Mr. Harper.

“Good. And now, if you will excuse me, I should like to be alone
for a little while.”

He went out of the tent, and I followed him.

“What are you going to do, Poirot?” I asked.

“I am going to think, Hastings. I am going to think very hard.”

He sat down on a stone and buried his face in his hands. I left
him there and went for a walk in the desert. My mind was in a
whirl. I could not believe that Sir Guy’s death was natural. And
yet, what other explanation was there?

I was still thinking when I saw Poirot coming towards me. His face
was transformed. He looked like a man who has made a great
discovery.

“Hastings,” he cried, “I have it! I have it at last!”

“What have you found?” I asked.

“The truth, Hastings! The truth about the deaths of Sir John
Willard, Mr. Bleibner, and Sir Guy!”

“And what is it?”

“It is very simple, Hastings. Very simple indeed. But first, I
must have a little talk with Dr. Ames.”

“Dr. Ames? Why Dr. Ames?”

“Because he is the only one who can help me. Come, let us find
him.”

We found Dr. Ames in his tent. He was sitting at a table, writing.
He looked up as we entered.

“Well, Monsieur Poirot,” he said, “have you found out anything?”

“I have found out everything, Doctor,” said Poirot.

The doctor stared at him.

“Everything? What do you mean?”

“I mean that I know who killed Sir John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, and
Sir Guy.”

The doctor’s face went white.

“What are you talking about?” he gasped. “They were not killed.
They died of natural causes.”

“That is what you would like us to believe, Doctor,” said Poirot.
“But it is not true. They were murdered, every one of them.”

“Murdered? By whom?”

“By you, Doctor,” said Poirot quietly.

The doctor sprang to his feet.

“You’re mad!” he cried. “Stark, staring mad!”

“I think not,” said Poirot. “Listen, and I will tell you how you
did it.”

“I won’t listen to another word!” shouted the doctor. “Get out of
my tent!”

“Stay where you are, Doctor,” said Poirot. “I have a revolver in
my pocket, and I am not afraid to use it.”

The doctor sank back into his chair.

“Go on,” he said hoarsely. “Tell me your ridiculous story.”

“It is not a story, Doctor,” said Poirot. “It is the truth. You
killed Sir John Willard because he was beginning to suspect you.
You killed Mr. Bleibner because he was going to leave his money
to the expedition instead of to his nephew, whom you had hoped to
influence. And you killed Sir Guy because he, too, was beginning
to suspect the truth.”

“And how did I kill them?” asked the doctor, with a sneer. “By
means of a curse?”

“No, Doctor. By means of a very modern and very deadly poison. A
poison that leaves no trace, and that produces the symptoms of
heart failure or blood poisoning, according to the way it is
administered.”

“And what is this poison?”

“It is a discovery of your own, Doctor. A discovery that you have
kept secret for your own purposes.”

The doctor laughed.

“You are even more mad than I thought,” he said. “There is no such
poison.”

“Oh, yes, there is, Doctor. I have found a bottle of it in your
medicine chest.”

The doctor’s face went a ghastly grey.

“You—you searched my chest?” he stammered.

“I did, Doctor. While you were at breakfast this morning. And I
found not only the poison, but also the anti-serum that you used
to protect yourself.”

The doctor was silent for a moment. Then he spoke in a low,
shaking voice.

“You are a very clever man, Monsieur Poirot. Very clever indeed.
But you have no proof. No one will believe your story.”

“I think they will, Doctor. Especially when they hear the
confession that you are going to write for me.”

“I will never write a confession!” cried the doctor.

“I think you will, Doctor. Because if you do not, I shall be
obliged to hand you over to the authorities in Cairo. And they
may not be as lenient as I am.”

The doctor looked at Poirot for a long time. Then he sighed.

“Very well,” he said. “I will write the confession. But on one
condition.”

“And what is that?”

“That you allow me to finish my work here. I have only a few more
days, and then I shall be finished.”

Poirot hesitated.

“I cannot promise that, Doctor,” he said. “But I will do what I
can.”

The doctor nodded.

“Thank you,” he said. “I will start the confession at once.”

He took up his pen and began to write. Poirot and I waited in
silence.

At last the doctor finished. He handed the paper to Poirot.

“There it is,” he said. “The whole story.”

Poirot read it through quickly.

“Thank you, Doctor,” he said. “This is exactly what I wanted.”

He turned to me.

“Come, Hastings. We must be going.”

We went out of the tent and started back towards our own.

“Poirot,” I said, “I don’t understand. Why did you let him finish
his work? He’s a murderer!”

“Because, Hastings, I knew that he would never finish it. He has
already taken the poison himself. He will be dead in a few
minutes.”

I gasped.

“You knew?”

“I knew, Hastings. It was the only way. He was a great scientist,
in his way, and it would have been a pity to see him end his life
on the gallows.”

We walked on in silence. The sun was setting over the desert,
casting long shadows across the sand. The Tomb of King Men-her-Ra
lay behind us, silent and mysterious.

The curse was lifted at last.

My only answer was a series of snores. My friend was already
wrapped in the deepest sleep.

The night passed quietly, and I was up and about early the next
morning. Poirot was already ahead of me, and I found him talking
to the two young men.

I was surprised at the change in him. Gone was the superstitious,
fanciful little man of yesterday. He was the Poirot I knew.
Practical, matter-of-fact, and extremely alert.

“Well, messieurs,” he was saying, “I’ve come to my conclusions.
The mystery is solved.”

“What?” cried Sir Guy. “Do you mean that there are no more
deaths to be feared?”

“That,” said Poirot, “I will not say. But I can tell you the
cause of the deaths we have had.”

“Well?”

“It was not the Curse of Men-her-Ra, but the curse of a living
man.”

The three men stared at him.

“I will explain. We have here four deaths. One heart failure,
one blood poisoning, one suicide, and one tetanus. All dissimilar,
yet all occurring within a month of the opening of the tomb. Let
us take them in order. Sir John Willard. Heart failure. A man of
sixty odd, who had been working hard and was perhaps a little
over-excited. Nothing unusual in that. Next, Mr. Bleibner. Blood
poisoning from a scratch on the thumb. Again, nothing unusual.
The nephew. Suicide. A young man who has led a dissipated life
and is at the end of his tether. Nothing unusual there. Lastly,
Mr. Schneider. Tetanus. A more unusual disease, certainly, but
not an impossible one. Taken separately, as I say, they are all
explicable. Taken together, the coincidence is, to say the least
of it, remarkable. Now, if we can find a link which connects
these four men, we may find a clue to the mystery.”

“But there is no link,” cried Sir Guy. “They were all totally
different.”

“On the contrary,” said Poirot, “there is a very strong link.
They were all of them interested in the estate of the late Mr.
Bleibner.”

“What?” I cried. “But Sir John Willard and Mr. Schneider had
nothing to do with Mr. Bleibner’s money.”

“Are you sure of that?” said Poirot. “Mr. Bleibner was a very
wealthy man. He had no children. His nephew was his only near
relation. If he died intestate, the nephew would inherit
everything. But Mr. Bleibner had frequently declared his
intention of leaving his money to the furtherance of Egyptology.
He had even discussed the matter with Mr. Schneider. Now, suppose
a will had been made, leaving everything to the expedition. Who
would benefit? Sir John Willard, as the head of the expedition,
and Mr. Schneider, as his colleague.”

“But the nephew is dead,” I pointed out.

“Exactly,” said Poirot. “And that is where the cleverness of
the murderer comes in. He knew that if the nephew died, the
money would go to the next-of-kin. And who is the next-of-kin?”

He paused, and his eyes travelled from one to the other of the
three men.

“Mr. Harper,” he said at last.

The young American started.

“Me? But I’m not even a relation.”

“Are you not?” said Poirot. “I think if we were to look into
your pedigree, we should find that you are a distant cousin of
Mr. Bleibner’s. And, as his next-of-kin, you would inherit his
fortune if he died intestate and his nephew were also dead.”

“It’s a lie!” cried Harper. “I never even knew I was a relation.”

“I think you did,” said Poirot. “And I think you saw a way to
make yourself a very rich man. You knew that Mr. Bleibner intended
to make a will in favour of the expedition. You had to prevent
that. You also had to get rid of the nephew. And you had to do
it in such a way that no one would suspect you. You chose the
Curse of Men-her-Ra as your screen.”

“It’s ridiculous!” cried Harper. “How could I have killed all
those men? I wasn’t even there when Sir John Willard died.”

“No,” said Poirot, “but you were there when the others died.
And as for Sir John Willard, his death was a godsend to you. It
gave you the idea for the whole thing. You knew that Mr. Bleibner
was in a nervous state. You played on his fears. You suggested
to him that he was under a curse. You even managed to infect
his thumb with some septic matter. And when the nephew came to
Egypt, you saw your chance. You followed him to New York, and
you—well, we will say you ‘persuaded’ him to commit suicide.
Perhaps you even provided the means.”

“This is all guesswork!” cried Harper. “You have no proof.”

“I have the proof of my own eyes,” said Poirot. “Last night, I
saw Anubis entering the tent of Dr. Ames. Now, why should Anubis
enter the tent of the doctor? Surely, if it were a supernatural
visitation, it would be the victim who was visited. But it was
not the victim. It was the doctor. And why? Because the doctor
was in the plot with you, Mr. Harper.”

The doctor, who had been listening in silence, now broke in.

“This is preposterous, Monsieur Poirot. Do you mean to accuse me
of being an accomplice to a murder?”

“I do,” said Poirot. “You were the one who provided the medical
knowledge. You were the one who ensured that Mr. Bleibner’s
scratch became septic. You were the one who saw to it that Mr.
Schneider died of tetanus. And you were the one who dressed up
as Anubis last night to keep up the illusion of the curse.”

“It’s a lie!” cried the doctor. “A pack of lies!”

“Is it?” said Poirot. “Then perhaps you can explain why, when
I searched your tent this morning, I found this?”

He held up a small bottle.

“A bottle of tetanus germs,” he said. “A very unusual thing
to find in a doctor’s travelling kit, surely?”

The doctor turned pale. For a moment he seemed about to speak,
but then, with a sudden movement, he snatched the bottle from
Poirot’s hand and dashed it to the ground.

“You’ll never prove it!” he cried. “Never!”

And before anyone could stop him, he had rushed out of the tent.

“Stop him!” cried Sir Guy.

But it was too late. A moment later, a shot rang out.

We rushed out of the tent to find the doctor lying on the sand,
a revolver in his hand. He was dead.

Poirot sighed.

“A pity,” he said. “I should have liked to have seen him in
the witness-box. But perhaps it is better so.”

“And Harper?” I asked.

“Mr. Harper,” said Poirot, “will, I think, find it difficult
to explain his part in the affair. Especially when the New York
police begin to look into his past.”

He turned to Sir Guy.

“And now, my friend, I think you may continue your excavations
in peace. The Curse of Men-her-Ra is at an end.”

“But how did you know?” I asked, as we were returning to Cairo.

“_Mon ami_,” said Poirot, “it was the camomile tea. When Hassan
brought it to me last night, I noticed that it had a peculiar
taste. A taste that I recognized. It was the taste of a very
powerful sleeping draught. I realized then that someone wanted
me out of the way for the night. And who would have access to
such a drug but the doctor? From that moment, I knew that he
was the man I was looking for. The rest was easy.”

“And the tetanus germs?” I asked.

“A little deception, Hastings. The bottle contained nothing
more dangerous than distilled water. But it was enough to break
the doctor’s nerve. As I have always told you, it is the little
grey cells that matter.”

And Poirot, with a satisfied smile, began to brush the dust from
his coat.

I got no answer, and I turned, a little annoyed. My annoyance was
quickly changed to concern. Poirot was lying back across the rude
couch, his face horribly convulsed. Beside him was the empty cup.
I rushed to his side, then dashed out and across the camp to Dr.
Ames’s tent.

“Dr. Ames!” I cried. “Come at once.”

“What’s the matter?” said the doctor, appearing in pyjamas.

“My friend. He’s ill. Dying. The camomile tea. Don’t let Hassan
leave the camp.”

Like a flash the doctor ran to our tent. Poirot was lying as I left
him.

“Extraordinary,” cried Ames. “Looks like a seizure—or—what did you
say about something he drank?” He picked up the empty cup.

“Only I did not drink it!” said a placid voice.

We turned in amazement. Poirot was sitting up on the bed. He was
smiling.

"I have the habit of the most extreme caution," said Poirot, stepping to the floor with his usual agility. "The tea, I did not swallow it. On the contrary, I have it here, in this little bottle which I had prepared for just such an eventuality. It was a small comedy, you see, to see who would be the most—shall we say—interested in my sudden indisposition. And you, Doctor, you arrived with a most commendable speed. But I do not think it was Hassan who put the little extra something in the cup. No, Hassan is a faithful servant; he merely brought what was given to him by another. The 'Anubis' we saw earlier tonight—that was a very clumsy touch, was it not? It was meant to prepare our minds for a supernatural death, to make a murder look like the work of a god."

“I did not drink it,” repeated Poirot, “for the very good reason
that I have no desire to join the late King Men-her-Ra just yet.”
He stepped lightly from the bed, his eyes twinkling with a sudden
sharp intelligence that replaced his previous air of superstitious
dread. Dr. Ames stood frozen, the empty cup still in his hand, his
face a mask of bewilderment. “You see, Hastings,” Poirot continued,
turning to me, “when one is surrounded by the ‘occult,’ one must
take precautions. I observed our friend Hassan very closely when
he brought this cup, but I was even more interested in what would
happen after it was delivered. As for the tea—it is a pity to
waste it, but I preferred to pour it into a small bottle I had
concealed in my hand. It will be most interesting to see what the
analyst in Cairo has to say about it.”

“I have not the least desire to be the fifth victim of the
Pharaoh,” remarked Poirot. He looked at the doctor with a
twinkle in his eye. “You see, Dr. Ames, it is quite simple. I
suspected that my little friend the camomile tea might be—how
shall we say?—seasoned. So I make the play-act, the comedy, to
see who would be the most interested in my demise. And behold,
it is you who arrive the first, with such admirable speed! No,
do not touch the cup, I pray of you. We shall keep it for a
little analysis.”

"You see, Dr. Ames," said Poirot, his eyes twinkling with a sudden dangerous light, "I have a most suspicious nature. I did not drink the excellent camomile tea of the good Hassan; instead, I diverted it into a small receptacle for future chemical analysis. It was a little 'mise en scène' to see who would be the first to arrive at my deathbed. But let us put aside the tea for a moment and speak of more interesting matters—of the young Rupert Bleibner, for instance. You knew him, did you not? He came here to borrow money from his uncle, and he failed. But he had a 'good friend' here—a medical friend, perhaps—who told him a very sad story.
