He told him that he had contracted the beginnings of leprosy, and that the only 'merciful' way out was a quick death. And being a medical man, this friend was able to provide the means of that death, just as he had provided the 'septic' germ for the uncle's thumb and the 'tetanus' for Mr. Schneider."

“I did not drink it,” Poirot repeated, his eyes twinkling with a
mischievous light. “I have a certain—prejudice, shall we say?—against
drinks brought to me in the dead of night, even by the devoted
Hassan. I merely poured the liquid into a small bottle for future
analysis and then, as you saw, I performed the little comedy for
your benefit. It was a test, you see—a test of the nerves.”

Dr. Ames stared at him, his face pale in the lamplight.

“A test of whose nerves?” he asked at last.

“Of everyone’s,” replied Poirot. “But specifically, of the man who
wished me dead. Now, Hastings, if you will be so kind as to fetch
Mr. Harper and Dr. Tosswill—and Hassan also. The time has come for
the little grey cells to explain the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’.”

“No,” he said gently. “I did not drink it. While my good friend
Hastings was apostrophizing the night, I took the opportunity of
pouring it, not down my throat, but into a little bottle. That
little bottle will go to the analytical chemist. No”—as the doctor
made a sudden movement—“as a sensible man, you will understand that
violence will be of no avail. During Hastings’ brief absence to
fetch you, I have had time to put the bottle in safe keeping. Ah,
quick, Hastings, hold him!”

But the doctor had not moved. He was staring at Poirot with a
curious expression on his face. He seemed suddenly to have
shrunken into himself.

“It’s no use,” he said, in a curiously flat voice. “You’ve won,
Monsieur Poirot. You’re a cleverer man than I thought. But you’ll
never prove anything—never.”

“Wait,” said Poirot, “I have more to say. You were saying,
Hastings, that you felt the fascination of the desert. I, too,
feel it, but in another way. I feel the fascination of its
mystery. It was that mystery that I came here to solve. And it is
solved.”

I looked at him in amazement.

“You mean,” I cried, “that it is—not the curse?”

“No,” said Poirot, “it is not the curse. It is something much
more modern and much more—lethal. Dr. Ames, you are a very clever
man, but you have made one or more mistakes. Your first mistake
was in thinking that I was a superstitious fool. I am not.”

“And the others?” asked the doctor.

“The others,” said Poirot, “we will discuss later. For the
moment, I will merely say that I have a very complete theory as
to the deaths of Sir John Willard, Mr. Bleibner, and his nephew.”

I sprang forward, and, after a brief struggle, the doctor was
overpowered. I could see the sweat on his brow, and his eyes had
the look of a trapped beast.

“What’s the meaning of this?” he snarled.

“It means,” said Poirot, “that I have come to a conclusion. I am
no believer in the occult, my friend. I believe in the more modern
and more effective method—the poisoner. For what does your medical
science tell us? That it is possible to produce certain symptoms
which resemble the results of natural causes. We have heart
failure, we have blood poisoning, we have tetanus. And then,
finally, we have—what should we have in my case? If I had swallowed
that potion which was so thoughtfully prepared for me, what should
the diagnosis have been?”

“_Eh bien_,” Poirot went on, his voice taking on a new resonance,
“I will tell you. In all those cases, the same hand has been at
work—the hand of a cold-blooded and calculating murderer. It was
not the curse of a dead King that struck down Sir John Willard.
It was the hand of a living man.”

But the doctor had already collapsed, his head buried in his hands.
Poirot stood over him.

“I was right, then,” he said. “You are the man we want. The triple
murderer. Oh, yes, I know it all. It was not the curse of
Men-her-Ra. It was the curse of greed.”

The doctor did not move. He was a broken man.

“Your first victim was Sir John Willard. That was a simple matter.
A dose of digitalis, I think? Then came Mr. Bleibner. A scratch,
it was easy to ensure that it should become septic. And then the
nephew in New York. You knew he was coming to Egypt, and you
met him there and warned him against his uncle. You told him that
his uncle would never give him a penny. And when the old man did
die, you wrote to the nephew and told him that his uncle had
disinherited him. In his despair, the poor fellow killed himself.
And lastly Mr. Schneider. He had grown suspicious, perhaps? So
he had to be removed. Tetanus, you said. It is easy for a doctor
to manage that. And then you tried to get rid of me. But I was
one too many for you.”

The doctor looked up.

“How did you know?” he whispered.

“I didn’t,” said Poirot simply. “I only suspected. But when I saw
your face as you looked at the empty cup, I knew I was right.
You see, I have what you call the ‘_œil de lynx_’.”

He turned to me.

“Fetch Sir Guy and Dr. Tosswill, Hastings. We must have some
witnesses to this confession.”

The doctor had made a sudden dash for the door of the tent. I
threw myself upon him. He was a powerful man, and we were locked
in a desperate struggle. Poirot, with more activity than I should
have given him credit for, joined in the fray. Together we managed
to overmaster him.

“And now,” said Poirot, “if you will be so good as to search his
pockets, Hastings.”

I did so. In a small case I found a hypodermic syringe.

“Good!” said Poirot. “I think we have our man. Dr. Ames, it is
unfortunate that you should have attempted to poison me. It was
a mistake, a great mistake. I have been watching you, monsieur,
ever since I arrived. I saw that you were uneasy. You were afraid,
and you had reason to be afraid.”

“You’re mad,” cried the doctor, between his teeth. “What have I
done?”

“A series of murders, Monsieur le docteur. The death of Sir John
Willard, of Mr. Bleibner, of his nephew in New York, and lastly,
of Mr. Schneider.”

I sprang forward, but the doctor was too quick for me. In a
second, his hand was at his mouth. He fell back on his bed.
Poirot was by his side in a moment.

“Cyanide,” he said briefly. “A quick death. It was the only way
out for him.”

I looked at the little man in amazement.

“You mean—it was Dr. Ames?”

“Precisely.”

“But the Curse? The—the dog-headed god?”

“Ah, that, my friend, was an old friend of mine, a young man from
one of the neighbouring camps. He is a clever actor, and he enjoyed
the part. He has a great talent for such things. I had already
concluded that someone was using the ‘Curse’ as a screen for
murder, and when I saw the figure of Anubis, I knew I was right.
It was too theatrical, too well-staged. It was meant to frighten
us—or perhaps to provide a supernatural explanation for what was
to follow.”

“But why Dr. Ames?” I asked, still bewildered. “What was his
motive?”

I misunderstood Poirot’s anxiety. Eager to save my friend, I flung
myself in front of him. But the doctor’s swift movement had another
meaning. His hand went to his mouth, a smell of bitter almonds
filled the air, and he swayed forward and fell.

“Another victim,” said Poirot gravely, “but the last. Perhaps it
is the best way. He has three deaths on his head.”

“Dr. Ames?” I cried, stupefied. “But I thought you believed in some
occult influence?”

“Did you, Hastings? That was most successful. When I began my
nonsense about Magic, I saw the doctor’s eye upon me. He thought
me a fool. He was right from his point of view. But he also thought
me a dangerous fool. That is what I wanted. He thought I was on
the wrong track, and yet I was getting too near for his comfort.
So he decided to finish me with the camomile tea. I knew he would.
I have had several little conversations with the good Hassan. He
is a devoted servant, but he will do anything for money. Dr. Ames
was paying him to do certain things. I, too, was paying him to
inform me of what the doctor was up to.”

“Then it was the doctor—all the time?”

“From the first. But I had no proof. How could I have proof? It
all began when I heard of young Rupert Bleibner’s death. Rupert
was an outcast, a beach-comber, but he was his uncle’s heir.
Supposing his uncle were to die, and he were to die shortly after,
who would inherit the Bleibner millions?”

“I don’t know. Who?”

“Dr. Ames. He was Rupert’s only friend. They had been in the South
Seas together. The doctor had a hold over the young man. He sent
him to Egypt, knowing his uncle was there, and that his uncle would
not be glad to see him. Then he killed the uncle, and later, the
nephew. But the first death, that of Sir John Willard, was a pure
accident. It gave him the idea for the others. He saw the use he
could make of the ‘curse.’ The second death, that of Mr. Bleibner,
was easily managed. A little septicæmia. And then the nephew in
New York. That was the most difficult of all. But it was done. And
then Schneider. He was beginning to get suspicious. A little tetanus
toxin. He would have finished Sir Guy, too, if it hadn’t been for
Lady Willard’s foresight in sending for us. He knew the game was
up. That is why he tried to finish me.”

“And the jackal-headed figure?”

“That was Hassan. A little more of the doctor’s money. He was
unwilling, but the doctor’s hold over him was strong. Hassan,
too, will be the better for a change of air.”

Poirot sighed. “A very clever man, this Dr. Ames. But he forgot
one thing. He forgot the little grey cells of Hercule Poirot.”

“My friend, I did not believe it. But it was essential that the
guilty person should think I did. He was a clever man, Dr. Ames,
a very clever man. He had planned his crimes with most consummate
skill. But he forgot one thing. He forgot the little Hercule
Poirot!”

“But how did he do it?” I asked.

“Listen. He was the medical attendant of the expedition. He had
all the necessary knowledge. Sir John Willard died of heart
failure—nothing more easy to simulate than that. Then Mr.
Bleibner—septicaemia. That, too, can be induced. And then the
nephew in New York. The doctor had been in New York, you remember.
He had visited the nephew, had given him some subtle poison,
and—most important of all—had suggested to him the idea of
remorse. The letter was a masterpiece.”

“But why?” I asked. “What was the motive?”

“The motive? A very old one, Hastings. Money. Mr. Bleibner was a
very rich man. He had no near relations but this nephew. If the
nephew died, and Mr. Bleibner died, who would inherit the money?”

“I don’t know,” I said.

“I do. Dr. Ames. He had lived in New York for some years, and he
had managed to get himself appointed as Mr. Bleibner’s heir in case
of the nephew’s death. It was a very clever plot.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“Ah, there he was less successful. Mr. Schneider had begun to
suspect. He had to be removed. Tetanus—a very painful death,
Hastings, but one that is easily induced by a medical man.”

“And the jackal-headed figure?”

“That was a little piece of theatricality on the part of the doctor.
He wanted to keep up the idea of the ‘Curse’. He did it very well,
I must admit. But he made one mistake. He gave me that cup of
camomile tea. He thought I was a foolish, superstitious old man.
He forgot that I have a very keen sense of smell. The smell of
strychnine is very distinctive, Hastings.”

“But Hassan?” I asked. “He brought the tea.”

“Yes, and the doctor had put the strychnine in it before he gave
it to him. He thought that Hassan would be blamed. It was a very
clever plot, but, as I said, he forgot the little Hercule Poirot.”

Poirot sighed.

“It is a sad world, Hastings. But at least we have saved the young
Sir Guy. And now, if you will excuse me, I think I will go to
sleep. It has been a very trying day.”

I looked at my little friend. He was already composing himself for
slumber. I went to the door of the tent and looked out over the
desert. The moon was shining, and the Pyramids stood out cold and
clear against the sky. The mystery of Egypt seemed more profound
than ever.

But, as Poirot had said, the “Curse of Men-her-Ra” was at an end.

“I believe in the force of superstition, Hastings,” said Poirot
mildly. “It is one of the greatest forces the world has ever
known. Think for a moment of the situation. Dr. Ames was the
beneficiary under Mr. Bleibner’s will—no, not exactly that, for
there was no will. But he was his only near relation. He was the
son of Mr. Bleibner’s only sister. He had been a medical student
in London when the war broke out, and had gone to the front with
the R.A.M.C. After the war he went to Egypt as medical officer
to the expedition. He was a clever man, but a bit of a gambler.
He had large debts. He knew that if his uncle died he would inherit
his money.”

“But how did he manage it?” I asked.

“It was simple enough. Sir John Willard’s death was a natural one.
It gave him the idea. Mr. Bleibner had a slight scratch on his
thumb. It was an easy matter to infect it with a virulent culture.
The nephew’s death followed. It was Dr. Ames who attended him in
Cairo, and who gave him the idea that he had contracted some
horrible and incurable disease. The young man, in a fit of despair,
shot himself. Then came Mr. Schneider. He had to be removed because
he was suspicious. He had seen something, or heard something. A
dose of tetanus toxin did the work there.”

“But the jackal-headed figure?” I asked.

“Ah, that was a little touch of my own. I wanted to see how the
members of the party would react to it. Dr. Ames was the only one
who was not genuinely alarmed. He knew it was a hoax. He also knew
that I was onto him, and he tried to silence me. He chose the most
unlikely person to bring the poisoned cup—Hassan, the faithful
servant. But he forgot that I have a very suspicious nature.”

“And Dr. Tosswill?” I asked.

“A very learned man, but quite a child in some ways. He was easily
led by the nose. And Mr. Harper?”

“A very nervous young man,” said Poirot. “He will be glad to get
back to New York.”

“And Sir Guy?”

“He will continue his father’s work. He is a brave young man.”

“It’s a strange case,” I said.

“A very strange case,” agreed Poirot. “But the most interesting
part of it is the way in which the force of superstition was used
to cover a very modern crime. It shows how little human nature
changes through the centuries.”

I looked at the little man with a new respect. He had seen through
the veil of mystery which had surrounded the Tomb of King Men-her-Ra,
and had brought a cold-blooded murderer to justice.

“It was a great piece of work, Poirot,” I said.

“It was a very pretty little problem,” he replied modestly. “But,
oh, my friend, the sand! The terrible, all-pervading sand! Let us
make haste to return to a civilization where there are streets and
houses, and where the palm-trees are planted in rows!”

“I believe in the force of superstition, Hastings,” said Poirot
mildly. “I believe it is a very real force. It is the best mask
for a crime. In this case, the criminal was at some pains to
cultivate it. He was the one who suggested that the dog-headed
deity should be seen walking about the camp. He was the one who
made sure that everyone was talking about the Curse. But let us
sit down, my friend, and I will tell you all.”

“Wait,” I cried. “I don’t understand. How did you know it was Dr.
Ames?”

“It was the death of young Rupert Bleibner that first started me
on the right track. He was a wastrel and a failure, but he was
Mr. Bleibner’s only near relation. If both his uncle and his
uncle’s friend, Sir John Willard, were to die, who would benefit?
Not Rupert, for his uncle had disinherited him. But who would
benefit if Rupert also died? I asked myself that question, and the
answer was—Dr. Ames.”

“But how?” I asked. “I don’t see it.”

“It was simple enough. Dr. Ames was an old friend of Rupert
Bleibner’s. He had known him in his beach-combing days. He knew
that Rupert was a weak, easily-led character. He also knew, what
no one else knew, that Mr. Bleibner had made a will leaving the
bulk of his fortune to Dr. Ames for the furtherance of his
archæological work. It was a very natural thing for a man with no
near relations to do.”

“But Rupert was his nephew,” I protested.

“Exactly. And if there was no will, the money would go to Rupert.
But Mr. Bleibner had made a will. Dr. Ames knew that. He also knew
that if he could persuade Rupert to kill his uncle, and then commit
suicide from remorse, he, Dr. Ames, would be doubly safe. He would
inherit under the will, and there would be no one to question it.”

“But Sir John Willard?” I asked. “Why did he have to die?”

“Sir John was a very different type of man. He was a keen,
observant scientist. He was already beginning to be suspicious of
Dr. Ames. He had noticed certain things—I don’t know what—but enough
to make him a danger. So Sir John had to go. A little digitalin in
his morning coffee—it was easily done. Then Mr. Bleibner—a little
septic culture on a scratch. And finally, young Rupert in New
York. A letter from his ‘friend’ Dr. Ames, telling him that his
crime was discovered, that the police were on his track, and
suggesting suicide as the only way out. It was a cold-blooded,
diabolical plan.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“Mr. Schneider was an accident. He happened to see Dr. Ames
experimenting with his cultures. He was a man of a curious and
enquiring turn of mind. He asked too many questions. So he, too,
had to be removed. Tetanus is a painful death, Hastings, but a
very effective one.”

“But the Anubis figure?” I asked. “Who was that?”

“Dr. Ames himself, of course. He wanted to keep up the atmosphere
of the supernatural. He knew that if people were looking for a
ghost, they wouldn’t be looking for a murderer. It was a clever
touch, that.”

“And the camomile tea?”

“Ah, that was his last desperate effort. He knew I was getting
dangerously near the truth. He tried to poison me, and then, if
he had succeeded, he would have blamed it on Hassan. It was a
bold move, but it failed.”

Poirot sighed.

“A clever man, Dr. Ames. A very clever man. But he made the
mistake of underestimating Hercule Poirot.”

He looked down at the dead man.

“He has taken the easy way out. Perhaps it is better so. It saves
the scandal—and the long, weary process of the law.”

He turned to me with a smile.

“And now, my friend, let us go and find Sir Guy. I think we can
assure him that the Curse of Men-her-Ra is at an end.”

I followed him out into the night. The desert lay calm and peaceful
under the stars. The mystery of the ages seemed to brood over it,
but the air was no longer thick with the sense of evil. The spirit
of the dead King was appeased.

As we walked towards Sir Guy’s tent, Poirot stopped for a moment
and looked up at the Sphinx.

“You see, Hastings,” he said, “it has the air happy now. It
smiles.”

And, indeed, in the flickering light of our torches, it seemed as
though the great stone face was indeed smiling—a smile of infinite
wisdom and peace.

“I am not the only one who can play a part, Hastings. I knew that
unless I could create an atmosphere of superstition, of things
supernatural, I should never catch my man. He was far too clever
for that. He thought me a superstitious old fool, and he showed
his hand. Did you not see him when I was talking about the magic
of the Middle Ages? He could hardly keep his face grave. He was
playing with me, as he thought. But it was I who was playing with
him. And when I went off and made my diagrams in the sand—then he
really was amused. He thought he could do what he liked with me.
And he tried.”

“Then it was he who dressed up as Anubis?”

“Of course. But he did it for your benefit and for that of Sir
Guy, not for mine. He wanted to keep the atmosphere of the
supernatural alive. He knew that I was a superstitious man—or
thought I was—and that I should be only too ready to believe that
the god of the dead was at work. That was why he gave me the
poisoned cup. He thought I should drink it and—die of heart
failure.”

“But why did he want to kill these people?”

“Because he was the heir to Mr. Bleibner’s money.”

“I don’t understand. I thought he had no heirs.”

“You are thinking of the nephew. That was a very clever piece of
work on the doctor’s part. He had known the nephew in New York,
had even, I suspect, been his medical attendant. He knew that the
young man was a physical and mental wreck. He also knew that Mr.
Bleibner was a very wealthy man. What more simple than to suggest
to the nephew that he should go and see his uncle in Egypt?
The young man did so, they had a quarrel, and the nephew returned
to New York and committed suicide. But first, at the doctor’s
suggestion, he had made a will, leaving everything to his ‘dear
friend, Dr. Ames.’ The doctor knew that Mr. Bleibner had made no
will. Therefore, if he died, his money would go to his only
relative, his nephew. And if the nephew died, it would come to the
doctor. It was a very pretty little plot.”

“But the other deaths? Sir John Willard and Mr. Schneider?”

“I have no doubt that they were also planned by the doctor. Sir
John’s death was a simple matter of a heart stimulant. Mr.
Schneider’s was even more ingenious. Tetanus is a disease which
is easily communicated. A scratch, a little soil, and the thing
is done. The doctor was always on the spot. He saw his opportunity
and he took it. He was a very clever man, but he was not quite
clever enough for Hercule Poirot.”

“And Hassan?” I asked. “What was his part in it?”

“Hassan? Oh, Hassan was just a devoted servant who suspected
something was wrong and did his best to warn his young master.
He did not know what it was, but he felt the presence of evil.”

“And the diagrams in the sand?” I asked, smiling.

“They were very necessary,” said Poirot, with a twinkle in his eye.
“They were part of the ‘atmosphere’ which was to catch our criminal.
Also they kept you, Hastings, from being too inquisitive!”

And with a little chuckle, Poirot returned to his bed.

“But the sea!” he groaned. “The sea on the way back!”


  •   •   •   •   •   •   •

“You misunderstood me, Hastings. What I meant was that I believe
in the terrific force of superstition. Once get it firmly
established that a series of deaths are supernatural, and you might
almost stab a man in broad daylight, and it would still be put down
to the curse, so strongly is the instinct of the supernatural
implanted in the human race. I suspected from the first that a man
was taking advantage of that instinct. The idea came to him, I
imagine, with the death of Sir John Willard. A fury of superstition
arose at once. As far as I could see, nobody could derive any
particular profit from Sir John’s death. Mr. Bleibner was a
different case. He was a man of great wealth. The information I
received from New York contained several suggestive points. To
begin with, young Bleibner was reported to have said he had a good
friend in Egypt from whom he could borrow. It was tacitly understood
that he meant his uncle, but it seemed to me that in that case he
would have said so outright. The words suggest some boon companion
of his own. Another thing, he scraped up enough money to take him
to Egypt, his uncle refused outright to advance him a penny, yet
he was able to pay the return passage to New York. Some one must
have lent him the money.”

“All that was very thin,” I objected.

“Perhaps, but it was enough to give me a clue. I began to look
about for a possible friend of Rupert Bleibner’s. Now, who were
the members of the party? Dr. Tosswill, Mr. Schneider, Mr. Harper,
Dr. Ames and Hassan. Who of these might have been at any of the
South Sea islands with him? Not Dr. Tosswill, he has been in the
British Museum for twenty years. Schneider? I had to find out
about him. Harper? He was of the same age as young Bleibner.
Ames? He was just about the age to have been a medical man on some
island in the Pacific. It seemed to me that either he or Harper
was our man. In either case, it would be someone whom Rupert
Bleibner would be likely to take into his confidence. If he had
the intention of doing away with his uncle, the doctor would be
a most useful ally.”

“And it was the doctor?” I said. “But why?”

“Because he knew that Mr. Bleibner had made no will, and that,
his nephew being his only relation, the money would go to him.
Now, if Rupert were to die also, who would get the money? Dr.
Ames. You see, he had been Rupert’s friend, he had lent him the
money to go to Egypt, he had even, perhaps, suggested the murder.
Then, once his uncle was dead, Rupert, who was a weak,
dissipated character, would be easily led to believe that he had
committed a crime, or at least that he was responsible for his
uncle’s death. He would be in the doctor’s power. But there was
a more direct way. If Rupert died before he could inherit, the
money might pass to his next of kin—or, as was more likely in
this case, if the doctor had played his cards well, he might have
persuaded Rupert to make a will in his favour. I had to find out
if such a will existed.”

“And did it?” I asked.

“I found it in his desk just now,” said Poirot. “A simple
document, leaving everything to his ‘dear friend, Dr. Ames.’ It
was witnessed by two of the native servants. No doubt Ames
intended to produce it at the right moment.”

“And Schneider’s death?”

“That was a mistake. Schneider had begun to be suspicious. He
was a clever man, and he was not so easily gulled by the ‘curse’
as the others. He had to be removed. Tetanus is a very useful
disease for a doctor to produce.”

“But the figure of Anubis?” I asked. “What was that?”

“A little piece of theatricality on the part of the doctor. He
knew the effect it would have on the superstitious minds of the
expedition. It was a clever touch, but it overshot the mark. It
made me certain of my man. No spirit would need to masquerade in
a mask and a piece of cloth. It was a very human device.”

“And the camomile tea?”

“Ah, that was his last desperate effort. He knew I was getting
dangerously near the truth. If I were to die of some mysterious
malady, it would only be one more victim of the ‘curse.’ He
little knew that I was prepared for him.”

“It’s a horrible story,” I said with a shudder.

“Yes,” said Poirot. “The greed of gold—it is a terrible thing.
But Justice has been done. The ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’ is at an
end.”

We stood for a moment in silence, looking out over the moonlit
desert. The mystery of the ages seemed to enfold us. Then Poirot
turned back into the tent.

“And now, Hastings, let us see if we can get a little sleep. I
feel that I have earned it.”

I agreed with him. We had both had a long and trying day. But
as I lay down on my bed, I could not help thinking of the tragic
fate of Dr. Ames. A man of talent and ability, he had allowed
the lust for wealth to lead him into a career of crime. It was
a melancholy thought.

But Poirot’s voice broke in on my reflections.

“Hastings,” he said, “do you think my moustaches will be quite
themselves by tomorrow morning? This sand, it is truly
deplorable.”

I laughed and told him I thought they would be all right. And
with that, we both fell into a sound sleep.

THE END.

“Exactly. Then came the third death—that of young Bleibner himself.
He had committed suicide. Remorse, it was suggested. But why?
Supposing that he had a friend in Egypt who, for his own reasons,
wished the old man out of the way. He suggests to the nephew a
means of getting rid of his uncle, something that cannot be
traced—a germ, for instance. The old man dies. The nephew is
overcome with remorse. He has killed his uncle. Then he receives
a further blow. His uncle has not left him his money after all.
In his despair he kills himself.

“It was just a theory, but I decided to go to Egypt. I saw at once
that of the people in the camp, only one could have done it—the
doctor. His position made him the only person who could have had
access to the necessary cultures. Schneider’s death from tetanus
confirmed my suspicions. A culture of tetanus is easily
manageable.”

“But the motive?” I asked.

“The motive was simple. Mr. Bleibner, it appeared, had made no
will. In that case his money would go to his next of kin. Who was
his next of kin? His nephew. And who was his nephew’s next of kin?
That was what I had to find out. I cabled to New York and found
that the nephew’s next of kin—was Dr. Ames.”

I gasped.

“So that was it!”

“Precisely. He had to get rid of the uncle and the nephew. He had
them both in his power. It was easy to work on the nephew’s
fears—to suggest the germ—to lend him the money for his journey.
The rest was easy. He probably told the young man that he had
already administered the germ to his uncle, and that the only thing
for him to do was to get away. Then, when the news of the death
reached New York, the nephew would believe himself a murderer.
The letter he left behind him was exactly what might have been
expected.”

“And what of the jackal-headed figure?” I asked.

“Ah, that,” said Poirot, with a smile. “That was a little device
of my own. I wanted to see how the doctor would react to the
supernatural. He reacted as I expected—by an immediate and
energetic search for the human agency. It was not the reaction of
a man who really believed in the curse. As for Hassan, I had
already had a little talk with him. He is a very intelligent man,
and he was only too ready to help me. It was he who, at my
request, appeared in the guise of Anubis. And it was he who
brought the drugged cup of camomile tea. I had told him exactly
what to do. I wanted to see if the doctor would take the
opportunity. He did.”

“It’s a wonderful case,” I said. “The Curse of Men-her-Ra!”

“The Curse of Men-her-Ra,” said Poirot. “It was a very clever
idea. But it was not quite clever enough.”

He looked at his boots.

“And now,” he said, “if only I can find a way to get this sand
out of my boots, I shall be a happy man.”

“It was, Hastings, it was. But then I have seen several points in
it that you have missed. For instance, young Bleibner’s letter on
his return. He referred to himself as a leper. Now, in the case of
blood-poisoning, the face is often terribly disfigured. It was, I
felt sure, his uncle’s death that he was referring to. He had killed
him, but how? Tetanus? I did not think so. It was a more subtle
poison. Then, three days ago, Schneider died. Why? Why should
anyone want to kill him? I did not know, until I found out that
he and Ames had known young Bleibner. Ames, I have since discovered,
spent some years in the South Seas. He and young Bleibner were
evidently friends. He must have known that the young man was a
failure and a spendthrift. When he saw the way the wind was blowing
in the matter of the ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra,’ he saw his opportunity.
He had first to get rid of Sir John Willard. That was easy enough.
Sir John was an old man, and his heart was weak. A little extra
exertion, a little excitement, and the thing was done. Then came
Mr. Bleibner’s turn. He was a more difficult subject. But Ames was
his medical attendant. He could easily manage to infect a small
scratch with some virulent culture. Then he had to get rid of the
nephew. He had already prepared the way by lending him money, and
encouraging him to think he would be his uncle’s heir. When the old
man died, and it was found he had left no will, the nephew would
be his legal heir. He then managed to make the young man believe
that he had accidentally killed his uncle, and that the only way
out was suicide. A very pretty scheme!”

“But why Schneider?” I asked.

“Because Schneider was the only person who knew that Ames and
young Bleibner had been friends. He might have mentioned it at
any moment. Ames couldn’t risk that. He’d already killed two men,
another didn’t matter.”

“And Hassan?”

“I have no doubt he was in the doctor’s pay. He may have known
more than was good for him. He certainly tried to frighten us
away. The figure of Anubis was, of course, the doctor himself. It
was a clever touch, that.”

“And you, Poirot?”

“I? Oh, I am a very lucky man. I have a very good friend in
Captain Hastings. He would never allow me to be poisoned.”

I looked at him suspiciously. I have never been quite sure how
much Poirot really believed in the Curse of Men-her-Ra. Even to
this day he will not discuss the subject.

The little man was busy with his clothes-brush.

“_Enfin!_” he said, with a sigh of relief. “The dust, it is gone.
Now, if you will be so good as to help me with my packing, we will
start for Cairo by the first available means. I have an appointment
with my coiffeur.”

“Wait. He goes back to New York and commits suicide. In a letter
he writes of himself as a ‘leper.’ That was the first definite
clue. In New York, leprosy is a rare disease. But in Egypt, or
the East, it is common enough. What if he were not a leper? What
if some one had told him that he had contracted the disease?”

“And that some one was Dr. Ames?”

“Exactly. He was the only person who could have done so with
authority. He was his ‘good friend.’ For some years he had been
waiting for the old man to die. Then came the opening of the tomb,
and the death of Sir John Willard. Dr. Ames saw his opportunity.
If he could persuade young Bleibner that he had contracted a
loathsome and incurable disease, the young man’s suicide would be
a foregone conclusion. The uncle would then be his next victim.
He knew that the old man was in the habit of making no will. But
he did not reckon on the old man’s obstinate determination to
leave his money to the Museum. Mr. Bleibner, however, did not live
to carry out his threat. Dr. Ames took care of that. He was
murdered, and the nephew was already dead. The estate would then
go to the next of kin, a cousin in New York, who, in his turn,
died——”

“You mean,” I cried, “that the Dr. Ames—the doctor—has murdered
every one of them?”

“Yes, Hastings. He was the only one who could have done it. A
scratch, a little septic poisoning, a dose of tetanus—all so
simple. And who would suspect him? No one. The ‘Curse of
Men-her-Ra’ was the talk of the world.”

“But Schneider?”

“He was an expert. He might have suspected. Ames was taking no
chances. As for me, he tried to get rid of me by a dose of
cyanide. He was a clever man, but he forgot one thing. He forgot
the ‘_petites cellules grises_’ of Hercule Poirot.”

Poirot sighed, then his face clouded.

“And my boots,” he lamented. “Regard them, Hastings. Covered with
the sand of the desert. Never shall I get them clean again.
Never!”

“I quite agree with you, Hastings. It was thin, but it was enough
to make me wonder. Then came the third death, that of the nephew
himself. He left a letter in which he spoke of himself as a leper.
Now, as we know, he had no such disease. I asked myself at once,
Was it possibly a literal statement? Had he indeed been told that
he had contracted that most dread of all diseases? If so, who told
him? The only doctor in the party was Dr. Ames. I remember then
that young Bleibner was reported to have said when in Egypt that
there was ‘something wrong’ with him. Suppose that ‘something
wrong’ was only some trifling ailment, but that the doctor, for
his own ends, chose to pronounce it leprosy. The poor young man
would be naturally overwhelmed, and the doctor would have him
completely in his power. In that state he would be only too glad
to borrow money from his ‘friend’ the doctor. Then, when he was
back in New York, the news of his uncle’s death would reach him.
He would realize that, far from being a penniless outcast, he was
now a man of enormous wealth. Why then should he commit suicide?
Unless, indeed, he believed that he was a leper. Under those
circumstances, life would indeed be a burden. If, on the other
hand, the doctor had been making away with his uncle, what more
simple than to make use of the nephew’s remorse? I do not know yet
exactly what passed between them, but I imagine that the doctor
persuaded the young man that it was he himself who had
inadvertently caused his uncle’s death. The letter he left behind
him was a very clever piece of work. It was at once a confession
and a suicide note.”

“But Schneider?” I interrupted. “Why should he have killed
Schneider?”

“But there was more. Hastings, there occur often enough words
spoken metaphorically which are taken literally. The opposite can
happen too. In this case, words which were meant literally were
taken metaphorically. Young Bleibner wrote plainly enough: ‘I am
a leper,’ but nobody realized that he shot himself because he
believed that he had contracted the dread disease of leprosy.”

“What?” I ejaculated.

“It was the doctor, Ames, who had told him that he was a leper.
Wait, Hastings. I will explain. It was Ames who had taken
advantage of the superstitious frenzy to rid himself of his
unwelcome creditors. For, you see, the doctor had a secret to
keep. He was a gambler, and he had been using Mr. Bleibner’s money
to pay his debts. He was also, it seems, the ‘good friend’ that
young Bleibner had in Egypt. It was from him that the young man
had borrowed the money for his return journey. Ames knew that
sooner or later the truth must come out. He must get rid of Mr.
Bleibner. He had a great advantage. He was the doctor to the
expedition. He could choose his time and his method. He decided on
septicæmia. It was a simple matter to infect a small scratch on
Mr. Bleibner’s thumb. But he must also get rid of the nephew, who
knew too much of his financial affairs. He did so by the cruelest
of all methods—by making him believe he had contracted leprosy.
The young man, in a fit of despair, committed suicide. Then came
the death of Schneider. He had to go, too. He was a keen man of
business, and he had already begun to ask awkward questions.”

“And the tetanus?” I asked.

“It was the doctor. I suspected him when he told us he had been
present at the death of both Sir John Willard and Mr. Bleibner.
It was easy for him to suggest heart failure and blood-poisoning.
The motive was simple—gain. He had probably some hold over young
Bleibner, and together they plotted the uncle’s death, but the
young man was weak. When it was accomplished, he was struck with
remorse, and then the doctor told him he had contracted leprosy.”

“But the doctor wouldn’t have gained anything by that?”

“Oh, yes, he would. He had no intention of letting his confederate
survive to tell the tale. Besides, he must have known that Mr.
Bleibner had made no will and that his money would go to his next-of-kin.
Sir Guy Willard? That was another matter. He was a wealthy young
man and Dr. Ames was his medical attendant. A series of deaths
from a curse—it was a wonderful opportunity. And Schneider, too,
had to be got rid of.”

“But why did you pretend to believe in the supernatural?” I asked.

“Because it is by those methods that you catch your criminal,”
declared Poirot. “I knew that he would try to remove me, and I
gave him his opportunity. I took care to show him I was
superstitious, and I even went so far as to suggest that I believed
the deaths were due to some occult influence. I knew that he would
rely on that and try to poison me. If I had been on my guard, he
might have suspected and tried some other way.”

“And Hassan?” I asked.

“Hassan was a good servant, Hastings, but he was also a tool in
the doctor’s hands. It was the doctor who suggested the camomile
tea to him. He is a clever man, Dr. Ames, and it is a pity that
he has used his brains for evil. But, _mon ami_, even the cleverest
criminals make mistakes. He should have known that Hercule Poirot
is not easily deceived.”

“Yes, Hastings. Ames told him that he was suffering from leprosy
and would be a social outcast for life. The young man, who had
returned to New York and was already in low water, believed it.
With the death of his uncle, Dr. Ames’s next victim, the money
would pass to the nephew, and if the nephew died it would go to
the next of kin. Now Mr. Bleibner had no relations, so he made a
will leaving everything to the man who was his friend and
physician—Dr. Ames. But I had to find out how the three deaths
had been accomplished. Sir John’s was simple, a weak heart, and
the excitement of the discovery. Or a little help—digitalis,
perhaps. Then Mr. Bleibner. Septicæmia from a poisoned thumb.
That suggested at once that the poison had been introduced on
purpose. Then we have Mr. Schneider. He died of tetanus. That was
a more difficult matter. Tetanus is a disease which takes some
time to develop, and the anti-serum was not at hand. It was clear
to me then that the murderer must have some knowledge of
medicine.”

“How did he manage it?” I asked.

“Yes, Hastings. I saw at once that he had been tricked. He had
already been in a bad state of health, and it would be easy to
persuade him that some trifling skin affection was in reality the
dreaded scourge. A little suggestion, a few books on the subject
left in his way, a casual word or two, and the trick was done. He
shot himself in a fit of despair. He had been made to believe
himself a leper.”

“I see,” I said slowly. “But who would do such a thing? And why?”

“Exactly, Hastings. It was then that I began to see. Suppose the
death of Sir John Willard had put into some one’s head the idea of
using the ‘Curse’ as a cloak for murder. Now, who was that some
one? Some one who had a medical knowledge, some one who was on the
spot. Not Dr. Tosswill, who was a scientist but not a medical man.
Not the secretary, Harper, for he had not been with the party long
enough. But Ames—Ames, who had been an associate of young Bleibner’s
in his wilder days. He knew of the young man’s arrival in Egypt,
he knew of his uncle’s refusal of money. He may even have been the
very friend Rupert Bleibner came to see. It was Ames who told him
that he had contracted leprosy, and it was Ames who lent him the
money to return to New York. The poor boy, believing himself an
outcast from society, took his own life. The uncle’s death followed
hard upon. It was easy for the doctor to ensure that a slight
scratch should become septic—to us it is known as septicæmia, to
the world it was the ‘Curse.’ Mr. Schneider’s death was equally
simple. A little culture of tetanus—and once more the ‘Curse’!”

“And now?” I asked. “Sir Guy Willard?”

“Yes, he was to have been the next victim. And then, I suppose,
with the expedition broken up, the doctor would have been free to
enjoy the fortune he had inherited from his friend, the elder
Bleibner. For it seems that Mr. Bleibner had made a will in favour
of his ‘dear friend and medical adviser, Dr. Ames.’”

“It was the clever invention of a diabolical mind. Young Bleibner
was suffering from some minor skin trouble, he had lived in the
South Sea Islands, where the disease is common enough. Ames was a
former friend of his, and a well-known medical man, he would never
dream of doubting his word. When I arrived here, my suspicions were
divided between Harper and Dr. Ames, but I soon realized that only
the doctor could have perpetrated and concealed the crimes, and I
learnt from Harper that he was previously acquainted with young
Bleibner. Doubtless the latter at some time or another had made a
will or had insured his life in favour of the doctor. The latter
saw his chance of acquiring wealth. It was easy for him to inoculate
Mr. Bleibner with the deadly germs. Then the nephew, overcome with
despair at the dread news his friend had conveyed to him, shot
himself. Mr. Bleibner, whatever his intentions, had made no will.
His fortune would pass to his nephew and from him to the doctor.”

“And Mr. Schneider?”

“That was pure chance, Hastings. His death might have been the
result of an accident, or he might have become suspicious and
threatened to expose the doctor. Who can say? The main thing was
that Dr. Ames, who had seen his opportunity, and had already used
it, was not to be turned aside. He was a man of strong will, and
he had a certain power over others. He had already, I fancy,
suggested to young Willard that the curse of the Pharaohs was at
work. That was a stroke of genius, Hastings, because it meant that
any death that occurred would be at once attributed to the curse.
But he did not reckon with Hercule Poirot.”

“And Hassan?” I asked. “He, at least, was innocent?”

“The death of Mr. Schneider was to have been the last of the
series. He was a most inconvenient witness to any of the doctor’s
actions, and a man who would never have believed in the
supernatural. Tetanus is a terrible death, and a doctor would have
no difficulty in inoculating his victim with the germs. The cup of
camomile tea was for me. He saw that I was not to be hoodwinked,
and his only safety lay in my death. It was a well-thought-out
crime, but he forgot one thing. He forgot Hercule Poirot.”

Poirot’s face, which had been serious enough, now wore its usual
expression of self-satisfaction. I had been thinking things over.

“Another victim. The doctor must have found out that Schneider
was aware of the old man’s intention of leaving his money elsewhere.
He must have known that the American intended to speak, and he
silenced him for ever. It was a cold-blooded and most ingenious
crime.”

“But the jackal-headed figure?” I persisted. “And your diagrams
in the sand?”

Poirot smiled.

“_Mon ami_, I had to keep the doctor’s mind off me. I knew that
he would try to remove me, but that he would wait for a favourable
opportunity. I gave him that opportunity. I pretended to be
credulous, to believe in the supernatural. I knew that he would
think me an easy victim. He did. He chose what he thought would
be a safe and easy method. He did not know that I was on my guard.”

“And Hassan?”

“I have no doubt he was an unconscious tool. He was devoted to
his master, and his simple mind was easily worked upon. The doctor
used him as his messenger.”

“And Sir Guy Willard?”

“He is safe enough now. The ‘Curse of Men-her-Ra’ is at an end.”

I sighed.

“It’s a wonderful story,” I said. “The power of superstition.”

“Yes,” said Poirot, “it is a very powerful thing. And to-day,
Hastings, I have used it to catch a murderer.”

He looked at me with a little twinkle in his eyes.

“You, too, Hastings, you were a little bit afraid, were you not?”

“I? Not at all!” I declared stoutly.

Poirot chuckled.

“_C’est bien_, then we will say no more about it. And now, for
the love of Heaven, let us get away from this cursed sand and back
to civilization!”

“That was to make the ‘Curse’ more probable. Schneider was the
only man who knew that his uncle had intended to leave his money
to the expedition. His death was necessary. The tetanus germs
must have been easy enough for a medical man to procure. I
suspected that the anti-serum would be of no avail, even if it
ever arrived in time, and I took the opportunity to prove my
theory.”

“How?” I asked.

“By my little drama this evening. I suspected that the doctor,
fearing my interference, would try to get rid of me. I gave him
every opportunity. Hassan was merely a tool. The doctor told him
that the camomile tea was a certain cure for the evil spirits.
I saw him go into the doctor’s tent with the cup. He is a simple
fellow, and he would never dream that he was being used as an
instrument of murder.”

“And the jackal-headed figure?” I asked.

“That was also part of the doctor’s plan to keep up the atmosphere
of superstition. I have no doubt that it was he who donned the
mask and played the part of Anubis. He knew the effect it would
have upon the minds of the superstitious natives and even upon
ourselves.”

“It was a narrow escape for you, Poirot,” I said, with a shudder.

“_Pas du tout_, my friend. I have lived too long to be caught by
the same trick twice. As for the doctor, it is better so. He has
expiated his crimes in the only way possible.”

I looked out across the desert. The moon was rising, and in its
pale light the Pyramids stood out, silent and mysterious. The curse
of Men-her-Ra was ended, but at what a cost!

“The murder of Mr. Schneider was more or less of a necessity.
Wait a moment, Hastings, I’m getting it all out of order. Sir
John Willard had died of heart failure. He was an elderly man,
and it was quite possible that his death was a natural one. But
to a mind like Dr. Ames’s, it suggested a possibility. He saw how
the death was being exploited by the newspapers. He saw the way
cleared for a series of murders which should be attributed to the
unlucky influence of the Tomb. Mr. Bleibner was his first victim.
Then Mr. Schneider, who, I think, must have suspected something.
The doctor was a clever man, he didn’t use any ordinary poison.
A few tetanus germs, easily and quickly injected, and the deed
was done. But Sir Guy Willard? His death would have been the most
significant of all. I feel sure that it was for him that the fatal
draught was intended. The doctor was taking no chances. If the
young man was once dead, he would have no more to fear from any
awkward questions.”

“But how did you know?” I asked. “What made you suspect?”

“I have my own methods, Hastings. I don’t jump to conclusions, I
reason. I felt from the first that there was a human agency behind
it all. I’ve known many clever criminals, but I’ve never met one
who could control the spirits of the dead. And when I saw that
Anubis-headed figure, I knew that someone was trying to frighten
us. It was a clumsy device, and one that could only have been
carried out by someone who knew the camp well.”

“But the native, Hassan?”

“We cannot be sure. He knew young Bleibner too, remember, and may
have suspected something, or, again, the doctor may have thought
that a further death motiveless and purposeless would strengthen
the coils of superstition. Furthermore, I will tell you an
interesting psychological fact, Hastings. A murderer has always a
strong desire to repeat his successful crime, the performance of
it grows upon him. Hence my fears for young Willard. The figure of
Anubis you saw to-night was Hassan, dressed up by my orders. I
wanted to see if I could frighten the doctor. But it would take
more than the supernatural to frighten him. I could see that he
was not entirely taken in by my pretences of belief in the occult.
The little comedy I played for him did not deceive him. I suspected
that he would endeavour to make me the next victim. Ah, but in
spite of _la mer maudite_, the heat abominable, and the annoyances
of the sand, the little grey cells still functioned!”

I was silent for a moment, then I said:

“But what of the dog-headed figure?”

“Ah, Hastings, did I not tell you? That was Hassan, my faithful
confederate for the evening. I had to convince the doctor that I
was a credulous fool, the better to lead him on. He was a clever
man, a very clever man, but he forgot that Hercule Poirot has a
very certain nose for a criminal, even when that criminal is
protected by the shadow of a Pharaoh!”

“Then Dr. Ames was the man?”

“Exactly, Hastings. He was a most cold-blooded and ruthless
criminal. He had calculated everything to a nicety, but his greed
was his downfall. He could not resist the opportunity of adding
another victim to the list.”

“But how did you know it was he?”

“I did not know for certain until to-night. But my suspicions were
directed towards him from the first. He was the only person who
had the knowledge and the opportunity to commit the crimes. And
his manner when I questioned him was most significant. He was too
insistent upon the scientific side of the case. He was too anxious
to prove that there was no such thing as the curse of the Pharaohs.”

“And what about the other suspects?”

“Dr. Tosswill is a man of science, but he is also a man of
integrity. Mr. Harper is a nervous young man, but he is not a
murderer. And Hassan, though he is a devoted servant, has not the
brains to carry out such a series of crimes. No, it could only be
Dr. Ames.”

“It’s a wonderful case, Poirot,” I said. “I don’t know how you
manage to see through it all.”

“It is simple, Hastings. One has only to use the little grey cells.
But come, let us get some sleep. To-morrow we must make
arrangements for our return to England.”

“It was indeed a masterpiece of cold-blooded, calculating crime,”
I remarked, still somewhat dazed by the revelation. “To use the
very fears and legends of an ancient people as a cloak for murder—it
is almost beyond belief. And to think that he almost succeeded in
silencing even you, Poirot!”

“Almost, Hastings, but not quite,” Poirot replied, with a modest
shrug. “He underestimated the vigilance of Hercule Poirot. He
thought that by playing upon the strings of the supernatural, he
could blind me to the hard, cold facts of science and human greed.
But he forgot that while the spirits of the past may haunt the
desert, it is the living who commit the crimes of the present.”

“It was the camomile tea that did it,” I cried. “But how did you
know?”

“I did not know,” admitted Poirot. “I only suspected. Hassan
brought it to me. But Dr. Ames had prepared it, had he not?”

“How should I know?”

“_Eh bien_, it was easy to see. There was the smell, the bitter
almonds—cyanide. The doctor had been very careful to use only such
poisons as could be attributed to natural causes. Tetanus,
septicæmia, heart failure. But for me he must have something more
drastic. He was a man of quick decisions, and he knew that his time
was short.”

“And Hassan?” I asked. “Is he not a confederate?”

I gazed at him in admiration.

“And Hassan? How did he come into it?”

“Hassan was a most efficient ally. I told him I was a magician, and
he believed me. He did exactly as I told him. He is a good fellow.”

“But you were really in danger?” I asked.

“_Mon ami_, there is always danger. But I have my little ways. One
does not arrive at the truth without a certain amount of risk. To-day
we return to Cairo, and from there to London. I have had enough of
this Egypt. The dust, it is everywhere. It is not a country for a
civilized man.”

Poirot proved to be perfectly right in his premises. Young Bleibner,
some years ago, in a fit of drunken merriment, had made a jocular
will, leaving “my cigarette case you admire so much and everything
else of which I die possessed which will be principally debts to
my good friend Robert Ames who once saved my life from drowning.”

The case was a very interesting one, and showed the danger of those
popular superstitions which are always ready to be tapped by a
unscrupulous mind. As we sailed away from Egypt, I looked back at
the Pyramids. They stood out against the sky, eternal and
unfathomable. Behind them, somewhere in the heart of the desert,
rested the body of a man who had sought to use their ancient
shadows to cover his modern crimes, but who had forgotten that
there are forces of justice as old and as patient as the sands of
Egypt themselves. Poirot, however, was not looking at the
Pyramids; he was looking at the sea, and his face was very green.

The case was hushed up as far as possible, and, to this day, people
talk of the Curse of Men-her-Ra and the fatalities which attended
the breaking of the seal of the Tomb. But since then no more deaths
have occurred, and Sir Guy Willard has finished his excavations in
peace. He is still a firm believer in the occult, but Poirot,
brushing his grey suit with meticulous care, merely smiles and
murmurs, “It is the little grey cells, Hastings, the little grey
cells!”

The case was hushed up as far as possible, and, to this day, people
talk of the “Curse of Men-her-Ra” and the vengeance of the dead
King; but for my part, I believe that the little grey cells of my
friend Hercule Poirot are more than a match for any spirit, ancient
or modern, that ever walked the earth.

The case was hushed up as much as possible, and, to this day, people
talk of the Curse of Men-her-Ra and the strange series of deaths
connected with the opening of the Tomb. But for the efforts of a
little Belgian detective of whom you may have heard, the secret
of the Magician of the Tombs might never have been brought to light.

The case was hushed up as far as possible, and, to this day, people
talk of the Curse of Men-her-Ra and the strange series of deaths
which attended the opening of the Tomb. But Poirot and I know
better. Although, as Poirot says, it was the Force of Superstition
that killed.

The case was hushed up as far as possible, and, to this day, people
talk of the remarkable series of deaths in connection with the Tomb
of Men-her-Ra as a triumphal proof of the vengeance of a bygone
king upon the desecrators of his tomb—a belief which, as Poirot
pointed out to me, is contrary to all Egyptian belief and thought.
